text:
**Chapter 1**

I am a cat. I have no name yet. I cannot tell where I was born. The only thing I remember is crying "meow, meow" in a dim, damp place. It was here that I first saw a human being. Moreover, I later learned that this human was a student, the most ferocious kind among humans. It is said that these students sometimes catch us and cook us for a meal. However, at that time, I had no such thoughts, so I did not find it particularly frightening. When I was lifted up in his palm, I only felt a soft, fluffy sensation. Settling a little on his palm, I looked at the student's face, which was my first encounter with what is called a human. I still remember the strange feeling I had at that moment. First of all, a face that should be adorned with fur was smooth and shiny, like a kettle. Since then, I have met many cats, but I have never encountered one like this. Moreover, the middle of the face protruded too much. From that hole, smoke occasionally puffed out. It was quite choking, and I felt truly weak. I only recently learned that this was the tobacco that humans smoke. For a while, I sat comfortably in the palm of the student, but soon he began to move at an incredible speed. I could not tell if it was the student moving or if it was just me, but my eyes spun around uncontrollably. My chest felt tight. I thought I would surely not survive when suddenly there was a thud, and sparks flew from my eyes. I remember up to that point, but after that, no matter how hard I tried to think, I could not grasp what happened. When I became aware again, the student was gone. Not a single one of my many siblings was in sight. Even my crucial mother had hidden herself away. Moreover, unlike the previous place, it was unbearably bright. It was so bright that I could hardly keep my eyes open. What on earth was going on? I crawled out slowly, only to find it extremely painful. I had been suddenly abandoned from the straw into a thicket of bamboo. Finally, after much effort, I crawled out of the thicket and saw a large pond ahead. I sat in front of the pond, pondering what I should do. I had no particular wisdom. After a while, I thought that if I cried, perhaps the student would come back to get me. I tried meowing, "meow, meow," but no one came. Meanwhile, the wind rustled over the pond, and the sun began to set. My stomach was very hungry. Even if I wanted to cry, no voice came out. There was no choice; I decided to walk slowly toward wherever there might be food. It was incredibly difficult. As I forced myself to crawl along, I finally stumbled upon a place that smelled distinctly of humans. Thinking that somehow I would be alright if I entered here, I squeezed through a hole in a broken bamboo fence and slipped into a certain residence.

It is a strange thing, but if that bamboo fence had not been broken, I might have starved to death on the roadside. They say a tree's shade is a wonderful thing. This hole in the fence has become my passage to visit the neighbor's cat, Mikeko, even to this day. Now that I had sneaked into the residence, I had no idea what to do next. It was getting dark, I was hungry, it was cold, and rain began to fall, leaving me with no time to spare. With no other option, I walked toward the bright and warm-looking place. Looking back now, I realize that I had already entered the house. Here, I had the opportunity to see humans other than the student again. The first I encountered was Osan. She was even more violent than the previous student, and as soon as she saw me, she grabbed my neck and threw me outside. I thought, "No, this won't do," so I closed my eyes and left my fate to the heavens. However, I could not endure the hunger and cold. I once again looked for an opportunity and crawled into the kitchen. But soon, I was thrown out again. I remember being thrown out and crawling back in, repeating this same thing four or five times. During that time, I truly grew weary of Osan. After I stole her three rice balls and returned the favor, I finally felt relieved. Just as I was about to be tossed out one last time, the master of the house came out, saying something about the commotion. The maid, holding me up, said to the master that this homeless little kitten keeps coming into the kitchen no matter how much they throw it out. The master, twisting the black hair under his nose, gazed at my face for a while, and then said, "Well then, let it stay inside," and went back inside. It seemed the master was not much of a talker. The maid, looking displeased, tossed me into the kitchen. Thus, I finally decided to make this house my home. My master rarely faces me. His profession is said to be a teacher. When he returns from school, he goes straight into his study and hardly ever comes out. The family thinks he is a tremendous scholar. He also tries to present himself as a diligent scholar. However, in reality, he is not as hardworking as they say. Sometimes, I sneak a peek into his study, and I often find him taking a nap. Occasionally, he drools on the book he has been reading. He has a weak stomach, and his skin has a pale yellow hue, showing signs of lethargy and lack of vitality. Yet, he eats a lot. After eating a large meal, he drinks Takajiyase, and after that, he spreads out his books. After reading two or three pages, he becomes sleepy and drools on the book. This is his nightly routine. Even as a cat, I sometimes ponder. Being a teacher seems to be a very easy job. If one were born a human, becoming a teacher would be the best.

If one can get away with sleeping this much, it is something even a cat could do. Nevertheless, according to my master, there is nothing more difficult than being a teacher, and he complains about it every time a friend visits. When I first moved into this house, I was greatly disliked by everyone except my master. Wherever I went, I was rebuffed and ignored. The extent to which I was not valued can be seen in the fact that even to this day, I have not been given a name. I had no choice but to stay as close to my master as possible. When he read the newspaper in the morning, I would always sit on his lap. When he took a nap in the afternoon, I would always sit on his back. This was not necessarily because I liked my master, but because I had no other option. After various experiences, I decided to sleep on the rice container in the morning, on the kotatsu in the evening, and on the porch during sunny afternoons. However, the most comfortable place was to snuggle into the bed of the children at night. These children, aged five and three, would sleep together in one bed at night. I would always find a spot between them and somehow squeeze in. Unfortunately, if one of the children woke up, it would lead to a great disaster. The younger child, especially, was of poor quality and would cry out loudly in the middle of the night, "The cat is here! The cat is here!" This would inevitably wake my nervous, weak-stomached master, who would come flying out from the next room. Just the other day, I was severely spanked on my behind with a finger. **Chapter 1**

I have come to the unavoidable conclusion that the more I coexist with humans and observe them, the more they reveal themselves to be selfish creatures. This is especially true of the small child with whom I occasionally share a bed. When it suits their whims, they will turn people upside down, cover their heads with bags, throw them out, or shove them into a corner. Yet, if I so much as attempt to retaliate, the entire household will rally together to chase me down and persecute me. Just the other day, I sharpened my claws on the tatami, and my mistress became extremely angry, making it difficult for me to enter the room afterward. While others trembled on the wooden floor of the kitchen, I remained completely unfazed. My esteemed neighbor, Shiro-kun, often remarks that there is nothing more unfeeling than humans. Recently, Shiro-kun had four kittens born, but on the third day, the student living in that house took them to the back pond and abandoned them, despite their number. Shiro-kun shed tears as he recounted the entire incident, insisting that we cats must wage war against humans to eradicate them if we are to fully experience parental love and live a beautiful family life.

I find his argument entirely valid. Moreover, my neighbor, Mikeko-kun, is greatly indignant, claiming that humans do not understand the concept of ownership. In our kind, it is established that whoever first finds a morsel of food, whether it be the head of a sardine or the belly of a loach, has the right to consume it. If the other party does not adhere to this rule, it is only reasonable to resort to force. Yet, it seems that humans have no such concept, and the delicacies we discover are invariably snatched away for their benefit. They rely on their strength to unjustly take what we are entitled to eat. Shiro-kun lives in a military household, while Mikeko-kun has a lawyer as his master. As for me, I reside in a teacher's home, and in matters like these, I find myself more optimistic than either of them. As long as I can manage to get through each day somehow, I am content. After all, no matter how prosperous humans may be, they cannot thrive forever. It is better to patiently await the right season for cats. Speaking of selfishness, let me share a story about how my master failed due to his own whims. Originally, this master is not particularly skilled at anything, but he has a tendency to dabble in various pursuits. He writes haiku and sends submissions to the hototogisu (a type of cuckoo), submits new-style poetry to the Myojo (a literary magazine), writes English sentences riddled with mistakes, and at times becomes obsessed with archery, learns to sing, or even plays the violin with a wheezing sound. Unfortunately, none of these endeavors have amounted to anything. Yet, once he starts, he becomes excessively enthusiastic despite his weak stomach. He sings in the back room, completely unfazed by being nicknamed "Back Room Sensei" by the neighbors, and he continues to repeat this like a fool. Everyone bursts out laughing at his foolishness. One day, about a month after I moved in, on a payday, my master returned home in a flurry, carrying a large package. I wondered what he had bought, and it turned out to be watercolor paints, brushes, and a type of paper called Wattman. It seemed he had decided to stop singing and writing haiku and instead pursue painting. Indeed, from the next day onward, he spent every day in his study, neglecting his naps to paint. However, when I looked at what he had produced, it was impossible to tell what he had painted. Perhaps he realized this himself, for one day, when a friend of his who studies aesthetics came over, I overheard the following conversation. "Really, I can't seem to paint well. It looks easy when I see others do it, but when I take up the brush myself, I find it unexpectedly difficult." This was my master's reflection. Indeed, there is no denying the truth in that.

His friend, peering at my master's face through gold-rimmed glasses, said, "Of course, you can't paint well from the start. First of all, you can't create a painting solely from imagination indoors. The great Italian master Andrea del Sarto once said, 'If you want to paint, you must capture nature as it is. In the heavens, there are stars; on the earth, there is dew; in the air, there are birds; on land, there are beasts; in the pond, there are goldfish; on the withered tree, there are crows. Nature is a grand masterpiece.' If you wish to paint something that resembles a painting, you should try sketching from life."

"Is that so? I had no idea Andrea del Sarto said such things. That makes perfect sense. Indeed, it is true," my master said, overly impressed. Behind the gold rims, a mocking smile could be seen. The next day, as usual, I went out to the porch and was pleasantly napping when my master unexpectedly emerged from the study and began doing something behind me. I woke up and, squinting my eyes for a moment to see what he was doing, found him completely absorbed in channeling Andrea del Sarto. I could not help but stifle a laugh at this sight. As a result of being teased by his friend, he had begun by sketching me. I had already had enough sleep and was bursting to yawn. However, I thought it would be rude to move while my master was so earnestly holding the brush, so I endured it quietly. He was now sketching my outline and adding color to my face. I must confess, as a cat, I am certainly not of superior quality. In terms of my back, fur, and facial features, I do not dare to think I surpass other cats. However, no matter how unattractive I may be, I cannot help but feel that the strange form my master was depicting was entirely unrepresentative of me. For one, the color was wrong. I have a coat of pale gray with marbled patterns like lacquer, reminiscent of a Persian cat. This is an undeniable fact that anyone can see. Yet, looking at my master's coloring, it was neither yellow nor black, neither gray nor brown, nor a mixture of these colors. It was a hue that could only be described as something other than a single color. Moreover, the most puzzling thing was that there were no eyes. Of course, this was understandable since he was sketching me while I was asleep, but without even the semblance of eyes, it was impossible to tell whether I was a blind cat or just a sleeping one. I secretly thought that no matter how skilled Andrea del Sarto might be, this was beyond hope. However, I could not help but admire his enthusiasm. I wanted to remain still for his sake, but I had been feeling the urge to relieve myself for some time. My internal muscles were restless.

It had become impossible to delay even for a moment, so I had no choice but to excuse myself, stretching out my legs, lowering my head, and letting out a big yawn. Once this happened, it was clear that remaining still was no longer an option. Since I had already disrupted my master's plans, I thought I might as well go to the back and relieve myself. As I began to crawl away, my master, with a voice mixed with disappointment and anger, shouted from the room, "You fool!" It is his habit to call someone a fool whenever he insults them. He does not know how to express any other form of insult, so it cannot be helped. However, it is rude to call someone a fool without considering the feelings of the one who has endured it. If I had at least received some kindness when I climbed onto his back, I could have accepted this tirade, but since he has never done anything to make my life easier, to call me a fool for relieving myself is too much. Humans, by their nature, tend to become arrogant as they grow complacent with their own abilities. Unless someone stronger than them comes along to put them in their place, who knows how far their arrogance will go? While I can tolerate selfishness to this extent, I have heard reports that should cause me to lament the moral failings of humans several times more than this. **Chapter 1**

There is a tea garden of about ten tsubo behind my house. It is not large, but it has a charming atmosphere and is a pleasant spot bathed in sunlight. Whenever my little ones are too noisy for me to take a comfortable nap, or when I feel particularly bored and my stomach is not quite right, I often come out here to cultivate my spirit. It was around two o'clock on a gentle day in early spring when, after a delightful nap following lunch, I made my way to this tea garden for some exercise. As I sniffed each tea plant's roots, I approached the western side of the cedar fence, where I found a large cat sprawled out, completely oblivious to the world, having toppled a withered chrysanthemum. He lay there, snoring loudly, seemingly indifferent to my approach. I could not help but be secretly astonished by his boldness; how could one sleep so soundly in a garden where intruders might lurk? He was a pure black cat. The sun, just past noon, cast transparent rays upon his skin, making it seem as if invisible flames were igniting from the soft fur that sparkled in the light. He possessed a magnificent physique that could be called the king among cats. He was certainly twice my size. As I stood there, lost in admiration and curiosity, a gentle spring breeze lightly stirred the branches of the paulownia tree above the cedar fence, causing a few leaves to fall into the thicket of withered chrysanthemums. The king opened his perfectly round eyes wide.

I still remember it well. Those eyes sparkled far more beautifully than the amber that humans so cherish. He did not move. The light that seemed to shoot from the depths of his gaze gathered upon my diminutive forehead, as if to say, "What on earth are you?" I thought it somewhat beneath a king to speak in such a manner, yet the power behind his voice could easily intimidate even a dog, and I felt a twinge of fear. However, I thought it would be dangerous not to greet him, so I replied as calmly as I could, "I am a cat. I do not yet have a name." Yet at that moment, my heart was certainly beating more fiercely than usual. He responded with a tone of great disdain, "What, a cat? How ridiculous! Where do you live?" Such audacity! "I live at the house of the teacher here," I replied. "I figured as much. You look terribly thin," he remarked, puffing himself up. From his words, it seemed he did not think much of my background. However, judging by his plumpness, it appeared he was well-fed and living comfortably. I could not help but ask, "And who might you be?" "I am Kuro, the rickshaw man's black cat," he declared boldly. Kuro was notorious in this area as a rough cat. But being a rickshaw cat, he was strong yet utterly unrefined, which made him rather unpopular among others. He had become a target of mutual avoidance. Upon hearing his name, I felt a slight shiver of discomfort, but at the same time, a sense of disdain arose within me. I thought I would first test his level of ignorance and posed the following question. "Which is greater, a rickshaw man or a teacher?"  
"The rickshaw man is undoubtedly stronger. Have you seen your master? He is nothing but skin and bones."  
"You seem quite strong for a rickshaw cat. I suppose you get to eat well there," I replied. "Me? I could find food anywhere I go. You should stop wandering around the tea garden and follow me for a bit. In less than a month, you’ll be unrecognizably fat."  
"I'll hope for that. However, it seems to me that the house of the teacher is larger than that of the rickshaw man."  
"You fool, no matter how big it is, it won't fill my belly."  
He seemed greatly offended, his ears twitching like bamboo shoots, and he departed with a huff. From that point on, I became acquainted with Kuro, the rickshaw man's black cat. Afterward, I frequently encountered Kuro. Each time, he would exude the arrogance befitting a rickshaw man. The scandal I had previously heard about was, in fact, something I learned from him.

One day, as usual, I was lounging in the warm tea field with Kuro, engaging in various idle chit-chat, when he repeated his familiar bragging story with an air of novelty. Afterward, he directed a question at me: “How many mice have you caught so far?” I considered myself far more knowledgeable than Kuro, but I was well aware that when it came to physical strength and courage, I could not compare to him at all. However, when faced with this question, I found myself at a loss for words. Nevertheless, the truth is the truth, and I could not lie, so I replied, “Actually, I have been intending to catch them but haven’t yet.” Kuro shook his long whiskers, which were taut at the tip of his nose, and laughed heartily. Kuro, by nature, lacks something in his bragging, and if I feigned admiration and purred in appreciation of his bravado, he became an exceedingly manageable cat. Having come to understand this dynamic since getting closer to him, I thought it foolish to defend myself and worsen my position. Instead, I resolved to let him talk about his own exploits to divert the conversation. So, I calmly suggested, “Given your age, you must have caught quite a few, haven’t you?” Sure enough, he leaped at the chance to boast. “Not many, but I’ve caught about thirty or forty,” he replied proudly. He continued, “I could handle a hundred or two hundred mice by myself, but that weasel is a different story. I had a terrible experience with one once.” “Oh, really?” I interjected, feigning interest. Kuro blinked his large eyes and said, “It was during last year’s big cleaning. My master crawled under the porch with a bag of lime, and out jumped a big weasel, startled.” “Hmm,” I responded, pretending to be impressed. “But a weasel is just a bit bigger than a mouse. I thought I could chase it down, but it ended up cornering me in the muddy ditch.” “Well done!” I cheered him on. “But when it came down to it, that little rascal let out a foul stench at the last moment. Ever since then, whenever I see a weasel, I feel sick to my stomach.” At this point, he raised his front paw and rubbed his nose several times, as if still sensing the odor from last year. I felt a bit sorry for him. Wanting to lighten the mood, I said, “But when it comes to mice, you must be their worst nightmare. You’re such a master at catching them, and you eat so many that you’ve grown fat and shiny.” This question, intended to flatter Kuro, surprisingly yielded the opposite result. He sighed deeply and said, “Thinking about it, it’s rather pointless. No matter how many mice I catch—there’s no one as shameless as humans in this world. They take all the mice I catch and bring them to the police station. Since no one knows who caught them at the station, they give me five sen each time.

My master has made about one yen and fifty sen off my efforts, yet he has never fed me anything decent. Humans are the best thieves, you know.” Even Kuro, who was uneducated, seemed to grasp this reasoning, and he became quite indignant, bristling his back fur. I felt a bit uneasy, so I decided to change the subject and headed home. From that moment on, I resolved never to catch a mouse again. However, I did not become Kuro's subordinate to hunt for anything other than mice. It was far more comfortable to sleep than to feast. It seems that when a cat lives in a teacher’s house, it takes on the nature of a teacher. If I’m not careful, I might end up with a weak stomach. Speaking of teachers, it seems my master has recently come to realize that he has no hope in watercolor painting. On December 1st, he wrote the following in his diary:

“I met a person named ○○ for the first time at today’s meeting. They say he has led quite a debauched life, but indeed he has the air of a connoisseur. Such a person is usually liked by women, so it would be more appropriate to say that ○○ was compelled to lead a debauched life rather than that he chose it. I hear that his wife is a geisha; how enviable! Most of those who speak ill of debauchery are often those who lack the qualifications to indulge in it. Furthermore, among those who consider themselves debauchees, many lack the qualifications as well. These people engage in it without necessity, forcing themselves into it. It’s much like my own watercolor painting; I have no intention of graduating from it. Nevertheless, I still consider myself a connoisseur. If one can become a connoisseur simply by drinking at restaurants or entering waiting rooms, then I too could be a respectable watercolor artist. Just as it would be better if I didn’t paint at all, it is far superior to be a simpleton from the mountains than to be a foolish connoisseur.”

I find it hard to agree with his connoisseur theory. Moreover, to envy a geisha as a wife is a foolish thought that a teacher should never express, yet his critical eye regarding his own watercolor painting is indeed sharp. Despite his self-awareness, my master’s vanity is difficult to shake off. Two days later, on December 4th, he wrote this in his diary:

“Last night, I dreamed that someone had taken my poorly done watercolor and framed it beautifully, hanging it on the transom. Upon seeing it framed, I suddenly felt I had become quite skilled. I was very pleased. I thought it was a fine piece, and as I admired it alone, dawn broke, and I awoke to find that I was still as clumsy as ever, which became clear with the morning sun.”

It seems my master carries the burden of his unfulfilled dreams of watercolor painting even into his sleep.

At this rate, he is not likely to become a watercolor artist, nor a so-called connoisseur. **Chapter 1**

The day after my master dreamed of watercolor painting, the usual bespectacled aesthete visited him after a long absence. As soon as he sat down, he opened with, “How is the painting coming along?” My master, maintaining a calm demeanor, replied, “I have been diligently practicing sketching as you advised, and indeed, it seems that when one sketches, one becomes aware of the shapes and subtle color variations of things that one had previously overlooked. It appears that the development of painting in the West has resulted from a long-standing emphasis on sketching. Truly, Andrea del Sarto is remarkable.” He did not even hint at his diary, yet he continued to express admiration for Andrea del Sarto. The aesthete chuckled and scratched his head, saying, “Actually, my friend, that’s nonsense.” “What do you mean?” my master asked, still unaware that he had been mocked. “What I mean is that the Andrea del Sarto you are so taken with is a fabrication of mine. I never thought you would take it so seriously. Hahaha!” he exclaimed with great delight. I could not help but imagine what might be recorded in his diary that day. This aesthete, who scattered such nonsense and took pleasure in deceiving others, seemed entirely unconcerned about how the Andrea del Sarto incident might resonate with my master’s emotions, and he continued to prattle on with the following: “You know, it’s amusing how people take jokes seriously, provoking a great sense of the absurd. The other day, I told a student that Nicholas Nickleby advised Gibbon to stop writing his monumental history of the French Revolution in French and to publish it in English instead. That student, who has a remarkable memory, repeated my words earnestly at a lecture of the Japanese Literary Society, which was quite comical. There were about a hundred listeners at that time, and they all listened intently.” He then continued with another amusing story. “Recently, at a gathering with a certain literary figure, the subject of Harrison’s historical novel, Theophano, came up. I remarked that it is the finest among historical novels, especially the part where the female protagonist dies, which is truly haunting. A teacher sitting across from me, whom I had never met before, chimed in, ‘Yes, indeed, that part is a masterpiece.’ At that moment, I realized that this man, like me, had not read the novel.” My master, who is somewhat neurotic and sensitive, widened his eyes and asked, “What will you do if the other party has read it and finds out you’re spouting nonsense?” It was as if he felt that deceiving others was acceptable, but he would be in trouble if the truth were to come to light.

The aesthete remained unfazed. “Well, then I would just say I confused it with another book or something,” he replied, laughing heartily. This aesthete, though wearing gold-rimmed glasses, has a nature similar to that of Kuro, the rickshaw man’s black cat. My master remained silent, puffing out his cheeks as if to say that he lacked such courage. The aesthete, therefore, looked at him as if to say that painting is indeed difficult, and added, “However, while jokes are jokes, painting is genuinely a challenging endeavor. I’ve heard that Leonardo da Vinci once instructed his students to sketch the stains on the walls of temples. Indeed, if you enter a snow closet and attentively observe the walls where rain leaks, you can naturally create quite a beautiful pattern. Pay attention and try sketching; you’ll surely produce something interesting.” “You’re trying to deceive me again, aren’t you?” “No, this is certainly true. It’s quite an extraordinary statement, something da Vinci might say.” “Indeed, it is extraordinary,” my master conceded, half-surrendering. However, it seems he still has not attempted to sketch in the snow closet. Kuro, the rickshaw man’s black cat, has since become lame. His once glossy fur is gradually losing its color and falling out. In his eyes, which I once praised as more beautiful than amber, there is now a buildup of eye discharge. What particularly caught my attention was his waning vitality and the deterioration of his physique. On the last day I encountered him in the usual tea garden, when I asked how he was, he replied, “Like a weasel’s last fart, I’m at the mercy of the balance beam of a fishmonger.”

Amid the red pines, a few clusters of crimson leaves scattered like dreams of the past, and the red and white camellias had completely shed their petals. As the winter sun’s rays quickly slanted on the south-facing porch of three and a half mats, the days when the cold winds did not blow became increasingly rare, and I felt that my napping time had also been shortened. My master goes to school every day. Upon returning, he barricades himself in his study. When people come, he complains about the teachers. He rarely engages in watercolor painting anymore. He even stopped using Takaji Astase, claiming it was ineffective. The children, however, tirelessly attend kindergarten. When they return, they sing songs, play with balls, and occasionally dangle me by my tail. I do not eat lavish meals, so I do not particularly gain weight, but I am reasonably healthy and manage to get through each day without becoming lame. I never catch mice. I still dislike Osan. They have yet to give me a name, but since desires are boundless, I intend to live my life as an unnamed cat in this teacher’s household.

**Chapter 2**

I have become somewhat famous since the New Year, and as a cat, it is gratifying to feel a bit proud. Early on New Year’s Day, a picture postcard arrived for my master. This was a New Year’s greeting from a certain painter friend of his, painted with red at the top and deep green at the bottom, featuring an animal squatting in the middle rendered in pastels. My master, in his usual study, examined the painting from the side and from above, remarking that it was a beautiful color. Having already been impressed, he thought he might stop looking, yet he continued to view it from various angles. He twisted his body, extended his hand, and peered at it as an elderly person might when looking at the three faces of a person. He even brought it close to his nose, and if he didn’t stop soon, my knees would shake with anxiety. Just when I thought the commotion had finally calmed down, he murmured softly, “What on earth is this animal?” My master was impressed by the colors of the postcard, but since he could not discern the identity of the animal depicted, it seemed he had been troubled by it for some time. While pondering whether it was such an inscrutable postcard, I opened my eyes just enough to look calmly, and there was no mistaking it: it was my own portrait. Though he may not have mastered Andrea del Sarto like my master, as a painter, he had rendered both form and color quite well. Anyone who looked at it would undoubtedly recognize it as a cat. A person with even a little discernment would clearly see that it was not just any cat, but me. To think that he would struggle so much without realizing such a clear fact made me feel a bit sorry for humans. If only I could let him know that the painting was of me. Even if he did not understand that it was me, at the very least, I wanted him to know that it was a cat. However, humans are creatures who are utterly unable to comprehend the language of my feline kind, so regrettably, I left it at that.

I would like to make a brief note to the readers: it is quite unfortunate that humans have a tendency to regard me with a tone of casual disdain, as if I were nothing more than a mere cat. To think that from the dregs of humanity, cows and horses were created, and from the dung of cows and horses, cats were manufactured, is a notion that might be common among those teachers who wear a haughty expression while remaining oblivious to their own ignorance. From an outsider's perspective, it is hardly a dignified sight. No matter how much one may be a cat, such a crude and simple origin cannot be the case. To the untrained eye, all cats may appear to be one and the same, equal and indistinguishable, but upon entering the world of cats, one finds it to be quite complex. The phrase "ten people, ten colors," which applies to the human world, can be directly applied here as well. In terms of appearance, nose shape, fur texture, and leg structure, each cat is different. From the thickness of the whiskers to the arrangement of the ears and the droop of the tail, there is not a single cat that is identical to another. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the differences in beauty, lack of beauty, preferences, and tastes are as varied as the stars in the sky. Despite such clear distinctions existing, the human eye, fixated on notions of superiority and other such ideas, fails to recognize even the most basic aspects of my nature, let alone the nuances of my appearance. There is an old saying that "like seeks like," and indeed, a rice cake maker knows rice cakes, and a cat knows cats; thus, only a cat can truly understand matters pertaining to cats. No matter how advanced humans may become, this remains an insurmountable barrier. Moreover, to speak of reality, they are not as remarkable as they believe themselves to be, making it all the more difficult. Furthermore, my master, who lacks empathy, is a man who does not even understand that the first principle of love is to fully comprehend one another. He clings to his study like a bad oyster, never having opened his mouth to the outside world. It is rather amusing that he wears a face that seems to be profoundly enlightened. The proof of his lack of enlightenment is right in front of him, yet he shows no sign of realization, casually remarking that this year must be the second year of the Russo-Japanese War, and it is likely a painting of a bear or something of the sort. As I ponder these thoughts while dozing on my master's lap, the maid soon brings in a second picture postcard. Upon looking, I see several imported cats lined up in a row, holding pens, opening books, and studying. Among them, one cat has left its seat and is dancing a Western-style jig at the corner of the desk.

Above it, in Japanese ink, is written in bold characters, "I Am a Cat," and to the right, a haiku about cats enjoying a spring day can be seen. This postcard, sent by my master's former pupil, should be easily understood by anyone who sees it, yet my oblivious master seems not to grasp its meaning and tilts his head in puzzlement, muttering, "Is this year the Year of the Cat, perhaps?" It seems he is still unaware of how famous I have become. Just then, the maid brings in a third postcard. This time, it is not a picture postcard. It reads "Happy New Year," and beside it, it says, "Please convey my regards to the cat, if you would be so kind." Even my master, who is usually quite slow on the uptake, seems to finally realize something, letting out a grunt as he looks at my face. His gaze, different from before, now seems to carry a hint of respect. It seems only natural that my master, who had previously been unrecognized by the world, would suddenly take on a new demeanor, all thanks to me. At that moment, the gate's latticework jingles, chime, chime, chime. It is likely a visitor; if so, the maid will go to receive them. I have resolved not to leave my master's lap except when the fishmonger Ume-kun comes, so I remain comfortably seated as before. However, my master looks anxious, as if he has been cornered by a moneylender, glancing toward the entrance. It seems he finds the prospect of receiving New Year guests and having to entertain them with drinks rather distasteful. If humans could be this obstinate, it would be commendable. He could have gone out early, but he lacks even that courage. He is truly revealing his oyster-like nature. After a while, the maid returns to announce that Kangetsu has arrived. This Kangetsu fellow was also a former pupil of my master, but now he has graduated and is said to be doing much better than my master. For some reason, this man often comes to visit my master. When he comes, he brings along a string of remarks that seem to suggest he has a woman who is infatuated with him, or that the world is interesting or dull, or that it is both terrifying and alluring. It is puzzling why he would come to share such conversations with a withered man like my master, but it is all the more amusing that my oyster-like master occasionally responds to such discussions.

"I have been somewhat remiss in my correspondence. The truth is, I have been quite active since last year’s end, and though I think to go out, my feet just don’t seem to head in that direction," he said, twisting the cord of his haori (traditional jacket) while looking rather mysterious. "Which direction do your feet head in, I wonder?" the master asked with a serious expression, pulling at the cuffs of his black cotton haori. This haori was made of cotton and had short sleeves, from which a bit of the undergarment peeked out on both sides. "Heh heh heh, a slightly different direction," Kangetsu laughed. Upon closer inspection, I noticed he was missing one of his front teeth today. "What happened to your tooth?" the master shifted the topic. "Oh, I happened to eat some shiitake mushrooms somewhere," he replied. "What did you eat?" "Well, I ate a bit of shiitake. When I tried to bite through the cap with my front teeth, it broke off." "To chip a front tooth on a shiitake? That sounds rather old-fashioned. It might make for a haiku, but it won’t win any hearts," he said, giving my head a light pat. "Ah, so that cat is the one you mentioned? Quite fat, isn’t it? It wouldn’t lose to Kuro, the rickshaw man’s cat, that’s for sure. A fine specimen," Kangetsu praised me greatly. "I’ve grown quite a bit recently," I thought, feeling a bit proud as he patted my head. Although I was pleased with the praise, my head was slightly sore. "The other night, we had a little concert," Kangetsu continued, returning to his previous topic. "Where?" "Oh, you needn’t concern yourself with that. We had three violins accompanied by a piano, and it was quite entertaining. When there are three violins, even if they’re not very good, it’s still enjoyable. There were two women, and I joined in, and I thought I played quite well myself." 

"Hmph, and who were those women?" the master asked, a hint of envy in his voice. Although the master usually had a face like a withered tree in winter, he was not at all indifferent to women. Once, after reading a certain Western novel, he remarked that one character fell for nearly every woman he encountered. He was impressed by the satirical observation that this character would fall in love with nearly seventy percent of the women he met. Such a fickle man, I thought, how could he lead a solitary life? Some say it’s due to unrequited love, others claim it’s because of a weak stomach, and still others say it’s because he’s timid and lacks money. Regardless, he is not a person of such historical significance in the Meiji era, so it hardly matters. However, it is true that he was curious about Kangetsu’s female companion.

Kangetsu, looking amused, picked up a piece of kamaboko (fish cake) with his chopsticks and bit it in half with his front teeth. I worried he might chip another tooth, but this time he was fine. "Oh, they are both daughters of a certain household, you wouldn’t know them," he replied somewhat distantly. "I see," the master said, pondering the implications. Kangetsu seemed to think it was a good time to change the subject. "What lovely weather we’re having! If you’re free, shall we take a walk together? With the fall of Port Arthur, the city is quite lively," he suggested. The master, looking more interested in the identities of the women than the fall of Port Arthur, seemed to ponder for a moment before finally making up his mind. "Well then, let’s go," he said decisively, standing up. He was still wearing his black cotton haori and an old, worn-out cotton quilted garment that his brother had given him twenty years ago. No matter how durable the fabric, wearing it continuously is bound to wear it thin. In places, it had become so thin that sunlight shone through, revealing the stitches from patches sewn on from behind. The master’s attire showed no distinction between the end of the year and the New Year. He had no everyday clothes or formal wear. When he went out, he would just thrust his hands into his pockets and saunter out. Whether it was because he had nothing else to wear or simply found it troublesome to change, I could not tell. However, I was certain this was not due to unrequited love. After the two had left, I took the liberty of finishing off the remaining piece of kamaboko that Kangetsu had bitten into. I, too, was no ordinary cat these days. I believed I had enough qualifications to be considered a cat of the caliber of those who stole gray goldfish or perhaps one of the cats from the time of Momokawa Nyōen. I had no interest in Kuro, the rickshaw man’s cat. Taking a piece of kamaboko wouldn’t draw any remarks from anyone. Moreover, the habit of sneaking snacks while avoiding the eyes of others is not something limited to us felines. Osan, for instance, often pilfers rice cakes while his wife is away, taking them and then taking them again. It’s not just Osan; even the children, who are said to be receiving refined upbringing from their mother, exhibit this tendency. A few days ago, two children woke up unusually early and, while the master and his wife were still asleep, sat down at the dining table. They usually share a bit of the bread that the master eats in the morning, sprinkled with sugar, but that day, the sugar bowl was right there on the table with a spoon beside it. Since there was no one to distribute the sugar as usual, the older child soon scooped a spoonful of sugar from the bowl and poured it onto their plate.

The younger one, seeing this, did the same, pouring an equal amount onto their own plate. For a while, they glared at each other, but then the older one took the spoon again and added another scoop to their plate. The younger one quickly followed suit, matching their sister’s portion. Then the sister scooped another spoonful. The younger one, not to be outdone, added another scoop. The sister reached for the bowl again, and the younger one grabbed the spoon once more. Before long, their plates were piled high with sugar, and the bowl was left empty. Just then, the master emerged from the bedroom, rubbing his sleepy eyes, and put the sugar they had just poured back into the bowl. In such moments, it seems that humans might possess a sense of fairness derived from selfishness that surpasses that of cats, yet their wisdom appears to be inferior to ours. I thought it would have been better for them to finish it off before it piled up so high, but as usual, my words would not reach them, so I could only watch silently from atop the rice container.

The master, who had gone out with Kangetsu, returned late that evening, and the following day, he sat down to breakfast around nine o'clock. From my vantage point atop the usual rice container, I observed him silently eating his zoni (a traditional soup). He took a bite, then another, alternating his consumption. The pieces of mochi were small, yet he managed to eat six or seven pieces, leaving just one last piece in the bowl before he set down his chopsticks, signaling that he was done. If anyone else were to act so selfishly, they would hardly be tolerated, but he, basking in his own authority, was unfazed as he gazed at the charred remains of mochi floating in the murky broth. When his wife brought out some Takajiya starch from the back of the cupboard and placed it on the table, he declared, "I won't drink that; it doesn't work." 

"But I've heard it has great benefits for starchy foods, so you should try it," she insisted, eager for him to consume it. "Starch or whatever, it won't do," he stubbornly replied. "You really are quite fickle," his wife muttered to herself. "It's not that I'm fickle; it's that the medicine doesn't work." 

"Yet you said just the other day how effective it was, and you took it every single day," she countered. "Last time it worked for me, but these days it doesn't," he replied, almost like a refrain. "If you keep starting and stopping like that, no matter how effective the medicine is, it won't work. You need to be more consistent; otherwise, your weak stomach won't recover like other ailments," she said, glancing at Osan, who was holding a tray. "That is indeed true. You won't know if it's a good or bad medicine unless you try it a bit longer," Osan supported his wife without hesitation. "Whatever, I won't drink it, so I won't. What do women know about such things? Just be quiet," he snapped. "Well, I am a woman," his wife said, thrusting the Takajiya starch in front of him, trying to force him into submission. Without saying a word, he stood up and shuffled into his study. His wife and Osan exchanged glances and chuckled. At times like this, if I were to follow him and jump onto his lap, I would surely find myself in trouble, so I quietly circled around the garden and climbed up to the porch of the study, peering through the gap in the shoji. There, I found him engrossed in a book by a man named Epictetus. If I could understand it as usual, there might be something impressive about it. After five or six minutes, he slammed the book down onto the desk. I thought that was probably the case, yet I continued to pay attention, and this time he pulled out his diary and jotted down the following:

"Strolled with Kangetsu around Nezu, Ueno, Ikebukuro, and Kanda.

In front of the waiting room at Ikebukuro, a geisha was fluttering her fan while wearing a spring kimono with a hem pattern. The outfit was beautiful, but her face was exceedingly unattractive. She somewhat resembled my own cat."

There was no need to specifically mention me as an example of an unattractive face. If I were to visit a barber and have my face shaved, I wouldn't be so different from humans. It is precisely this human vanity that causes problems. As I turned the corner at Hodan, another geisha appeared. This one was a tall, slender beauty with well-formed shoulders, and her light purple garment was elegantly worn. She smiled, revealing her white teeth, and said, "Gen-chan, I was just busy last evening..." However, her voice was as hoarse as a crow's, which greatly diminished her charm, and I lost interest in finding out who this so-called Gen-chan was, so I walked out onto Onarimichi with my hands in my pockets. Kangetsu seemed to be somewhat restless. Nothing is as difficult to understand as human psychology. I could not discern whether the master's current mood was one of anger, elation, or if he was seeking solace in the philosopher's legacy. It was impossible to tell if he was sneering at the world or wishing to mingle with it, if he was irritated by trivial matters, or if he was completely indifferent to everything. In contrast, cats are simple creatures. If we want to eat, we eat; if we want to sleep, we sleep; when we are angry, we are fiercely angry, and when we cry, we cry with all our might. First and foremost, we never keep a useless diary. There is no need to do so. Humans, like the master, who have two sides to their nature, may feel the need to write a diary to express their hidden selves in a dark room, but for us cats, every action, every moment, is a true diary, so there is no need for such troublesome efforts to preserve our true selves. If I had time to keep a diary, I would rather lie down on the porch. "I had dinner at a certain tavern in Kanda. After a long time, I drank two or three cups of Masamune sake, and this morning my stomach feels quite good. I think evening drinks are best for a weak stomach. Of course, Takajiya starch is out of the question. No matter what anyone says, it won't work. Something that doesn't work simply doesn't work."

He launched into an unwarranted attack on Takajiya starch. It felt as if he were fighting with himself. This morning's irritation was manifesting itself here. Perhaps the true essence of human diaries lies in such moments. The other day, someone said that skipping breakfast would improve my stomach, so I tried not eating breakfast for two or three days, but all I experienced was a rumbling belly without any benefits. Another advised me to absolutely avoid pickles.

According to him, all stomach ailments stem from pickled foods. If I could just eliminate pickles, the source of my stomach issues would dry up, and recovery would be assured. For about a week, I refrained from pickles, but since I saw no particular improvement, I started eating them again. When I asked another friend, he said that it was limited to abdominal massage therapy. However, it had to be the right kind. If I had someone perform the ancient Minagawa-style massage once or twice, most stomach ailments could be cured. Yasui Ikken was very fond of this massage technique. Even a bold figure like Sakamoto Ryoma occasionally received treatment, so I promptly went to the upper Negishi area to try it out. However, they said that unless they massaged my bones or turned my organs upside down, it would be difficult to cure me, and they employed a rather brutal method of massage. Afterwards, I felt as if my body had turned to cotton and I was in a state of stupor, so I decided to stop after just one session. A certain friend insisted that I should avoid solid foods altogether. So, I spent a day living solely on milk, but during that time, my stomach made such loud noises that it felt like I was about to burst, and I couldn't sleep all night. Another suggested that if I breathed using my diaphragm and exercised my internal organs, my stomach's function would naturally improve, so I was told to give it a try. I did attempt it a little, but it left me feeling uneasy in my belly. Sometimes I would remember and focus intently, but after five or six minutes, I would forget. When I tried not to forget, my diaphragm would bother me, making it impossible to read or write. The aesthetician Meitei saw me in this state and joked that I looked like a man about to give birth, so I stopped doing it recently. Another doctor suggested that I should eat soba, so I promptly tried alternating between kake and mori soba, but all that did was upset my stomach without any benefits. I have tried every possible method to cure my long-standing stomach weakness, but all have failed. However, I can say for certain that the three cups of Masamune I drank last night with Kangetsu had a definite effect. From now on, I shall drink two or three cups every evening.

This will certainly not last long. My master's heart changes incessantly, much like my own eyeballs. He is a man who cannot maintain anything for long. Moreover, while he worries about his stomach ailment in his diary, he outwardly puts on a brave front, which is quite amusing. The other day, a certain scholar, a friend of his, came to visit and argued from a certain perspective that all illnesses are nothing but the result of ancestral sins and one's own wrongdoings. It seemed he had done quite a bit of research, for his reasoning was clear, and his argument was well-structured and impressive. Unfortunately, my master does not possess the intellect or knowledge to refute this. However, since he is suffering from a stomach ailment, it appears he wanted to defend himself somehow and maintain his dignity. Thus, he said, “Your theory is interesting, but that Carlyle was weak in the stomach,” as if to imply that his own stomach weakness was honorable because Carlyle had the same affliction. His friend countered, “Just because Carlyle was weak in the stomach doesn’t mean that every weak-stomached person can become Carlyle,” and my master fell silent. It seems that, despite being rich in vanity, it is indeed better not to be weak in the stomach. Starting to drink in the evenings from tonight is rather ridiculous. Upon reflection, the fact that I ate so much zoni (a traditional soup with mochi) this morning might be influenced by last night’s debauchery with Kangetsu over some sake. I, too, felt a sudden desire to try some zoni. I am a cat, but I eat most things. I do not have the energy to venture as far as the tavern down the alley like Kuro, the rickshaw man's black cat, nor am I in a position to be as extravagant as the calico cat at the koto teacher's place on New Road. Therefore, I find that I am surprisingly less picky. I eat the bread that children have dropped, and I lick the rice cakes. The pickles are exceedingly unappetizing, but out of curiosity, I once had a couple of pieces of takuan (pickled daikon). Upon tasting, it is a strange thing; I can eat most things. To say, “I don’t like this, I don’t like that,” is a luxurious whim that a cat living in a teacher's house should not indulge in. According to my master, there was a novelist in France named Balzac. This man was quite the extravagant one—though this does not refer to his palate, but rather to the lavishness of his writing. One day, Balzac wanted to name a character in his novel, but he could not find a name he liked no matter how hard he tried. Then, a friend came to visit, and they went out for a walk together. The friend, of course, was unaware of Balzac's intention to find a name, so when they went out, Balzac walked aimlessly, merely looking at the shop signs.

However, he still could not find a name that pleased him. He wandered around with his friend, who followed him without understanding the situation. They ended up exploring Paris from morning till night. On their way back, Balzac suddenly noticed a tailor's sign. Upon seeing it, he found the name Marcus written there. Balzac clapped his hands and exclaimed, “This is it! This is the one! Marcus is a fine name. If I add the initial Z to it, it will create a name that is simply perfect. It must be Z. Marcus is truly splendid. No matter how much I thought I had come up with a good name myself, there always seemed to be something contrived about it that made it uninteresting. Finally, I have found a name I like,” completely forgetting about the inconvenience he was causing his friend, and he was delighted. However, to have to explore Paris for an entire day just to name a character in a novel is quite a laborious affair. If one could indulge in such extravagance, it would be quite nice, but with a master as miserly as I have, such thoughts are far from my mind. It is a natural consequence of my circumstances to feel that anything will do as long as I can eat. Thus, my sudden craving for zoni is not the result of luxury, but rather a thought that I should eat while I can, recalling that perhaps some leftover zoni from my master’s meal might still be in the kitchen. …I will go check the kitchen.

This morning, the rice cake I saw is stuck to the bottom of the bowl in the same color I saw this morning. I must confess that I have never once put a rice cake in my mouth. It looks delicious, yet there is also something a bit unsettling about it. I scrape the greens that are resting on top with my front paw. Looking at my claws, I see that the outer skin of the rice cake has caught on them and feels sticky. When I sniff it, it has the aroma reminiscent of rice being transferred from the pot to the serving container. Should I eat it or not? I glance around. Fortunately or unfortunately, no one is here. Osan is pecking at the feathers with a face that looks the same in both spring and winter. The children are in the inner room singing "What Does the Rabbit Say?" If I am to eat it, now is the time. If I miss this opportunity, I will have to live without knowing the taste of rice cake until next year. In this moment, I, as a cat, have grasped a profound truth: "Difficult opportunities compel all creatures to dare to do what they do not prefer." To be honest, I do not desire to eat this zoni (a type of soup with rice cakes) that much. In fact, the more I observe the state of the bowl, the more unsettling it becomes, and I lose my desire to eat it. If Osan were to open the back door at this moment, or if I could hear the footsteps of the children approaching, I would have abandoned the bowl without hesitation, and the thought of zoni would not have crossed my mind until next year. However, no one is coming; no matter how much I hesitate, no one is coming. I feel as though I am being urged to eat it quickly. Peering into the bowl, I wish someone would come soon. Yet, still, no one comes. I must ultimately eat the zoni. Finally, I let my entire body weight drop onto the bottom of the bowl and took a small bite of the rice cake. Given the force I exerted, I should have been able to bite through most things, but to my surprise! Just as I thought I could pull my teeth away, I found I could not. When I tried to bite down again, I could not move. The rice cake is a demon, I realized, but it was already too late. Just like a person who falls into a swamp and sinks deeper with every attempt to pull their feet out, the more I bit, the heavier my mouth became, and my teeth would not move. There was a response from my teeth, but just having that response did not allow me to resolve the situation. Mr. Meitei, the aesthetician, once remarked that my master was a man who could not be easily understood, and indeed, that was a clever observation. This rice cake, like my master, could not be easily dealt with either. No matter how much I bit, it seemed there would never be a moment when I could divide it as easily as splitting ten into three.

In this moment of torment, I inadvertently stumbled upon a second truth: "All creatures intuitively predict the suitability or unsuitability of things." I had already discovered two truths, but the rice cake sticking to my teeth brought me no joy whatsoever. My teeth were absorbed into the flesh of the rice cake, and it hurt unbearably. I had to finish eating quickly and escape before Osan arrived. The children's singing seemed to have stopped; they must surely be rushing to the kitchen. In the height of my torment, I wagged my tail in circles, but it had no effect. I raised and lowered my ears, but that did not help either. Upon reflection, I realized that my ears and tail had no relation to the rice cake. In short, I realized that I was merely wasting my efforts in waving and raising them. Finally, I thought that I would have to use my front paws to knock the rice cake off. First, I raised my right paw and stroked around my mouth. Just stroking it would not break it apart. Next, I stretched out my left paw and tried to draw a sharp circle around my mouth. Such a curse would not make the demon fall away. Thinking that persistence was key, I moved my paws back and forth, but still, my teeth remained dangling in the rice cake. How troublesome! I decided to use both paws at once. Then, strangely enough, at that moment, I was able to stand on my hind legs. It felt as though I were not a cat. Whether I was a cat or not, at this point, I did not care; I was determined to do whatever it took until the demon of the rice cake fell away, and I began to scratch my face wildly. My front paws were moving so vigorously that I almost lost my balance. Each time I leaned, I had to adjust with my hind legs, so I could not stay in one place, and I was darting around the kitchen. I was surprised at how skillfully I was managing to stay upright. A third truth suddenly presented itself: "In times of danger, one can do what they normally cannot do. This is called divine assistance." Fortunate to receive divine assistance, I was fighting desperately against the demon of the rice cake when I suddenly felt the presence of footsteps approaching from the back. If a person were to come now, it would be a disaster, so I became even more frantic, racing around the kitchen. The footsteps grew closer. Alas, it seems divine assistance was a bit lacking. I was finally spotted by the children. "Oh look, the cat is eating zoni and dancing!" they exclaimed loudly. The first to hear this was Osan. Abandoning her feather and paddle, she rushed in from the back, exclaiming, "Oh my!" My mistress, dressed in a crepe kimono, said, "What a troublesome cat!" Even my master came out of his study, saying, "You foolish creature!" Only the children found it amusing.

And then, as if they had all agreed, they burst into laughter. I was angry, it was painful, and I could not stop dancing; I was at my wits' end. Just as the laughter was beginning to die down, a five-year-old girl said, "Mother, the cat is quite something," and the laughter erupted again with a force that felt like a storm. I had seen enough of human indifference, but I had never felt so resentful as I did at that moment. Finally, even divine assistance disappeared, and as usual, I found myself crawling on all fours, performing the disgraceful act of rolling my eyes in confusion. It seemed even Osan felt pity and said to my master, "Well, let’s take the rice cake away from him." Osan looked at my mistress with an expression that suggested, "Shall we let him dance some more?" My mistress wanted to see the dance but had no desire to see it at the cost of my life, so she remained silent. "If you don’t take it away, he’ll die; hurry and take it away!" my master urged Osan again. Osan, looking as if she had just awakened from a dream halfway through a delicious meal, grabbed the rice cake with a disinterested expression. I thought my front teeth might all break, just like Kangetsu said. It was unbearable, as they ruthlessly pulled on the teeth that were firmly embedded in the rice cake. As I experienced the fourth truth, "All comfort must be traversed through hardship," I looked around in bewilderment, only to find that the household had already retreated to the inner room.

When I make such a blunder, it feels somewhat awkward to be seen by Osan while staying indoors. So, I thought it best to ease my mind and visit Mikeko, the koto teacher's cat, who lives nearby. Mikeko is a renowned beauty in this area. I may be a cat, but I have a fair understanding of human emotions. Whenever I see my master's bitter face or endure Osan's harsh remarks, and my spirits are low, I always visit this female friend of mine to engage in various conversations. Before I know it, my heart feels light, and I forget all my worries and troubles, feeling as if I have been reborn. The influence of women is indeed immense. Peering through the gap in the fence, I wondered if she was there, and there was Mikeko, sitting gracefully by the porch, wearing a new collar for the New Year. The roundness of her back is indescribably beautiful. It embodies the beauty of curves. The way her tail bends, the angle of her legs, and the languid flick of her ears are beyond description. She sits elegantly in a sunlit spot, her body exhibiting a calm and composed demeanor, yet her smooth fur, glistening in the spring light, seems to ripple gently as if stirred by a breeze. I was momentarily entranced by her beauty, but as I regained my senses, I called out softly, "Mikeko, Mikeko," waving my front paw. Mikeko responded, "Oh, Mr. Cat," as she descended from the porch. The bell attached to her red collar jingled pleasantly. Ah, she even has a bell now that it's the New Year; what a lovely sound! While I was admiring it, she came closer and said, "Oh, Mr. Cat, Happy New Year," wagging her tail to the left. Among the cats in the neighborhood, only Mikeko calls me "Mr. Cat." As I still have no name, she is the only one who respects me and addresses me as "Mr." because I live in a teacher's house. I don't mind being called "Mr.," so I respond, "Yes, yes." "Ah, Happy New Year! You've done a splendid job with your grooming," I said. "Yes, it was bought for me by the koto teacher last New Year's Eve. Isn't it nice?" she replied, jingling her collar. "Indeed, it sounds wonderful. I have never seen anything so splendid since I was born." "Oh, really? Everyone has one," she said, jingling again. "Isn't it a lovely sound? I'm so happy," she continued to jingle. "It seems your teacher really dotes on you," I remarked, hinting at my envy in comparison to my own situation. Mikeko, being innocent, replied, "It's true! It's just like having my own child," laughing innocently. Cats can laugh too, you know. It is a mistake for humans to think that nothing can make them laugh except themselves. I laugh by making my nostrils triangular and vibrating my throat, so humans would not understand. "By the way, what is your master?" I asked. "Oh, my master? That's a strange one.

It's the koto teacher," she answered. "I know that, but what is his status? He must have been quite a distinguished person in the past," I inquired. "Yes," she replied. While waiting for you, the princess Komatsu... Inside the sliding door, the koto teacher began to play the koto. "Isn't it a lovely sound?" Mikeko boasted. "It seems nice, but I can't really tell. What is it, exactly?" I asked. "That? That's something or other. The koto teacher loves that," she explained. "He is sixty-two years old. Quite sturdy, isn't he?" If he has lived to sixty-two, he must indeed be sturdy. I responded with a "Hmm." It seemed a bit dull, but there was no other answer to give, so it couldn't be helped. "He used to be of quite a good status, you know. He always says so," she continued. "Oh? What was he originally?" I asked. "He is the nephew of the woman who married the sister of the koto teacher's secretary," she replied. "What did you say?" "The sister of the koto teacher's secretary married..." "I see. Please wait a moment. The sister of the koto teacher's secretary..." "Oh, that's not right. It's the sister of the koto teacher's secretary..." "Alright, I understand. It's the koto teacher's, right?" "Yes." "The secretary's, right?" "That's right." "Married?" "She married the sister." "Yes, yes, I made a mistake. She married the sister's husband." "The nephew's daughter, that's what it is." "The nephew's daughter?" "Yes. Got it?" "No, it seems quite confusing and unclear. Ultimately, what relation does this have to the koto teacher?" "You really don't understand much, do you? That's why I said she is the daughter of the nephew of the woman who married the sister of the koto teacher's secretary, haven't I been saying that from the start?" "I understand that completely, but..." "As long as you understand that, it's fine, isn't it?" "Yes," I conceded, as I had no choice but to surrender. Sometimes, we must engage in convoluted conversations.

When the sound of the koto stopped abruptly within the sliding doors, the voice of the koto teacher called out, "Mikeko, Mikeko, it's time for your meal." Mikeko, looking pleased, replied, "Oh, the teacher is calling me, so I’ll be going back, if that’s all right?" Even if it were inappropriate, there was no helping it. "Then do come back to play again," the teacher said, jingling a bell as she hurried to the garden, but she suddenly returned, looking worried and asked, "You look quite unwell. Are you all right?" Since it was unlikely that I had been dancing after eating zoni (a traditional New Year soup), I replied, "Oh, it’s nothing in particular, but I have a bit of a headache after thinking too much. I thought talking with you might help, so I actually came out." "I see. Take care of yourself. Goodbye," she said, appearing somewhat reluctant to leave. With that, my energy from the zoni had completely returned. I felt quite good. As I intended to pass through the usual tea garden on my way back, I stepped on the melting frost pillars and peeked out from the ruins of Kenninji Temple, only to see Kuro, the rickshaw man's black cat, lounging on top of a withered chrysanthemum, stretching. I was no longer the kind of cat who feared Kuro, but I thought it would be a hassle to engage in conversation, so I decided to pass by with a nonchalant expression. Kuro, as is his nature, would never remain silent if he sensed that someone was looking down on him. "Hey, nameless Gonbei, you’ve been perched quite high lately, haven’t you? No matter how much you’ve eaten off a teacher’s plate, you shouldn’t be so arrogant. You’re not amusing at all," he remarked. It seemed Kuro was still unaware of my newfound fame. I wanted to explain, but he was not the type to understand, so I resolved to offer a polite greeting and excuse myself as quickly as possible. "Well, Kuro, congratulations. You’re as lively as ever," I said, raising my tail and turning to the left. Kuro raised his tail but did not return the greeting. "What’s so congratulatory? If it’s New Year’s, then you’re the one who’s perpetually in a festive mood. Watch out for that blowhard over there," he retorted. The phrase "that blowhard over there" seemed to be a derogatory expression, but I could not grasp its meaning. "Excuse me, but what do you mean by 'that blowhard over there'?" I inquired. "Hmph, you’re asking about that when you’re in such poor shape? It means you’re a New Year’s fool," he replied. While "New Year’s fool" is poetic, the meaning behind it was even more unclear than the phrase about the blowhard. I wanted to clarify, but I knew that I would not receive a clear answer, so I stood there silently, facing him. I felt somewhat at a loss.

Then, suddenly, Kuro’s wife shouted loudly, "Hey, the salmon I left on the shelf is gone! This is terrible. That black beast must have taken it again. What a detestable cat!" Her voice shook the tranquil air of early spring, disturbing the peace. Kuro, with a lazy expression that seemed to say he could care less about her yelling, leaned forward with his square jaw, signaling me to listen. Until now, I hadn’t noticed during my exchange with Kuro, but looking down, I saw a piece of salmon bone, muddy and equivalent to two sen and three rin, rolling beneath his feet. "You’re still at it, I see," I said, forgetting the previous conversation and offering a compliment. Kuro was not the type to easily forgive such trivial matters. "What do you mean by 'still at it'? A piece or two of salmon is nothing. You’re talking as if you’re looking down on me. I am, after all, Kuro, the rickshaw cat," he said, raising his right front paw to scratch his shoulder instead of rolling up his sleeves. "I’ve known you were Kuro from the start." 

"Knowing that and still saying such things, what does that mean?" he retorted, blowing hot air in annoyance. If he were human, I would have been grabbed by the collar and shoved around. Feeling somewhat exasperated, I thought to myself that this was becoming a troublesome situation when I heard Kuro’s wife’s loud voice again. "Hey, Nishikawa! Hey, Nishikawa! I need you to bring me a pound of beef right away! Do you understand? A pound of tender beef!" Her order for beef shattered the silence of the neighborhood. "Hmph, shouting like that just because you order beef once a year. A pound of beef is something to boast about to the neighbors, isn’t it?" Kuro scoffed, bracing himself on all fours. I had no way to greet him, so I remained silent and watched. "A pound isn’t something I can accept, but there’s no helping it. Just keep it for now; I’ll eat it later," he said, as if it were something specially prepared for him. "This time it’s a real feast. Splendid, splendid," I said, trying to send him off as best as I could. "It’s none of your business. Be quiet," he snapped, suddenly hurling a chunk of the crumbled frost pillar at my head with his hind legs. While I was startled and brushing off the mud from my body, Kuro slipped under the fence and disappeared somewhere. He must have gone to spy on Nishikawa’s beef. When I returned home, the room felt unusually spring-like, and even the sound of my master’s laughter was cheerful. Curious, I approached my master, who was sitting by the open sliding door, and saw an unfamiliar guest. He was a serious-looking student, neatly parted hair, wearing a cotton haori and small trousers.

Upon seeing the corner of my master’s hand warmer, I noticed a business card that read "Kangetsu, a friend of Tofu," which indicated this guest’s name and that he was a friend of Kangetsu. Since the conversation between my master and the guest was already underway, I could not grasp the context, but it seemed to be about Meitei, the aesthetician I had introduced last time. 「So, he said there’s an interesting theme, so you must come along with me,」 the guest said calmly. 「What is it? Is there a theme about going to eat Western food for lunch?」 The host poured more tea and pushed it in front of the guest. 「Well, I didn’t understand what that theme was at the time, but since it was that person, I thought there must be something interesting about it...」 

「Did you go together? I see.」 

「However, I was surprised,」 the host said, almost as if to say, “Did you see that?” while giving a light tap on my head, which was resting on his lap. It hurt a little. 「It must have been some foolish farce again. That man has a knack for that,」 he suddenly recalled the Andrea del Sarto incident. 「Hehe. You said you wanted to try something unusual, didn’t you?」 

「What did you eat?」 

「First, we looked at the menu and talked about various dishes.」 

「Before you ordered, right?」 

「Yes.」 

「And then?」 

「Then he tilted his head and looked at the waiter, saying there didn’t seem to be anything unusual. The waiter, determined not to lose, suggested duck roast or veal chop, to which the gentleman replied that he wouldn’t come all the way here just to eat such commonplace dishes. The waiter, not understanding what “commonplace” meant, made a strange face and fell silent.」 

「That’s right.」 

「Then he turned to me and said, “When you go to France or England, you can eat quite a variety of dishes, but in Japan, no matter where you go, it’s all the same, and I just can’t bring myself to enter a Western restaurant,” with an air of disappointment. Overall, I wonder if that gentleman has ever traveled abroad.」 

「What? Meitei travel abroad? He has the money and the time, and if he wanted to go, he could go anytime, but I suppose this is just a clever joke about a place he intends to visit in the future,」 the host said, thinking he had made a clever remark, and chuckled. The guest did not seem particularly impressed. 「Is that so? I thought perhaps he had traveled abroad without my noticing, and I was listening earnestly. Besides, he was describing dishes like slug soup and frog stew as if he had seen them,」 

「He must have heard that from someone; he’s quite the master at lying, you know.」 

「It seems so,」 he said, gazing at the daffodils in the vase. There was a hint of disappointment in his expression. 「So that theme was it, then,」 the host pressed.

「No, that was just the introduction; the main topic is yet to come.」 

「Hmm,」 the host interjected with a curious exclamation. 「Then, since slugs and frogs are really not something you can eat, I thought we might settle for something like a tochi-menbo (a type of dish), and since you were consulting me, I casually said that would be fine.」 

「Heh, tochi-menbo is quite unusual.」 

「Yes, it is indeed unusual, but the gentleman was so serious that I didn’t notice it at the time,」 he seemed to be apologizing to the host for his carelessness. 「And then what happened?」 the host asked indifferently. He showed no sympathy for the guest's apology. 「Then I told the waiter to bring two servings of tochi-menbo, and the waiter asked if it was menchi-bo (another dish), but the gentleman corrected him with an even more serious expression, saying it was not menchi-bo but tochi-menbo.」 

「Is that so? Is there even such a dish as tochi-menbo?」 

「Well, I thought it was a bit strange, but the gentleman was so composed, and on top of that, he was quite knowledgeable about Western cuisine, so at that moment, I completely believed he had traveled abroad, and I added my voice to his, telling the waiter it was tochi-menbo, tochi-menbo.」 

「What did the waiter do?」 

「The waiter, thinking back now, it’s really quite comical, took a moment to ponder and said, “I’m very sorry, but we don’t have tochi-menbo today; however, we can prepare menchi-bo for you right away,” to which the gentleman looked very disappointed and said, “Well, it seems I’ve come all this way for nothing. Is there any way you could arrange for tochi-menbo?” He then handed the waiter a twenty-sen coin, and the waiter said he would consult with the chef and went to the back.」 

「It seems you really wanted to eat tochi-menbo.」 

「After a while, the waiter came back and said, “I’m truly sorry, we can prepare it if you order it, but it will take a little time.” To which Meitei-sensei, calm as ever, replied, “Well, we have time since it’s New Year’s, so let’s wait a bit and eat,” and then took out a cigar from his pocket and began to smoke. I had no choice but to take out a Japanese newspaper from my pocket and start reading, and the waiter went back to consult again.」 

「That’s quite a hassle, isn’t it?」 the host said, shifting his position as if he were reading a war report. 「Then the waiter came out again and said, “Recently, the ingredients for tochi-menbo have run out, and we can’t find them at Kameya or Yokohama’s No. 15, so I’m very sorry,” looking quite pitiful. The gentleman said, “That’s a problem; I came all this way,” and looked at me, repeating himself over and over. I couldn’t remain silent, so I chimed in, “It’s truly regrettable, indeed.”」 

「You’re quite right,」 the host agreed.

What he found so agreeable, I couldn’t understand. 「Then the waiter, looking quite sorry, said, “When the ingredients come in, please do ask for it.” When the gentleman asked what ingredients were used, the waiter just laughed and didn’t answer. When the gentleman pressed him, saying, “It must be some Japanese-style haiku poet,” the waiter replied, “Yes, that’s right, and that’s why we can’t find them in Yokohama lately, so I’m truly sorry.”」 

「Ahahaha, is that the punchline? That’s amusing,」 the host laughed louder than usual. His knees shook, and I almost fell off. The host laughed without a care. It seemed he suddenly felt pleased to know he was not the only one who had fallen for the Andrea del Sarto incident. 「Then the two of us went outside, and he said, “How about that? It went well, didn’t it? Using tochi-menbo as a theme was quite clever,” and he was quite pleased with himself. I had to say I was deeply impressed, but in truth, lunch had been delayed, and I was very hungry and in a weak state.」 

「That must have been a bother,」 the host finally expressed sympathy. To this, I had no objections. After a while, the conversation paused, and the sound of my throat growling reached the ears of both host and guest.
