Tofu gulped down the now-cold tea and said, “Actually, I came here today because I have a small request to make of you, Mr. Kushami,” adjusting his demeanor. “Oh, what is it?” the master replied, equally composed. “As you know, I have a fondness for literature and the arts…” “That’s fine,” he interjected, pouring more oil on the fire. “A group of like-minded individuals has recently organized a reading club, and we intend to meet once a month to continue our studies in this field. We already held our first meeting last year at the end of December.” “I’d like to ask, when you say reading club, does that mean you read poetry and prose with some sort of rhythm?” “Well, we plan to start with works from the ancients and gradually include original creations from our members.” “When you say works from the ancients, do you mean something like Bai Juyi’s ‘Song of the Pipa’?” “No.” “Or perhaps Buson’s ‘Spring Breeze on the Horse Path’?” “No.” “Then what kind of works did you read?” “Recently, we performed a play by Chikamatsu.” “Chikamatsu? The Chikamatsu of jōruri?” The two of them were not thinking of the same Chikamatsu. When Chikamatsu was mentioned, they were referring to the playwright. The master, hearing this, thought Tofu must be quite foolish, while he absentmindedly patted my head. In a world where there are humans who believe they are loved by those who glare at them from the bushes, it is hardly surprising that such a mistake would occur, and I allowed myself to be patted without concern. “Yes,” Tofu replied, glancing at the master’s expression. “So, do you read alone, or do you perform roles?” “We performed roles and acted it out together. The main idea is to express sympathy for the characters in the work and to bring out their personalities, adding gestures and movements. The aim is to portray the people of that era as closely as possible, whether they are young ladies or servants, so that they seem to come alive.” “Well then, isn’t it just like a play?” “Yes, except we don’t have costumes or set pieces.” “Pardon my curiosity, but did it go well?” “I think it was a success for a first meeting.” “And the play you performed, the one about the lovers, what was it about?” “It’s about a boatman taking passengers to the Yoshiwara.” “That sounds like quite a dramatic scene,” the teacher tilted his head slightly. The smoke from the rising sun wafted past his ear and around his face. “Oh, it wasn’t such a big deal. The characters were just the passengers, the boatman, a courtesan, a waitress, and a servant, along with the audience,” Tofu said nonchalantly. The master made a slightly bitter face upon hearing the name of the courtesan, but it seemed he had no clear understanding of the terms waitress, servant, and audience, so he posed a question.

“Is a waitress a maidservant at a brothel?” “I haven’t studied it well, but I think a waitress is a maid at a tea house, and a servant is something like an assistant in a women’s room.” Tofu, who had just said they would use gestures to portray the characters, seemed not to fully understand the nature of the servant and waitress. “I see, so the waitress is one who serves at a tea house, and the servant is someone who attends to the brothel. Now, what about the audience? Is it a person or a specific place? If it’s a person, is it a man or a woman?” “I think the audience is always male.” “What role do they play?” “Well, I haven’t looked into that yet. I’ll research it later.” I glanced up at the master’s face, thinking that if they were to perform with such a lack of understanding, it would surely result in something absurd. The master appeared unexpectedly serious. “So, who else was involved in the reading besides you?” “There were various people. The courtesan was played by a law student named K, who had a mustache and spoke with a sweet, feminine tone, which was a bit strange. And the courtesan had a fit at one point…” “Do you have to have fits even in a reading?” the master asked anxiously. “Well, expressions are important,” Tofu maintained his artistic demeanor. “Did you manage to have a fit well?” the master quipped. “A fit was a bit too much for the first meeting,” Tofu replied, also making a quip. “By the way, what role did you play?” the master inquired. “I was the boatman.” “Oh, you were the boatman.” The tone of his voice seemed to imply that if he could be the boatman, then I could at least play the audience. Eventually, he confessed, “Was being the boatman too much for you?” Tofu showed no signs of being offended. In a calm tone, he replied, “As the boatman, the event ended up being a bit anticlimactic. You see, there were four or five female students living next door, and somehow they found out that there was a reading that day and came to listen from outside the window. Just as I was getting into character as the boatman, thinking everything was going well, my gestures must have been a bit too exaggerated, and the female students, who had been holding back until then, suddenly burst into laughter. It was quite a shock, and it was awkward, so I couldn’t continue, and we ended up breaking up the meeting there.” For a reading that was deemed a success as a first meeting, one could only imagine what a failure would look like, and I couldn’t help but laugh. I felt a rumble in my throat. The master continued to gently pat my head. It is a blessing to be laughed at and cherished by someone, but there is also something a bit eerie about it. “That was quite an incident,” the master remarked, as if delivering a eulogy at the start of the new year.

“For the second meeting, we plan to be more ambitious and grand, and that is precisely why I came today. I would like to ask you to join us and lend your support.” “I certainly can’t manage to have fits,” the master, being somewhat passive, began to decline. “No, you don’t have to have fits. Here is the list of supporters,” Tofu said, carefully pulling out a small notebook from a purple furoshiki. “I would like you to sign it and affix your seal.” He placed the notebook open before the master’s knees. Looking at it, I saw the names of well-known literary doctors and scholars neatly lined up. “Well, I wouldn’t mind becoming a supporter, but what obligations does that entail?” Mr. Kushami appeared to be concerned. “Obligations? There’s really nothing you must do. Just writing your name to express your support is enough.” “In that case, I’ll join,” the master said, suddenly feeling lighthearted upon realizing there were no obligations. Knowing that there was no responsibility, he looked as if he would sign his name to any treasonous document. Furthermore, to have his name listed among such renowned scholars was an unparalleled honor for the master, who had never encountered anything like this before, so it was no wonder he responded with such enthusiasm. “Excuse me for a moment,” the master said, entering the study to fetch his seal. I plopped down onto the tatami mat. Tofu picked up a piece of castella from the plate of sweets and stuffed it into his mouth. He looked as if he was struggling for a while. I recalled the incident with the zoni from this morning. When the master came out of the study with the seal, Tofu’s castella had settled in his stomach. The master seemed unaware that the plate of sweets was completely empty. If he were to notice, I would be the first to be suspected. After Tofu left, the master entered the study and looked at the desk, where, before he knew it, a letter from Meitei had arrived. “Happy New Year…”

The master thinks that today’s letter is unusually serious. There is hardly anything serious in Mr. Meitei’s letters, and the other day, for instance, I received one that said, “Since there are no women to fall in love with afterwards, and no love letters from anywhere, I am glad to report that I am managing to get by without incident.” Compared to that, this New Year’s letter is exceptionally worldly. “I would like to visit for a moment, but contrary to my brother’s passive philosophy, I plan to greet this unprecedented New Year with as positive an attitude as possible. Therefore, I am extremely busy every day, as you can imagine…”

Indeed, knowing that man, the master agrees with Mr. Meitei in his heart that he must be busy frolicking around during the New Year. “Yesterday, I stole a moment to prepare a feast of tochi menbo (a type of sweet) for Tofu, but unfortunately, due to a lack of ingredients, I was unable to fulfill that intention, which is most regrettable…”

The master smiles silently, thinking that things are starting to return to their usual state. “Tomorrow is a karuta (Japanese card game) gathering hosted by a certain baron, the day after is the New Year’s banquet of the Aesthetics Society, the day after that is a welcome party for Professor Toribe, and the day after that…”

How noisy, the master thinks, skipping over the rest. “As you can see, with the series of gatherings for Noh performances, haiku meetings, tanka meetings, and new poetry meetings, I will be busy attending events without a break for the time being. Therefore, I humbly ask for your forgiveness for my inability to respond to your greetings with a proper visit…”

The master thinks it is not worth going at all and decides to reply to the letter. “When you come to visit next time, I would like to prepare dinner for you after a long time. Although my cold kitchen has no rare delicacies, I will at least try to provide some tochi menbo starting now…”

Still going on about tochi menbo, the master feels a bit offended. “However, due to a recent shortage of tochi menbo ingredients, it is uncertain whether I will be able to procure any in time. If that is the case, I could offer you peacock tongues instead…”

The master thinks he has weighed both options. “As you know, the amount of tongue meat from one peacock is hardly enough to fill a pinky finger, so to satisfy my brother’s hearty appetite…”

What a lie, the master thinks, dismissing it as nonsense. “Surely, I must capture at least twenty or thirty peacocks. However, while peacocks can be seen here and there in zoos and at Asakusa’s Hanayashiki (flower park), they are nowhere to be found in ordinary bird shops, which is quite a dilemma…”

The master thinks he is worrying about this all on his own and feels no gratitude.

“The cooking of peacock tongues was once very popular during the height of Rome, and it was secretly a delicacy that I have long desired…”

What is this “I have long desired”? The master is extremely cold toward this. “Until the sixteenth or seventeenth century, peacocks were considered an indispensable delicacy at banquets throughout Europe. I recall that when the Earl of Leicester invited Queen Elizabeth to Kenilworth, he indeed used peacock…”

If he is going to talk about the history of peacock dishes, it doesn’t seem like he’s that busy after all, the master grumbles. “Anyway, with the continuous feasting as we have lately, even I, as a cat, will inevitably become weak in the stomach like my brother before long…”

That “like my brother” is unnecessary. The master mutters that there’s no need to make me the standard for weak stomachs. “According to historians, the Romans held banquets two or three times a day. If one were to have meals two or three times a day, even the healthiest person would surely experience digestive issues. Therefore, naturally, one would end up like my brother…”

Again with “like my brother,” how rude. “However, those who sought to balance luxury and hygiene recognized the need to maintain their digestive health while indulging in excessive amounts of rich food. Thus, they devised a secret method…”

The master suddenly becomes interested. “They would always take a bath after eating. After bathing, they would vomit everything they had swallowed before the bath, cleansing their stomachs. After this cleansing of the stomach, they would return to the table and indulge in delicacies until they were satisfied. Once satisfied, they would bathe again and expel everything. By doing this, they could gorge on their favorite foods without causing any harm to their internal organs. This is what I believe to be a twofold benefit…”

Indeed, it is a twofold benefit, the master thinks with envy on his face. “In the twentieth century, with frequent transportation and an increase in banquets, not to mention the second year of the Russo-Japanese War, we, as citizens of a victorious nation, have arrived at a time when we must certainly study the Romans’ method of bathing and vomiting. Otherwise, even the great citizens of our nation will inevitably become stomach patients like my brother in the near future…”

Again with “like my brother,” what an irritating man, the master thinks.

“At this time, if someone knowledgeable about Western affairs were to study ancient history and legends, discover this long-abandoned secret method, and apply it to Meiji society, it would not only serve to prevent calamities before they arise but also allow us to repay the kindness of indulging in pleasures…”

Something seems odd, the master thinks, scratching his head. “Therefore, I have been perusing the writings of Gibbon, Monson, Smith, and others, but I have yet to find a clue to this discovery, which is quite disappointing. However, as you know, once I set my mind to something, I have a nature that will not cease until I succeed. Thus, I believe I will soon revive the vomiting method. I will report to you as soon as I make this discovery, so please be aware of this. Therefore, I would like to prepare the tochi menbo and peacock tongues for you after this discovery, as it would be convenient not only for me but also for my brother, who is already suffering from a weak stomach…”

What? Have I finally been taken in? The master thinks, having read it all with such seriousness because the writing was so earnest. Mr. Meitei must be quite the idle person to play such a prank at the start of the New Year, the master chuckles. After that, four or five days passed without any particular events. Watching the white porcelain narcissus gradually wilt and the blue-stemmed plum blossoms in the vase slowly begin to open, I thought it was boring just to linger around, so I decided to visit Mikeko, but I couldn’t find her. At first, I thought she was out, but on the second attempt, I learned she was sick in bed. While hiding in the shadow of the water basin’s leaves, I listened to the koto teacher and the maid talking through the shoji (sliding door). “Is Mikeko eating her food?” “No, she hasn’t eaten anything since this morning. I’ve kept her warm and let her lie in the kotatsu (heated table).” That doesn’t sound very cat-like. It’s as if she’s being treated like a human. On one hand, I feel envious when comparing her situation to mine, but on the other hand, I am pleased to see the cat I love receiving such generous treatment. “It’s really troublesome, you know. If she doesn’t eat, her body will just get weaker.” “That’s true. Even we can’t work the next day if we don’t eat at least once a day.”

The maid responds as if the cat is a more superior creature than herself. In reality, in this household, the cat may indeed be more valued than the maid. 「Did you take it to the doctor?」  
「Yes, that doctor is quite peculiar. When I took Mikeko in my arms to the examination room, he tried to take my pulse, thinking I had caught a cold. No, the patient is not me.

When I placed Mikeko back on my lap, he chuckled and said that he couldn't understand a cat's illness, and if I just left it alone, it would heal in time. Isn't that rather infuriating? I was so annoyed that I said, 'Well, if that's the case, I won't have you look at her. She's a very important cat,' and promptly returned home with Mikeko tucked in my arms.」  
「Indeed, indeed.」  
The phrase "indeed, indeed" is certainly not something I would hear in my own household. It is a phrase that can only be used in the presence of someone like the Empress Dowager, and I was quite impressed by its elegance. 「It sounds like you're saying something mournful, but...」  
「Yes, she must have caught a cold and has a sore throat. Anyone who catches a cold will have a cough, you know...」  
Only a maidservant under the Empress Dowager would use such excessively polite language. 「Moreover, these days, there are ailments like tuberculosis, you know.」  
「Truly, with all these new diseases like tuberculosis and plague cropping up lately, we must be vigilant and cautious. There’s nothing good about being careless during these times.」  
「In the old shogunate days, there was nothing decent among those who didn't take care, so you must be careful too.」  
「Is that really the case?」  
The maidservant was greatly moved. 「Even though you say she has a cold, she didn't seem to be out and about much...」  
「Well, you see, I've made some bad friends lately.」  
The maidservant spoke with the air of someone revealing a state secret. 「Bad friends?」  
「Yes, that scruffy tomcat from the teacher's place on the main street.」  
「The teacher, you mean that person who makes that rude noise every morning?」  
「Yes, the one who sounds like a goose being strangled every time he washes his face.」  
That description of a goose being strangled is quite apt. My master has a habit of making strange noises without restraint when he gargles in the bath every morning, poking his throat with a toothpick. When he's in a bad mood, he makes a ruckus, and when he's in a good mood, he gets even louder. In other words, whether he's in a good or bad mood, he makes a ruckus without pause. According to my mistress, he didn't have this habit before moving here, but once he started, he hasn't stopped for a single day. It's a rather troublesome habit, and I, as a cat, can hardly imagine why he persists with it so patiently. Still, to call him a "scruffy cat" is quite a harsh judgment, and I perk up my ears to listen further. 「I wonder what curse he thinks he’s casting with such a voice.

Before the Restoration, even a servant or a sandal bearer knew proper etiquette, and in the estate town, there wasn't a single person who washed their face like that.」  
「That’s surely true.」  
The maidservant was excessively impressed and kept using "indeed."  
「With a master like that, it’s no wonder he’s a stray cat. If he comes around again, give him a good whack.」  
「I’ll certainly give him a whack. Mikeko's illness is entirely his fault, so I’ll surely take my revenge.」  
What an outrageous injustice I’ve suffered. I couldn't get close to that rascal, and thus returned without meeting Mikeko. Upon returning, I found my master in his study, pen in hand, seemingly lost in thought. I thought he would surely be angry if I mentioned the rumors I had heard from the koto teacher, but ignorance is bliss, as they say, and he was mumbling to himself, pretending to be a noble poet. At that moment, Meitei, who had said he was too busy to come by for a while, floated in. 「Are you composing some new poetry? If you come up with something interesting, do show it to me,」 he said. 「Hmm, I thought it was a pretty good piece of writing, so I thought I’d try translating it,」 my master replied, opening his mouth with a heavy air. 「Writing? Whose writing is it?」  
「I don’t know whose it is.」  
「An anonymous author, huh? There are quite a few good pieces by anonymous authors, so they shouldn’t be underestimated. Where did you find it?」  
「In the Second Reader,」 my master answered calmly. 「The Second Reader? What about the Second Reader?」  
「The fine writing I’m translating is in the Second Reader.」  
「You can’t be serious. Are you trying to tackle the curse of the peacock’s tongue at a critical juncture?」  
「I’m not like you, a braggart,」 he said, twisting his mustache. He was quite composed. 「Once, someone asked Sanyo if there were any fine writings lately, and he showed a debt collection notice written by a horse driver, saying, 'This is probably the finest writing of late.' So perhaps your aesthetic sense is unexpectedly sharp. Go ahead and read it; I’ll critique it for you,」 Meitei said, sounding like the authority on aesthetic sense. My master began reading in a voice like a Zen monk reciting the teachings of Daido Kokushi. 「Giant, gravity.」  
「What is this giant gravity?」  
「It’s the title, 'Giant Gravity.'」  
「What a strange title; I don’t understand its meaning.」  
「It’s meant to imply a giant that has the name of gravity.」  
「That seems a bit forced, but since it’s the title, I suppose I’ll let it slide. Now, let’s read the text; your voice is good, so it should be quite interesting.」  
「Don’t mix things up,」 he warned beforehand and began reading again. I gazed out the window. Children were playing, throwing a ball. They tossed the ball high into the air.

The ball ascended higher and higher. After a while, it came falling down. They threw the ball high again. Once more, three times. Each time the ball fell back down. I asked, "Why does it fall? Why doesn’t it just keep going up?"  
「Because the giant lives underground,」 the mother replied. 「He is gravity incarnate. He is strong. He pulls everything toward himself. He pulls houses down to the ground. If he didn’t, they would float away. The children would float away too. Did you see the leaves fall? That’s because the giant gravity calls them. There may be times when a book falls. That’s because giant gravity is calling it. The ball goes up into the sky. Giant gravity calls. When it calls, it falls back down.」  
「Is that all?」  
「Hmm, that’s a bit sweet, isn’t it?」  
「No, I’m quite impressed. I’ve received a splendid return for my trouble.」  
「It’s not a return or anything; I just thought it was genuinely good, so I translated it. Don’t you think so?」 he said, peering over his gold-rimmed glasses. 「I’m truly astonished. I never thought you had such skill. I’ve been thoroughly taken in this time; I concede, I concede,」 he muttered to himself, talking away. My master was completely oblivious. 「I have no intention of making you concede. I just thought it was an interesting piece of writing, so I translated it.」  
「No, it’s really interesting. It has to be like this to be genuine. It’s astonishing. I’m humbled.」  
「There’s no need to be so humbled. I’ve recently given up watercolor painting, so I thought I’d try my hand at writing instead.」  
「How can it compare to watercolor painting, which is indiscriminately equal in black and white? I’m utterly impressed.」  
「If you praise me like that, I’ll get even more motivated,」 my master continued, completely misunderstanding the situation.

Just then, Kangetsu entered, apologizing for his previous rudeness. "Ah, pardon me. I was just listening to a remarkable piece of writing and had just vanquished the spirit of the tochi menbo," Mr. Meitei hinted at something incomprehensible. "Oh, is that so?" Kangetsu replied with an equally baffling greeting. Only the master showed no sign of excitement. "The other day, at your introduction, a man named Tofu came by." "Ah, did he? That Tofu is an exceedingly honest man, but he has some peculiarities, so I thought he might be a bother. However, he insisted on being introduced..." "It's not that he was a bother, really..." "When he came here, didn't he say something about his own name?" "No, it seems he didn't mention anything like that." "Is that so? It's his habit to explain his name to anyone he meets for the first time." "What kind of explanation does he give?" Mr. Meitei, eager to hear, interjected. "He gets quite sensitive if you read his name, Tofu, by sound." "Oh, really?" Mr. Meitei said, pulling out a cigarette from his gold-leaf tobacco pouch. "He always insists, 'My name is not Tofu; it is Kochi.'" "How strange," he mused, inhaling deeply. "This obsession stems entirely from his literary fervor. If you read it as Kochi, it becomes a phrase meaning 'near and far,' and moreover, he takes pride in the fact that his name rhymes. That's why he complains that if people read it as Tofu, they fail to appreciate his painstaking effort." "That is indeed peculiar," Mr. Meitei chuckled, exhaling smoke from his belly. The smoke hesitated midway, caught in his throat. He grasped his pipe and coughed. "When he came the other day, he mentioned that he was ridiculed by the female students while serving as the narrator at a reading session," the master said with a laugh. "Yes, yes," Mr. Meitei replied, tapping his knee with his pipe. I, feeling uneasy, distanced myself a little. "At that reading session, when I treated them to tochi menbo, that story came up. They plan to invite well-known literary figures for the second session and would like to have you attend as well. When I asked if he would be doing another of Chikamatsu's works, he said, 'No, this time I've chosen something entirely new, the Golden Demon.' I asked him what role he would play, and he said, 'I will be the shrine maiden.' Tofu as the shrine maiden should be interesting. I intend to attend and cheer him on." "That sounds amusing," Kangetsu replied with a strange laugh. "However, that man is genuinely sincere and lacks any superficiality, which is good. He is entirely different from Meitei." The master took both Andrea del Sarto and the peacock's tongue and the revenge of the tochi menbo all at once. Mr.

Meitei, seemingly unfazed, laughed, "Well, I suppose I am merely a mere footnote in the annals of history." "That seems about right," the master said. In truth, he did not understand the term "mere footnote," but having been a teacher for so long, he had learned to apply his classroom experiences to social situations. "What does 'mere footnote' mean?" Kangetsu asked earnestly. The master glanced at the floor and said, "That narcissus was something I bought and arranged after returning from the bath last winter, and look how well it holds up." He awkwardly diverted the conversation from the "mere footnote." "Speaking of last winter, I had a truly strange experience," Mr. Meitei said, spinning his pipe like a grand performance. "What kind of experience? Do tell," the master sighed, feeling he had abandoned the "mere footnote" far behind. When he heard Mr. Meitei's strange experience, it went something like this:

"I believe it was on the twenty-seventh of last December. That Tofu sent a message requesting to stay with me to discuss literary matters, and I was eagerly awaiting his arrival all morning, but he was quite late. While I was having lunch and reading Barry Pain's humorous writings in front of the stove, I received a letter from my mother in Shizuoka. She still thinks of me as a child and cautions me, saying not to go out at night in the cold, that while cold baths are good, I must keep the room warm with the stove to avoid catching a cold, and various other pieces of advice. Indeed, parents are truly kind; no one else would care like that. Even I, who usually takes things lightly, felt deeply moved at that moment. Yet, thinking about it, it would be a waste to just dawdle like this. I must write a great work to elevate my family's name. I want to make it known in the Meiji literary world that Mr. Meitei exists while my mother is still alive. As I continued reading, I thought to myself, 'You are indeed fortunate.' It was written that while the Russo-Japanese War had begun, the young men were enduring great hardships for their country, and here I was, leisurely enjoying myself as if it were the New Year during the end of the year. — I certainly am not playing around as my mother thinks — Following that, there was a list of names of my friends from elementary school who had died or been injured in this war. As I read each name, I felt the world growing dull and humanity becoming tiresome. At the very end, it said, 'If I reach that age, will this be the last time I celebrate the New Year's soup?' It was written in such a way that it made me feel uneasy, and I wished for Tofu to arrive soon, but he still did not come. Eventually, it became time for dinner, so I thought I would write a reply to my mother and jotted down a dozen or so lines.

My mother's letter was over six feet long, but I could never manage such a feat, so I always kept it to about ten lines. Since I had been sitting still all day, my stomach felt strange and uncomfortable. I thought that when Tofu arrived, I would keep him waiting, so I decided to take a walk while dropping the mail. For some reason, I found myself heading towards the banks of the river rather than to Fujimicho. That night, it was slightly cloudy, and the cold wind blew from across the moat, making it very chilly. A train from Kagurazaka whistled as it passed below the embankment. It felt terribly lonely. Thoughts of evening, death in battle, old age, and the transience of life raced through my mind. People often say that one might be tempted to hang themselves, and I thought that perhaps such thoughts could lead one to feel inclined towards death. I glanced up and realized that I had unknowingly come right under that pine tree."

"That pine tree, what is it?" the master interjected, interrupting the sentence. "The Pine of the Hanging Neck," Mr. Meitei replied, narrowing his eyes. "The Pine of the Hanging Neck is at Kōtai, isn't it?" Kangetsu rippled the conversation.

"At the Kōno-dai, there is the Pine of the Bell Hanger, and at Dote Sanban-cho, there is the Pine of the Neck Hanger. The reason these names were given is due to an old saying that anyone who comes under this pine feels an urge to hang themselves. There are dozens of pines on the embankment, but when one thinks of hanging, they invariably end up hanging from this particular tree. It happens two or three times a year without fail. For some reason, one cannot muster the will to die from any other pine. Upon closer inspection, the branches conveniently extend horizontally towards the road. Ah, what a fine branch structure! It would be a shame to leave it as is. I wonder if I could somehow entice a human to hang from it; is there anyone coming by? As I looked around, unfortunately, no one appeared. It can't be helped; perhaps I should hang myself. No, no, if I were to hang myself, I would lose my life; that would be dangerous, so I shall refrain. However, there is a tale that the ancient Greeks would mimic hanging at banquets as a form of entertainment. One person would climb onto a platform and put their neck in a noose, at which point the others would kick the platform away. The one who had their neck in the noose would loosen the rope and jump down simultaneously. If that were indeed the case, there would be no particular fear in trying it myself. As I reached for the branch, it bent just right. The way it bent was truly aesthetic. Imagining my neck caught and swaying made me feel indescribably happy. I thought I would definitely do it, but then I considered that if Tofu were waiting, it would be unfortunate. So, I decided to first meet Tofu and discuss matters as promised, and then I would return home."

"Is that how the town prospered?" the master asked. "How amusing," Kangetsu said with a grin. "When I returned home, Tofu was not there. However, today I had some pressing matters and could not go out, and I had received a note saying we would meet again someday, which finally put my mind at ease. I thought, 'Now I can hang myself without worry,' and promptly put on my geta and hurried back to the original spot to see..." he said, looking at the faces of the master and Kangetsu with a composed expression. "What did you see?" the master asked, slightly impatient. "Indeed, we are entering the climax," Kangetsu twisted the cord of his haori. "Upon looking, I found that someone had already come and was hanging there ahead of me. Just one step behind, you see. What a pity! When I think about it, at that moment, I must have been possessed by the Grim Reaper. According to Zeimus, my existence in the real world and the underworld beneath my subconscious were interacting through some kind of causal law.

Isn't it truly a mysterious thing?" Meitei replied with a composed demeanor. The master, thinking he had been had again, said nothing and chewed on his kuya-mochi, making muffled sounds. Kangetsu carefully raked the ash in the hibachi, looking down and smiling, but soon opened his mouth in a very calm tone. "Indeed, upon hearing it, it seems like a strange occurrence that might not happen at all. However, I myself recently had a somewhat similar experience, so I have no doubt about it at all."

"Oh, did you also feel like hanging yourself?" 

"No, mine was not about hanging. This happened just around the same time last year, and moreover, it occurred at almost the same hour as the incident you mentioned, which makes it even more mysterious."

"How interesting," Meitei said, also munching on his kuya-mochi. "That day, there was a year-end party and a concert at a friend's house in Mukojima, and I took my violin along. About fifteen or sixteen young ladies and their husbands gathered, and it was quite a lively affair, everything seemed to be going splendidly. After dinner and the concert, as conversations were flowing and the hour was getting late, I was thinking of taking my leave when the wife of a certain doctor came over and quietly asked me if I was aware of the illness of Ms. ○○ko. Since I had seen her just two or three days prior and she appeared perfectly fine, I was surprised and asked for details. I learned that she had suddenly developed a high fever that very night and had been rambling incoherently, and while that alone would be fine, it seemed that my name was mentioned among her delirious utterances."

The master, of course, and even Meitei did not utter the usual platitudes like "That's unfortunate," but listened quietly and attentively. "When they called a doctor to examine her, it seemed that while they couldn't determine the exact illness, the fever was severe enough to affect her brain, and they diagnosed that if the sleeping medicine did not work as hoped, it could be dangerous. Upon hearing this, I felt a certain unpleasant sensation arise within me. It was a heavy, suffocating feeling, as if the surrounding air had suddenly solidified and was squeezing me from all sides. On my way home, that thought consumed my mind, and I felt unbearably distressed. That beautiful, lively, healthy Ms. ○○ko..."

"Excuse me, but wait a moment. I've been listening, and I've heard the name ○○ko mentioned a couple of times now. If it's not too much trouble, I would like to know," he said, glancing at the master, who also replied with a noncommittal "Hmm."

"Well, that might cause trouble for her, so let's leave it at that."

"Are you planning to go on in such an unclear and vague manner?"

"Please don't scoff; this is a very serious matter...

In any case, when I think about how that lady suddenly fell ill, it fills me with a sense of transience, and my entire vitality seemed to suddenly go on strike, leaving me feeling utterly drained, and I staggered to Azumabashi. Leaning against the railing and looking down, I couldn't tell if it was high tide or low tide, but the black water seemed to be just swirling without movement. A rickshaw came racing from the direction of Hanakawado and crossed the bridge. As I watched the light of its lantern fade away, it gradually shrank until it disappeared at the Sapporo Beer place. I looked back at the water. Then, from far upstream, I heard a voice calling my name. How strange; at this time, there shouldn't be anyone calling me, so I wondered who it could be and peered into the dark water, but I couldn't see anything. It must be my imagination. I thought I should hurry home, but as I took one or two steps, I heard that faint voice calling my name again from afar. I stopped and strained my ears to listen. By the third time I was called, while holding onto the railing, my knees began to tremble. The voice seemed to come from far away or perhaps from the bottom of the river, but it was unmistakably ○○ko's voice. Without thinking, I replied, 'Yes!' That reply was so loud that it echoed in the still water, and I was startled by my own voice, looking around in surprise. I saw no one—no people, no dogs, no moon, nothing. At that moment, I felt myself being drawn into this 'night,' and an overwhelming desire to go to the source of that voice surged within me. The voice of ○○ko pierced my ears, sounding pained, pleading, and seeking rescue, so this time I answered, 'I will come right away,' and leaned half my body over the railing, gazing down at the black water. It seemed to me that the voice calling me was seeping up from beneath the waves. I thought it must be under this water, and finally, I climbed onto the railing. I resolved that if I was called again, I would jump in, and as I stared at the current, that pitiful voice floated up like a thread. I thought, 'This is it!' and gathered my strength, leaping up as if I were a small stone, and then I fell without hesitation."

"So you really jumped in?" the master asked, his eyes wide with surprise. "I didn't intend to go that far," Meitei said, pinching the tip of his nose.

"After I jumped in, I felt faint and was lost in a daze for a while. Eventually, when I came to my senses, I found it cold, but there was no sign of wetness anywhere, nor did I feel as if I had drunk any water. I must have jumped in, yet it was truly strange. Realizing something was off, I looked around and was astonished. I had intended to leap into the water, but mistakenly jumped right in the middle of the bridge, which was indeed quite disappointing. It was merely a matter of getting the front and back mixed up that prevented me from reaching that place where the voice came from." Kangetsu was grinning while, as usual, fiddling with the strings of his haori. "Hahaha, this is amusing. It's quite strange how similar it is to my own experience. It would indeed make for a fine subject for Professor James. If it were turned into a descriptive essay under the title 'Human Sensitivity,' it would surely astonish the literary world... And how is that ○○ko's illness?" Meitei inquired further. "When I went there a few days ago at the beginning of the year, I found the maid playing with feathers inside the gate, so it seems she has fully recovered," came the reply. The master had been deep in thought until this moment, finally opening his mouth to assert, "I have something too."

"Something? What do you have?" Of course, Meitei had no regard for the master. "My own experience was from last year's end."

"Everyone's experiences from last year's end are strangely coincidental," Kangetsu laughed, a piece of kuzu mochi stuck between his missing front teeth. "Isn't it the same day and time?" Meitei interjected. "No, it seems the days were different. It was around the twentieth. My wife asked me to take her to hear Setsu Daijo instead of the New Year's gift, and while I wouldn't mind taking her, when I asked what the story was for today, she referred to the newspaper and said it was Unagidani. I dislike Unagidani, so I decided to skip it that day. The next day, my wife brought the newspaper again and said it was Horikawa, which should be fine. However, I found Horikawa to be lively with shamisen but lacking substance, so I decided to skip that too, and my wife sulked as she withdrew. The following day, my wife said it was Sanjusangendo, and she insisted she wanted to hear the Sanjusangendo of Setsu. I don't know if you dislike Sanjusangendo, but since she wants to hear it, would it be alright for you to accompany me? Thus, we had a bit of a negotiation. If you want to go that much, then it would be fine to go, but since it's a once-in-a-lifetime event, it's bound to be crowded, and I doubt we could get in even if we tried.

Originally, to go to such a place, there should be a teahouse involved, and one must negotiate to reserve a proper seat, so it's not good to act outside of the usual procedures. Regrettably, I suggested we skip it today." At this, the wife shot him a fierce look, saying, "I’m a woman, so I don’t know such complicated procedures, but both Ohara’s mother and Suzuki’s Kimiyo went to hear it splendidly without following the proper procedures. No matter how much of a teacher you are, you shouldn’t make such a fuss over a simple outing. You’re being too much," she cried. "Well then, if it can't be helped, let's go. After having dinner, I conceded to take the train. If we're going, we must arrive by four o'clock; we can't dawdle," she suddenly insisted with vigor. When I asked why we had to be there by four, she explained that if we didn't go early, we wouldn't be able to get a spot, just as Kimiyo from Suzuki had told her. "So if we miss four o'clock, it's no good, right?" I pressed, to which she affirmed, "Yes, it's no good." Then, curiously, I suddenly began to feel chills. "Your wife?" Kangetsu inquired. "No, my wife is perfectly fine. It was me. I felt as if I were like a deflated balloon, suddenly shrinking, and before I knew it, my eyes were spinning, and I couldn't move."

"Sounds like an acute illness," Meitei added.

"Oh dear, what a predicament I find myself in. My wife has a wish that comes only once a year, and I absolutely want to fulfill it. I have never repaid her for all the times I’ve scolded her, ignored her, burdened her with my troubles, or made her take care of the children. Today, fortunately, I have some time, and I also have four or five bills in my pocket. If I take her along, we can go. She must want to go, and I want to take her. I absolutely want to take her, but I am feeling such chills and my vision is blurring that I can't even think about getting on the train, let alone taking off my shoes to get out. Oh, how pitiful it is! The more I think about it, the worse the chills get, and my vision blurs even more. If I could just see a doctor quickly and take some medicine, I would surely be fine before four o'clock. After that, I could consult with my wife and send for Dr. Amaki, but unfortunately, he was on duty last night and hasn’t returned from the university yet. He said he would be back around two o'clock, and that he would come as soon as he returned. What a bother! If I could just drink some almond water now, I would surely be cured before four o'clock, but when luck is against you, nothing goes as planned, and the budget I had for enjoying my wife's delighted smile seems to be slipping away. My wife, with a resentful expression, asks if I really cannot go. I will go, I will definitely go. I assure her that I will be fine before four o'clock, so she can rest easy. I tell her to wash her face and change her clothes and wait, but while I say this, my heart is filled with infinite emotions. The chills grow stronger, and my vision becomes increasingly dizzy. If I cannot recover by four o'clock and fulfill my promise, knowing my wife’s narrow-mindedness, I can only imagine what she might do. It has become a pitiful situation. What should I do? Considering the worst-case scenario, I thought it might be my duty as a husband to explain the principles of change and the inevitability of death to her, so that if something were to happen, she would not be thrown into a panic. I quickly called my wife to the study. I asked her if she understood the Western proverb "many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip," even though she is a woman. She replied, "Who knows such foreign words? You know I don’t understand English, yet you deliberately use it to tease me. Very well, since I cannot speak English anyway, if you like it so much, why didn’t you marry a graduate of a Christian school?" She said this with such a fierce demeanor that it completely derailed my carefully laid plans. I tried to explain that my use of English was not meant to be malicious.

It truly came from my deep love for her, and if she interpreted it otherwise, I would have no ground to stand on. Moreover, I had been feeling dizzy and chilly, and in my haste to explain the principles of change and the inevitability of death, I had forgotten that she did not understand English and unwittingly used it. Reflecting on this, I realized it was my fault; it was a complete oversight. This failure only intensified my chills. My vision continued to blur. My wife went to the bath as instructed, undressed, and began to prepare herself, taking out a kimono from the chest and changing into it. She was ready to go at any moment. I was in a state of anxiety. I thought how nice it would be if Dr. Amaki would arrive quickly, and when I looked at the clock, it was already three o'clock. There was only one hour left until four. "Shall we be off soon?" my wife asked, peeking through the open door of the study. It seemed strange to compliment my own wife, but I had never found her more beautiful than at that moment. Her skin, polished with soap, glistened, reflecting the black crepe haori she wore. Her face shone with the hope of hearing the music of the koto, glowing from both tangible and intangible sources. I felt a strong urge to satisfy that hope and take her out. Just then, I thought I might as well splurge and go, and as I took a deep breath, Dr. Amaki finally arrived. Everything went according to plan. However, when I explained my condition, Dr. Amaki examined my tongue, held my hand, tapped my chest, stroked my back, pulled down my eyelids, rubbed my skull, and pondered for a while. "I feel a bit uneasy," I said. The doctor calmly replied, "No, it shouldn’t be anything serious." "Is it alright for me to go out a little?" my wife asked. "Yes," the doctor said, but he continued to think. "As long as you don’t feel worse..." "I do feel worse," I interjected. "Well, I’ll give you some quick medicine and a water remedy," he said. "Ah, it seems a bit dangerous," I remarked. "No, there’s really nothing to worry about. You mustn’t get too nervous," the doctor said before leaving. It was already past three-thirty. I sent the maid to fetch the medicine. At my wife's insistence, she dashed out and quickly returned. It was just before four o'clock. There were still fifteen minutes until four. Then, around fifteen minutes before four, I suddenly felt nauseous, even though I had been fine until then. My wife poured the water remedy into a teacup and placed it in front of me, so when I picked up the cup to drink, a wave of nausea surged from my stomach. Reluctantly, I set the cup down. My wife urged, "You should drink it quickly." I felt it would be rude not to drink and leave. I resolved to gulp it down, but again the nausea stubbornly interfered.

As I tried to drink, I kept putting the cup down. Just then, the clock in the tea room chimed four times. Ah, it’s four o'clock! I can’t dawdle any longer! I picked up the cup again, and strangely enough, with the sound of four o'clock, the nausea completely subsided, and I was able to drink the remedy without any difficulty. By around ten minutes past four, I began to understand why Dr. Amaki was considered a skilled physician; the chills and dizziness vanished like a dream, and the illness that had made me think I could not stand was suddenly completely gone, which was a great relief."

"Did you then go to the Kabukiza together?" Meitei asked, looking puzzled. "I wanted to, but since it was past four, my wife insisted we couldn’t go, so we had to cancel. If only Dr. Amaki had come just fifteen minutes earlier, I would have fulfilled my duty, and my wife would have been satisfied. It’s truly unfortunate that it came down to just a fifteen-minute difference. I still think about how dangerous it could have been."

Having finished his story, the narrator finally seemed to feel he had fulfilled his duty. Perhaps he felt he had saved face with both of them. Kangetsu, as usual, showed his missing tooth while laughing and said, "That is indeed unfortunate."

Meitei, with a bewildered expression, remarked, "Your wife is truly fortunate to have such a kind husband as you." From behind the shoji, a cough from my wife could be heard, as if to say, "Ahem."

**Chapter 1**

I was quietly listening to the conversation of the three men in turn, but I felt neither amusement nor sadness. I thought that humans are creatures who, to pass the time, force their mouths to move, laughing at things that are not funny and taking delight in things that are not interesting. I had long been aware of my master's capricious and narrow-minded nature, but since he usually did not speak much, there seemed to be some points that were hard to understand. There was a slight sense of fear regarding those points I could not grasp, but after hearing their conversation, I suddenly felt a desire to scorn them. Why could he not listen to the two men’s talk in silence? What profit could there be in engaging in foolish banter, determined not to lose? I wondered if Epictetus had written anything about such matters. In short, my master, Kangetsu, Meitei, and Tofu are all idle gentlemen of peace, and while they appear to be as serene and unaffected as a gourd swaying in the wind, in reality, they are still filled with worldly desires and cravings. The spirit of competition, the urge to win, flickers even amidst their everyday banter, and it is a pity to see them become one with the common folk they usually deride, more so than cats.

However, the fact that their verbal exchanges do not carry the usual pretentiousness of half-wits might be considered a slight merit. Thinking this, the conversation of the three suddenly lost its interest, and I thought to check on Mikeko. I turned towards the garden entrance of the koto teacher. The New Year decorations had already been removed, and ten days had passed since the start of the year, but the gentle spring sun illuminated the world all at once from a deep sky without a single cloud, making the small garden of less than ten tsubo (about 33 square meters) appear more vibrant than on the morning of the New Year. There was a single cushion on the porch, and no human figure was in sight, with the shoji (sliding paper door) completely closed. I wondered if the koto teacher had gone to take a bath. It did not matter if the teacher was absent, but I was concerned about Mikeko. It was so quiet that there was no sign of anyone, so I climbed onto the porch with my muddy paws and lay down in the middle of the cushion, which felt quite pleasant. I dozed off, forgetting about Mikeko, when suddenly I heard a human voice from inside the shoji. “Thank you for your hard work. Is it done?” The koto teacher was indeed not absent. “Yes, I’m sorry for the delay. When I went to the carver’s, they said it had just been completed,” came the reply. “Let me see. Ah, it turned out beautifully; this will surely bring peace to Mikeko. The gold should not wear off, right?”

“Yes, I pressed them, and they said they used high-quality materials, so it should last longer than a human’s memorial tablet… Also, they said it would look better if the character for ‘honor’ in ‘Mikeko’ was slightly altered, so they made some adjustments.”

“Let’s quickly place it on the altar and offer some incense.”

Mikeko seemed to sense something was amiss and stood up on the cushion. “Chime, Namu Mikeko, Namu Amida Buddha, Namu Amida Buddha,” the koto teacher’s voice rang out. “You should also offer your prayers.”

“Chime, Namu Mikeko, Namu Amida Buddha, Namu Amida Buddha,” now it was the maid’s voice. My heart suddenly raced. Standing on the cushion, I did not even move my eyes like a wooden cat. “It is truly regrettable. It seems she caught a slight cold at first,” someone said. “If only Dr. Amaki had given her some medicine, it might have helped,” another replied. “Indeed, that Dr. Amaki is to blame; he has been far too dismissive of Mikeko,” someone else chimed in. “One should not speak ill of others. This is simply fate.”

It seems Mikeko had been examined by Dr. Amaki. “In the end, I believe it was that stray cat from the teacher’s house on the main street that lured her out recklessly,” one of them said.

“Yes, that beast is the enemy of Mikeko.”

I wanted to defend myself a little, but I held my tongue and listened patiently. The conversation paused for a moment. “The world is not free for everyone. A beautiful creature like Mikeko tends to die young, while the ugly stray cats thrive and cause mischief…” 

“That’s exactly right. A lovely cat like Mikeko is sought after with bells and drums, yet there are not two like her.”

Instead of saying “two cats,” they said “two beings.” It seemed the maid believed that cats and humans were of the same kind. Now that I thought about it, the maid’s face bore a striking resemblance to us felines. “If only I could take Mikeko’s place…” 

“When that stray from the teacher’s house dies, it would be just as you wish,” someone said. If it were to happen just as they wished, it would be a bit troubling. I had never experienced what it was like to die, so I could neither say I liked it nor disliked it. However, the other day, it was so cold that I crawled into the fire extinguisher, and the maid, unaware of my presence, closed the lid on me from above. The agony I felt then was terrifying to even think about. According to Shiro’s explanation, if that suffering continued for a little longer, I would die. If I could die in Mikeko’s place, I would have no complaints, but if I had to endure that suffering to die, I would not want to die for anyone. “However, even cats have their sutras recited for them and receive posthumous names, so there should be no regrets.”

“That is true; she is indeed fortunate. But if I may express a desire, it seems the sutra recited by that monk was rather brief.”

“It seemed a bit too short, so when I asked, ‘Isn’t it a bit early?’ the monk from Gokeiji replied, ‘Yes, I did a little something for her, but since she is a cat, this should be sufficient for her to reach the Pure Land,’” they said. “Oh my… But that stray…”

I had often asserted that I had no name, yet this maid continued to call me “stray, stray.” What an impudent creature. “Given the depth of your sins, no matter how precious the sutra, there is no way to be saved.”

I lost track of how many times the word “stray” was repeated after that. I abandoned the endless conversation midway and slipped off the cushion, leaping down from the porch, causing all eighty-eight thousand hairs on my body to bristle at once. After that, I never approached the koto teacher’s neighborhood again. By now, the teacher himself would likely be receiving a brief prayer from Gokeiji. Recently, I have lacked the courage to go out. It feels as if the world is enveloped in a languid haze. I have become a neutered cat, no less than my master. I have come to think it is no wonder that people comment on how he is shut away in his study, lamenting a lost love.

I have yet to catch a mouse, and at one point, even Osan proposed expelling me, but my master knows that I am not an ordinary cat, so I continue to lounge about this house. In this regard, I deeply appreciate my master’s kindness while also expressing my respect for his keen insight without hesitation. It does not anger me that Osan mistreats me without knowing who I am. If one day, the great sculptor left Zengoro were to come forth and carve my likeness into the pillars of the gate, and if Japan’s own Stanran were to take pleasure in painting my portrait on canvas, then those dull-witted fools would finally feel ashamed of their ignorance.

Mikeko is dying. Kuro is no match for her, and I feel a slight sense of loneliness, but fortunately, I have made acquaintances among humans, so I do not find it too dull. Recently, there was a man who wrote to request a photograph of me to send to my master. The other day, someone went out of their way to deliver Okayama’s famous Kibi dango addressed to me. Gradually, as I receive sympathy from humans, I find myself forgetting that I am a cat. I feel as if I have unwittingly drawn closer to humans, and I have no intention of gathering my fellow cats to challenge the two-legged teachers. Moreover, there are times when I even think of myself as one of the human world, which is quite an evolution. I do not mean to disdain my fellow cats. However, it is only natural to seek comfort among those of similar temperament, and I would be a bit troubled if this were to be labeled as a change of heart, frivolity, or betrayal. It seems that those who resort to such language to insult others are often inflexible and miserly men. When I shed the habits of a cat, I cannot simply burden myself with the affairs of Mikeko and Kuro. I want to evaluate their thoughts and actions on par with humans. This is not unreasonable. Yet, it is regrettable that my master, who thinks of me as just another ordinary cat, devoured the Kibi dango without so much as a greeting to me. He has yet to take my photograph and send it. While this could be seen as a grievance, my master is my master, and I am I; it is only natural that our perspectives differ. Since I am pretending to be human, it is somewhat difficult to write about the actions of a cat that does not socialize. I suppose I will have to rely on the reputations of Meitei and Kangetsu. Today is a fine Sunday, and my master has sluggishly emerged from his study, laying out his writing brush, inkstone, and manuscript paper beside me, and is muttering something to himself. I pay attention, thinking he is likely producing a draft and making strange sounds as a prelude. After a while, he writes “Kōichi” (香一) in bold strokes. I wonder if it will turn into a poem or a haiku; it seems a bit too clever for him. Before I can dwell on it, he finishes writing “Kōichi” and starts a new line, saying, “I have been thinking of writing about the natural hermit.” The brush stops there, not moving further. My master twists his neck while holding the brush, but it seems he has no particular idea, so he starts licking the tip of the brush. As I watch, his lips turn black, and then he draws a small circle beneath it. He puts two dots inside the circle for eyes, draws a nose with flared nostrils in the center, and stretches his mouth into a straight line. This is neither prose nor haiku.

It seems my master has lost interest in his own work, and he hastily smudges the face he has drawn. He starts a new line again. According to his thinking, he believes that simply changing lines will make it into a poem, a praise, a narrative, or something else entirely. Eventually, he writes in a unified style, “The natural hermit studies space, reads the Analects, eats sweet potatoes, and lets his nose run,” a rather jumbled piece of writing. He then reads it aloud without reservation, laughing more than usual, “Hahaha, how amusing!” but decides, “Let’s erase the part about letting his nose run; that’s a bit harsh,” and strikes through that line. Instead of just one line, he draws two or three lines, creating neat parallel lines, even allowing the lines to extend into other lines without concern. It seems he cannot create another line, so he abandons the brush and starts twisting his mustache. In a display of “I will show you the prose I twist out from my mustache,” he twists it fiercely, raising and lowering it, when suddenly his wife appears from the tea room and sits right in front of him. “You, just a moment,” she calls. “What is it?” my master replies with a voice like a gong being struck underwater. Not satisfied with his response, she calls again, “You, just a moment.” “What is it?” This time, he sticks his thumb and index finger into his nostrils and yanks out a nose hair. “This month is a bit short…” “It shouldn’t be short; I’ve already paid the doctor and the drugstore, and I paid the bookstore last month. This month should have a surplus,” he says, calmly inspecting the nose hair he has pulled out as if it were a rare spectacle. “But you eat rice and bread and lick jam, so…” “How many cans of jam have you licked?” “Eight this month.” “Eight? I don’t remember licking that many.” “It’s not just you; the children lick it too.” “No matter how much they lick, it shouldn’t amount to more than five or six yen,” my master says, nonchalantly planting each nose hair carefully on the manuscript paper. They stand upright like pins because they have flesh attached. My master, feeling a sudden discovery, blows gently on them. Due to their stickiness, they do not fly away. “How stubborn,” my master says, blowing with all his might. “It’s not just jam; there are other things we need to buy,” his wife says, her cheeks brimming with displeasure. “There may be,” my master replies, digging his fingers back into his nostrils and yanking out another nose hair. Among the various colors, there is one pure white hair. My master, astonished, stares at it as if it were a hole, and then presents it to his wife’s face, still pinched between his fingers. “Oh, no!” she grimaces and pushes his hand away.

“Just look, it’s a gray hair among the nose hairs,” my master says, appearing greatly moved. Even his wife, unable to help herself, laughs as she retreats to the tea room. It seems the economic discussion has been abandoned. My master returns to the natural hermit. Having chased away his wife with a nose hair, my master seems relieved, as if to say, “Now I can write my manuscript,” but the brush still does not move. “Eating sweet potatoes is unnecessary; I’ll omit that line,” he finally decides to erase that line as well. “Kōichi is a bit too abrupt, so let’s drop it,” he mercilessly strikes it out. What remains is the line, “The natural hermit studies space and reads the Analects.” My master thinks this seems a bit too simple, but he finds it troublesome, so he decides to abandon the prose and just write the title, vigorously drawing a poorly executed orchid in a four-character style on the manuscript paper. All his painstaking efforts are rendered useless. He then flips the paper over and writes, “Born in space, delving into space, dying in space. Ah, the natural hermit is empty and vacant,” stringing together incomprehensible words when, as usual, Meitei enters. Meitei seems to believe that other people’s homes are just as much his own, entering without asking for permission, and sometimes even breezing in through the back door, a man who has shed all worries, hesitations, and troubles somewhere along the way. 「Is it the giant's gravity again?」 I asked my master while standing. "Yes, I’m not always writing about the giant's gravity. I’m currently selecting the epitaph for the Natural Master," he said grandiosely. "Natural Master, huh? Is that a name like 'Accidental Boy'?" Meitei said, as usual, spouting nonsense. "Is there really such a thing as 'Accidental Boy'?" 

"Well, there’s nothing like that, but I thought that might be the case." 

"I don’t think I’ve heard of 'Accidental Boy,' but I do know the Natural Master; he’s a man you know." 

"Who on earth gave him such a name as Natural Master?" 

"It’s that fellow Sorozaki. He graduated and entered graduate school, researching a topic on spatial theory, but he studied too hard and died of peritonitis. Sorozaki was my close friend, you know." 

"Even if he was a close friend, that doesn’t mean he was a bad person. But who on earth transformed Sorozaki into the Natural Master?" 

"That would be me; I gave him that name. After all, there’s nothing more vulgar than the names given by monks," he boasted, as if it were a very elegant title. Meitei laughed and said, "Well then, let me see this epitaph." He picked up the manuscript and read aloud in a loud voice, "Born in space, delving into space, dying in space.

Empty and void, Natural Master, alas!" 

"Indeed, this is good; it suits the Natural Master well," my master said happily. "Isn’t it good?" 

"We’ll carve this epitaph into a stone and throw it behind the main hall like a weight stone. How elegant! The Natural Master will surely be at peace." 

"I intend to do just that," my master replied very seriously, but then added, "I’ll excuse myself for a moment; I’ll be back soon, so please entertain the cat while I’m gone." Without waiting for Meitei’s reply, he left nonchalantly. Unexpectedly tasked with entertaining Mr. Meitei, I couldn’t afford to appear unfriendly, so I climbed onto his lap, purring and being charming. Then Meitei said, "Well, you’ve certainly gotten quite fat, haven’t you?" and rudely grabbed my scruff, lifting me into the air. "With those hind legs dangling like that, you won’t catch any mice... What do you think, madam, can this cat catch mice?" He seemed to think I wasn’t enough, so he addressed the lady in the adjacent room. "This cat doesn’t just catch mice; he eats ozoni and dances," the lady chimed in, unexpectedly revealing an old grievance. I felt a bit embarrassed while being dangled in the air. Meitei still wouldn’t let me down. "Indeed, he looks like he could dance. Madam, this cat has a face that you can’t let your guard down with. He resembles the cat from the old picture books," he said, speaking freely while repeatedly engaging the lady in conversation. She, looking somewhat troubled, set aside her needlework and came into the room. 「How dreadfully boring it is, let’s go home now,” I said, pouring tea and placing it in front of Meitei. “Where has he gone, I wonder?” “He’s a man who never asks permission to go anywhere, so I can’t say for certain, but he’s probably gone to see the doctor.” “Mr. Amaki, you mean? It’s unfortunate for him to be caught up with such a sickly person.” “Indeed,” the wife replied simply, as if she had nothing more to say. Meitei didn’t seem to care at all. “How have you been lately? Is your stomach feeling any better?” “I can’t really tell if it’s better or worse. No matter how much Mr. Amaki treats me, I don’t think my stomach will heal if I keep eating nothing but jam,” the wife subtly expressed her earlier grievances to Meitei. “So he’s eating that much jam? He’s acting just like a child.” “It’s not just jam; these days he’s been eating a lot of grated daikon, claiming it’s good for his stomach…” “That’s surprising,” Meitei exclaimed. “I read in the newspaper that there’s something called diastase in grated daikon.” “I see, so that’s his idea to compensate for the damage done by the jam. Quite clever, ha ha ha,” Meitei said, clearly amused by the wife’s complaints.

“Just the other day, he even made a baby eat some…” “Jam?” “No, grated daikon… You see, he says to the boy, ‘Come here, your father has something delicious for you,’ and when he occasionally shows affection for the child, he ends up doing such foolish things. A few days ago, he picked up our daughter and put her on top of the dresser…” “What was the idea behind that?” Meitei interpreted everything with a sense of purpose. “There was no idea at all; he just told her to jump down from there. She’s only three or four years old, so there’s no way she could do something so reckless.” “I see, that was a bit too thoughtless. But he’s a good-natured person at heart.” “If he had poison in his heart, he wouldn’t be able to endure it,” the wife said, her spirit rising. “Well, there’s no need to complain so much. As long as we can live comfortably day by day, that’s what matters. Mr. Kushami, for instance, doesn’t indulge in pleasures, doesn’t care about his attire, and has become quite a respectable household man,” Meitei said, giving an unexpected sermon in a cheerful tone. “But you’re quite mistaken…” “Are you doing something behind the scenes? It’s a world where one mustn’t let their guard down,” he replied lightly. “I don’t indulge in other pleasures, but I keep buying books that I don’t even read. If only they would buy them wisely, it would be fine, but he goes to Maruzen and takes as many as he likes, and when the end of the month comes, he acts as if he doesn’t know anything. Last year, by the end of the year, I had accumulated so many that it became quite a problem.” “Oh, it doesn’t matter if he brings home books. When the bill collector comes, just tell him you’ll pay soon, and he’ll leave,” Meitei said dismissively. “Even so, we can’t keep dragging it out like this,” the wife said, looking disheartened. “Then I’ll explain the situation and try to reduce the book expenses.” “How can you say that? It’s not easy to get through to him. Just the other day, he said I’m not fit to be a scholar’s wife, that I don’t understand the value of books at all. He said there’s a story from ancient Rome that I should listen to for the sake of future generations.” “That sounds interesting. What’s the story?” Meitei became intrigued. It seemed more out of curiosity than sympathy for the wife. “Well, there was a king named Tarquin in ancient Rome…” “Tarquin? That’s a bit odd,” Meitei interjected. “I can’t remember the names of the Chinese characters; they’re too complicated for me. I heard he was the seventh generation.” “Ah, the seventh generation Tarquin is indeed peculiar. So what happened with him?” “Well, a woman came to the king with nine books, asking him to buy them.” “I see.” “When the king asked how much she wanted for them, she quoted an exorbitant price.

When he asked if she could lower it a bit, she suddenly threw three of the nine books into the fire.” “What a waste!” “It’s said that among those books, there were prophecies or something that couldn’t be found elsewhere.” “Oh?” “When the king saw that nine books had become six, he thought the price should have gone down a bit, so he asked how much for the six. But she wouldn’t lower it at all. When he protested that it was outrageous, she took three more and tossed them into the fire. The king, still reluctant, asked how much for the remaining three, and she insisted on the price for all nine. Even as the number of books dwindled from nine to six, then six to three, the price remained unchanged. If he pressed her further, she might burn the last three as well, so the king ultimately paid a high price for the remaining three books…” “How about that? From this story, you should understand the value of books a little better, don’t you think?” The wife prompted Meitei for a response, trying to establish the family’s wisdom. Even Meitei seemed a bit at a loss, fidgeting with a handkerchief from his sleeve to amuse me. “But, my dear,” he suddenly exclaimed, as if struck by a thought. “Because he buys so many books and fills them up, people say he’s somewhat of a scholar. Just the other day, I saw a review of Mr. Kushami in a literary magazine.” “Really?” the wife turned to him, clearly concerned about her husband’s reputation. “What did it say?” “Oh, just a couple of lines. It said, ‘Mr. Kushami’s writing flows like clouds and water.’” The wife smiled a bit. “Is that all?” “Then it went on to say, ‘Just when you think it’s coming, it suddenly disappears, and when it departs, it forgets to return.’” The wife made a strange face. “Was that a compliment?” “Well, it’s probably a compliment,” Meitei said, casually dangling the handkerchief in front of me. “Books are just tools for trade, so it’s not surprising to be a bit eccentric.” Meitei seemed to think he was coming from a different angle. “Eccentric? Well, that’s a bit eccentric indeed. Those who study are all like that anyway,” he offered a somewhat evasive defense. “Just the other day, when he came home from school, he found it too troublesome to change his clothes, so he sat down at the table to eat without even taking off his coat. He placed the meal on the kotatsu, and I was sitting there with the rice pot, and it was quite amusing…” “It sounds like a highbrow inspection of some sort. But that’s what makes Mr. Kushami, Mr. Kushami—after all, it’s not ordinary,” he complimented in a bittersweet manner. “Whether it’s ordinary or not, women can’t tell, but still, it’s a bit too reckless,” the wife retorted.

“But it’s better than ordinary,” he insisted, and the wife, dissatisfied, challenged, “In the first place, everyone keeps saying ordinary, but what exactly is ordinary?” “Ordinary? Well, it’s hard to explain…” “If it’s that vague, then ordinary might not be so bad,” she countered, employing a woman’s logic. “It’s not vague; I understand it perfectly well; it’s just difficult to explain.” “Isn’t it just that anything you dislike is called ordinary?” she said, unwittingly making a pointed remark. Now Meitei had to come up with some sort of explanation for what ordinary meant. “My dear, ordinary refers to those who, at the age of twenty-eight or twenty-nine, lie around in thought without saying a word, and when the weather is fine, they always go out with a gourd to the riverbank.” “Are there really people like that?” the wife asked, not understanding, and offered a vague response. “I can’t make heads or tails of it,” she finally conceded. “So you mean to attach the head of Pendennis to the body of Bakin and wrap it in European air for a year or two?” “Would that make it ordinary?” Meitei chuckled without answering. “You don’t need to go through all that trouble to make it ordinary. Just take a middle school student and add the head of the clerk from Shirokiya, and divide it by two, and you’ll have a fine ordinary person.” “Is that so?” the wife looked puzzled, still tilting her head in disbelief. 「Are you still here?」 the master said, having returned without my noticing and sitting down beside Meitei. 「To say 'are you still here' is a bit harsh; I told you I would be home soon, so please wait.」 

「Well, that’s just how things are, isn’t it?」 replied the lady, glancing at Meitei. 「While you were out, I heard all your stories.」 

「Women are often too talkative; it would be good if humans could maintain silence like this cat,」 the master said, stroking my head. 「I hear you made a baby taste grated daikon, huh?」 

「Hmm,」 the master laughed, 「but even babies these days are quite clever. Ever since then, when I ask the boy where it hurts, he always sticks out his tongue, which is quite amusing.」 

「It’s cruel to train him like a dog. By the way, Kangetsu should be arriving soon,」 Meitei remarked. 「Kangetsu is coming?」 the master asked, looking puzzled. 「Yes, I sent him a note asking him to come to Mr. Kushami’s house by one o'clock this afternoon.」 

「He’s a man who does as he pleases without considering others’ circumstances. What does he want with Kangetsu?」 

「Oh, today’s request isn’t for our amusement; it’s Mr. Kangetsu’s own demand. He said he wants to practice for a lecture he’s giving at the Physical Society. He asked me to listen, so I thought it would be just right for Mr. Kushami to hear it too.

So I decided to invite him to your house—after all, you have plenty of free time, don’t you?—and he’s not a man who would cause any trouble, so you should listen.」 Meitei was swallowing his words alone. 「I don’t understand anything about physics lectures,」 the master said, sounding a bit indignant at Meitei’s unilateral decision. 「However, this topic isn’t some dry and flavorless thing about magnets and nozzles. It’s an extraordinary subject on the mechanics of hanging, so it’s worth listening to,」 Meitei replied. 「You, having nearly been hanged yourself, should listen, but as for me…」 

「You seem like a person who would get chills at the Kabukiza, so it’s unlikely you’ll want to listen,」 he quipped, as usual. The lady chuckled and retreated to the next room, glancing back at the master. The master, in silence, continued to stroke my head. At that moment, he was particularly gentle in his caress. About seven minutes later, as ordered, Kangetsu arrived. Today, since he was to give a lecture in the evening, he wore an unusually splendid frock coat, with a freshly laundered white collar, raising his manliness by about twenty percent. 「I’m a little late,」 he said calmly as he greeted them. 「We’ve been waiting for you for quite some time,」 the master said, looking at him. The master, having no choice, replied, 「Hmm.」 Kangetsu was in no hurry. 「May I have a glass of water, please?」 he asked. 「Ah, so you’re going to do this properly; next, you’ll be asking for applause, I suppose,」 Meitei exclaimed to himself. Kangetsu took out his manuscript from within his coat and slowly said, 「Since this is practice, please feel free to critique me.」 He then began his rehearsal for the lecture. 「To execute a criminal by hanging is a method that has primarily been practiced among the Anglo-Saxon peoples. If we trace back to ancient times, hanging was mainly used as a method of suicide. Among the Jews, it was customary to kill a criminal by stoning. If we study the Old Testament, the term 'hanging' is recognized as meaning to suspend the body of a criminal for wild beasts or carnivorous birds to feast upon. According to Herodotus, it seems that the Jews had a strong aversion to exposing corpses at night, even before they left Egypt. The Egyptians would decapitate criminals and nail only their torsos to a cross, exposing them at night. The Persians…」 

「Kangetsu, it seems you’re drifting further from the topic of hanging; are you alright?」 Meitei interjected. 「I’m just about to get into the main argument, so please bear with me a little longer. …Now, as for the Persians, it seems they also used crucifixion for executions.

However, whether they nailed them while still alive or after death, I’m not quite sure…」 

「That’s something we don’t need to know,」 the master said, yawning in boredom. 「I still have many things I’d like to discuss, but since it might be a bother…」 

「Rather than 'it might be a bother,' it would be better to say 'please come,' don’t you think, Mr. Kushami?」 Meitei reproached again, and the master replied, 「It’s the same either way.」 

「Now, let’s get to the main topic,」 Kangetsu said. 「Saying 'let’s get to the main topic' sounds like something a lecturer would say. A speaker should use more refined language,」 Meitei interjected again. 「If 'let’s get to the main topic' is vulgar, then what should I say?」 Kangetsu asked, sounding a bit annoyed. 「It’s hard to tell whether Meitei is listening or just interjecting. Kangetsu, don’t mind that busybody and just get on with it,」 the master urged, trying to get through the difficult part as quickly as possible. 「I said it in a huff, like a willow, didn’t I?」 Meitei continued to speak nonchalantly. Kangetsu couldn’t help but burst into laughter. 「In truth, the use of hanging as a method of execution, according to my research, appears in the twenty-second book of the Odyssey. Specifically, it’s the passage where Telemachus hangs twelve of Penelope’s maids. I could read the text in Greek, but it might seem a bit showy, so I’ll refrain. If you look from line four hundred sixty-five to four hundred seventy-three, you’ll understand.」 

「It’s better to skip the Greek; otherwise, it sounds like you’re boasting that you can speak Greek, don’t you think, Mr. Kushami?」 

「I agree; it’s better not to say such things that sound so needy,」 the master chimed in, unusually siding with Meitei. Neither of them could read Greek at all. 「Then let’s skip those two or three lines for tonight and move on to the next point—ah, I must say. Imagining this hanging now, there are two methods to execute it. The first is that Telemachus ties one end of the rope to a post with the help of Eumaeus and Philoetius. Then, he makes knots at various points along the rope, placing the heads of the women into these knots, and when he pulls the other end, it lifts them up.」 

「In other words, it’s like the women hanging like shirts at a Western laundry, right?」 

「Exactly. Then the second method is to tie one end of the rope to the post as before and raise the other end high to the ceiling.
