From that high rope, several other ropes are lowered, with loops made for the women’s necks, and at the crucial moment, the platform beneath the women’s feet is removed.」 

「To put it another way, it’s like hanging a lantern ball from a curtain of ropes; that’s not mistaken, is it?」 

「I’ve never seen a lantern ball, so I can’t say for sure, but if there is one, it would be something like that. —Now, I will demonstrate that the first method is fundamentally untenable from a mechanical standpoint.」 

「Interesting,」 Meitei said, and the master agreed, 「Yes, interesting.」 

「First, let’s assume the women are hung at equal distances. Also, let’s assume the rope connecting the two women closest to the ground is horizontal. We’ll denote the angles formed by the rope with the horizontal as α1, α2, …, α6, and the forces acting on each section of the rope as T1, T2, …, T6, while T7 = X represents the force at the lowest part of the rope. W, of course, is the weight of the women, as you know. Do you understand?」

Meitei and the master exchanged glances and said, "I understand for the most part." However, the degree of "for the most part" was something both of them had concocted on their own, so it might not apply to others. "Now, according to the well-known theory of average values concerning polygons, we can establish the following twelve equations: T1cosα1 = T2cosα2…… (1) T2cosα2 = T3cosα3…… (2) ……" "That should be enough equations," the master said brusquely. "Actually, this formula is the crux of the speech," Kangetsu seemed quite reluctant to let it go. "Then let’s just ask about the crux," Meitei appeared somewhat abashed. "If we skip this formula, the valuable mechanical research will be rendered completely useless…" "No need to be so polite; just skip it…" the master said nonchalantly. "Then, as you command, though it’s unreasonable, let’s skip it." "That would be best," Meitei clapped his hands in a peculiar manner. "Then, moving to England, we find the word 'gallows'—that is, 'garuga'—in Beowulf, so it seems that the punishment of hanging must have been practiced from this era. According to Blackstone, if a criminal sentenced to hanging does not die due to the condition of the rope, he should receive the same punishment again, but strangely enough, in Piers Plowman, there is a line that states even a notorious criminal cannot be hanged twice. Well, I don’t know which is true, but it often happens that one does not die from a single hanging. In 1786, there was a notorious criminal named F* (small kana character 'hi', 1-6-84) who was hanged. However, due to a strange turn of events, when he jumped from the platform the first time, the rope broke. When they tried again, the rope was too long, and his feet touched the ground, so he still did not die. Finally, on the third attempt, a spectator helped him to his demise," he recounted. "Good grief," Meitei suddenly perked up at this point. "What a close call for death," even the master seemed to be in high spirits. "There’s something even more interesting; they say that when one is hanged, their height increases a little. This has been measured by doctors, so it cannot be mistaken." "That’s a novel idea. What do you think, Kushami? If we hung you for a bit, you might grow tall enough to be like a human," Meitei turned to the master, who surprisingly looked serious and asked, "Kangetsu, is there a chance that one could grow taller and come back to life?" "That’s utterly impossible. Being hanged stretches the spinal cord, so to put it simply, it’s not so much that one grows taller as it is that they get damaged," he replied. "Well then, let’s not do it," the master conceded.

The speech was still quite lengthy, and Kangetsu was supposed to delve into the physiological effects of hanging, but due to Meitei’s incessant interruptions with whimsical remarks and the master yawning without restraint, they eventually stopped midway and went home. That evening, I could not know how Kangetsu had behaved or what eloquence he had displayed, as those events occurred far away. A couple of days passed without incident, but one afternoon around two o'clock, Meitei, as usual, came in with a carefree air, as if he were a child. Upon taking a seat, he suddenly exclaimed, "Have you heard about the Takawana incident involving Tofu?" with the enthusiasm of someone announcing the fall of Port Arthur. "No, I haven’t; I haven't seen him lately," the master replied gloomily as usual. "Today, I came all the way to report on Tofu's blunder," he said, clearly busy. "You speak of such grand matters; you are truly an outrageous man." "Hahaha, rather than outrageous, it’s more like shameless. Please make that distinction, as it pertains to my honor." "It’s the same thing," the master scoffed. He was a pure and natural eccentric. "Last Sunday, it seems Tofu went to the Takawana Senkaku Temple. Why, in this cold weather—first of all, going to a place like Senkaku Temple nowadays makes one seem like a country bumpkin who doesn’t know Tokyo." "That’s Tofu’s business. You have no right to stop him." "Indeed, I have no right. Rights don’t matter, but there’s an exhibition called the Preservation Society of the Relics of the Loyalists within that temple. Do you know about it?" "No." "You don’t know? Well, I’m surprised. No wonder you were so eager to defend Tofu. It’s a shame for a Tokyoite not to know about Senkaku Temple." "One can still be a teacher without knowing," the master continued to play the role of the natural eccentric. "That’s fine, but while Tofu was there looking around, a German couple came in. At first, they asked him something in Japanese. However, as you know, he’s the kind of man who can’t resist using German. He started chatting away in German. Surprisingly, he did quite well—though in hindsight, that was the source of his trouble." "What happened next?" the master finally became intrigued. "The German saw a lacquered inro by the famous artist Gengō and asked if he could buy it. Tofu’s reply was amusing; he said that since Japanese are all upright gentlemen, it would be impossible to sell it. That part was quite lively, but then the German seemed to think he had a good interpreter and kept asking questions." "What kind of questions?" "Well, if he could understand it, there wouldn’t be any worries, but he spoke so fast and asked such random questions that Tofu couldn’t grasp any of it.

Occasionally, he thought he understood, but then they would ask about a tsuba or a kanzashi. Since he had never learned how to translate Western tsuba or kanzashi, he was at a loss." "That’s understandable," the master sympathized, comparing it to his own situation as a teacher. "Meanwhile, curious onlookers began to gather around, and eventually, Tofu and the German were surrounded. Tofu’s face turned red, and he was flustered, easily losing his initial bravado." "What ended up happening?" "In the end, Tofu couldn’t take it anymore and said 'sayonara' in Japanese and hurriedly left. He thought 'sayonara' was a bit strange, so when he asked if they said 'sayonara' to Westerners, he found out that it was indeed 'sayonara,' but since the other party was a Westerner, he adjusted it to 'sayonara.' Tofu is a man who doesn’t forget to harmonize even in difficult times, and I was impressed." "Sayonara is fine, but what about the Westerner?" "The Westerner was left dumbfounded, staring blankly. Hahaha, isn’t that amusing?" "It doesn’t seem particularly funny. It’s you who came all the way to report this that’s far more amusing," the master said, shaking the ash from his rolled cigarette into the fire pot. Just then, the bell at the lattice door rang sharply, and a sharp female voice called out, "Excuse me." Meitei and the master exchanged glances and fell silent.

As I observed that female visitors were a rarity in my master's home, the owner of that sharp voice entered, rubbing her double-layered crepe fabric against the tatami mat. She appeared to be just over forty years of age. Her bangs stood up high like a levee under construction, protruding at least half the length of her face towards the heavens. Her eyes slanted sharply, resembling a steep slope, drawn straight up and opposing each other on either side. This straightness could be described as thinner than a whale. Only her nose was disproportionately large, as if it had been stolen from someone else and affixed to the center of her face. It stood out alone in her small garden of about three tatami mats, like a stone lantern moved to a spirit shrine, yet it somehow felt out of place. This nose, the so-called "key nose," had once risen to its utmost height, but then, in modesty, it sagged midway, drooping forward and peering down at the lips below. Such a remarkable nose led me to think that when this woman spoke, it was not her mouth that was doing the talking, but rather her nose that was articulating. To pay my respects to this grand nose, I have since decided to refer to her as Hanako, the Nose. After exchanging initial greetings, Hanako surveyed the room and remarked, "What a splendid residence you have." My master, thinking to himself, "What a lie," puffed away at his cigarette. Meitei, gazing at the ceiling, subtly prompted my master, saying, "Hey, is that a leak or just the grain of the wood? There’s a strange pattern appearing." When my master replied, "Of course, it's a leak," Meitei responded with a nonchalant, "That's nice." Hanako felt indignant at the ignorance of these social misfits. For a while, the three of us sat in silence. "I came here to ask you something," Hanako resumed the conversation. "Ah," my master replied, extremely coldly. Realizing this wouldn't do, Hanako continued, "Actually, I live nearby—at the corner house down that alley." "Is that the large Western-style house with the warehouse? No wonder there's a sign saying Kaneda there," my master finally seemed to recognize Kaneda's Western house and warehouse, but his level of respect for Mrs. Kaneda remained unchanged. "The truth is, I have a guest, and I wanted to discuss it with you, but the company is extremely busy," she said, casting a slightly more shrewd glance this time. My master remained utterly unmoved. Hanako's manner of speaking had already begun to annoy me, as it was too presumptuous for a woman meeting someone for the first time. "There isn't just one company; I manage two or three," she continued.

"And in each company, I hold a significant position—I'm sure you know." She wore an expression that seemed to say, "Aren't you impressed?" My master, who was typically very modest when it came to professors or doctors, had a strangely low regard for businessmen. He believed that a middle school teacher was far superior to a businessman. Even if he didn't believe it, he had resigned himself to the fact that his rigid nature would never allow him to benefit from the patronage of wealthy entrepreneurs. No matter how powerful or wealthy the other party was, he was utterly indifferent to their interests, thinking that he would never have to rely on them. Thus, apart from the scholarly community, he was extremely naïve about other fields, particularly the business world, where he had no idea who was doing what. Even if he did know, he felt no respect or admiration for them. Hanako, on her part, had no idea that such a peculiar person existed in this corner of the world, living under the sun. She had interacted with many people in the world so far, but she had never encountered a case where someone introduced themselves as Mrs. Kaneda and did not receive a change in treatment. No matter what gathering she attended or how high-ranking the individuals present were, she could always carry herself as Mrs. Kaneda. How could she expect anything less from this dusty old scholar, who, when she mentioned her house at the corner of the alley, would surely be astonished and not even inquire about her profession?

“Do you know a man named Kaneda?” the master asked casually of Meitei. “I certainly do. Mr. Kaneda is a friend of my uncle. He came to the garden party the other day,” Meitei replied seriously. “Oh, and who is your uncle?”  
“Baron Makiyama,” Meitei said, becoming even more serious. Before the master could say anything, Hanako suddenly turned around and looked at Meitei. He was wearing a combination of Oshima tsumugi and some old sarasa fabric, looking quite composed. “Oh, you are a friend of Baron Makiyama’s—how rude of me not to have realized it. We often speak of Baron Makiyama at the inn, as he has been so kind to us,” he said suddenly, using polite language and even bowing. Meitei laughed, “Oh really, ha ha ha.” The master was taken aback and silently watched the two of them. “I believe you have also asked Baron Makiyama for help regarding your daughter’s marriage…”  
“Is that so?” Meitei seemed a bit taken aback by this sudden turn of conversation. “Actually, I’ve received many requests from various parties, but given my status, I can’t just settle for any proposal…”  
“Quite right,” Meitei finally seemed to relax. “I came to ask you about that,” Hanako suddenly turned to the master and returned to a more serious tone. “I hear that a man named Mizushima Kangetsu often visits your place. What kind of person is he?”  
“Why do you want to know about Kangetsu?” the master replied bitterly. “Surely it’s related to your daughter’s marriage, and you want to know a bit about Kangetsu’s character,” Meitei interjected with quick wit. “If I could find that out, it would be quite convenient…”  
“Then you’re saying you want to marry your daughter to Kangetsu?”  
“It’s not that I want to marry her off,” Hanako suddenly countered the master. “There are other suitors as well, so I wouldn’t want to force her into anything.”  
“Well then, there’s no need to inquire about Kangetsu,” the master said, becoming agitated. “But you wouldn’t want to keep it a secret, would you?” Hanako replied, becoming somewhat combative. Meitei sat between them, holding his silver pipe like a fan, internally shouting “What a mess!”  
“Did Kangetsu say he absolutely wants to marry her?” the master shot back directly. “He didn’t say he wanted to, but…”  
“Are you thinking he might want to?” the master seemed to have figured out that this was a woman’s matter. “The conversation hasn’t progressed that far, but I wouldn’t think Kangetsu would be entirely uninterested,” Hanako retorted, regaining her footing. “Is there any indication that Kangetsu has fallen for your daughter?” The master leaned back, as if challenging her to speak up. “Well, that seems to be the case,” Hanako replied, and this time the master’s challenge didn’t yield any results.

Meitei, who had been enjoying the spectacle so far, seemed to be piqued by Hanako’s words and leaned forward, placing his pipe down. “Did Kangetsu write her a love letter? How delightful! With the New Year approaching, another story will add to the gossip,” he thought to himself, pleased. “It’s not just a love letter; it’s something much more intense,” Hanako interjected, getting involved. “Do you know about this?” the master asked, looking at Meitei with a fox-like expression. Meitei, in a foolish tone, replied, “I don’t know; if I did, I’d tell you.”  
“No, both of you know about it,” Hanako declared triumphantly. “Really?” both men responded in unison, intrigued. “If you’ve forgotten, I can tell you. Last year, there was a concert at Mr. Abe’s residence in Mukojima, and Kangetsu attended. That night, something happened at Azumabashi—though I won’t go into details, as it might trouble the parties involved. But with that much evidence, I think it’s sufficient, don’t you?” She adjusted her posture, her diamond-studded ring glinting as she spoke. Her prominent nose seemed to radiate an unusual aura, making both Meitei and the master appear as if they were nonexistent. The master, of course, and even Meitei seemed taken aback by this unexpected revelation, sitting there for a while like a patient who had just recovered from a fever, but as the shock wore off, a sense of absurdity surged forth. The two of them burst into laughter, as if they had agreed upon it, “Ha ha ha ha ha.” Hanako alone seemed to feel that laughing at this moment was quite rude and glared at the two of them. “Is that your daughter? Indeed, that’s quite something. You’re absolutely right, aren’t you, Mr. Kushami? Kangetsu must be in love with your daughter… there’s no point in hiding it anymore, let’s confess,” she said. “Uh-huh,” the master simply replied. “You really shouldn’t keep it a secret; the matter is quite obvious,” Hanako became even more self-satisfied. “Well, there’s no helping it now. I’ll present all the facts regarding Kangetsu for your reference. Hey, Mr. Kushami, you’re the master here, but if you keep grinning like that, nothing will get resolved. Secrets can be terrifying, you know. No matter how much you try to hide them, they will eventually come to light. —But it’s strange, isn’t it? How did Mrs. Kaneda find out about this secret? It’s truly astonishing,” Meitei rambled on to himself. “I’m not careless on my end either,” Hanako said smugly. “It seems you’re almost too careful. Who did you hear this from?”  
“I heard it from the rickshaw man who’s just behind here.”  
“From the rickshaw man with the black cat?” the master’s eyes widened. “Yes, he’s been quite useful regarding Kangetsu.

Every time Kangetsu comes here, I have the rickshaw man report back to me on what he says.”  
“That’s quite invasive,” the master exclaimed loudly. “Whatever you may say, it’s not my concern. It’s all about Kangetsu,” Hanako replied, showing no signs of embarrassment. “It’s not just the rickshaw man. I’ve also heard quite a bit from the koto teacher on Shinmichi,” she added. “About Kangetsu?”  
“Not just about Kangetsu,” she said, sounding a bit ominous. The master thought he should be alarmed, but then he remarked, “That teacher acts so refined, as if he’s the only one with a human face. What a fool.”  
“Excuse me, but she’s a woman. You’re mistaken,” Hanako’s tone became increasingly revealing of her background. This was beginning to sound like a quarrel, but Meitei, as always, seemed to be enjoying the debate, listening with the same expression as a spectator watching a cockfight.

The master, realizing that he was no match for Hanako in a battle of insults, found himself compelled to maintain a silence for a while. Finally, as if a thought had struck him, he said, "You keep saying that it seems like Kangetsu has fallen in love with the young lady, but what I've heard is a bit different, don't you think, Meitei-kun?" He sought Meitei's support. "Well, according to that story, it was the young lady who first fell ill — I heard something about her speaking deliriously," Meitei replied. "That's not true at all," Mrs. Kaneda interjected with a clear and straightforward manner of speaking. "Still, Kangetsu certainly said he heard it from Dr. ○○'s wife," the master continued. "That's our angle, you see. I asked Dr. ○○'s wife to try and catch Kangetsu's attention," he explained. "Did Dr. ○○'s wife agree to that knowing what it entailed?" 

"Yes. But even if she agreed, it wouldn't come for free; she’s been using various means to make it happen."

"Are you determined not to return until you’ve thoroughly investigated Kangetsu’s affairs?" Meitei seemed a bit put off and used a rougher tone than usual. "Not at all, my friend. There's no harm in talking, so let’s discuss it, Kushami-kun. Mrs. Kaneda, whether it’s me or Kushami, we’ll share all the facts concerning Kangetsu, so if you could kindly listen in order, that would be most convenient."

Hanako finally came to an understanding and began to pose a question. The previously rough manner of speaking returned to its usual politeness when addressing Meitei. “I hear Mr. Kangetsu is also a Bachelor of Science, but what exactly is his area of expertise?” The master answered seriously, “He is studying the Earth's magnetism in graduate school.” Unfortunately, the meaning of this was lost on Hanako, who responded with a puzzled “Oh?” while wearing a confused expression. “If he studies that, can he become a doctor?” she asked. “Are you saying that one must become a doctor to pursue it?” the master inquired, looking somewhat displeased. “Yes. There are plenty of mere Bachelors, after all,” Hanako replied nonchalantly. The master cast a more unpleasant glance at Meitei. “We cannot guarantee whether you will become a doctor or not, so let’s discuss something else,” Meitei suggested, not in the best of moods. “Is he still studying that Earth—whatever it is?” “A couple of days ago, I delivered a lecture on the mechanics of hanging at the Science Association,” the master said, unaware of the implications. “Oh dear, hanging? He must be quite the eccentric. If he’s involved in such hanging, he certainly won’t become a doctor,” Hanako remarked. “It’s difficult for the person to hang themselves, but as for the mechanics of hanging, it’s not impossible to become one,” the master replied. “Is that so?” Hanako now looked at the master, gauging his expression. Sadly, she was unable to grasp the meaning of mechanics, leaving her unsettled. However, perhaps considering the implications for Mrs. Kaneda’s reputation, she merely observed the master’s expression for clues. His face was sour. “Is there anything else you’re studying that’s easier to understand?” “Well, the other day I wrote a paper discussing the stability of acorns and its relation to celestial movements,” the master said. “Do they study acorns at university?” “I’m not sure, as I’m an amateur myself, but since Mr. Kangetsu is doing it, it seems worth researching,” Meitei coolly teased. Hanako appeared to have given up on academic questions, deciding to change the topic. “On a different note—didn’t you break two of your front teeth eating shiitake mushrooms this New Year?” “Yes, the broken part got stuck to a kuzu mochi,” the master suddenly brightened at this question, feeling it was within his domain. “Aren’t you a rather dull person? Why didn’t you use a toothpick?” “I’ll be sure to mention it next time we meet,” the master chuckled. “If your teeth break from shiitake mushrooms, it must mean they’re in pretty bad shape, don’t you think?” “I wouldn’t say they’re good—right, Meitei?” “There’s nothing good about them, but they have a bit of charm. It’s strange that they’re still not filled in.

They’ve become quite the spectacle, still having kuzu mochi stuck to them,” Meitei observed. “Are you leaving your broken teeth as they are because you can’t afford to get them fixed, or is it just a matter of taste?” “You don’t have to worry, as you won’t be known for long as someone with missing front teeth,” Meitei’s mood began to improve gradually. Hanako shifted the topic again. “If you have any letters or anything written by the person, I would like to take a look.” “I have plenty of notes, take a look,” the master said, bringing over thirty or forty sheets from his study. “You don’t need to see so many—just two or three of them…” “Let me pick out a few good ones for you,” Meitei said, pulling out a postcard. “Oh, you can draw too? Quite skillful, let me see.” As she looked it over, she exclaimed, “Oh dear, it’s a raccoon. Why would you choose to draw a raccoon of all things? It’s still recognizable as a raccoon, which is curious.” “Read the text on it,” the master said with a laugh. Hanako began to read it like a maid reading the newspaper. “On the night of the old lunar year, the mountain raccoons held a garden party and danced merrily. The song says, ‘Come now, on this night of the year, even the mountain women won’t come. Supokopon no pon.’” “What’s this? It’s mocking people, isn’t it?” Hanako complained. “Don’t you like this celestial maiden?” Meitei pulled out another card. It depicted a celestial maiden dressed in a flowing robe, playing the biwa. “Her nose seems a bit too small,” Hanako remarked. “What? That’s quite normal. Read the text instead.” The text read: “Once upon a time, there was an astronomer. One night, as usual, he climbed to a high platform and gazed at the stars with all his heart when a beautiful celestial maiden appeared in the sky, playing a music so delicate that it could not be heard in this world. The astronomer, forgetting the biting cold, became entranced. In the morning, he was found frozen to death, his corpse covered in white frost. This is a true story, as that lying old man said.” “What’s the meaning of this? There’s no meaning at all. Can someone like this really be a Bachelor of Science? It seems more like something that would be read in a literary club,” Kangetsu was thoroughly unimpressed. Amused, Meitei presented the third card. This one was printed with a woodblock of a sailboat, with some text scattered beneath it. “The sixteen little girls who stayed the night, with no parents, cried like the plovers on the rough shore, crying like the plovers waking from their dreams.” “That’s quite good, I’m impressed. It’s quite talkative, isn’t it?” “Is it talkative?” “Yes, this would go well with a shamisen.” “If it goes well with a shamisen, it’s the real deal. How about this?” Meitei carelessly offered.

“No, I’ve seen enough for now. I understand that it’s not so dull, so I’ll pass on the rest,” Hanako concluded, satisfied. It seemed she had exhausted most of her inquiries regarding Kangetsu. “I apologize for my rudeness. Please keep my visit a secret from Mr. Kangetsu,” she made a rather selfish request. It appeared she believed she must inquire about everything concerning Kangetsu, but that nothing about herself should be revealed to him. Both Meitei and the master responded with a disinterested “Ah,” and as she stood up, she added, “I will express my gratitude in due time.” As the two men returned to their seats, Meitei asked, “What was that?” The master echoed, “What was that?” Both posed the same question. From the back room, it seemed Mrs. Kaneda could no longer hold back, as a muffled laugh was heard. Meitei called out in a loud voice, “Madam, madam, a commonplace specimen has arrived! When it gets to that level, it’s quite impressive. Now, don’t hold back, laugh to your heart’s content!”

My master, with a dissatisfied tone, remarked, “First of all, that face is unappetizing,” and spoke with a certain malice. Meitei immediately took up the comment, adding, “That nose is stationed right in the center of the face, looking quite proud.” “And it’s crooked too,” he continued. “It’s a bit hunched over. A hunched nose is rather too extravagant,” he laughed, finding it amusing. “It’s a face that seems to conquer its husband,” my master said, still looking disgruntled. “It looks like something that was left unsold in the nineteenth century and is now on display in the twentieth,” Meitei said, uttering peculiar remarks. Just then, Mrs. Kushami came out from the inner room and cautioned, “If you keep speaking ill like that, the rickshaw man’s deity will surely punish you.” “A little punishment is good medicine, my dear,” Meitei replied. “However, to speak ill of someone’s face is rather low. After all, no one chooses to have such a nose, and besides, the other party is a lady, so it’s rather harsh,” he defended Mrs. Kaneda’s nose while simultaneously defending his own appearance indirectly. “What a terrible thing to say! That’s not a lady; that’s a fool, isn’t it, Meitei?” “She may be a fool, but she’s quite a remarkable person. She’s been scratched quite a bit, hasn’t she?” “What does she think a teacher is?” “She thinks of him as someone akin to the rickshaw man. To be respected by such a person, one must become a doctor. The fact that you haven’t become a doctor is your own narrow-mindedness, isn’t it, my dear? Isn’t that right?” Meitei said, glancing back at his wife with a smile. “A doctor is utterly out of the question,” my master said, feeling abandoned even by his wife. “It might still happen, so don’t look down on it. You wouldn’t know, but once there was a man named Isocrates who wrote great works at the age of ninety-four. Sophocles astonished the world with his masterpieces at nearly a hundred years old. Simonides composed beautiful poetry at eighty. Even I…” “That’s ridiculous! With your stomach ailment, how could you possibly live that long?” his wife calculated his lifespan accurately. “How rude! — Go ask Dr. Amaki and see! It’s because you dress me in this wrinkled black cotton haori and this patched kimono that I’m ridiculed by such a woman. From tomorrow, I’ll wear something like what Meitei has on, so get it ready.” “Get it ready? We don’t have anything so splendid. Mrs. Kaneda only started being polite to Mr. Meitei after hearing your uncle’s name. It’s not about the kimono,” his wife cleverly shifted the blame. Upon hearing the word “uncle,” my master suddenly remembered and asked Meitei, “I’ve never heard that you have an uncle before.

Is it really true?” Meitei, as if he had been waiting for this moment, replied, “Yes, that uncle of mine is quite a fool — he has managed to survive from the nineteenth century all the way to today,” glancing between my master and his wife. “Oh ho ho ho ho, you say the funniest things! Where does he live?” “He lives in Shizuoka, but it’s not just living. He lives with a topknot on his head, which is quite embarrassing. When told to wear a hat, he boasts that at his age, he has never felt cold enough to wear one — ‘It’s cold, so sleep more,’ he says, claiming that four hours of sleep is sufficient for a human. Sleeping more than four hours is a luxury, and he gets up before dawn. So, I’ve had to train myself to reduce my sleep to four hours. When I was young, I couldn’t help but feel sleepy, but recently, I’ve finally entered a state of great joy where I can sleep as I please. It’s only natural that at sixty-seven, he can’t sleep anymore. He thinks he has succeeded entirely by his own self-discipline, even though neither his training nor his melons have anything to do with it. When he goes out, he always carries a folding fan with him.” “What does he do with that?” “I don’t know what he does with it; he just carries it. Perhaps he thinks of it as a substitute for a cane. However, something strange happened recently,” he said, now addressing Mrs. Kushami. “Oh?” she responded with a noncommittal reply. “This spring, he suddenly sent a letter asking for a top hat and frock coat to be sent urgently. I was a bit surprised, so I inquired by mail, and he replied that he himself would wear them. He ordered them to be procured in time for a celebration in Shizuoka on the twenty-third. What’s funny is that in the order, he wrote that I should buy a hat of a reasonably sized fit, and for the clothes, I should measure and order them from Daimaru…” “Do they make clothes at Daimaru these days?” “Oh, he must have confused it with Shirokiya.” “Even if they measured, it wouldn’t be feasible.” “That’s the nature of my uncle.” “What happened then?” “Well, I had no choice but to measure and send them.” “You’re quite reckless. Did it arrive in time?” “Well, somehow or other, it worked out. When I looked at the national newspaper, it said that on that day, old Makiyama was unusually in a frock coat, holding the usual folding fan…” “It seems he didn’t let go of the folding fan.” “Yes, when he dies, I think I’ll make sure to put the folding fan in the coffin.” “Still, it was good that he wore the hat and clothes well.” “However, that was a big mistake. Just when I was thankful that he managed to go safely, a little while later, a package arrived from the country.

I thought it was a gift of some sort, but when I opened it, it was the very top hat, with a letter attached saying, ‘Although you kindly procured it, it’s a bit too large, so please send it back to the hat shop to have it resized. The resizing fee will be sent from here in a money order.’” “I see, that’s quite foolish,” my master said, feeling greatly satisfied to discover that there are those even more foolish than himself. Then he asked, “And what happened next?” “What could I do? I had to wear it myself.” “That hat?” my master chuckled. “Is that gentleman a baron?” his wife asked, intrigued. “Who?” “That uncle with the folding fan.” “Oh, he’s just a Confucian scholar. In his youth, he was fixated on Zhu Xi’s teachings or something, so he lives with a topknot under the electric light, looking quite dignified. There’s nothing to be done,” he said, rubbing his chin excessively. “Still, you called him Baron Makiyama earlier,” Meitei pointed out. “Yes, you did say that; I heard it in the tea room,” his wife agreed with my master on this point. “Did I? Ah ha ha ha ha,” Meitei laughed for no particular reason. “That’s a lie. If I had an uncle who was a baron, I would have become a department head by now,” he said nonchalantly. “I thought something was strange,” my master said, looking both pleased and worried. “Oh my, how can you tell such a lie so seriously? You must be quite good at spinning tall tales,” his wife expressed her admiration. “I’m not as good as that woman,” he replied. “You’re not one to be outdone either.” “But my dear, my tall tales are mere fabrications. That woman’s are all calculated, with ulterior motives, and they’re notorious lies. It’s troublesome.

If the wisdom of a monkey is mixed with the innate sense of humor, even the god of comedy would have to lament the lack of discerning individuals.” My master lowered his gaze and said, “Who knows.” His wife laughed and replied, “It’s the same thing.”

吾輩は今まで向う横丁へ足を踏み込んだ事はない。角屋敷の金田とは、どんな構えか見た事は無論ない。聞いた事さえ今が始めてである。主人の家で実業家が話頭に上った事は一返もないので、主人の飯を食う吾輩までがこの方面には単に無関係なるのみならず、はなはだ冷淡であった。しかるに先刻図らずも鼻子の訪問を受けて、余所ながらその談話を拝聴し、その令嬢の艶美を想像し、またその富貴、権勢を思い浮べて見ると、猫ながら安閑として椽側に寝転んでいられなくなった。しかのみならず吾輩は寒月君に対してはなはだ同情の至りに堪えん。先方では博士の奥さんやら、車屋の神さんやら、二絃琴の天璋院まで買収して知らぬ間に、前歯の欠けたのさえ探偵しているのに、寒月君の方ではただニヤニヤして羽織の紐ばかり気にしているのは、いかに卒業したての理学士にせよ、あまり能がなさ過ぎる。と言って、ああ云う偉大な鼻を顔の中に安置している女の事だから、滅多な者では寄り付ける訳の者ではない。こう云う事件に関しては主人はむしろ無頓着でかつあまりに銭がなさ過ぎる。迷亭は銭に不自由はしないが、あんな偶然童子だから、寒月に援けを与える便宜は尠かろう。して見ると可哀相なのは首縊りの力学を演説する先生ばかりとなる。吾輩でも奮発して、敵城へ乗り込んでその動静を偵察してやらなくては、あまり不公平である。吾輩は猫だけれど、エピクテタスを読んで机の上へ叩きつけるくらいな学者の家に寄寓する猫で、世間一般の痴猫、愚猫とは少しく撰を殊にしている。この冒険をあえてするくらいの義侠心は固より尻尾の先に畳み込んである。何も寒月君に恩になったと云う訳もないが、これはただに個人のためにする血気躁狂の沙汰ではない。大きく云えば公平を好み中庸を愛する天意を現実にする天晴な美挙だ。人の許諾を経ずして吾妻橋事件などを至る処に振廻わす以上は、人の軒下に犬を忍ばして、その報道を得々として逢う人に吹聴する以上は、車夫、馬丁、無頼漢、ごろつき書生、日雇婆、産婆、妖婆、按摩、頓馬に至るまでを使用して国家有用の材に煩を及ぼして顧みざる以上は――猫にも覚悟がある。幸い天気も好い、霜解は少々閉口するが道のためには一命もすてる。足の裏へ泥が着いて、椽側へ梅の花の印を押すくらいな事は、ただ御三の迷惑にはなるか知れんが、吾輩の苦痛とは申されない。翌日とも云わずこれから出掛けようと勇猛精進の大決心を起して台所まで飛んで出たが「待てよ」と考えた。吾輩は猫として進化の極度に達しているのみならず、脳力の発達においてはあえて中学の三年生に劣らざるつもりであるが、悲しいかな咽喉の構造だけはどこまでも猫なので人間の言語が饒舌れない。よし首尾よく金田邸へ忍び込んで、充分敵の情勢を見届けたところで、肝心の寒月君に教えてやる訳に行かない。主人にも迷亭先生にも話せない。話せないとすれば土中にある金剛石の日を受けて光らぬと同じ事で、せっかくの智識も無用の長物となる。これは愚だ、やめようかしらんと上り口で佇んで見た。

しかし一度思い立った事を中途でやめるのは、白雨が来るかと待っている時黒雲共隣国へ通り過ぎたように、何となく残り惜しい。それも非がこっちにあれば格別だが、いわゆる正義のため、人道のためなら、たとい無駄死をやるまでも進むのが、義務を知る男児の本懐であろう。無駄骨を折り、無駄足を汚すくらいは猫として適当のところである。猫と生れた因果で寒月、迷亭、苦沙弥諸先生と三寸の舌頭に相互の思想を交換する技倆はないが、猫だけに忍びの術は諸先生より達者である。他人の出来ぬ事を成就するのはそれ自身において愉快である。吾一箇でも、金田の内幕を知るのは、誰も知らぬより愉快である。人に告げられんでも人に知られているなと云う自覚を彼等に与うるだけが愉快である。こんなに愉快が続々出て来ては行かずにはいられない。やはり行く事に致そう。

向う横町へ来て見ると、聞いた通りの西洋館が角地面を吾物顔に占領している。この主人もこの西洋館のごとく傲慢に構えているんだろうと、門を這入ってその建築を眺めて見たがただ人を威圧しようと、二階作りが無意味に突っ立っているほかに何等の能もない構造であった。迷亭のいわゆる月並とはこれであろうか。玄関を右に見て、植込の中を通り抜けて、勝手口へ廻る。さすがに勝手は広い、苦沙弥先生の台所の十倍はたしかにある。せんだって日本新聞に詳しく書いてあった大隈伯の勝手にも劣るまいと思うくらい整然とぴかぴかしている。「模範勝手だな」と這入り込む。見ると漆喰で叩き上げた二坪ほどの土間に、例の車屋の神さんが立ちながら、御飯焚きと車夫を相手にしきりに何か弁じている。こいつは剣呑だと水桶の裏へかくれる。「あの教師あ、うちの旦那の名を知らないのかね」と飯焚が云う。「知らねえ事があるもんか、この界隈で金田さんの御屋敷を知らなけりゃ眼も耳もねえ片輪だあな」これは抱え車夫の声である。「なんとも云えないよ。あの教師と来たら、本よりほかに何にも知らない変人なんだからねえ。旦那の事を少しでも知ってりゃ恐れるかも知れないが、駄目だよ、自分の小供の歳さえ知らないんだもの」と神さんが云う。「金田さんでも恐れねえかな、厄介な唐変木だ。構あ事あねえ、みんなで威嚇かしてやろうじゃねえか」「それが好いよ。奥様の鼻が大き過ぎるの、顔が気に喰わないのって――そりゃあ酷い事を云うんだよ。自分の面あ今戸焼の狸見たような癖に――あれで一人前だと思っているんだからやれ切れないじゃないか」「顔ばかりじゃない、手拭を提げて湯に行くところからして、いやに高慢ちきじゃないか。自分くらいえらい者は無いつもりでいるんだよ」と苦沙弥先生は飯焚にも大に不人望である。「何でも大勢であいつの垣根の傍へ行って悪口をさんざんいってやるんだね」「そうしたらきっと恐れ入るよ」「しかしこっちの姿を見せちゃあ面白くねえから、声だけ聞かして、勉強の邪魔をした上に、出来るだけじらしてやれって、さっき奥様が言い付けておいでなすったぜ」「そりゃ分っているよ」と神さんは悪口の三分の一を引き受けると云う意味を示す。
なるほどこの手合が苦沙弥先生を冷やかしに来るなと三人の横を、そっと通り抜けて奥へ這入る。

Though I have paws like a cat, they make no clumsy sounds wherever I walk. It is as if I tread upon the sky, glide through the clouds, strike a bell in the water, or beat a koto in a cave; I savor the exquisite taste of the finest sake and am aware of both warmth and chill beyond mere words. There are no ordinary Western-style houses, no model kitchens, and no rickshaw gods, nor Gonsuke, nor rice cookers, nor young ladies, nor housemaids, nor Mrs. Kaneda, nor her husband. I go where I please, listen to the tales I wish to hear, stick out my tongue, wag my tail, and return leisurely with my whiskers held high. In particular, I pride myself on being the most skilled navigator of this road in all of Japan. I sometimes wonder if I might not be descended from the bloodline of the cat-bane mentioned in the grass double picture books. They say that a toad has a luminous pearl on its forehead, but my tail contains, without a doubt, a family recipe that mocks all of humanity, alongside the teachings of gods and the Buddha. To stroll through the Kaneda household's corridor without anyone noticing is easier than the Nioh stepping on a piece of konnyaku (a type of yam cake). At that moment, I found myself admiring my own prowess, realizing that it is indeed thanks to my tail, which I usually hold in high regard. I thought to pay homage to the great deity of my tail and pray for long-lasting fortune, and I lowered my head slightly, but it seemed I was a bit off in my approach. I must bow towards my tail as much as possible. When I tried to turn my body to look at my tail, it naturally followed suit. When I twisted my neck to catch up with it, my tail also maintained the same distance and dashed ahead. Indeed, being a spiritual object that contains the universe within a mere three inches, it is far beyond my grasp. After circling my tail seven and a half times, I grew weary and decided to stop. My vision blurred a little. I lost my sense of direction for a moment. Not caring, I wandered about chaotically. I heard Mrs. Kaneda's voice behind the sliding door. I paused, standing still, pricking my ears to listen, holding my breath. "Isn't it a bit cheeky for a poor teacher?" she exclaimed in her usual shrill voice. "Yes, what a cheeky fellow. I think I’ll tease him a bit for that. There are some national treasures at that school, you know." 

"Who’s there?" 

"Tsuki Pinsuke and Fukuchi Kishago are there, so let’s ask them to play a trick on him." 

I did not know where Kaneda-kun hailed from, but I was somewhat surprised to find such peculiar names gathered in one place.

Kaneda-kun continued, "Is that fellow an English teacher?" 

"Yes, according to the rickshaw god, he specializes in teaching something like English riddles." 

"Well, he’s probably not a very good teacher." 

I couldn’t help but feel a bit impressed. "The other day, when I met Pinsuke, he said, 'There’s a strange fellow at my school. When a student asked him what 'bancha' (a type of tea) is in English, he seriously replied that it is 'Savage tea,' and it has become a joke among the teachers. It’s because of such teachers that others are troubled and inconvenienced.'" 

"That sounds just like him, with a face that looks like he’d say something like that, and he has such a ridiculous beard." 

"What a suspicious fellow." If a bearded man is suspicious, then a cat could be considered suspicious as well. "And that Meitei or Hebereke fellow, what a ridiculous character he is. I thought, 'How could my uncle Baron Makiyama have such a face?'" 

"It’s foolish to take seriously the words of someone whose origins you don’t know." 

"It’s foolish to belittle someone too much, isn’t it?" she replied, sounding quite disappointed. Strangely enough, there was not a word about Kangetsu-kun. I wondered if the rumors had already spread before I stealthily arrived, or if he had already flunked out and was not in anyone’s thoughts. I had my concerns, but there was nothing to be done. After standing there for a while, I heard the sound of a bell from the room across the hallway. There must be something going on over there. I decided to head in that direction without delay. When I arrived, I saw a woman talking loudly by herself. Judging by the similarity of her voice to Mrs. Kaneda’s, this must be the very lady who had caused Kangetsu-kun to attempt to drown herself. Alas, I could not see her beautiful figure through the sliding door. Therefore, I could not ascertain whether she had a large nose in the middle of her face or not. However, considering the tone of her conversation and her heavy breathing, it seemed she was not entirely unremarkable. The woman kept chattering away, but I could not hear the voice of her interlocutor at all; it must be that device they call a telephone. "You’re from Yamato, right? I’m going tomorrow, so please hold onto three quail eggs for me, okay? — Did you understand? — What, you don’t understand? Oh dear. I said to hold onto three quail eggs. — What? — You can’t hold onto them? There’s no way you can’t, you must! — Hehehe, you’re joking, aren’t you? — What do you mean, I’m joking? — You’re really making fun of me. Who are you, anyway? Nagayoshi? I don’t understand what you mean by that. Tell the god to get on the line! — What? I can explain anything? — You’re being rude. Do you know who I am? I’m Kaneda! — Hehehe, I know very well.

You’re really foolish, aren’t you? — I’m Kaneda, you know. — What? — Thank you for your continued patronage? — What’s there to be thankful for? I don’t want to hear any thanks! — Oh, you’re laughing again. You must be quite the fool. — Is that what you say? — If you keep making fun of me, I’ll hang up the phone. Is that okay? You won’t be troubled, will you? — If you don’t speak up, I won’t understand, so please say something." 

It seemed that Nagayoshi had hung up the phone, as there was no response. The young lady, in a fit of anger, began to ring the bell furiously. At her feet, a small dog startled and suddenly began to bark. Realizing I could not afford to be careless, I quickly jumped down and hid beneath the porch.

At that moment, I heard footsteps approaching along the corridor, followed by the sound of a sliding door being opened. Someone has come, I thought, straining to listen. "Miss, your father and mother are calling for you," came a voice that sounded like a maid. "I don't know," the young lady replied, delivering a sharp retort. "They said they have something to discuss, so please call the young lady," the maid insisted. "You're so noisy! I told you I don't know," the young lady shot back with a second retort. "It seems they have business regarding Mr. Mizushima Kangetsu," the maid tried to be considerate and smooth things over. "I don't know anything about Kangetsu or Suigetsu—I'm sick of it! He has a face like a gourd that’s lost its way," she delivered a third retort, which the unfortunate Mr. Kangetsu would receive in absentia. "Oh, when did you tie your hair up?" The maid, relieved, offered as simple a greeting as she could manage. "How cheeky of you, for a maid," the young lady responded with a fourth retort from another angle. "And you've put on a new half-collar, haven't you?" "Yes, I received it from you the other day, and I thought it was too nice to wear, so I kept it in the trunk, but since the old one got so dirty, I thought I might as well wear it now." "When did I ever give you something like that?" "This New Year, you went to Shirakiya and bought it—it's the one dyed with the wrestling match list in uguisu green. You said it was too plain for me, so you wanted to give it to me." "Oh, how dreadful! It suits you so well. It's infuriating." "I'm honored." "I didn't mean it as a compliment; I find it infuriating." "Oh." "If it suits you that well, why did you keep quiet about it?" "Oh." "If it suits you that much, it shouldn't look strange on me either, should it?" "I'm sure it would suit you very well." "Knowing it looks good on you, why keep quiet? And here you are, wearing it so smugly—how mean!" The retorts continued to fly without end. Just as I was listening intently to see how the situation would develop, I heard Kaneda-kun calling the young lady loudly from the adjoining room, "Tomiko! Tomiko!" The young lady, with no choice, replied, "Yes," and left the telephone room. Following her was a small dog, a little larger than I, with a face that seemed to gather its eyes and mouth at the center. I slipped out through the back, using my usual stealth, and hurried back to my master's house. My exploration had yielded a satisfactory result. Upon returning, I felt as if I had suddenly moved from a beautiful house to a dirty place, as if I had entered a dim cave from a sunny mountaintop.

During my exploration, I had been distracted by other matters and had not paid attention to the decorations, sliding doors, or the condition of the shoji, but now, feeling the inferiority of my dwelling, I found myself longing for what is called the ordinary. It seemed to me that practical businessmen were indeed more admirable than teachers. I thought it was a bit strange, so I consulted my tail, and sure enough, it confirmed my thoughts from the tip. When I entered the sitting room, I was surprised to find that Meitei had not yet returned, with his half-smoked tobacco rolled up and stuck into the brazier like a beehive, sitting cross-legged and talking about something. Before I knew it, even Mr. Kangetsu had arrived. My master was lying with his head resting on his hands, gazing absentmindedly at the leaking ceiling. It was, as always, a gathering of the peaceful and carefree.

"Mr. Kangetsu, the name of the lady who spoke of you in a delirium seems to have been a secret at the time, but it should be fine to talk about it now," Meitei began to tease. "As long as it concerns only me, I don't mind discussing it, but it might be a bother to the other party."

"Is it still not okay?" 

"Moreover, I made a promise to Dr. ○○'s wife."

"Was it a promise not to speak of it?"

"Yes," replied Mr. Kangetsu, twisting the cord of his haori as usual. The cord was a shade of purple that should not be found on sale. "That color is a bit too much like the Tenpo era," the master said, lying down. "Indeed, it is certainly not something from the Russo-Japanese War era. One would need to wear a haori with a standing aoi crest to match such a cord. When Oda Nobunaga entered into marriage, he tied his hair with a tea whisk, and I believe it was a cord much like this," Meitei's complaints were as long as ever. "In fact, this was used by my grandfather during the Choshu Expedition," Mr. Kangetsu said seriously. "Perhaps you should donate it to a museum. It is somewhat unbecoming for a physicist like you, Mr. Kangetsu, to dress like a leftover samurai," the master remarked. "I could follow your advice, but there are people who say it suits me very well—"

"Who would say such a tasteless thing?" the master exclaimed, turning over in bed. "Well, it is someone you don't know—"

"It doesn't matter if I don't know. Who is it, anyway?"

"It was a lady from the past."

"Hahaha, she must be quite the tea connoisseur. Shall I take a guess? Is she the one who called your name from the bottom of the Sumida River? Why not wear that haori again and perfect your Buddhist practice?" Meitei interjected from the side. "Hehehe, she is no longer calling from the depths of the water. She is in the pure world towards the dry direction..."

"It doesn't seem very pure; that nose is quite toxic," the master remarked. "Eh?" Mr. Kangetsu looked puzzled. "The nose from the alley just barged in here. We were truly surprised, weren't we, Mr. Kushami?"

"Indeed," the master replied, sipping tea while lying down. "Whose nose are you talking about?"

"Your dear, eternal lady's mother."

"Eh?"

"The wife of Kaneda came to inquire about you," the master explained seriously. I observed Mr. Kangetsu's reaction, wondering if he would be surprised, pleased, or embarrassed, but he remained unperturbed. In his usual calm tone, he said, "I suppose it is a request for me to marry that girl," and twisted the purple cord again. "However, that's quite different. That mother of hers is the owner of a magnificent nose..." Meitei began to say, but the master interrupted, "Hey, you, I've been thinking of a haiku about that nose since earlier."

From the next room, his wife began to giggle.

"You really are carefree. Have you made any progress?"

"A little. The first line goes, 'This face with a nose festival.'"

"And then?"

"The next line is, 'Offering sacred sake to this nose.'"

"What about the next line?"

"I haven't gotten any further than that."

"How amusing," Mr. Kangetsu chuckled. "How about adding, 'Two holes, faintly visible'?" Meitei suggested, ready to create. Then Mr. Kangetsu said, "Wouldn't it be better to say, 'Deep within, not a hair is seen'?" They were both stringing together nonsense when, near the fence, a group of four or five people could be heard shouting, "Imado-yaki raccoon, Imado-yaki raccoon!" 

The master and Meitei were a bit startled and peered through the gap in the fence to see, "Wahaha!" a voice of laughter echoed, followed by the sound of footsteps scattering away. "What do they mean by 'Imado-yaki raccoon'?" Meitei asked the master, puzzled. "I have no idea," the master replied. "Quite a lively atmosphere," Mr. Kangetsu commented. Meitei suddenly stood up, recalling something, and said, "I have long studied this nose from an aesthetic perspective, and I would like to present a portion of my findings for your attentive ears."

The master, taken aback by the suddenness, stared at Meitei in silence. Mr. Kangetsu said quietly, "I would certainly like to hear it."

"I have looked into it variously, but the origin of the nose remains unclear. The first point of suspicion is that if we assume it to be a practical tool, two holes are more than enough. There is no need for it to protrude so far into the wind. Yet, how did it come to protrude so much as you see?"

He pinched his own nose to demonstrate. "That doesn't seem to protrude all that much," the master remarked bluntly. "Nevertheless, it certainly does not retract. Just because there are two holes side by side does not mean that it cannot lead to misunderstandings, so I must caution you in advance. According to my humble opinion, the development of the nose is a remarkable phenomenon resulting from the natural accumulation of the subtle act of humans blowing their noses."

"That is a rather—" Mr. Kangetsu protested, as a physicist would. "Your skepticism is entirely valid, but proof is in the pudding. The bone is here, so there is no denying it. The bone has formed, yet the mucus still flows. When it flows, one cannot help but blow their nose. This action causes the sides of the bone to be worn down, transforming it into a narrow, high prominence—truly a terrifying effect. Like water dripping through stone, like the head of a skull shining with light, the nose becomes firm and straight."

"Still, yours is quite bulbous," the master commented. "The performer himself has a fear of exposing his own parts, so I shall refrain from discussing that.

However, I would like to introduce the nose of Mrs. Kaneda as the most developed and magnificent treasure of the world."

Mr. Kangetsu involuntarily gasped. "However, when something reaches an extreme, it may differ in grandeur, but it also becomes somewhat frightening and hard to approach. That bridge of the nose is undoubtedly splendid, but it may be a bit too steep. Among the ancients, Socrates, Goldsmith, or Thackeray had noses that were structurally quite commendable, and it is precisely those commendable aspects that give them charm. A nose is not valuable simply for being high; it is precious for being peculiar. In the common saying, 'Dumplings over noses,' from an aesthetic perspective, I believe that someone like Meitei is quite appropriate."

Mr. Kangetsu and the master chuckled, "Hehehe."

Meitei himself laughed joyfully. "Now, what I have just expounded upon—"

"Sir, your expounding sounds a bit like a lecturer, so let’s refrain from that," Mr. Kangetsu interrupted, seeking revenge for the previous day. "Very well, then I shall wash my face and start over. —Ah— I would like to touch upon the balance between the nose and the face. If we speak of the nose alone, Mrs. Kaneda possesses a nose that would not be embarrassing to show anywhere—even at an exhibition on Kurama Mountain, it would likely win first prize. Alas, that nose was made without consultation with the eyes, mouth, or any other features. Julius Caesar's nose is undoubtedly remarkable. But what if we were to cut off Caesar's nose and place it on the face of our cat? Imagine a hero's nose towering in a space as small as a cat's forehead, like placing the Great Buddha of Nara on a Go board—it would be a complete loss of proportion, detracting from its aesthetic value. Mrs. Kaneda's nose, like Caesar's, is indeed a noble and heroic prominence. However, what about the facial conditions surrounding it? Of course, they are not as inferior as our cat's. Yet, like a lady afflicted with epilepsy, with a furrowed brow and narrow eyes, it is a fact that we must lament, 'This face has this nose.'"

Just as Meitei's words trailed off, a voice from behind said, "They are still talking about noses. What a bold fellow he is."

"It's the rickshaw man's god," the master informed Meitei. Meitei began again, "To unexpectedly encounter new listeners of the opposite sex behind us is a deep honor for the performer. Especially to have added a touch of charm to this dry lecture with such a melodious voice is truly an unexpected joy. I will try to avoid being too colloquial to not offend the attention of the lovely ladies present, but I will now delve into a somewhat complicated issue of mechanics, so it may be difficult for the ladies to understand; I ask for your patience."

Mr.

Kangetsu grinned at the mention of mechanics. "What I am trying to prove is that this nose and this face are utterly incompatible. It violates the golden rule of Tsai Sing, and I intend to derive it strictly from the principles of mechanics. First, let H be the height of the nose. α is the angle formed by the intersection of the nose and the plane of the face. W, of course, is the weight of the nose, as you all know. Do you understand most of this?"

"How could we?" the master replied. "What about you, Mr. Kangetsu?"

"I find it a bit hard to understand myself."

"That's a problem. I thought you, being a physicist, would understand. This formula is the crux of the speech, and if I omit it, all my efforts will be in vain—well, it can't be helped. I will skip to the conclusion."

"Is there a conclusion?" the master asked, intrigued. "Of course! A speech without a conclusion is like a Western meal without dessert. —Listen closely, both of you, this is the conclusion. —Now, considering the theories of Wilhoyt and Weissman in conjunction with the above formula, we must allow for the hereditary nature of congenital forms. Furthermore, the psychological conditions that arise in conjunction with this form, even if there is a strong theory that acquired traits do not inherit, must be recognized as a necessary result to some extent. Therefore, it can be inferred that the child born of a nose that is incongruous with its status will have some abnormality in that nose. Mr. Kangetsu, being still young, may not yet recognize any particular abnormalities in the structure of Miss Kaneda's nose, but such heredity has a long incubation period, and at any moment, with a drastic change in climate, it may suddenly develop and swell like that of her mother. Thus, according to Meitei's theoretical proof, it seems safer to abandon this marriage for now. I believe our master here, as well as the cat lord lying there, would have no objections."

The master finally sat up and said, "Of course not. Who would want to marry someone like that? Mr. Kangetsu, you shouldn't either."

I let out a couple of meows to express my agreement. Mr. Kangetsu showed no particular sign of agitation, saying, "If that is the gentlemen's intention, I can abandon it, but if the lady takes it to heart and falls ill, that would be a sin..."

"Hahaha, that would be a sin of charm," the master insisted fervently, "There’s no way anyone would marry her; she's not worth it. She was the first to come to my house and try to put me in my place.

Such an arrogant person."

Then, again near the fence, a group of three or four people laughed, "Wahaha!" One of them said, "What a proud fool he is!" Another added, "He probably wants to get into a bigger house." Yet another shouted, "It's unfortunate, but no matter how much he boasts, he's just a coward."

The master stepped out onto the porch, raising his voice to match, "Shut up! Why come all the way to shout under the fence?"

"Wahaha! Savage Chi! Savage Chi!" they jeered in unison. The master, in a great rage, suddenly stood up, grabbed his cane, and rushed out into the street. Meitei clapped his hands and said, "How amusing! Go on, go on!" Mr. Kangetsu twisted the cord of his haori and grinned. I followed the master, peering through the broken fence into the street, where the master stood idly, poking the ground with his cane. There was not a single person passing by, and he looked a bit like a fox caught in a trap.

Four

I stealthily slipped into the Kaneda residence, as usual. To say "as usual" requires no further explanation. It is a phrase that indicates a degree of frequency, so much so that one might say it has become a habit. Once one has done something, one wishes to do it again; and once one has attempted something twice, the desire to try it a third time is not limited to mere human curiosity. Even a cat, too, must be recognized as possessing this psychological privilege, having been born into this world. It is only when one repeats an action three times or more that it is crowned with the term "habit," and this behavior evolves into a necessity of life, much like in humans. If one were to raise doubts about why I frequent the Kaneda residence so often, I would like to pose a question to humans first: why do they inhale smoke through their mouths only to exhale it through their noses? If they shamelessly puff out something that is neither nourishing nor medicinal, I would rather not have them chastise me too loudly for entering and exiting the Kaneda household. The Kaneda residence is my tobacco. To say "sneak in" carries a connotation that is somewhat misleading; it sounds as if I were a thief or an illicit lover, which is quite unpleasant to hear. My visits to the Kaneda residence are not for the purpose of stealing bonito fillets or to engage in secret conversations with that pug-nosed fellow whose eyes and nose are grotesquely close together. — What detective? — That is utterly preposterous. I believe that among the various lowly professions in the world, there is none more contemptible than that of a detective or a moneylender. Indeed, I once felt an uncharacteristic sense of chivalry for a cat and observed the movements of the Kaneda household from a distance for the sake of Kangetsu, but that was merely a one-time occurrence, and since then, I have never engaged in any disgraceful behavior that would shame a cat’s conscience. — Then why use such dubious words as "sneak in"? — Ah, that is indeed a matter of great significance. Originally, according to my thoughts, the vast sky exists to cover all things, and the earth exists to support all things — no matter how stubbornly humans may argue, they cannot deny this fact. Now, considering how much effort humanity expends to create this vast sky and earth, it seems they have not contributed a single ounce. There is no law that allows one to claim ownership of something one has not created. One may claim ownership without issue, but there is no reason to prohibit others from entering.

To foolishly enclose this vast expanse of earth with fences and stakes, declaring certain plots as private property, is akin to someone attempting to stake a claim in the azure sky, declaring, "This part is my sky, and that part is his." If one can slice up land and trade ownership by the square foot, then it would be equally valid to sell the air we breathe by the cubic foot. If selling air is impossible and claiming the sky is unjust, then private ownership of land is also unreasonable. Thus, believing in such a perspective and adhering to such a principle, I, therefore, go wherever I please. Of course, I do not go to places I do not wish to visit, but in the direction I aspire to go, I make no distinction between east, west, south, or north; I stroll along with a calm demeanor. There is no reason for me to be considerate of someone like Kaneda. — However, the sorrow of a cat is that it cannot possibly compete with humans in strength. In this world, where there is a saying that strength is right, no matter how reasonable my position may be, a cat's arguments will not hold. If I were to force my way through, I might unexpectedly find myself in the unfortunate position of being caught by Kuro, the rickshaw man's black cat, who might suddenly devour the pole of a fishmonger. In a situation where reason is on my side but power is on the other, should I bend my reasoning and submit without question, or should I slip past the eyes of power and uphold my own reasoning? Naturally, I would choose the latter. Since I cannot avoid the fishmonger’s pole, I must sneak in. It is permissible to enter a person's residence, so I have no choice but to do so. For this reason, I sneak into the Kaneda residence. As I sneak in more frequently, although I have no intention of being a detective, it is inevitable that the circumstances of the Kaneda family, which I do not wish to see, imprint themselves on my unwilling mind. I have come to notice that Mrs. Hanako wipes only her nose every time she washes her face, that Miss Tomiko carelessly devours Abe River rice cakes, and that Kaneda himself — Kaneda is a man with a low nose, unlike his wife. Not just his nose, but his entire face is flat. One might wonder if the face he bore when he was a child, pressed against a dirt wall by a bully, has remained unchanged for forty years, for it is indeed a remarkably flat face. It is certainly a gentle and harmless face, but it lacks any variation. No matter how angry he gets, his face remains flat.

— That Kaneda, while eating tuna sashimi, pats his own bald head with a splat, and since he is not only low-nosed but also short, he carelessly wears a tall hat and high geta (traditional wooden sandals), which the rickshaw man finds amusing and tells the students about, while the students express their admiration for his keen observations — these are but a few of the countless details. Recently, I have taken to passing through the side entrance and peering over the garden from the shadow of the hillock. Once I ascertain that the sliding doors are firmly closed and the atmosphere is quiet, I gradually make my way in. If I hear lively voices or fear being seen from the tatami room, I will circle the pond to the east and sneak out beneath the eaves without anyone noticing. I have no recollection of doing anything wrong, so there is nothing to hide or fear; however, when faced with the lawless nature of humans, I can only resign myself to misfortune. If the world were filled with people like Kumisaka Nagaharu, even the most virtuous gentlemen would likely adopt an attitude similar to mine. Kaneda is a dignified businessman, so he surely does not have the same concerns as Kumisaka Nagaharu, but I have heard that there are those who do not regard others as human. If one does not consider others human, one certainly would not regard a cat as a cat. Thus, for a cat, regardless of how virtuous it may be, one cannot afford to let down one’s guard within the confines of another’s home. However, it is precisely this inability to let down my guard that makes it somewhat amusing for me, and perhaps my frequent comings and goings at the Kaneda household are motivated by a desire to experience this danger. I shall reflect on this further and, when I have thoroughly dissected the cat's mind, I will share my findings. As I pressed my chin against the grass on the hillock, I surveyed the scene, wondering what was happening today. The fifteen-tatami mat guest room was wide open to the spring of Yayoi, and inside, Mr. and Mrs. Kaneda were engaged in conversation with a visitor. Unfortunately, Mrs. Hanako's nose was turned toward me, glaring straight down at my forehead across the pond. It was the first time in my life that I had been glared at by a nose. Fortunately, Kaneda was facing the guest, so I could not see the usual flat part of his face, but instead, I could make out the location of his nose. Only his salt-and-pepper mustache was growing haphazardly from a good spot, so I could easily conclude that there must be two holes above it. I imagined that if the spring breeze were to blow only on such a smooth face, it would surely be quite pleasant. The guest had the most ordinary appearance among the three.

However, being ordinary, there was nothing particularly noteworthy to introduce about him. While "ordinary" may sound pleasant, to have been born into the Meiji era with a face of such utter mediocrity is rather pitiable. As usual, I would have to go beneath the eaves to overhear their conversation to understand. "…So my wife went all the way to that man's place to inquire about the situation…" Kaneda was speaking in his usual breezy manner. While breezy, there was not the slightest hint of harshness. His language was as flat and expansive as his face. "Indeed, that man taught Mizushima-san, so — indeed, what a good idea — indeed," the guest was full of "indeeds." 

"But somehow, I can't quite grasp the point,"

"Ah, Mr. Kushami is truly indecisive—ever since the time I shared a boarding house with him, he has been remarkably wishy-washy—no wonder you were troubled," the guest turned to Mrs. Kaneda. "Troubled or not, I have never been treated so poorly in someone else's house until this age," Mrs. Kaneda huffed, as was her custom. "Did I say something rude? He has always been stubborn—after all, he has been a teacher specializing in reading for ten years, so you can understand," the guest smoothly adjusted his tone. "No, it’s hardly worth discussing; when my wife asks him something, he responds with a greeting that is as cold as steel..."

"That’s quite unacceptable—when one studies a little, arrogance tends to sprout, and when one is poor, it leads to a sense of resentment—there are indeed many lawless people in this world. They fail to notice their own lack of effort and recklessly attack those who have wealth, as if they were robbing them of their fortune—it's astonishing, really, ahahaha," the guest was in great delight. "Indeed, it is utterly absurd; such behavior ultimately stems from ignorance of the world, and I thought it might be good to teach him a lesson by giving him a little push."

"Well, that must have been quite a response; it is indeed something that would benefit him," the guest was already in agreement with Mr. Kaneda before knowing how he had pushed back. "However, Mr. Suzuki, what a stubborn man he is! Even at school, he won't speak a word to Mr. Fukuchi or Mr. Tsuki. I thought he was just intimidated and silent, but the other day, he chased our student with a cane—thirty faces down, well, how could he have done such a foolish thing? He must be a bit mad from frustration."

"How could he have done such a violent thing...?" It seemed even the guest was a bit suspicious of this. "Well, he just said something as he passed in front of that man, and suddenly, he dashed out barefoot with a cane. Even if he said something trivial, he’s not a child; he’s a bearded old monk and a teacher, no less."

"Indeed, he is a teacher," the guest said, and Mr. Kaneda echoed, "Because he is a teacher." It seemed that all three of them unexpectedly agreed that as a teacher, one must endure any insult like a wooden statue. "Moreover, that Meitei fellow is quite the drunkard. He spouts useless nonsense. I have never met such a peculiar person."

"Ah, Meitei, I see he is still blowing hot air. Did you meet him at Mr. Kushami's? He’s unbearable. He used to be part of our self-cooking group, but he looked down on people too much, so we often quarreled."

"Anyone would get angry at that. It’s one thing to lie, but to say that one must keep up appearances or that one must not offend—it’s common for anyone to say things they don’t mean in such situations.

However, that man lies without needing to; it’s utterly intolerable. What does he gain from spouting such nonsense? I am amazed at how brazenly he can say it."

"Quite right; it’s troublesome because it’s a lie born from indulgence."

"Even the matter of Mr. Mizushima, which you went to hear about seriously, has turned into a complete mess. I am furious and vexed—but still, duty is duty, and it’s too much for someone to go to another's house to ask questions and pretend not to know, so later I had the rickshaw man take a dozen beers. But you know what? He said there was no reason to accept such a thing and told me to take it back. I said it was a token of gratitude, so please accept it, but he replied—how rude!—that while he licks jam every day, he has never drunk anything bitter like beer, and just went inside without another word—what a ridiculous excuse, isn’t it?"

"That’s terrible," the guest seemed genuinely irritated this time. "That’s why I invited you here today," Mr. Kaneda’s voice was heard after a brief pause. "Such a fool should be dealt with from the shadows, but there are still some troublesome matters..."

As he spoke, he tapped his bald head as if eating tuna sashimi. Of course, I was under the porch, so I couldn’t see whether he actually tapped it or not, but I had grown quite accustomed to the sound of that bald head. Just as a nun can distinguish the sound of a wooden fish, I could tell from the sound alone that it was indeed his bald head. "So, I wanted to trouble you a bit..."

"Please feel free to ask me anything I can do—I have been appointed to work in Tokyo, and it is entirely due to the various concerns you have had for me," the guest readily accepted Mr. Kaneda’s request. From this tone, it seemed that this guest was indeed someone who relied on Mr. Kaneda. The events were becoming increasingly interesting; the weather was so pleasant today that I had come without any intention of doing so, but I never expected to gain such good material. It was like someone going to a temple during the equinox and unexpectedly being treated to rice cakes. I listened intently from under the porch, curious about what Mr. Kaneda would ask of the guest. "That strange fellow, Mr. Kushami, for some reason is advising Mr. Mizushima against marrying Mr. Kaneda's daughter—right, Mrs. Kaneda?"

"It’s not just advising; he’s saying there’s no way anyone would be foolish enough to marry such a man’s daughter. He’s telling Kangetsu not to marry her at all."

"How dare he speak of such a thing? What an outrageous thing to say!"

"It’s not just talk; the rickshaw man’s wife came to inform me about it."

"Mr. Suzuki, what do you think?

As you can see, it’s quite a troublesome situation, isn’t it?"

"It is indeed troublesome; unlike other matters, this is not something that outsiders should meddle in. Even Mr. Kushami should understand this much. What on earth is going on?"

"That’s why I’m asking you, since you shared a boarding house with Mr. Kushami during your student days, and now, after all this time, you were once close. I’m asking you to meet him and clearly explain the pros and cons. He may be angry, but if he’s in the wrong, and as long as he behaves himself, we can take care of his personal convenience and refrain from doing anything that might offend him. However, if he insists on being obstinate, we will respond in kind—after all, such stubbornness only harms him."

"Yes, you are absolutely right; foolish resistance will only harm him and bring no benefit, so I will make sure to convey this well."

"Also, there are various proposals regarding the daughter, so I can’t guarantee she will definitely be sent to Mr. Mizushima, but as I hear more, it seems she is not lacking in either learning or character, so if she studies hard and becomes a doctor in the near future, it might not be out of the question to hint that she could be married off."

"If you say that, it will encourage her to study. That sounds good."

"Then, it’s a strange thing, but—though it doesn’t suit Mizushima at all, that odd fellow Kushami calls himself 'teacher' and seems to listen to whatever Kushami says, which is quite troublesome. After all, it’s not just Mizushima; no matter what Kushami says to interfere, it doesn’t particularly bother me…"

"Poor Mizushima," Mrs. Kaneda interjects. "I’ve never met Mizushima, but in any case, if we could form a connection here, it would be a lifetime of happiness, and I’m sure he has no objections."

"Yes, Mizushima is eager to marry, but those oddballs like Kushami and Meitei keep saying this and that, so it’s a bit of a hassle."

"Well, that’s not a good thing; it’s quite unbecoming behavior for someone with a decent education. I often visit Kushami to discuss matters."

"Ah, if it’s not too much trouble, I would like to ask a favor. Actually, Kushami knows the most about Mizushima, but when my wife went to see him the other day, she couldn’t get much information because of the current situation, so I’d like you to inquire about his character and talents."

"Understood. Since today is Saturday, if I go now, I should be back before long. I wonder where he lives these days."

"Just go straight past here, turn right, and after a short distance to the left, you’ll find a crumbling black fence," Mrs. Kaneda instructs. "Then it’s quite nearby. No problem. I’ll stop by on my way back. After all, I’ll understand the general layout once I see the sign."

"Sometimes there’s a sign, and sometimes there isn’t. They probably stick a business card with rice paste on the gate. If it rains, it will peel off. Then on sunny days, they stick it back up again. So the sign is hardly reliable. It would be better to hang a wooden plaque at least. Really, he’s a person whose thoughts are utterly incomprehensible."

"That’s quite surprising. However, if you hear it’s a crumbling black fence, you should be able to figure it out."

"Yes, there’s only one such dirty house in the neighborhood, so it’ll be easy to find. Oh, and if that doesn’t help, there’s a good clue: just look for a house with grass growing on the roof, and you can’t go wrong."

"That’s quite a distinctive house, ha ha ha."

I must return before Suzuki-kun arrives; it would be somewhat inconvenient otherwise. Having heard this much of the conversation, I’m satisfied. I slip through the eaves, round the snow pit to the west, and emerge from behind the mound, hurrying back to the house with the grass-covered roof, putting on a nonchalant face as I circle around to the tatami room. My master has laid a white blanket on the porch and is lying on his stomach, basking in the lovely spring sun.

The sunlight is surprisingly fair, making even a shabby house with a target of penpen grass on the roof seem cheerfully warm, but sadly, the blanket is anything but spring-like. The manufacturer intended it to be white when woven, and the foreign goods store sold it as white, and my master bought it with the order for white, but—after all, it’s been twelve or thirteen years since then, and the era of white has long passed; it is now in a phase of discolored gray. Whether this blanket will last until it transforms into another dark color is questionable. Even now, it is already worn thin, with the vertical and horizontal threads clearly visible, so calling it a blanket is already a presumptuous affair; it would be more appropriate to simply call it a "tto" (a rag). However, my master seems to believe that as long as it lasts one year, two years, five years, or even ten years, it must last a lifetime. Quite a carefree notion. Now, as for that fateful blanket, I wonder what he is doing lying on it as I see him supporting his protruding chin with both hands, holding a rolled cigarette between the fingers of his right hand. That’s all there is to it. Of course, behind his dandruff-laden head, the great truths of the universe may be spinning like a wheel of fire, but from an external perspective, one would never dream of such a thing. The cigarette’s ember gradually creeps toward the mouthpiece, and a small stick of ash falls onto the blanket without my master caring. He is intently watching the smoke rising from the cigarette. The smoke dances in the spring breeze, swirling in layers, drifting toward the roots of my mistress’s dark, flowing hair. —Oh, I was supposed to mention my mistress. I had forgotten. My mistress, with her back turned to my master—what a rude thing for her to do! But there’s nothing particularly rude about it. Courtesy and rudeness depend entirely on mutual interpretation. My master rests his chin on his hands near her backside, and she, unfazed, places her dignified rear end right in front of his face. The two of them are a transcendent couple who have escaped the constraints of etiquette and formality within a year of their marriage. —Now, with her back turned to my master, I wonder what she is thinking, taking advantage of today’s fine weather to wash her excessively long green-black hair with seaweed and raw egg, and carelessly sprinkling it over her shoulders, all while silently and diligently sewing a sleeveless garment for the child. In fact, she has brought out a futon made of crinkled silk and a sewing box to dry her hair, respectfully turning her back to my master. Perhaps my master has brought his face near the area where her backside is located.

Thus, the smoke from the cigarette flows richly between her flowing black hair, and my master gazes at the unusual sight of the flickering heat waves. However, smoke, by its nature, does not stay in one place; it rises upward, so if my master wants to see this curious spectacle of smoke entangled in her hair, he must certainly move his eyes. My master begins his observation from the waist, gradually moving up along her back, over her shoulders and neck, and just as he finally reaches the crown of her head, he gasps in surprise. —Right in the center of my mistress’s head, where he has pledged to grow old together, there is a large, round bald spot. Moreover, that bald spot reflects the warm sunlight, now shining brightly as if it were a moment of triumph. When my master unexpectedly makes this remarkable discovery, his eyes show ample surprise amid the dazzling light, and he stares intently, regardless of the fierce rays dilating his pupils. When my master saw this bald spot, the first thing that came to his mind was the family heirloom of the altar, which had been adorned with offerings for generations. His family is of the Shinshu sect, and it is customary in Shinshu to lavish money on the altar that is not commensurate with one’s status. My master remembers that in his childhood, there was a dimly decorated cabinet in the family storehouse, and within that cabinet hung a brass lamp that was always lit, even during the day.
