In the surrounding darkness, this lamp shone relatively clearly, and the impression he had of that light when he saw it many times as a child must have been evoked by the sight of his mistress’s bald spot. The lamp went out in less than a minute. This time, he recalls the dove of Kannon. The dove of Kannon and my mistress’s bald spot seem to have no relation whatsoever, but in my master’s mind, there is a close association between the two. When he was a child, whenever he went to Asakusa, he would always buy beans to feed the doves. A plate of beans cost two bun (a unit of currency), and they came in a red earthenware bowl. That bowl, in color and size, closely resembles this bald spot. "Indeed, it does resemble," my master says, as if genuinely impressed, to which my mistress responds, "What do you mean?" without even glancing his way. "What do you mean? You have a large bald spot on your head, you know. Are you aware of that?"

"Yes," she replies, still not stopping her work. There’s no sign of her being embarrassed. A truly transcendent model of a wife. 「Is it something that has been there since you came to be my wife, or did it develop after our marriage?」 the master asked. If it had been there before she came, then he had been deceived, though he did not voice this thought, keeping it to himself.

「I can’t remember when it appeared; what does it matter? A bald head is nothing to worry about, is it?」 she replied, having come to a great understanding. 「What do you mean it doesn’t matter? It’s your own head, isn’t it?」 the master said, a hint of anger in his voice. 「Because it’s my own head, it doesn’t matter, does it?」 she retorted, but it seemed she was a little concerned after all, as she placed her right hand on her head and began to stroke her bald spot. 「Oh, it’s grown quite large; I didn’t think it would be this big,」 she remarked, and it appeared she had finally realized that her baldness was rather excessive for her age. 「Women get bald here because they tie their hair up in a bun, so everyone ends up bald,」 she began to defend herself a little. 「If everyone got bald at that rate, by the time they reach forty, they’d all be like kettles! That must be a disease. It might be contagious; you should see Dr. Amaki soon, while there’s still time,」 the master said, repeatedly stroking his own head. 「You talk about others, but you have white hairs growing in your nostrils, don’t you? If baldness is contagious, then white hairs must be contagious too,」 she said, a bit irritated. 「White hairs in the nostrils aren’t visible, so they don’t cause harm, but a bald head—especially a young woman’s bald head—is quite unsightly. It’s a disgrace.」

「If it’s a disgrace, then why did you marry me? You chose to marry me, and now you call me a disgrace…」

「I didn’t know! I truly didn’t know until today. If you’re so proud, then why didn’t you show me your head before you came to marry?」

「What a foolish thing to say! Is there any country where a head examination is required to pass before marrying?」

「I can tolerate the baldness, but you are exceptionally short. It’s terribly unsightly.」

「You can tell at a glance if someone is short; you knew I was short from the very beginning, didn’t you?」

「That’s true, I knew that, but I thought you might grow taller, so I married you.」

「At twenty, you think you’ll still grow taller? You must think very little of me,」 she said, throwing her sleeveless garment aside and turning toward the master, ready to argue further depending on his response. 「There’s no law that says you can’t grow taller at twenty. I thought that after marrying you, if I fed you well, you might grow a little taller,」 he said, earnestly presenting a strange argument when suddenly the doorbell rang vigorously, accompanied by a loud voice asking for entry. It seemed that Suzuki-kun had finally found Mr. Kushami’s lair in search of penpen grass. The lady decided to postpone the quarrel for another day, hurriedly gathering her sewing box and sleeveless garment and escaping into the tea room.

The master rolled up a gray blanket and tossed it into the study. Soon after, when he saw the business card brought by the maid, he looked a bit surprised, but then dismissed it, entering the back room while still clutching the card. It was entirely unclear why he had suddenly gone into the back room or why he had taken Suzuki Tojuro’s business card with him, making it even more difficult to explain. In any case, the one who was truly inconvenienced was the business card, which had been ordered to accompany him to the unpleasant place. The maid arranged a sarasa cushion in front of the floor and withdrew, saying, “Please sit here.” Afterward, Suzuki-kun looked around the room. After inspecting the fake woodblock print titled “Flowers Blooming in All Nations” hanging on the wall and the cherry blossoms in a vase of cheap celadon from Kyoto, he suddenly noticed that a cat was sitting there, looking quite composed on the cushion. It goes without saying that this was I, the narrator cat. At that moment, a slight storm of emotion stirred within Suzuki-kun, though it did not show on his face. This cushion had undoubtedly been laid out for him. Before he could sit on the cushion prepared for him, a strange animal was calmly squatting there without any prior notice. This was the first condition that disrupted Suzuki-kun’s mental equilibrium. If the cushion had been left unoccupied, allowed to flutter in the spring breeze, he might have intentionally expressed humility and waited on the hard tatami until the master said, “Please, go ahead.” However, the fact that an animal had already taken its place on the cushion he was meant to occupy was intolerable. If it were a human, he might have yielded, but a cat was another matter entirely. The fact that the occupant was a cat made it all the more unpleasant. This was the second condition that disrupted Suzuki-kun’s mental equilibrium. Finally, the cat’s attitude was most infuriating. It seemed to be gazing at him with round, unremarkable eyes, as if to say, “Who are you?” while sitting arrogantly on a cushion it had no right to occupy. This was the third condition that destroyed his mental equilibrium. With such grievances, one might think it reasonable to grab my neck and drag me off, yet Suzuki-kun remained silent and watched. It is inconceivable that a dignified human would fear a cat enough to refrain from taking action, so why he did not dispose of me quickly and express his discontent is entirely due to Suzuki-kun’s sense of self-restraint as a human being.

If he had resorted to physical force, even a child of three shaku (about 90 cm) could easily handle me, but considering the importance of maintaining his dignity, even Suzuki Tojuro, Kaneda-kun’s right-hand man, could do nothing about the cat deity sitting squarely in the center of that two-shaku square. Even in a place where no one could see, to have a dispute over seating with a cat would be somewhat detrimental to human dignity. To seriously contend with a cat over right and wrong is indeed very childish and absurd. To avoid this dishonor, one must endure a certain degree of inconvenience. However, the more one must endure, the greater the resentment toward the cat grows, so Suzuki-kun would occasionally glance at my face and make a bitter expression. I found it amusing to see Suzuki-kun’s disgruntled face, so I tried to maintain an expression of indifference as much as possible. While this silent drama unfolded between Suzuki-kun and me, the master emerged from the back room, adjusting his clothing, and sat down, saying, “Ah,” but when he noticed that the business card he had been holding was nowhere to be seen, it seemed that Suzuki Tojuro’s name had been sentenced to an indefinite term in that unpleasant place. Before long, the master, thinking that this fellow had grabbed my collar and tossed me aside, threw me against the wall. “Now, please sit down. How rare! When did you come to Tokyo?” the master asked, offering the cushion to his old friend. Suzuki-kun flipped it over slightly before sitting down. “I didn’t inform you because I’ve been busy, but actually, I’ve been returning to the head office in Tokyo for some time now…”

“That’s wonderful! It’s been quite a while since we last met. This is the first time since you went to the countryside, isn’t it?”

“Yeah, it’s been almost ten years. Well, I do come to Tokyo occasionally, but I’ve been so busy with work that I’ve often had to excuse myself. Please don’t think poorly of me. The company is quite busy, unlike your profession.”

“Ten years makes quite a difference,” the master said, looking up and down at Suzuki-kun. Suzuki-kun had his hair stylishly parted, wore a British-style tweed suit, and even sported a flashy collar ornament, with a gold chain glimmering on his chest, making it hard to believe he was an old friend of Mr. Kushami. “Yeah, I’ve had to hang on to things like this,” Suzuki-kun said, repeatedly showing off his gold chain. “Is that real?” the master asked, making an impolite inquiry. 「It’s eighteen yen, you know,” Suzuki-kun replied with a laugh, “but you’ve aged quite a bit. You must have a child by now, is it just one?”  
“No.”  
“Two?”  
“No.”  
“Still more? Then it must be three.”  
“Yeah, there are three.

I don’t know how many more there will be.”  
“You’re still as carefree as ever. How old is the oldest now? It must be quite a bit.”  
“Yeah, I’m not sure exactly, but probably around six or seven.”  
“Hahaha, it’s nice to be a teacher, so carefree. I should have become a teacher too.”  
“Go ahead and try; you’ll hate it in three days.”  
“Is that so? It seems so refined, easygoing, with leisure time to study what you like. Being a businessman isn’t bad, but in our case, it’s no good. If you’re going to be a businessman, you have to aim higher. If you’re at the lower end, you end up spreading all sorts of insincere flattery and going out to receive disliked compliments; it’s quite foolish.”  
“I’ve hated businessmen since school days. They’ll do anything for money; they’re like common townsfolk from the old days,” he said, laying out his carefree thoughts before the businessman. “Not that—though I can’t say it’s all bad; there are some crude aspects too. In any case, you can’t get by without being prepared to deal with money and emotional entanglements. The thing is, money is a tricky beast—just the other day, I went to see a businessman and heard that you have to use triangular tactics to make money.”  
“Obligations, emotions, and shame—apparently, that’s what makes it triangular. Isn’t that interesting? Hahaha!”  
“Who’s that fool?”  
“He’s no fool; he’s quite a clever man, actually. He’s a bit famous in the business world. Don’t you know him? He’s just down the street.”  
“Kaneda? What about that guy?”  
“You’re quite angry, aren’t you? Oh, it’s just a joke. It’s a saying that you can’t accumulate money without a bit of that. You shouldn’t interpret it so seriously, like you do.”  
“The triangular tactics may be a joke, but what about that woman’s nose? If you went, you must have seen that nose.”  
“His wife? She’s quite a capable woman.”  
“I’m talking about the nose, the big nose. I even wrote a haiku about that nose the other day.”  
“What’s this haiku you’re talking about?”  
“You don’t know what a haiku is? You’re quite out of touch with the times.”  
“Oh, when you’re as busy as I am, literature is utterly impossible. Besides, I’ve never been one for the peculiar.”  
“Do you know what Shariman’s nose looks like?”  
“Hahaha, you’re so carefree. I don’t know.”  
“Ellington was nicknamed ‘Nose Nose’ by his subordinates. Do you know that?”  
“Why are you so fixated on noses? What’s the matter? It’s fine if a nose is round or pointed.”  
“Not at all. Do you know Pascal?”  
“Again with the questions, it’s like I’m here to take an exam.

What about Pascal?”  
“Pascal said something like this.”  
“What did he say?”  
“If Cleopatra’s nose had been just a little shorter, the world would have undergone a great change.”  
“I see.”  
“Therefore, you shouldn’t dismiss noses so casually as you do.”  
“Well, fine, I’ll take care of it from now on. By the way, I came today because I have a little business with you—about that Mizushima you taught, um, Mizushima, I can’t quite remember. I hear he comes to your place often.”  
“Kangetsu?”  
“Yes, yes, Kangetsu. I came to ask you a little about that person.”  
“Is it about a marriage issue?”  
“Well, it’s somewhat related to that. When I went to Kaneda today…”  
“Didn’t that nose come by himself the other day?”  
“Is that so? Yes, that’s what his wife said. She thought of going to Mr. Kushami to inquire, but unfortunately, Meitei was there and interrupted, making it all confusing.”  
“It’s because he came with that nose.”  
“No, I’m not talking about you. It was because Meitei was there that I couldn’t ask anything too intrusive, so I was asked to go back and find out more. I’ve never been involved in such matters before, but if the parties involved don’t mind, it wouldn’t be a bad thing to step in and mediate.”  
“Thank you for your trouble,” the master replied coldly, but for some reason, upon hearing the phrase “the parties involved,” his heart stirred slightly. It felt as if a cool breeze had slipped through his sleeve on a muggy summer night. Originally, this master was a blunt, stubborn man, manufactured to be devoid of shine, but he was not a cold, unfeeling product of civilization. Whenever he spoke, he didn’t get angry and fume, but he could still grasp the news from here. The other day, he had quarreled with the nose because he disliked it, and the nose’s daughter was in no way at fault. He disliked businessmen, so it was no surprise that he also disliked Kaneda, who was a part of that world, but he had to say that this was a matter unrelated to the daughter herself. He had no feelings of gratitude or resentment toward her; Kangetsu was a student he loved even more than his own brother. If, as Suzuki-kun said, the parties involved were fond of each other, then it would not be the act of a gentleman to obstruct it indirectly. — Mr. Kushami still considered himself a gentleman. — If the parties involved were fond of each other—however, that is the issue. To change his attitude toward this matter, he must first ascertain the truth. “Does that girl want to go to Kangetsu? I don’t care about Kaneda or the nose, but what about the girl’s own intentions?”  
“Well, that is, um, what should I say—whatever it is—uh, she probably wants to go,” Suzuki-kun’s greeting was somewhat vague.

In truth, he had only intended to inquire about Kangetsu and report back, not confirming the young lady’s intentions. Thus, the smooth-talking Suzuki-kun appeared a bit flustered. “Those are rather ambiguous words,” the master said, as he couldn’t help but feel the need to confront him directly. “No, I must have expressed myself poorly. The young lady certainly has feelings for him. No, really—uh?—his wife told me so. She said that sometimes she speaks ill of Kangetsu, but deep down, she must really think highly of him.”  
“That girl?”  
“Yeah.”  
“What a suspicious person, speaking ill of him. First of all, doesn’t that mean she has no feelings for Kangetsu?”  
“That’s the thing; the world is strange, and sometimes people speak ill of those they like.”  
“What kind of fool would do that?” the master said, feeling no particular emotion upon hearing such subtleties of human nature. “There are plenty of such fools in the world, so it can’t be helped. In fact, Kaneda’s wife interprets it that way too. She says that she sometimes speaks ill of Kangetsu, like a confused gourd, so she must be thinking something in her heart.”  
The master, hearing this inexplicable interpretation, was so taken aback that he widened his eyes, speechless, staring at Suzuki-kun’s face as if he were a street fortune-teller. Suzuki-kun, sensing that he might be missing the mark, seemed to shift the conversation toward a direction where the master could make a judgment.

"Just think about it, can't you see? With that much wealth and such capability, they could send him to a suitable family anywhere. Kangetsu might be impressive, but in terms of status—no, that might be a bit rude to say—when it comes to wealth, well, anyone can see that it just doesn't match up. The fact that my parents are so worried that I have to go out of my way to visit is because the young man has an interest in Kangetsu, isn't it?" Mr. Suzuki explained with quite a clever reasoning. It seemed that this time the master was convinced as well, so he finally felt at ease. However, lingering here could lead to the risk of another outburst, so he realized it was best to move the conversation along and complete his mission as soon as possible. "And so, as I just said, the other party claims they don't want any money or property, but instead they want the qualifications that come with the person—qualifications, that is, a title. They boast that if he becomes a doctor, it would be acceptable. But let's not misunderstand. When Mrs. Kushami visited the other day, Meitei was there, saying all sorts of strange things—no, it’s not your fault. Mrs. Kushami praised you for being honest and straightforward. It was really Meitei's fault. So, if the young man could become a doctor, it would give him some standing in society, a sense of pride, you see. What do you think? Soon, Mizushima might submit his doctoral thesis and receive his doctorate. Well, as for Kaneda, he doesn’t need a doctorate or a bachelor’s degree; it’s just that society doesn’t make it so easy."

When I heard this, it began to seem not entirely unreasonable that they would request a doctorate from the other party. If it didn’t seem unreasonable, I felt inclined to do as Mr. Suzuki requested. The fate of the master lay entirely in Mr. Suzuki's hands. Indeed, the master was a simple and honest man. "Then, when Kangetsu comes next time, I’ll suggest he write a doctoral thesis. But first, I need to confirm whether he intends to marry Kaneda’s daughter."

"Confirming that? You can't just ask such a blunt question and expect things to work out. It’s best to subtly draw it out during a normal conversation."

"Draw it out?"

"Yes, though saying 'draw it out' might be misleading. You see, when you’re talking, it naturally becomes clear."

"You might understand that, but I can’t grasp what isn’t plainly stated."

"If you don’t understand, that’s fine. But I think it’s not good to meddle unnecessarily like Meitei did. Even if you don’t suggest it, this is something that should be left to the person’s discretion. So when Kangetsu comes next time, please try not to interfere as much as possible—no, I’m not talking about you, but about that Meitei.

With him around, there’s no way things will go smoothly." As I listened to the master speak ill of Meitei, just as he finished, Meitei himself floated in through the back door as if riding on the spring breeze. "Ah, what a rare visitor! When I’m like a familiar guest, Kushami tends to treat me rather rudely. It’s said that I only come to Kushami’s house once every ten years. This confection is better than usual, isn’t it?" he said, carelessly stuffing his mouth with the sweet. Mr. Suzuki was fidgeting. The master was grinning. Meitei was mumbling with his mouth full. I thought that this momentary scene could easily be the basis for a silent play. If silent dialogues in Zen are a form of telepathy, then this silent performance was clearly a curtain of telepathy as well. It was exceedingly brief, yet exceedingly sharp. "I thought you were a lifelong wanderer, but you’ve returned before I knew it. You must want to live long. Who knows what kind of fortune might come your way?" Meitei spoke to Mr. Suzuki as he would to the master, showing no signs of reservation whatsoever. Even among fellow lodgers, if you haven’t met for ten years, there’s a certain awkwardness, but with Meitei, such a demeanor was nowhere to be seen; whether that was admirable or foolish, I couldn’t quite tell. "Poor fellow, he’s not so foolish," Mr. Suzuki replied evasively, but he seemed somewhat unsettled, nervously fiddling with his usual gold chain. "Have you ridden the electric railway?" the master suddenly posed a strange question to Mr. Suzuki. "Today, I feel like I’ve come just to be teased by you all. No matter how much of a country bumpkin I am—I own sixty shares of the streetcar."

"That’s nothing to scoff at. I had eight hundred eighty-eight and a half shares, but unfortunately, most of them were eaten by bugs, and now I only have half a share left. If you had come to Tokyo a little earlier, I would have given you ten shares from the ones that weren’t eaten by bugs, but what a pity."

"Your tongue is still as sharp as ever. But joking aside, shares like that are worth holding onto; they only increase in value year by year."

"Indeed, even if it’s just half a share, if you hold it for a thousand years, you could build three warehouses. Both you and I are quite capable in that regard, but compared to that, Kushami is a pitiful case. When it comes to shares, he thinks of them as just a brother to radishes." As he reached for more of the sweet, he glanced at the master, who, catching Meitei's appetite, instinctively reached for the plate of treats. In this world, anything proactive has the right to be imitated by others. "I don’t care about shares, but I wanted to let Sorozaki ride the train at least once," the master said, gazing thoughtfully at the half-eaten sweet.

"If Sorozaki were to ride the train, every time he did, he’d end up in Shinagawa. It might be better for him to be carved into a stone tablet at Takuan instead."

"I heard that Sorozaki has passed away. What a pity; he was a good man with a fine mind, but what a loss," Mr. Suzuki said, and Meitei immediately took up the conversation. "His mind was good, but he was the worst at cooking rice. Whenever it was Sorozaki’s turn, I would go out and survive on soba."

"Indeed, the rice Sorozaki cooked was burnt and left me weak. To make matters worse, he always served cold tofu as a side dish, which was inedible," Mr. Suzuki recalled, bringing up grievances from ten years ago. "Kushami was Sorozaki’s close friend back then, and they would go out every night to eat sweet red bean soup together, but as a result, he’s now suffering from chronic stomach weakness. To tell the truth, Kushami has eaten more bowls of sweet red bean soup than Sorozaki, so it’s only natural that he should die before Sorozaki."

"What kind of logic is that? You, who called my sweet red bean soup a meal, went out every night with a bamboo sword to the back of the egg tombstone and got caught by a monk while you were banging on the stone monument," the master retorted, unwilling to lose to Meitei. "Ah, yes, yes, the monk said that hitting the Buddha’s head would disturb his peaceful sleep, so please stop. But while mine was a bamboo sword, this General Suzuki’s was a bare hand. I rolled around with the stone monument and knocked over about three of them."

"The monk’s anger at that time was truly fierce. He insisted that it must be restored to its original state, so when I asked him to wait until I could hire some laborers, he said that laborers wouldn’t do; to express repentance, you yourself must restore it, or you would go against the will of Buddha."

"Your appearance at that time was quite something; in a gold-striped shirt and a traditional loincloth, groaning in a puddle after the rain..."

"How irritating it is that you can draw that with such a composed face. I am not a man who gets angry easily, but at that moment, I truly thought it was rude. I still remember your words from that time; do you know them?"

"Who remembers words from ten years ago? However, I still recall that on the stone monument, it was inscribed: 'Kisen-in Don Ko-kaku, An'ei 5, Year of the Dragon, First Month.' That stone monument was made with an antique elegance. I almost wanted to steal it when I moved. It was truly a Gothic-style stone monument that conformed to the principles of aesthetics," Meitei again brandished his casual aesthetics. "That's fine, but your words went like this—'I intend to specialize in aesthetics, so I must sketch interesting occurrences in the world as references for the future. Feelings of pity or sympathy are not something a scholar like me should express.' You said that with such ease. I thought you were quite an unfeeling man, so I tore your sketchbook to shreds with my muddy hands."

"My promising artistic talent came to a halt and has not improved at all since that time. You broke my momentum. I hold a grudge against you."

"Don't be ridiculous. I am the one who feels resentful."

"Meitei was a braggart even back then," the master interjected, having finished his yokan (sweet bean jelly) and rejoining the conversation between the two. "He never fulfilled any promises. And when questioned, he never apologized, that so-called something-or-other. Back when the crape myrtle was blooming in the temple grounds, he said he would write a treatise on the principles of aesthetics before the flowers fell. I told him it was impossible; he could never manage it. Then Meitei replied, 'Though I may look like this, I am a man of strong will. If you doubt me, let us make a wager.' I took him seriously and bet that he would treat me to Western cuisine in Kanda or something. I thought he had no intention of writing anything, so I wagered, but deep down, I was a bit scared. I had no money to treat him to Western cuisine. However, the professor never even started writing. Days turned into weeks, and not a single page was produced. Eventually, when the crape myrtle had shed all its flowers, he remained unfazed, so I thought it was time to demand he fulfill his end of the bargain, but Meitei coolly brushed me off."

"Did he come up with some excuse again?" Suzuki interjected. "Yes, he is indeed a brazen man. I may not have any other talents, but I will never lose in willpower to you fellows," he stubbornly asserted. "Not a single page written, huh?" This time, Meitei himself asked. "Of course. At that time, you said, 'In terms of will, I will not yield an inch to anyone.' But unfortunately, my memory is particularly poor.

I had a sufficient will to write a treatise on aesthetics, but I forgot about it the day after I announced my intention to you. Therefore, the reason I could not produce the book before the crape myrtle fell was due to my memory's fault, not my will's. Since it is not a fault of will, I have no reason to treat you to Western cuisine," he boasted. "Indeed, this is a classic display of Meitei's character," Suzuki found it amusing for some reason. His tone was quite different from when Meitei was not present. Perhaps this is a trait of clever people. "What is so amusing about it?" The master still seemed angry. "That is unfortunate. That is why, to make up for it, I am searching for a peacock's tongue with money and drums. Well, don't be so angry; just wait. However, speaking of books, you know, I have brought you a major piece of news today."

"You are a man who brings major news every time, so I cannot let my guard down."

"However, today's news is truly remarkable. It is news without a price tag, not even a single rin. Do you know that Kangetsu has started drafting his doctoral thesis? I thought he would not engage in such a tedious task, being such an oddly opinionated man, but it seems he has some interest after all. You should definitely inform that nose of his; he might be dreaming of becoming a doctor these days."

Upon hearing Kangetsu's name, Suzuki made a gesture to the master, signaling that it was a topic to avoid. The master, however, did not understand at all. Earlier, when he met Suzuki and received his teachings, he had felt pity for Kaneda's daughter, but now, hearing Meitei's comments, he recalled the quarrel they had the other day. Remembering it was both comical and somewhat shameful. However, the fact that Kangetsu had started drafting a doctoral thesis was a splendid gift, and this was indeed a recent piece of remarkable news, not just any news, but a delightful and pleasing one. Whether he married Kaneda's daughter or not was of little consequence. In any case, it was wonderful that Kangetsu was becoming a doctor. I would not mind if a poorly made wooden statue like myself rotted in a corner of a sculptor's workshop, but I would like to see a well-crafted sculpture adorned with gold leaf as soon as possible. "Did he really start writing a thesis?" Ignoring Suzuki's signal, the master asked eagerly. "He is a man who often doubts what others say. —Though the issue is whether it's about acorns or the mechanics of hanging oneself, I can't say for sure. In any case, since it's Kangetsu, it must be something that would make his nose feel embarrassed."

Every time Meitei casually mentioned Kangetsu, Suzuki displayed signs of anxiety. Meitei, completely oblivious, remained unfazed.

"After that, he did further research, and recently, I discovered a theory about noses in Tristram Shandy. If only Kaneda's nose had been shown to Sterne, it would have made for excellent material; what a pity. Though it had ample qualifications to be remembered for ages, it will rot away as it is, which is truly unfortunate. Next time he comes here, I will sketch it for aesthetic reference," he continued to chatter nonsensically. "However, I hear that girl wants to go to Kangetsu," the master stated, repeating what he had just heard from Suzuki. Suzuki made a face that indicated this was troublesome and kept signaling the master, but the master remained completely oblivious. "That's a bit odd. Even a child like that can fall in love, but it probably isn't a serious love; it's likely just a crush on his nose."

"If it's just a crush, Kangetsu might as well take her."

"He might as well, but you were vehemently opposed to it the other day. You're awfully softening up today."

"I am not softening up; I will never soften up, but…"

"But what? Hey, Suzuki, since you are also one of the businesspeople, let me tell you for reference. That Kaneda fellow. To revere the daughter of that fellow as the wife of the world's genius, Mizushima Kangetsu, is a bit like mixing a lantern with a bell, and I think we, as friends, cannot let that go by without comment. Even you, as a businessman, must have some reservations about this."

"You are still as lively as ever. That's good. You haven't changed at all in ten years," Suzuki responded, trying to deflect. "If you are going to praise me, I could show you a bit more of my erudition. The ancient Greeks valued physical education highly and offered valuable prizes for all competitions, devising various incentives. However, strangely enough, there are no records of any rewards given for scholarly knowledge, and until today, I have been quite suspicious."

"That does seem a bit strange," Suzuki continued to match his tone. "Then just a couple of days ago, while studying aesthetics, I happened to discover the reason, and all my long-held suspicions were suddenly resolved. It was a thrilling revelation, like pulling a lacquer bucket, and I reached a state of ecstatic joy."

The words of Meitei were so grandiloquent that even the highly skilled Suzuki-kun wore a face that suggested he found it all too much to handle. The master, not wanting to say anything, merely tapped the edge of the sweet dish with his ivory chopsticks, looking down. Only Meitei continued to speak with great confidence. “Now, who do you think is the one who has clearly articulated the explanation of this contradictory phenomenon, rescuing our doubts from the abyss of darkness? It is none other than that philosopher of ancient Greece, the founder of the Peripatetic school, Aristotle himself, who is hailed as the scholar since the advent of learning. According to his explanation—ah, don’t bang on that sweet dish and listen attentively—what the Greeks receive as rewards in their competitions is more precious than the very skills they perform. Thus, it serves as both a prize and a means of encouragement. But what about knowledge itself? If one were to offer a reward for knowledge, it must be something of greater value than knowledge itself. But is there any treasure in this world that surpasses knowledge? Of course, there cannot be. To offer something inferior would only diminish the dignity of knowledge. They piled up a treasure trove of a thousand ryo (a unit of currency) on Olympus, exhausting the wealth of Croesus, in an attempt to provide a suitable reward for knowledge, yet they saw that no matter how they thought about it, it could never balance out. Thus, from that time onward, they decided to give nothing at all. It is clear that yellow, white, and blue coins cannot match knowledge. Now, armed with this principle, let us face the current issues. What is Kaneda but a person with eyes and a nose drawn on a banknote? To describe him with a peculiar phrase, he is merely an active banknote. If he is an active banknote, then his daughter would be something like an active postage stamp. On the other hand, what of Kangetsu? He graduated at the top of the highest seat of learning without a hint of fatigue, dangling the cord of his haori (a traditional jacket) from the time of the Chōshū expedition, studying the stability of acorns day and night, and still shows no signs of satisfaction, as he is about to publish a grand thesis that will soon overwhelm Lord Kelvin. He once happened to pass by Azumabashi and failed in the art of jumping into the river, but that was merely a momentary act typical of a passionate youth and hardly an event that would trouble him as a purveyor of knowledge. To use Meitei’s own metaphor, Kangetsu is an active library, a bullet crafted from twenty-eight grains of knowledge.

If this bullet were to explode at the right moment in the academic world—if it were to explode—then it surely would!”

At this point, Meitei seemed somewhat flustered, as the adjectives he usually used to describe himself did not come to mind, giving off a feeling of what is commonly referred to as a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail. But he quickly added, “Even if there were millions of active postage stamps, they would be reduced to dust. Therefore, Kangetsu cannot be with a woman so mismatched. It would be like marrying the wisest elephant among all beasts to the most greedy little pig. Wouldn’t you agree, Kushami-kun?” With that, he dismissed the matter, and the master resumed tapping the sweet dish in silence. Suzuki-kun, feeling somewhat deflated, replied, “That may not be the case.”

Having just spoken ill of Meitei, he knew that saying something reckless here could provoke a lawless person like the master into saying anything. It was wise to handle Meitei’s sharp tongue with care and navigate the situation safely. Suzuki-kun was a clever man. He believed that unnecessary resistance should be avoided at all costs, and that pointless arguments were relics of the feudal era. The purpose of life lay not in words but in action. If events progressed smoothly according to one’s own wishes, then the purpose of life was fulfilled. If events progressed without trouble, worry, or argument, then one could reach a state of bliss. Suzuki-kun succeeded after graduation through this blissful philosophy, hung a gold watch around his neck, accepted the Kaneda couple’s request through this same blissful philosophy, and successfully persuaded Kushami-kun to the point where the matter was nearly resolved. Just then, a wanderer, who seemed to possess a psychological mechanism beyond that of ordinary humans, entered the scene, causing a bit of surprise at his sudden appearance. The one who invented the philosophy of bliss was a gentleman of the Meiji era, the one who practiced it was Suzuki Tojuro-kun, and the one who was now troubled by it was also Suzuki Tojuro-kun. “You think you know nothing, and so you say it may not be the case, acting unusually refined and reserved. But did you see how that owner of the nose behaved when he came the other day? Even the most esteemed businessman would be utterly dismayed, wouldn’t you agree, Kushami-kun? You fought valiantly, didn’t you?” 

“Even so, it seems I have a better reputation than you.”

“Ah, ha ha ha! What a confident man you are! Otherwise, how could you go to school with students and teachers mocking you as ‘Savage Chi’? I, too, intend to have a will no less than anyone else, but I cannot be so thick-skinned; I truly admire you for that.”

“What’s so frightening about a few students and teachers grumbling?

Sainte-Beuve, a unique critic throughout history, was quite unpopular when he lectured at the University of Paris, and to defend himself against student attacks, he would always carry a dagger hidden in his sleeve. When Brunetchel attacked Zola’s novels at the same Paris university…”

“But you’re neither a university teacher nor anything of the sort. Just a mere teacher of Riddle, using such great figures as examples is like a small fish trying to compare itself to a whale; saying such things will only get you mocked even more.”

“Be quiet. Sainte-Beuve and I are just about the same kind of scholar.”

“What a grand perspective you have! But it’s dangerous to walk around with a dagger, so you’d better not imitate that. If a university teacher has a dagger, then a Riddle teacher would have something like a small knife. Even so, knives are dangerous, so it would be better to go to Nakamise and buy a toy air gun to carry around. It’s charming and nice. Isn’t that right, Suzuki-kun?” At this, Suzuki-kun finally felt relieved as the conversation shifted away from the Kaneda incident. “You remain as innocent and delightful as ever. After ten years, meeting you all feels like stepping out from a cramped path into a wide field. Our discussions among friends are never relaxed. We must be cautious about what we say, which is quite stressful and truly painful. It’s good to talk about things that are innocent. And speaking with friends from my student days is the best, as there’s no need for restraint. Ah, today I unexpectedly met Meitei-kun, and it was delightful. I have some business to attend to, so I must take my leave.” As Suzuki-kun stood to leave, Meitei said, “I’ll go too; I must head to the Japanese Bridge to the Performance Reform Society, so let’s go together.” “That’s just right; it’s been a while since we strolled together,” the two of them said, linking arms as they departed.

To write down the events of a full twenty-four hours without missing a single detail, and to read them without omission, would surely take at least twenty-four hours. Even for one such as I, who advocates for the art of descriptive writing, I must confess that this is an endeavor far beyond the capabilities of a mere cat. Therefore, it is quite regrettable that my master lacks the ability and patience to inform the readers of every peculiar word and action he engages in, despite his incessant and meticulous descriptions. Regrettable, indeed, but unavoidable. Even a cat requires rest. After Suzuki-kun and Meitei-kun returned, the wind blew in a sudden gust, and the night became as quiet as the softly falling snow. My master, as usual, retreated to his study. The children laid their pillows in the six-tatami room and went to sleep. Separated by a sliding door, in the south-facing room, my mistress lay down with her three-year-old daughter, Menko, nursing her. The day, hastened by the cloudy twilight, quickly faded, and even the sound of wooden clogs passing outside echoed distinctly into the tea room. From the boarding house in the neighboring town, the sound of a flute occasionally drifted in, providing a dull stimulus to my sleepy ears. Outside, it was likely quite hazy. After a dinner of abalone in a thin broth, my master certainly needed rest. I have faintly heard that there exists a phenomenon in the world referred to as "cat love," and that there are nights in spring when the local cats wander about in a state of excitement, unable to settle their dreams. However, I have yet to encounter such a psychological transformation. After all, love is a cosmic force. From the god Jupiter in the heavens above to the earthworm burrowing below, it is the nature of all beings to become enamored in this way. Thus, it is not surprising that we cats might express a vague delight and a somewhat troublesome aesthetic. Upon reflection, I too have once been infatuated with Mikeko. It is rumored that Tomiko Kaneda, the daughter of the triangle theorist Kaneda-kun, has even harbored feelings for Kangetsu-kun. Therefore, I hold no contempt for the frenzied dance of male and female cats under the spring night sky, but alas, even if I were invited, I find myself devoid of such feelings. At present, I only desire rest. With such drowsiness, I cannot even entertain thoughts of love. I lazily turned around to the edge of the children's futon and comfortably fell asleep. Suddenly, I opened my eyes and saw that my master had, without my noticing, come from the study to the bedroom and had slipped into the futon beside my mistress. It is a habit of my master to always bring a small book with him when he goes to bed.

However, he has never read more than two pages of it while lying down. Sometimes he merely places it by his pillow without even touching it. One might wonder why he goes to the trouble of bringing it if he does not intend to read it, but that is what makes him my master. No matter how much my mistress laughs or tells him to stop, he never agrees to abandon the practice. Every night, he dutifully brings unread books all the way to the bedroom. At times, he even brings three or four volumes at once. Just the other night, he brought Webster's dictionary with him. I surmise that this is a peculiar affliction of my master; just as a luxurious person cannot sleep without hearing the sound of the pine wind at Ryubundo, my master cannot sleep unless he has books by his side. Thus, for him, books serve not as reading material but as instruments to induce sleep. They are, in essence, a sleep-inducing tonic. Peeking in to see if anything was amiss tonight, I found a thin red book half-open and resting at the tip of my master's mustache. From the fact that his left thumb was wedged between the pages, it seemed he had read five or six lines tonight, which is quite remarkable. Next to the red book, as usual, the nickel pocket watch emitted a cold color unbefitting of spring. My mistress had thrown the nursing child about a foot away and was snoring with her mouth open, having kicked her pillow aside. I believe there is nothing more unbecoming in a human than to sleep with one's mouth agape. Cats, throughout their lives, have never suffered such embarrassment. After all, the mouth is a tool for making sounds, and the nose is for inhaling and exhaling air. It is true that in the northern regions, some humans, in their laziness, try to keep their mouths shut, resulting in a peculiar way of speaking through their noses, but I think it is even more unbecoming to breathe solely through the mouth while blocking the nose. First of all, it would be dangerous if mouse droppings fell from the ceiling. As for the children, they too were sprawled out in a manner not unlike their parents. The older sister, Tonko, stretched her right arm out as if to claim her right as the elder, resting it atop her younger sister's ear. In retaliation, the younger sister, Sunko, raised one foot and stomped on her sister's belly. Both had certainly rotated at least ninety degrees from their sleeping positions. Yet, despite this unnatural posture, both remained sound asleep without a hint of complaint. Indeed, the spring light is exceptional. This scene, innocent yet devoid of any artistic flair, seems to shine brightly as if urging one to cherish the beautiful night.

I looked around the room to see that it was quiet, with only the ticking of the clock, my mistress's snoring, and the distant sound of a maid grinding her teeth breaking the silence. This maid always denies it when accused of grinding her teeth. She stubbornly insists, "I have no recollection of ever grinding my teeth since the day I was born," and never concedes to correcting it, nor does she express any sympathy. She simply asserts that she has no such memory. Indeed, since it is a skill performed while asleep, it is likely she has no recollection. However, the fact remains that something can exist even if one is unaware of it, which is quite troublesome. There are people in the world who engage in wrongdoing while believing themselves to be virtuous. While it is innocent and commendable to have confidence in one's own innocence, the troublesome realities that affect others cannot simply be dismissed, no matter how innocent one may be. I believe such gentlemen and ladies belong to the same lineage as this maid. — The night seems to have grown quite late. There was a light knock on the kitchen's rain shutters, two soft taps. How strange; it is unlikely anyone would come at this hour. It is probably just the usual mouse. If it is a mouse, I have resolved not to catch it, so it may do as it pleases. — Another knock. This does not seem like a mouse. Even a mouse would be exceedingly cautious. The mice inside my master's house are like students from his school, always engaged in rowdy training, whether day or night, and they seem to take delight in startling my master from his peaceful dreams as if it were their vocation. Thus, they would have no reason to be so hesitant. That was certainly not a mouse. Now I hear the sound of someone lifting the rain shutters from below, and at the same time, the sliding door is being gently eased along its groove. It is definitely not a mouse. It must be a human. If a human is entering without asking for permission or unfastening the door at this late hour, it can only be either Meitei-sensei or Suzuki-kun. Perhaps it is the notorious thief I have heard so much about. If it is indeed the thief, I would very much like to see his esteemed face. The thief seems to have stepped boldly into the house, leaving great muddy footprints, and has advanced a couple of steps. Just as I thought it was the third step, he stumbled on the raised floorboard, making a sound that echoed through the night. I felt as if the fur on my back had been brushed the wrong way by a shoe brush. For a moment, there was no sound of footsteps. Looking at my mistress, she was still sleeping with her mouth open, blissfully exhaling the tranquil air. My master, I suppose, was dreaming of the red book wedged between his thumb.
Soon, I heard the sound of a match being struck in the kitchen. It seems even the thief cannot see as well in the dark as I can. It must be quite inconvenient for him.

At this moment, I pondered while crouching. Would the thief emerge from the tea room side, or would he turn left and pass through the entrance to the study? — The sound of footsteps came with the sliding door’s creak, and the thief finally crawled into the study. After that, there was no sound or sign of him. In the meantime, I realized that I wanted to wake my master and mistress quickly, but I had no idea how to do so. My thoughts spun around in my head like a waterwheel, without any clear plan. I thought about tugging at the edge of the futon to shake it, and tried it a couple of times, but it had no effect. I considered rubbing my cold nose against their cheeks, so I brought it close to my master’s face, but he merely stretched out his hand while still asleep and pushed my nose away as if to say, “No.” The nose is a vital spot for a cat, and it hurt tremendously. Since there was no other option, I decided to meow a couple of times to wake him, but for some reason, at that moment, my throat felt constricted, and I couldn't produce the sound I wanted. After much effort, I managed to let out a low sound, and to my surprise, my master showed no sign of waking, while suddenly the thief’s footsteps began again. They approached, crunching along the wooden floor. He had indeed come; at this point, I thought it was hopeless, and I resigned myself to hiding between the sliding door and the wicker trunk, watching for any movement. The thief’s footsteps stopped right in front of the bedroom’s sliding door. I held my breath, intensely curious about what he would do next. Upon reflection, I realized that when I’m catching a mouse, I never feel this way; my soul feels like it’s about to leap out of my eyes. I was truly grateful for the enlightenment that the thief had inadvertently provided me. Suddenly, the middle of the sliding door’s frame changed color as if wet by rain. Through it, something pale pink gradually became more vivid, and before I knew it, the paper tore, revealing a red tongue that flicked out. The tongue vanished into the darkness in an instant. Then, something that glimmered ominously appeared on the other side of the torn hole. Without a doubt, it was the thief’s eye. Strangely, that eye seemed to be focused solely on me, who was hiding behind the wicker trunk, without noticing anything else in the room. Though it was less than a minute, I felt as if my life was shortening under that gaze. Just as I decided I could no longer endure it and would leap out from behind the trunk, the bedroom’s sliding door slid open, and the waiting thief finally appeared before me.

As for the order of my narrative, I have the honor of introducing to you the unexpected guest, the thief himself, but before that, I would like to share a brief opinion for your consideration. Ancient gods are revered as omniscient and omnipotent. In particular, the god of Christianity still wears this mask of omniscience and omnipotence even today in the twentieth century. However, the omniscience and omnipotence that ordinary people conceive can sometimes be interpreted as ignorance and impotence. This is clearly a paradox. Yet, when I consider that I may be the only one to have unraveled this paradox since the creation of heaven and earth, a sense of vanity arises within me, suggesting that I am not just any cat. Thus, I feel compelled to present my reasoning here, to impress upon the proud humans that cats should not be underestimated. It is said that all things in heaven and earth were created by God, which implies that humans are also a product of divine creation. Indeed, it is written in the Bible that this is the case. Now, regarding humans, there is a fact that they have observed for thousands of years, marveling greatly at the profound mysteries while increasingly acknowledging God’s omniscience and omnipotence. This is none other than the fact that, despite the multitude of humans, there is not a single person in the world with the same face. The tools of the face are, of course, limited, and the general sizes are somewhat similar. In other words, they are all made from the same material, yet not a single one has resulted in the same outcome. When I think about how someone could conceive such a bizarre variety of faces from such simple materials, I cannot help but admire the skill of the creator. It must take a great deal of original imagination to achieve such variations. If a single artist, after exhausting their energy, can only produce a dozen or so different faces, then the divine craftsmanship that took on the task of creating humans must be truly exceptional. This is a feat that cannot be witnessed in human society, so it would not be inappropriate to call it an omnipotent skill. Humans seem to greatly fear God in this regard, and indeed, from their observational standpoint, such fear is quite reasonable. However, from a cat’s perspective, the same fact can be interpreted as evidence of God’s impotence. I believe it can be concluded that, even if not entirely incapable, there is certainly no greater ability than that of humans. It is said that God created as many faces as there are humans, but whether he had a plan from the beginning to achieve such variation, or whether he attempted to create all cats with the same face but ultimately failed, resulting in this chaotic state, is unclear.

The structure of their faces can be seen as a testament to God’s success while also bearing the marks of failure. It could be said to be omnipotent, but it would also not be inappropriate to describe it as impotent. The eyes of these humans are aligned on a flat plane, preventing them from seeing both sides at once, which is unfortunate, as they can only perceive half of things at a time. From another perspective, such a simple fact is constantly occurring in their society, yet they remain oblivious, overwhelmed by their own arrogance and consumed by God. If it is difficult to express variation in creation, then it is equally difficult to demonstrate thorough imitation. Asking Raphael to paint two identical images of the Virgin Mary would be as troublesome as demanding to see two completely different Madonnas. It might even be more difficult for Raphael to paint the same thing twice. It could be even more challenging to ask the great Kobo Daishi to write in the same style as yesterday, rather than simply requesting a different script. The language that humans use is entirely based on imitation. When they learn practical language from their mothers, nurses, or others, they have no ambition other than to repeat what they have heard. They strive to imitate as best they can. As this language, which is established through imitation, evolves over ten or twenty years, the natural changes in pronunciation demonstrate that they do not possess complete imitative ability. Pure imitation is thus exceedingly difficult. Therefore, if God could create humans in such a way that they could not be distinguished from one another, like a stamp, it would further demonstrate God’s omnipotence, while simultaneously allowing for the chaotic variety of faces we see today, which could indicate his impotence. I have forgotten why I engaged in such a discussion. Forgetting books is something even humans do, so I hope you will overlook it as a natural occurrence for a cat. In any case, when I caught sight of the thief emerging from the bedroom’s sliding door and appearing suddenly on the threshold, the above thoughts naturally welled up within me. Why did they arise? — If that question arises, I must reconsider. — Well, the reason is as follows. **Chapter 1**

When I beheld the face of the thief appearing before me with an air of nonchalance, I was struck by the fact that it possessed a feature so distinctive that it could instantly dispel my earlier doubts about the divine craftsmanship of the ordinary man. This feature was none other than the resemblance of his countenance to that of my dear friend, the handsome Mr. Kangetsu.

Of course, I do not have many acquaintances among thieves, but from the roughness of their deeds, I had imagined a face in my mind that was not entirely unfounded. I had concluded, in my own way, that it would be a face with small nostrils and eyes the size of a one-sen copper coin, crowned with a chestnut-like head. However, seeing is different from imagining; imagination is never as robust as reality. This thief was tall and slender, with a dark complexion and straight eyebrows, a remarkably spirited rogue. He appeared to be around twenty-six or twenty-seven years of age, which only made him resemble Kangetsu even more. If the divine could indeed produce two such similar faces, it would be unreasonable to regard it as a sign of incompetence. In fact, I was so taken aback by the resemblance that I wondered if Kangetsu himself had gone mad and dashed out in the middle of the night. It was only when I noticed the absence of a faint black stubble beneath his nose that I realized he must be a different person. Kangetsu was a handsome man with a bitter disposition, a creation so meticulous that he could easily win over Miss Tomiko Kaneda, who was often praised by Meitei. Yet, upon observing the thief's features, it was clear that he possessed an equal magnetic attraction towards women, not yielding an inch to Kangetsu. If Miss Kaneda were to be captivated by Kangetsu's gaze or charm, it would be only fair for her to be equally enamored by this rogue. Fairness aside, it defied logic. Ah, with such talent and an innate ability to grasp everything quickly, she would surely understand this much without needing to be told. Therefore, if this thief were to be presented in place of Kangetsu, she would undoubtedly shower him with all her love and achieve a harmonious union. Even if Kangetsu were swayed by the sermons of Meitei and this ancient bond were to be severed, as long as this thief remained in existence, there would be no cause for concern. I had anticipated the unfolding of future events to this extent, and for Miss Tomiko's sake, I finally felt a sense of relief. The existence of this thief was a crucial condition for ensuring Miss Tomiko's happiness in life. The thief was carrying something under his arm. Upon closer inspection, it was the old blanket that the master had carelessly tossed into the study earlier. Clad in a cotton padded jacket and a Hakata obi tied around his waist, his bare shins exposed from the knees down, he now lifted one foot to step onto the tatami. The master, who had been dreaming of biting his finger while reading a red book, suddenly turned over and exclaimed loudly, “Kangetsu!” The thief dropped the blanket and quickly pulled back the foot he had extended.

In the shadow of the shoji, two slender shins stood still, moving slightly. The master mumbled and grumbled as he pushed aside the familiar red book, scratching his black arm as if afflicted with a skin disease. After that, silence fell, and he removed his pillow and fell back asleep. It seemed that his utterance of “Kangetsu” was merely a sleep-talking whim. The thief stood for a while by the porch, observing the movements inside the room, and upon confirming that the master and his wife were sound asleep, he again placed one foot onto the tatami. This time, there was no sound of “Kangetsu.” Soon, the other foot followed suit. The six-tatami mat room, richly illuminated by the spring light, was sharply divided by the thief's shadow, casting darkness halfway up the wall above my head. When I turned to look, the shadow of the thief's face was vaguely moving at about two-thirds the height of the wall. Viewed only as a shadow, the handsome man appeared in a truly strange guise, like a monster with eight heads. The thief peered down at the sleeping face of the lady, grinning for some unknown reason. I was astonished to see that even his manner of laughing was a mimicry of Kangetsu. At the lady's bedside, there was a box, about four inches square and a foot and a half long, carefully placed as if it were a treasured item. This was the yam that Mr. Tatara Sampei, a resident of Karatsu in Hizen Province, had brought back as a souvenir during his recent visit. While it is not common to decorate one's bedside with yams, this lady was of a nature that lacked any sense of appropriateness regarding where to place things, as she would even put pickled daikon in her bedroom without a second thought. However, the thief, being no god, could not possibly know such a woman. Given the reverent way it was placed so close to her, it was only natural for him to assume it was a valuable item. The thief lifted the yam box slightly, and finding its weight to match his expectations, he appeared quite satisfied. As I thought, “Surely he will not steal the yam,” the thought of this handsome rogue stealing the yam suddenly struck me as amusing. However, it was dangerous to make a sound, so he remained silent and restrained. Eventually, the thief began to wrap the yam box carefully in the old blanket. He looked around for something to tie it with and fortunately found the crepe obi that the master had discarded when going to bed. The thief secured the yam box tightly with this obi and effortlessly hoisted it onto his back. It was not a very ladylike appearance.

Then, he stuffed two children's jackets into the master's baggy trousers, causing the area around his groin to bulge out like a snake that had swallowed a frog—or perhaps it would be more accurately described as a snake in its final month of pregnancy. In any case, it was a peculiar sight. If you doubt it, you may try it yourself. The thief wrapped the trousers around his neck. As for what he would do next, he spread the master's silk jacket like a large furoshiki and neatly folded in the lady's obi, the master's haori, and various other miscellaneous items. I was somewhat impressed by his skillful and adept handling. Then, he continued to tie together the lady's obi and shigoki (a type of sash) and secured the bundle in one hand. While looking around to see if there was anything else to take, he noticed a “Asahi” bag above the master's head, tossed it into his sleeve, and pulled out a stick from the bag to light it at the lamp. The delicious-looking smoke that he deeply inhaled and exhaled curled around the milky glass shade, and before it could dissipate, the sound of the thief's footsteps gradually faded away along the porch. The master and his wife remained sound asleep. Humans can be surprisingly oblivious. I, too, required a moment of rest. If I kept chattering away, my body would not hold up. When I finally fell into a deep sleep and awoke, the sky of Yayoi was brilliantly clear, and the master and his wife were conversing with a police officer at the back door. “Then, you entered from here and went around to the bedroom, correct? You were completely unaware while you were sleeping, I take it?”  
“Yes,” the master replied, looking somewhat embarrassed. “And when did the theft occur?” the officer asked, posing an unreasonable question. If they knew the time, there would have been no need for anything to be stolen. The oblivious master and his wife were repeatedly consulting each other regarding this inquiry. “What time was it?”  
“Well,” the lady pondered, seemingly thinking that if she thought hard enough, she would remember. “What time did you go to bed last night?”  
“I went to bed after you.”  
“Yes, I lay down before you.”  
“What time did you wake up?”  
“It must have been around seven-thirty.”  
“Then, what time do you suppose the thief entered?”  
“Well, it must have been in the middle of the night.”  
“That's obvious, but what time exactly?”

"One cannot truly understand without careful consideration," Mrs. Kushami still seems to be pondering. The police officer had only asked out of formality, so he feels no particular concern about when the incident occurred. He thinks it would suffice if the couple could provide any sort of answer, even if it were a lie, but since the husband and wife are engaged in a rather vague exchange, he appears to grow a bit impatient. "Then, the time of the theft is unknown, is it?" he says, to which the husband replies in his usual tone, "Well, yes." The police officer, without a hint of a smile, continues, "Then, on what date in the thirty-eighth year of Meiji did you lock up and go to bed, at which time the thief removed the shutters from such-and-such a window and sneaked in to steal several items? Please provide a written statement of your complaint. It should be a complaint that is not addressed to anyone in particular."

"Do I have to list each item?" 

"Yes, you will need to itemize them, stating how many haori (a traditional jacket) and their value, and so forth. — No, it’s pointless to go in and see now. The items are already gone," he says, leaving with an air of indifference. The husband brings out the inkstone to the center of the tatami room and calls for his wife, saying, "I will write the theft report now, so tell me everything that was stolen. Come on, speak up," he says in a tone as if they were about to quarrel. "Oh, how rude! Who do you think you are, demanding that I speak?" she replies, sitting down with her obi still wrapped around her. "What’s with that attitude? You look like a failed courtesan. Why didn’t you come out properly dressed?" 

"If this is bad, then please buy me something else. Whether I’m a courtesan or whatever, if I’m stolen from, it can’t be helped, can it?" 

"Did they even take your obi? What a cruel thief! Then I’ll start by writing down the obi. What kind of obi was it?" 

"What kind, you ask? Do you think I have so many? It was a black silk obi and a crepe obi sewn together."

"A black silk and crepe obi — how much is it worth?" 

"About six yen, I suppose." 

"How extravagant to wear such an expensive obi! From now on, stick to one that costs about one yen and fifty sen." 

"Is there even such an obi? This is why you’re so unfeeling. A wife, no matter how shabby she looks, if it suits her husband, it’s all fine, isn’t it?" 

"Well, whatever. What’s next?" 

"It’s a woven haori. That was given to me by Aunt Kōno, and even though it’s the same kind of woven fabric, it’s of a different quality than the current ones." 

"I don’t need to hear your explanations. What’s the price?" 

"Fifteen yen." 

"To wear a fifteen-yen haori is unbecoming of your status." 

"Isn’t it fine?

If you buy it for me, then it’s settled." 

"What’s next?" 

"A pair of black tabi (traditional socks)." 

"Yours?" 

"Of course, yours. The price is twenty-seven sen." 

"And then?" 

"A box of yam." 

"They even took the yam? Were you planning to boil it or make it into tororo (grated yam)?" 

"I don’t know what they were planning. Why don’t you go ask the thief?" 

"How much does it cost?" 

"I don’t know the price of yam." 

"Then let’s say it’s about twelve yen and fifty sen." 

"That’s ridiculous! No matter how much you dig it up from Karatsu, yam shouldn’t cost twelve yen and fifty sen!" 

"But you just said you don’t know." 

"I don’t know, but twelve yen and fifty sen is outrageous!" 

"What do you mean it’s outrageous when you don’t know? That doesn’t make any sense. That’s why I say you’re an otanchin paleologus." 

"What did you say?" 

"Otanchin paleologus." 

"What does that mean?" 

"It means whatever. And what about my kimono? It hasn’t shown up at all." 

"Anything else is fine. Just tell me the meaning of otanchin paleologus." 

"There’s no meaning to it." 

"Well, you could at least tell me. You must think I’m quite foolish. You probably think I don’t know English and are saying bad things about me." 

"Don’t say foolish things, just hurry up and finish. If you don’t file the complaint quickly, the items won’t be returned." 

"Even if I file a complaint now, it won’t matter. More importantly, please tell me what otanchin paleologus means." 

"What a noisy woman you are! I told you there’s no meaning." 

"Then, there are no more items left." 

"You’re being stubborn. Do whatever you want. I won’t write the theft report anymore." 

"I won’t tell you the list either. You can file the complaint yourself, so I won’t be troubled if you don’t write it." 

"Then I’ll just abandon it," the husband says, standing up abruptly and heading into the study. Mrs. Kushami retreats to the tea room and sits down in front of the sewing box. Both of them sit in silence, staring at the shoji (sliding paper doors) for about ten minutes without doing anything. At that moment, with a lively entrance, the donor of the yam, Tatara Sampei, comes in. Sampei was once a student in this household, but now he has graduated from law school and is employed in the mining department of a certain company. He is also a budding businessman, a junior to Suzuki Tojuro. Due to their previous relationship, Sampei often visits his old teacher’s humble abode and spends Sundays playing around before heading home, so he shares an informal relationship with the family. "Good day, Mrs. Kushami. What nice weather we have," he says, kneeling in front of her in his trousers, with a hint of a Karatsu accent. "Oh, Mr.

Tatara!" 

"Where has the teacher gone?" 

"No, he’s in the study." 

"Mrs. Kushami, if you study like the teacher, it’s poison, you know. It’s a rare Sunday after all." 

"It won’t do any good if you tell me; you should tell the teacher that." 

"Well, that’s true, but…" Sampei starts to say, looking around the room, "I don’t see the young lady today," and just as he half-asks Mrs. Kushami, Tonko and Sunko rush out from the next room. "Mr. Tatara, did you bring sushi today?" the elder sister Tonko remembers their previous promise and immediately prompts Sampei upon seeing his face. Sampei scratches his head and admits, "You remember well! I’ll definitely bring it next time. I forgot today." 

"Oh, how awful!" the sister says, and the younger sister immediately mimics her, saying, "Oh, how awful!" Mrs. Kushami finally lightens up a bit and smiles. "I didn’t bring sushi, but I did bring yam. Did the young lady eat it?" 

"What’s yam?" the sister asks, and the younger sister again mimics, "What’s yam?" as she asks Sampei. "Haven’t you eaten it yet? Hurry and have your mother boil it for you. The yam from Karatsu is different from the one in Tokyo and is delicious," Sampei boasts about his hometown, and Mrs. Kushami finally realizes, "Thank you very much for your kindness in bringing so much, Mr. Tatara." 

"How is it? Did you eat it? I packed it tightly in a box so it wouldn’t break, so it should still be long." 

"However, the yam you kindly brought was stolen by a thief last night." 

"A thief? What a foolish man! Is there really a man who loves yam that much?" Sampei expresses his astonishment. "Mother, did a thief break in last night?" the sister asks. "Yes," Mrs. Kushami replies lightly. "A thief broke in — and then — what kind of face did the thief have?" the younger sister asks this strange question. Mrs. Kushami, unsure how to respond, says, "He had a scary face," and looks toward Sampei. "A scary face? Do you mean a face like Mr. Tatara’s?" the sister asks, seemingly without pity, pressing for an answer. "What a rude thing to say!"

「Hahaha, is my face really that frightening? What a bother,」 he scratched his head. On the back of Tatara's head, there was a bald patch about an inch in diameter. It had appeared a month ago, and although he had consulted a doctor, it still showed no signs of healing easily. The first to notice this baldness was his sister, Tonko. "Oh, Tatara-san's head shines like Mother’s!"  
"I told you to be quiet."  
"Mother, the thief's head was shining last night too," this was a question from his younger sister.

Both his wife and Tatara couldn't help but burst out laughing, but since it was too bothersome to continue talking, his wife finally shooed the children away, saying, "Now, now, you two go play in the garden for a bit. Mother will give you some nice sweets soon." Then she turned back to Tatara and asked seriously, "What happened to your head?"  
"An insect has been eating it. It’s not healing well. Do you have any experience with this, ma'am?"  
"Oh dear, insects eating it? Well, since you have a topknot, it’s only natural for it to be a bit bald."  
"Baldness is all bacteria."  
"My baldness is not due to bacteria."  
"Ah, you want to be stubborn."  
"Not everything is bacteria. But there’s a term for baldness in English, isn’t there?"  
"Baldness is called 'bald' or something like that."  
"No, that’s not it; there’s a longer name, isn’t there?"  
"If you ask the teacher, you’ll find out right away."  
"The teacher won’t tell me, so I’m asking you."  
"I don’t know anything longer than 'bald.' What’s it like?"  
"It’s called 'Otanchin Paleologus.' 'Otanchin' means bald, and 'Paleologus' must mean head."  
"That might be true. I’ll go to the teacher’s study and look it up in Webster’s soon. But the teacher is quite peculiar. On such a fine day, staying indoors—oh dear, that won’t help his stomach ailment. You should suggest he go out for a cherry blossom viewing in Ueno."  
"You take him out. The teacher never listens to what women say."  
"Does he still lick jam these days?"  
"Yes, as usual."  
"Just the other day, he said my way of licking jam was too fierce, and it troubles him, but I don’t lick it that much. He must be mistaken; it’s certainly because the young lady and you lick it together—"  
"How rude, Tatara-san! Why would you say such a thing?"  
"But you look like you’d lick it too."  
"How can you tell that just by looking at my face?"  
"I can’t tell, but—then you don’t lick it at all?"  
"Well, I do lick it a little. What’s wrong with that? It’s mine, after all."  
"Hahaha, I thought so—however, about that thief, what a disaster it was! Did he only take the mountain yam?"  
"If it were just the mountain yam, it wouldn’t be a problem, but he took all our everyday clothes."  
"That’s quite troublesome, isn’t it? Will you have to borrow money again? If only this cat were a dog—what a shame. You must definitely get a big dog, madam. Cats are useless; they only eat—do they catch a mouse at least?"  
"I’ve never caught a single one. Truly, I’m a lazy and shameless cat."  
"Well, that’s just unacceptable. You should throw it away. I could take it and cook it."  
"Oh, Tatara-san, do you eat cats?"  
"I have.

Cats are quite delicious."  
"How bold of you!"  
I had heard rumors that among the lower-class students, there were savages who ate cats, but I never imagined that the very Tatara, whom I usually regarded with disdain, would belong to this same category. Not to mention, he is no longer a student; despite having graduated not long ago, he is now a dignified Bachelor of Law and an executive of the Rokuzui Trading Company, so my astonishment is indeed profound. The saying, "When you see someone, think of them as a thief," has already been proven by Kangetsu the Second, but to think of someone as a cat-eater is a truth I have only just come to realize thanks to Tatara. Living in this world brings knowledge, and while knowing is delightful, the dangers increase day by day, and one must be ever more vigilant. Becoming cunning or despicable, wearing a double-layered protective garment, all result from knowledge, and knowing is a sin of aging. The reason there are no decent old people is this principle; perhaps it would be wiser for me to perish in Tatara’s pot along with onions, I thought, as I shrank into a corner. Just then, the master, who had quarreled with his wife and retreated to the study, heard Tatara’s voice and lumbered into the tea room. "I hear you encountered a thief, sir. What a foolish thing to do," he immediately launched into. "The one who entered is the fool," the master considers himself wise above all. "The one who enters is foolish, but the one who was robbed is not very wise either."  
"Isn’t it the wisest of all to be like Tatara, who has nothing to lose?" his wife now supported her husband. "But the biggest fool is this cat. What on earth is it thinking? It doesn’t catch mice and just pretends not to notice when a thief comes. —Sir, won’t you give me this cat? It’s of no use just sitting here."  
"Go ahead, what will you do with it?"  
"I’ll cook and eat it."  
Upon hearing this shocking statement, the master let out a strange, weak laugh, but since he didn’t respond particularly, Tatara didn’t insist on wanting to eat it either, which was a stroke of unexpected luck for me. The master soon shifted the topic of conversation. "Cats are fine, but I’m cold because I’ve lost my clothes, and it’s unbearable," he said, feeling quite dejected. Indeed, it must be cold. Until yesterday, he had been wearing two layers of cotton, but today he was only in a thin kimono and short-sleeved shirt, having done no exercise since morning and just sitting around, so the insufficient blood was all working for his stomach and not circulating to his limbs at all. "Being a teacher is truly not good.

Even a little encounter with a thief makes one immediately troubled—why not change your mind and become a businessman?"  
"The teacher dislikes being a businessman, so saying that won’t help."  
His wife replied to Tatara from the side. She naturally wanted him to become a businessman. "How many years has it been since you graduated, sir?"  
"This is the ninth year," his wife glanced at the master. He neither confirmed nor denied it. "Even after nine years, your salary hasn’t gone up. No matter how much you study, no one praises you, and you’re all alone," he recited a line from a poem he had learned in middle school for his wife, but she didn’t quite understand it, so she didn’t respond. "Of course, I dislike being a teacher, but I dislike being a businessman even more," the master seemed to be pondering what he actually liked in his heart. "Since you dislike everything..."  
"Isn’t the only thing you don’t dislike your wife?" Tatara made a joke that didn’t quite suit him. "That’s the thing I dislike the most," the master’s reply was quite straightforward. His wife turned her head slightly, then looked back at him and said,  
"You must dislike being alive too, right?" trying to provoke him. "I don’t particularly like it," he replied surprisingly nonchalantly. This was quite hopeless. "Sir, if you don’t take a brisk walk, you’ll ruin your health. —And then become a businessman. Making money is really not a difficult task."

"Not making a single profit, yet you still—"
"But you only just started working at the company last year. Even so, you have more savings than the teacher."
"How much have you saved?" Mrs. Kushami asked eagerly. "Already fifty yen."
"What is your monthly salary, then?" This was also Mrs. Kushami's question. "Thirty yen. Out of that, five yen is set aside each month by the company, and they keep it for me to use when the time comes. —Why don't you buy a few shares of the Outer Moat Line with your pocket money? In three or four months, they’ll double in value. Honestly, if only you had a little money, it could easily become two or three times as much."
"If I had that kind of money, I wouldn't be troubled even if I encountered a thief."
"That's why I say it’s all about being a businessman. If you had pursued law or something and worked at a company or a bank, you would be earning three or four hundred yen a month by now. What a pity! —Do you know that engineer named Suzuki Tojuro?"
"Yes, he came yesterday."
"Is that so? I met him at a party the other day, and when I mentioned you, he said, 'Oh, so you were a student at Mr. Kushami's place? I used to live with Mr. Kushami in a temple in Koishikawa, cooking for ourselves. Next time I go, please send my regards; I’ll visit him sometime.'"
"I hear he just came to Tokyo recently."
"Yes, he was in a coal mine in Kyushu until recently, but he just got assigned to Tokyo. He’s quite good. He talks to me like a friend. —What do you think that man earns?"
"I don’t know."
"His salary is two hundred fifty yen, and he gets bonuses at New Year and Obon, so it averages out to four or five hundred yen. For a man like that, it’s quite a good deal, yet you, who specialize in leading, have been stuck with a meager salary for ten years. Isn’t that foolish?"
"Indeed, it is foolish," even someone like the master, who is a detached realist, has a concept of money that is no different from ordinary people. Perhaps it is precisely because he is in need that he desires money more than anyone else. Since Tatara had sufficiently boasted about the benefits of being a businessman, he had nothing more to say. "Madam, is a man named Mizushima Kangetsu coming to see the teacher?"
"Yes, he comes quite often."
"What kind of person is he?"
