"I hear he is very learned."
"Is he a handsome man?"
"Ho ho ho, he’s about as good-looking as Mr. Tatara."
"Is that so? So he’s about as good-looking as I am?" Tatara said seriously. "How do you know Kangetsu's name?" the master asked. "I was asked about him by someone the other day. Is he really someone worth asking about?" Tatara was already posturing as if he were more important than Kangetsu. "He is a much more remarkable man than you."
"Is that so?

More remarkable than me?" he neither laughed nor got angry. This was Tatara's characteristic. "Is he going to become a doctor soon?"
"I hear he is writing a thesis."
"How foolish. To write a doctoral thesis, I thought he would be someone who could talk a bit more."
"Still, you have quite the discerning eye," Mrs. Kushami said with a laugh. "When he becomes a doctor, he mentioned something about marrying someone’s daughter, but what kind of fool would do that? To become a doctor just to marry a daughter? It would be much better to give her to me than to someone like that," he said. "Who said that?"
"It was a man who asked me to inquire about Mizushima."
"Was it Suzuki?"
"No, I wouldn’t say something like that to him yet. He’s a big shot."
"Tatara, you’re a coward. You might act all high and mighty at home, but you shrink when you’re in front of someone like Suzuki."
"Yes. If I don’t, it’s dangerous."
"Tatara, shall we go for a walk?" the master suddenly said. Since it had been quite cold with just a single layer of clothing, he thought a bit of exercise would warm him up, which led him to propose this unprecedented motion. Tatara, who was always spontaneous, of course had no reason to hesitate. "Let’s go. Shall we go to Ueno? Should we go to Imozaka and eat some dumplings? Teacher, have you ever eaten those dumplings there? Madam, you should go and try them once. They’re soft and cheap. They also serve sake." While he was rambling on in his usual disordered manner, the master had already put on his hat and was heading downstairs to take off his shoes. **Chapter 1**

I find myself in need of a bit of rest. As for what my master and Mr. Tatara did in Ueno Park, and how many plates of dango they consumed at Imosaka, there’s no need for a detective to uncover such trivialities, nor do I have the courage to follow them. Thus, I must take this time to recuperate. Rest is a rightful claim that all living beings should demand from the heavens. Those who are obligated to exist in this world and move about must obtain rest in order to fulfill that obligation. If there is a god who says you were born to work and not to sleep, I would respond, as you have commanded, I was born to work, and therefore I ask for rest to work. Even a sturdy man like my master, who grumbles about machines, takes time off for himself occasionally, even on days other than Sunday. As for me, a creature of many feelings and resentments, who toils day and night, it is only natural that I require more rest than my master, even if I am merely a cat. However, I am somewhat troubled by the fact that just earlier, Mr. Tatara looked at me and insulted me as if I were nothing more than a useless luxury, incapable of anything but rest.

Those who are merely driven by material things, lacking any activity beyond the stimulation of the five senses, are a nuisance when it comes to evaluating others, as they only engage with the superficial. They seem to think that unless one is sweating and working hard, one is not working at all. It is said that a monk named Daruma sat in meditation until his legs rotted away, but even if he did not move until vines crept in through the cracks in the wall to block his eyes and mouth, he was neither asleep nor dead. His mind was always active, pondering exquisite principles like "kurosen mushō" (the state of being without thoughts). It is said that Confucians also have their own methods of quiet sitting. However, this does not mean sitting idly in a room, practicing tranquility. The vitality in their brains burns more fiercely than that of ordinary people. Yet, on the surface, they appear entirely calm and composed, leading the common eye to mistake these intellectual giants for mere sluggards or useless beings, and to voice baseless slanders. These common eyes are born with a defective vision that sees only the form and not the heart—indeed, Mr. Tatara Sampei, for example, is a prime representative of those who see only the form and not the heart. It is no wonder that he regards me as equivalent to excrement. Regrettably, even my master, who has read a few books and has some understanding of the true nature of things, agrees with the shallow Sampei without hesitation, leading to the absurdity of my skin being stripped off and sold to a shamisen maker, and my flesh being served to Mr. Tatara’s table. This would be a most serious matter. I have come into this world as a cat of great importance, destined to act with my head. There is a saying that a precious child does not sit on the ground, so to willingly pursue danger while espousing lofty ideals is not only a personal disaster but also a great affront to the will of heaven. Even a fierce tiger, when placed in a zoo, occupies a space next to a filthy pig, and a wild goose, when captured in a birdcage, shares the same fate as a chick. As long as I am among the common folk, I cannot help but become a common cat. If I am to be a common cat, I must not fail to catch mice. — I have finally resolved to catch mice. Recently, I have heard that Japan is at war with Russia. As a Japanese cat, I naturally support Japan. If possible, I would like to organize a mixed cat brigade to scratch at the Russian soldiers. Given my vigorous nature, if I set my mind to it, I could easily catch one or two mice even while sleeping.

It is said that a certain famous Zen master once answered someone who asked how to attain enlightenment by saying, "Like a cat watching a mouse." To catch a mouse like a cat means that if one does so, there will be no deviation from the goal. There is a saying that women are wise, but there is no proverb stating that a cat is wise and fails to catch mice. Thus, even a clever creature like myself should have no trouble catching mice. There should be no trouble at all; rather, the reason I haven't caught any thus far is simply that I have not wanted to. The spring day fades just like yesterday, and the occasional gust of wind brings in a flurry of blossoms that floats into the kitchen through the torn shoji, casting shadows in the bucket that appear white in the dim light of the kitchen lamp. Determined to achieve a great feat tonight and surprise everyone in the house, I realize I need to survey the battlefield in advance and familiarize myself with the terrain. The front line, of course, cannot be too wide. In terms of tatami mats, it might be about four mats wide, with half of one mat being the sink and the other half being the dirt floor where the sake shop and vegetable shop are served. The hearth is a splendid structure that seems out of place in a poor kitchen, with a shiny red copper pot, and behind it, there is a space of two shaku (about 60 cm) leading to where my abalone shell is located. The six shaku near the tea room serves as a cupboard for bowls, plates, and small dishes, further narrowing the already cramped kitchen, almost level with the exposed shelf that juts out sideways. Underneath it, a suribachi (grinding bowl) lies upside down, and the bottom of a small bucket faces me. Graters and small pestles are lined up beside it, while only the fire extinguisher stands quietly nearby. A single flexible rod hangs down from the center of the darkened barrel wood, with a large flat basket placed on top. This basket sways gently in the wind from time to time. I had no idea what this basket was for when I first arrived at this house, but after realizing that it was deliberately placed out of reach of cats to hold food, I came to deeply feel the malice of human nature.

Now, let us devise a battle plan. When it comes to where to wage war against the mice, it must, of course, be in places where they appear. No matter how convenient the terrain may be for us, if I stand alone waiting, it will hardly be a war at all. Here, it becomes necessary to study the exits of the mice. I stand in the middle of the kitchen, looking around in all directions, wondering from which side they might come. I feel somewhat like General Tōgō. The maid has gone to fetch hot water and has not yet returned. The children are particularly asleep. The master has come back from eating sweet dumplings at Imosaka and is still holed up in his study. As for the mistress—well, I do not know what she is doing. She is probably dozing off, dreaming of yams. Occasionally, a rickshaw passes by the gate, but after it goes by, the place feels even lonelier. My resolve, my spirit, the scene in the kitchen, the desolation all around—everything feels utterly tragic. I can’t help but think of myself as the Tōgō of cats. When one enters such a state of mind, it is common to feel a certain pleasure amidst the dread, but I discovered that beneath this pleasure lies a great worry. I am prepared for war against the mice, so I am not afraid of how many come, but the uncertainty of where they will emerge is indeed troublesome. From my meticulous observations, I have concluded that there are three possible routes for the mouse bandits to escape. If they are sewer rats, they will surely follow the pipes from the drain and circle around to the back of the stove. In that case, I will hide behind the fire extinguisher and cut off their retreat. Alternatively, they might sneak out through the hole in the plaster where the bathwater drains, unexpectedly jumping into the kitchen. If that happens, I will take my position on the lid of the pot and pounce down on them when they come into view. Then, as I look around again, I notice that the lower right corner of the cupboard door has been gnawed into a crescent shape, suggesting it might be a convenient exit for them. When I press my nose against it, I detect a faint mouse smell. If they were to burst out from here, I would use the pillar as a shield and strike from the side with a sudden claw. If they were to come from the ceiling, I look up and see the black soot glimmering in the lamp's light, as if hell itself were turned inside out; with my current skills, I could neither climb up nor descend. I doubt they would fall from such a high place, so I decide to relax my guard in that direction. Nevertheless, I am concerned about being attacked from three sides. If it’s just one mouse, I can handle it with one eye closed. If there are two, I have confidence that I can manage somehow.

But if there are three, no matter how instinctively I am expected to catch mice, I would be at a loss. Therefore, relying on a cat like Kuro, the rickshaw man’s black cat, for assistance would compromise my dignity. What should I do? When I ponder this and cannot come up with a good idea, I find it best to conclude that such a situation is unlikely to arise, as it brings me the most comfort. Moreover, one tends to think that things that are not governed by law will not happen. Just take a look at the world. The bride I received yesterday might very well die today; however, the groom is blissfully arranging auspicious things like “May you live a thousand years,” without a care in the world. The reason he is not worried is not because there is no cause for concern. No matter how much one worries, the law does not apply. In my case, while there is no substantial evidence to assert that a three-pronged attack will not occur, it is more convenient to believe that it will not happen for my peace of mind. Peace of mind is essential for all things. I, too, desire peace of mind. Hence, I conclude that a three-pronged attack will not occur. Yet, still feeling uneasy, I ponder what it could be, and eventually, I come to understand. The torment arises from my struggle to find a clear answer to which of the three strategies would be the most advantageous. I have a plan ready for when they emerge from the cupboard, another for when they appear from the bath, and yet another for when they crawl up from the drain, but I must decide on one of these strategies, which greatly confounds me. General Tōgō was said to have worried greatly about whether the Baltic fleet would pass through the Tsushima Strait, emerge into the Tsugaru Strait, or take the long route around the Sōya Strait, but now, imagining my own situation, I truly empathize with his predicament. I am not only similar to General Tōgō in the overall situation but also share his struggles in this particular position. As I become engrossed in devising strategies, suddenly, the torn sliding door opens, and Osan's face peeks through. The fact that only her face appears does not mean she lacks arms and legs. The other parts are not visible in the dim light of night, but her face stands out distinctly, illuminated by a strong hue that clearly catches my eye. Osan, with her cheeks even redder than usual, has returned from the bath and, perhaps chastened by last night’s events, is hastily locking the doors. I hear the master’s voice from the study, instructing her to place my stick by his pillow. I do not understand why one would adorn their pillow with a stick. Surely, he is not trying to imitate the heroic figures of the past, hoping to hear the dragon’s roar.

Yesterday it was yams, today it’s a stick; what will it be tomorrow? The night is still young, and the mice do not seem likely to emerge just yet. I require a moment of rest before the great battle. In the master’s kitchen, there are no sliding windows. In the sitting room, there is a place about a foot wide cut out in the transom, serving as a substitute for a sliding window, allowing the summer and winter winds to blow through. The wind, inviting the scattered cherry blossoms of the equinox, surprises me as I wake from my slumber; even the hazy moon has somehow made its way in, casting the shadow of the stove diagonally across the raised floor. After shaking my ears a few times to check if I have dozed off, I hear only the sound of the clock ticking, just as it did last night. It is already time for the mice to come out. From where will they emerge? I hear a clattering sound from inside the cupboard. It seems one is trying to tip over a small dish, holding it down with its feet. I crouch by the hole, waiting for it to come out. However, the scene of it emerging does not come to pass. The sound of the dish eventually stops, but now it seems something heavy, perhaps a bowl, is being knocked about, thudding intermittently. Moreover, it is happening just on the other side of the door, no more than three inches from my nose. Occasionally, I hear footsteps approaching the hole, but then they retreat, and not a single one shows its face. It is quite a long wait for me to remain still at the exit while the enemy is wreaking havoc just one door away. The mice are holding a grand ball in the soup bowl. If only Osan would open this door wide enough for me to slip in! What a thoughtless mountain girl she is. Now, from the shadow of the stove, I hear my shell clink. The enemy has come this way as well; I quietly approach on tiptoe and catch a glimpse of a tail disappearing beneath the sink. After a while, I hear the rinsing bowl clink against the metal basin in the bath. Just as I turn to look behind me, a large one, nearly five inches long, darts in, dropping the toothbrush pouch and rushing under the eaves. I leap after it, determined not to let it escape, but soon, it vanishes without a trace. Catching mice is more difficult than I had anticipated. I wonder if I lack the innate ability to catch them.

When I made my way to the bathroom, the enemy rushed out from the cupboard, wary of my presence, then leaped from the sink, making a commotion in three directions as they stood their ground in the middle of the kitchen. Whether to call them petty or cowardly, they were certainly not the foes of a gentleman. I ran back and forth, exhausting my mind and body at least fifteen or sixteen times, but in the end, I never succeeded even once. It is regrettable, but against such small-minded creatures, no strategy devised by any great General Tōgō would be effective. At first, I had courage, a sense of rivalry, and even a lofty aesthetic feeling of tragic heroism, but eventually, I became bored, foolishly sleepy, and tired, so I decided to sit right in the middle of the kitchen and not move. However, even if I did not move, if I kept my eyes darting in all directions, the enemy was small-minded, so they could not do much. The ones I thought were my foes turned out to be surprisingly stingy, and the feeling that war was honorable faded, leaving only a sense of disdain. Once that feeling of disdain passed, my spirit deflated, and I became dazed. After becoming dazed, I thought, let them do as they please; they cannot do anything clever anyway, and this contempt made me incredibly sleepy. Following this path, I finally grew drowsy. I shall sleep. Rest is necessary even amidst the enemy. From the open sliding window, facing sideways, a flurry of cherry blossoms was thrown in, and as the fierce wind swirled around me, one who had shot out from the cupboard like a bullet, without a moment to evade, bit into my left ear. The following black shadow, before I could think it would circle around behind me, hung from my tail. It was a matter of mere moments. I jumped up mechanically, without any purpose, gathering all my strength into my fur to shake off this monster. The one biting my ear lost its center and dangled limply from my profile. The soft tip of my tail, like a rubber tube, unexpectedly slipped into my mouth. With this last grip, I bit down on the tail as if to crush it, shaking it left and right, but only the tail remained between my front teeth while the body hit the wall covered in old newspapers and rebounded onto the raised board. As I got up, if I were to pile on without leaving any gaps, like kicking a ball, I would graze my nose and shrink my feet to stand on the edge of the step. He looked down at me from the shelf, and I looked up at him from the floorboards. The distance was five shaku (about 15 feet). In that space, the moonlight poured in horizontally, like a broad band stretched across the sky. I gathered strength into my front paws and finally tried to leap onto the shelf.

My front paws managed to grip the edge, but my hind legs flailed in the air. The black thing from before was biting down on my tail with a force that seemed unwilling to let go. I was in a precarious situation. I tried to deepen my grip with my front paws. Each time I tried to grip better, the weight of my tail made it shallower. If I slipped for two or three minutes, I would have to fall. I was in an even more precarious situation. The sound of my claws scraping against the shelf echoed harshly. This wouldn’t do, so as I pulled out my left front paw, I missed my grip perfectly, and I was left hanging from the shelf with only my right claw. The weight of myself and the thing biting my tail caused my body to twist precariously. At that moment, the monster that had been peering down from the shelf without moving until now, leaped down as if to throw a stone at my forehead from above. My claws lost their tenuous grip. The three entities merged into one and fell down, cutting through the moonlight vertically. The mortar that had been placed on the next step, along with the small bucket inside it and an empty jam can, all tumbled down together, inviting the fire extinguisher below, half rolling into the water jug and half onto the floorboards. Everything made an unusual noise in the dead of night, chilling even the soul of me, who was in a frenzy. “Thief!” my master shouted loudly as he burst out from the bedroom. He appeared holding a lamp in one hand and a cane in the other, radiating a light befitting his station, more brilliant than his drowsy eyes. I remained quietly crouched beside the abalone shell. The two monsters concealed themselves back into the cupboard. My master, with nothing to do, angrily asked, “What is it? Who made that loud noise?” even though there was no one to answer. As the moon tilted to the west, the area of white light became thinner, about half the size of a cut.

In such heat, even a cat cannot endure it. There is a story that a certain Sidney Smith from England once lamented that he wished he could shed his skin, meat, and just remain as bones to cool off. While I do not aspire to become just bones, I do feel the urge to wash this light gray, speckled fur coat of mine, or at least to put it in some middle-quality fabric for a while. From a human's perspective, cats may seem to lead a simple, carefree life, wearing the same expression all year round, and living without the burden of expenses. However, even a cat feels the heat and cold in its own way. Occasionally, I would not mind taking a dip, but the trouble is that once I use water over this fur coat, drying it becomes quite a challenge. Thus, I have endured the smell of sweat without ever passing through the warm curtain of the bathhouse until this age. Sometimes, I feel the urge to try using a fan, but since I cannot hold one, there is no point. When I think about it, humans are quite extravagant. They take the trouble to boil, grill, pickle, or season things that should be eaten raw, indulging in unnecessary efforts and delighting in their own complexity. Clothing is the same. To expect them to wear the same thing all year round like a cat might be a bit unreasonable for those who were born imperfectly, but there is no need to drape themselves in such a variety of things. When they rely on sheep, silkworms, or even cotton fields for their comfort, one could assert that such luxury is the result of incompetence. Even if we overlook food and clothing, it makes no sense to push this trend to the point where it affects survival. First of all, hair on the head grows naturally, so it would be simpler and better for them to leave it alone. Yet, they go to great lengths to create various styles and take pride in them. Those who call themselves monks always have their heads shaved. When it’s hot, they wear parasols on top. When it’s cold, they wrap their heads in hoods. What is the purpose of having a shaved head if they cover it up? Then there are those who use a meaningless saw-like tool called a comb to divide their hair into two equal parts, and if it’s not equal, they artificially create sections on their skull in a seven-to-three ratio. Some even have this division running from the crown of their head all the way to the back, resembling a counterfeit banana leaf. Next, they shave the top of their heads flat and cut the sides straight. They fit a square frame onto a round head, which can only be interpreted as a sketch of a cedar fence with a gardener inside. There are even tales of five-point cuts, three-point cuts, and one-point cuts, suggesting that eventually, there may be a trend for minus one-point cuts or minus three-point cuts.

In any case, I cannot understand what they intend to achieve by torturing themselves in such a way. First of all, it is extravagant to have four legs and only use two. If they walked on all four, they could move much more easily, yet they always manage with just two, leaving the other two dangling like a piece of dried cod, which is utterly ridiculous. From this, it seems that humans are far more idle than cats, and out of sheer boredom, they devise such antics to amuse themselves. What is amusing, however, is that these idle people, when approached, claim to be busy, busy, and their expressions certainly reflect a sense of busyness, to the point that one might think they are about to be consumed by their own busyness. Some of them look at me and say, “If only I could be as carefree as that cat.” If being carefree is what they desire, they should be like me and wear their fur coats even in summer. — That said, it is a bit hot. This fur coat is truly too warm. With this heat, I cannot even enjoy a proper nap. What to do? Having neglected my observations of human society for a long time, I thought today I might take a look at their drunken revelry after a long absence. Unfortunately, my master is exceedingly cat-like in this regard. He takes naps just as well as I do, and especially after the summer break, he does not engage in any human-like work, so no matter how much I observe, there is no incentive to do so. If only Meitei were to come by, my sensitive skin would respond somewhat, and I would be able to distance myself from the cat for a while. However, my master seems to think it is a good time for a visit, as someone is splashing water in the bathhouse without revealing their identity. It is not just the sound of water; occasionally, there are loud voices chiming in. “Ah, splendid!” “What a delightful feeling!” “One more!” The voices echo throughout the house. No one else would come to my master's home and make such loud and rude noises. It must be Meitei. Ah, he has finally arrived. I thought I could waste half the day with this, but he wipes his sweat and, as usual, barges into the tatami room, calling out, “Madam, what has become of Mr. Kushami?” His wife, who had been comfortably dozing off next to the sewing box in the adjacent room, startled awake at the sound that resonated in her eardrums and, with her eyes still half-closed, purposely opened them and came out to the tatami room, where Meitei had settled himself in a casual manner, fanning himself with a sashiko cloth. “Oh, welcome!” she said, albeit a bit flustered, adding, “I had no idea you were here,” while wiping the sweat from her nose and bowing. “No, I just arrived. I was just in the bathhouse getting water splashed on me by Osan.

I’ve just returned to life—how hot it is!” “These past few days, just sitting still makes me sweat, it’s terribly hot. But you seem to be well,” she said, still not wiping the sweat from her nose. “Yes, thank you. It’s just hot, so there’s not much change. But this heat is something else. My body feels so sluggish.” “I, for one, have never had a proper nap, but in this heat, I can’t help but…” “Do you take naps? That’s good. If you can nap during the day and sleep at night, that would be splendid,” he continued to speak cheerfully, but it seemed insufficient, so he added, “I, for one, don’t want to sleep. I envy people like Mr. Kushami who seem to sleep every time they come. But this heat is hard on a weak stomach. Even a healthy person, like today, would find it difficult to keep their head on their shoulders. But then again, if it’s on, it can’t be taken off.” 

“Madam, you still have something on your head, so you shouldn’t be able to sit still. Just the weight of your bun would make you want to lie down,” he said, and upon hearing this, she thought her bun had been exposed by her sleeping position and said, “Ho ho ho, what a sharp tongue,” while she fiddled with her hair.

Meitei, unconcerned with such matters, said, "Madam, yesterday I tried frying an egg on the roof." "What happened to the frying?" she asked. "The roof tiles were so beautifully baked that I thought it would be a waste just to leave them alone. So, I melted some butter and dropped the egg on it." "Oh my!" "But, as expected, the sun doesn't always cooperate. It wouldn't become half-cooked, so while I went down to read the newspaper, a guest arrived, and I completely forgot about it. This morning, I suddenly remembered and thought it should be fine, so I went back up to check." "What happened?" "Far from being half-cooked, it had completely run off." "Oh dear," his wife exclaimed, raising her eyebrows in astonishment. "However, it's strange that it's so cool during the Doyō season, and now it's starting to get hot," she continued. "Indeed, it is. Just the other day, it was chilly even in a thin garment, but suddenly it became hot from the day before." "If it were crabs, they would be crawling sideways, but this year's climate seems to be going backwards. It might be saying something like 'to go against the natural order is not good.'" "What do you mean by that?" "Oh, it's nothing. The way this climate is reversing is just like Hercules' cattle," he said, getting carried away with his odd remarks, which, of course, his wife did not understand. However, having been a bit put off by the earlier mention of reversing the natural order, she merely replied, "Oh, really," without asking for clarification. When not questioned further, Meitei felt that his efforts to bring up the topic had been in vain. "Madam, do you know about Hercules' cattle?" "I don't know of such cattle." "You don't know? Shall I give you a little lecture?" Since his wife couldn't quite refuse that, she replied, "Well, yes." "Long ago, Hercules brought some cattle," he began. "Is this Hercules a cattle herder?" "No, he is not a cattle herder. He is not the husband of a cattle herder either. This was back when there wasn't a single butcher shop in Greece." "Oh, is this a story about Greece? Then you should have said so," she replied, as she only knew the name of the country. "But it is Hercules, isn't it?" "Is Hercules from Greece?" "Yes, Hercules is a hero from Greece." "No wonder I didn't know. So what happened with that man—" "That man, you see, madam, fell asleep and was snoring away—" "Oh, how dreadful!" "While he was sleeping, the son of Vulcan came and—" "Who is Vulcan?" "Vulcan is a blacksmith. This blacksmith's son stole the cattle. However, he was pulling the cattle by the tail, so Hercules woke up and called out, 'Where are my cattle? Where are my cattle?' but he couldn't find them. Of course, he couldn't.

He didn't lead them forward by their footprints; he dragged them backward, backward. For a blacksmith's son, that was quite a feat," Meitei said, having already forgotten about the weather discussion. "By the way, what about your husband? Is he still napping? While napping may sound elegant in Chinese poetry, doing it daily like Kushami-kun is a bit too mundane. It’s like dying a little bit every day. Madam, if you wouldn't mind, could you wake him up?" When he urged her, she seemed to agree, saying, "Yes, it really is a problem. First of all, it’s just making him more unwell. He just had a meal." As she started to get up, Meitei said, "Madam, as for meals, I haven't had any yet." With a calm face, he spread rumors about something he hadn’t even asked about. "Oh my, I didn’t notice it was that time—then I suppose there’s nothing, but perhaps some tea over rice?" "No need for tea over rice; I’m fine without it." "Even so, you know, there’s nothing that would suit your taste," she said, adding a hint of sarcasm. Meitei, realizing this, replied, "No, I must decline tea over rice or any other kind of rice. I just had a feast prepared for me along the way, so I’ll have that here." He stated something that seemed impossible for an amateur to do. His wife merely said, "Well!" but in that "well," there was a mix of surprise, concern about his mood, and relief that it spared her the trouble. At that moment, the master came out, unusually loud, as if his sleep had been disturbed, and he stumbled out from the study. "What a noisy man as usual. Just when I was about to fall into a nice sleep," he said, yawning and wearing a sulky expression. "Ah, you’re awake. I’m terribly sorry to have disturbed your peaceful slumber. But it’s nice once in a while. Now, please sit down," he greeted, leaving one unsure of who was the guest. The master silently took his seat and, from a marquetry tobacco pouch, pulled out a "Morning Sun" cigarette and began to smoke. Suddenly, he noticed Meitei’s hat lying in the corner and said, "You bought a hat." Meitei immediately boasted, "What do you think?" as he presented it proudly to the master and his wife. "Oh, how beautiful! It’s very finely woven and soft," his wife said, stroking it repeatedly. "Madam, this hat is quite useful; it listens to everything I say," he said, clenching his fist and giving the Panama hat a light tap, which indeed created a hole the size of his fist. Before his wife could exclaim "Oh!" in surprise, he then pushed his fist inside from the other side, making the top of the hat poke up sharply. Next, he took the hat off and pressed the brim from both sides to show how it could be flattened. The crushed hat became as flat as soba noodles rolled out with a rolling pin.

He then rolled it up like a mat, starting from one end. "What do you think of this?" he said, showing the rolled-up hat tucked into his pocket. "How mysterious!" his wife exclaimed, as if watching a magic trick by Kitten Saiza. Seeing her excitement, Meitei seemed to get into the spirit of it, pulling the hat out from his left sleeve and saying, "There’s not a scratch on it," then placing the bottom of the hat on his fingertip and spinning it around. Just when one might think it was time to rest, he suddenly tossed it behind him and plopped down on it. "Are you alright?" even the master looked concerned. Of course, his wife, too, worriedly said, "If you break such a splendid hat, it would be terrible, so you should stop now." Only the owner was pleased, saying, "But isn’t it strange that it doesn’t break?" He pulled out the crumpled hat from beneath him and placed it back on his head, and miraculously, it instantly regained its shape. "What a truly durable hat! I wonder how that is," his wife said, increasingly impressed. "Oh, it’s nothing special; it’s just made to be like this from the start," Meitei replied to her while still wearing the hat. "Wouldn’t it be nice if you bought a hat like that?" his wife suggested to the master after a while. "But Kushami-kun has a splendid straw one, doesn’t he?" "However, the other day, a child stepped on it and ruined it." "Oh dear, that was quite careless!" "So, I thought it would be good to buy something as sturdy and beautiful as yours," she said, not knowing the price of the Panama hat, and kept urging the master, "You should get this one, right?"

Meitei took out a red case containing scissors from the right sleeve and showed them to his wife. "My dear, enough about the hat; take a look at these scissors. They are quite a handy tool, and you can use them in fourteen different ways." If these scissors hadn't appeared, the master would have been subjected to a Panama hat ordeal for his wife, but fortunately, thanks to her curiosity, which women are born with, she was spared this misfortune. I discerned that it was more a stroke of luck than Meitei's quick thinking. "How can these scissors be used in fourteen different ways?" As soon as I asked, Meitei replied in a tone full of pride, "I will explain each one, so listen closely. First, see this crescent-shaped notch here? You put a cigar in it and snip it off cleanly. Then, there’s a little mechanism at the base for handling wire. Next, if you flatten it and lay it sideways on paper, it serves as a ruler. The back of the blade has measurements marked, so it can also be used as a measuring stick. On the front, there’s a file attached, which you can use to smooth your nails. Now, if you insert this tip into the head of a screw and twist it, it can also serve as a hammer. If you push it in hard and pry, you can easily remove the lid from most nailed boxes. Moreover, the tip of this blade can be used as an awl. This part is for scraping off mistakes in writing, and if you separate them, it becomes a knife. And finally—now, my dear, this last one is quite interesting—there’s a ball here about the size of a fly's eye; just take a peek through it." 

"Oh no, you’re just going to make a fool of yourself again," she replied. "How can you be so distrustful? But just for a moment, look through it, will you? What? You don’t want to? Just a little bit." He handed the scissors to his wife. She hesitantly took them and pressed her eye against the spot where the fly's eye was, peering intently. "How is it?" 

"It looks quite dark." 

"It shouldn’t be dark. Turn it a bit more towards the shoji, and don’t lay the scissors flat—yes, yes, that should do it." 

"Oh my, it’s a photograph! Why would they attach such a small photo?" 

"That’s the interesting part," Meitei and his wife continued their exchange. The master, who had been silent until now, suddenly seemed eager to see the photo. "Hey, let me have a look too," he said, and his wife pressed the scissors against his face, saying, "It’s truly beautiful, a naked beauty!" and wouldn’t let go. "Hey, I just wanted a quick look!" 

"Well, just wait a moment. Such beautiful hair, it reaches down to her waist. She’s a terribly tall woman when she tilts her head back, but she is beautiful." 

"Come on, if you’re going to show it, at least show it properly," the master urged, growing impatient with his wife.

"Ah, please wait a moment, enjoy it thoroughly," she said as she handed the scissors to the master, just then Osan entered, announcing that the guest’s order had arrived, bringing two bowls of soba to the room. "My dear, this is my homemade treat. Excuse me, but I’m going to dig in right here," he said with a polite bow. His actions were both serious and playful, making his wife seem a bit flustered as she lightly replied, "Well, please go ahead," while watching him. The master finally tore his gaze away from the photo and said, "You know, in this heat, soba is poison." 

"Oh, it’s fine, you rarely get sick from what you love," he replied, lifting the lid off the steamer. "Freshly made is a blessing. Soba that’s overcooked and a person who’s absent-minded are both equally undesirable," he said, tossing condiments into the dipping sauce and stirring it recklessly. "You’re putting in too much wasabi; it’ll be too spicy," the master warned with concern. "Soba is meant to be eaten with sauce and wasabi, you know. You don’t like soba, do you?" 

"I prefer udon." 

"Udon is what horses eat. There’s nothing more pitiful than a person who doesn’t appreciate the taste of soba," he said, while carelessly plunging his chopsticks in, scooping up as much as he could to a height of about two inches. "My dear, there are various ways to eat soba. Beginners tend to carelessly dip it in sauce and chew it up in their mouths. That way, you lose the taste of the soba. You should hook it on the chopsticks like this," he said, lifting the chopsticks, and a long strand of soba lined up, dangling about a foot in the air. Meitei thought it was good enough and looked down, only to find twelve or thirteen strands still clinging to the bottom of the steamer. "This one is long, how about it, my dear? What do you think of this length?" he asked, seeking her confirmation. "That is indeed long," she replied, seemingly impressed. "You dip this long one in sauce just a third of the way and swallow it whole. Don’t chew; if you chew, you lose the taste of the soba. The smoothness as it slides down your throat is the essence," he declared, raising his chopsticks high. Finally, the soba left the ground. He received it into the teacup in his left hand, letting it drop slowly, soaking the end of the strand gradually. According to Archimedes’ principle, the amount of soba soaked would increase the volume of the dipping sauce. However, since the teacup already had sauce filled to eight-tenths, before even a quarter of the soba on Meitei’s chopsticks could soak, the cup was already full. The chopsticks halted five inches above the teacup and remained still for a while. It was no wonder they didn’t move; any slight shift would cause the sauce to overflow.

At this point, Meitei hesitated slightly, but in a flash, with the speed of a rabbit, he brought the chopsticks to his mouth, and with a slurping sound, the soba at the tip vanished. I noticed a couple of drops, like tears, flowing from the corners of Meitei’s eyes down his cheeks. Whether it was the wasabi’s kick or the difficulty of swallowing, I couldn’t tell. "Impressive! I can’t believe you swallowed that all at once," the master said in admiration, and "What a splendid performance!" his wife praised Meitei’s skill. Meitei said nothing, set down his chopsticks, and patted his chest a few times, "My dear, a steamer is usually eaten in three and a half or four bites. If you take longer, you can’t enjoy it properly," he said, wiping his mouth with a handkerchief and taking a moment to catch his breath. Just then, Kangetsu arrived, for some reason wearing a winter hat in this heat, with both feet covered in dust. "Ah, a fine gentleman has arrived, but since I was in the middle of eating, I’ll excuse myself for a moment," Meitei said, unabashedly lifting the remaining steamer from behind the crowd. This time, instead of the remarkable eating style from before, he used a handkerchief, and without the awkwardness of pausing to breathe, he easily finished off the two steamers. 「Kangetsu-kun, have you finished your dissertation yet?」 the master asked, and Meitei added from behind, 「Miss Kaneda is waiting, so do present it quickly.」 Kangetsu, as usual, let out a rather eerie smile and said, 「It’s a crime, so I want to submit it as soon as possible to put her mind at ease, but the problem is quite a problem, requiring a considerable amount of labor-intensive research.」 He spoke as if it were a serious matter, though it seemed hardly so. 「Indeed, the problem is a problem, so it can't be resolved just as Hanako says. However, with that nose of hers, it certainly has enough value to warrant some attention,」 Meitei responded in a manner befitting Kangetsu’s style. The master, comparatively serious, asked, 「What exactly is the problem with your dissertation?」 

「It’s about the effect of ultraviolet light on the electric action of a frog's eyeball,」 Kangetsu replied. 「That’s peculiar. As expected of Kangetsu-sensei, the frog's eyeball is quite the topic. What do you think, Kushami-kun? Shouldn’t we inform the Kaneda household about that issue before you finish your dissertation?」 The master did not engage with Meitei’s comment and asked Kangetsu, 「Is that really such a laborious study?」

「Yes, it’s quite a complex issue. First of all, the structure of the lens in a frog's eyeball is not something simple.

I’ll need to conduct various experiments, but I plan to start by making a round glass sphere.」 

「Making a glass sphere is no trouble if you go to a glass shop,」 Meitei interjected. 「How can you say that?」 Kangetsu replied, slightly taken aback. 「Originally, circles and straight lines are geometric concepts, and ideal circles or straight lines that fit those definitions do not exist in the real world.」

「If they don’t exist, then just discard the idea,」 Meitei chimed in. 「So, I thought I’d try to create a sphere that is sufficient for experimentation. I started doing that the other day.」

「Have you made any progress?」 the master asked casually. 「Is it possible?」 Kangetsu replied, but realizing this sounded somewhat contradictory, he added, 「It’s quite difficult. As I gradually polish it, I think one side’s radius is too long, so I try to reduce that, and then the other side becomes longer. Just when I manage to grind it down, the overall shape becomes distorted. After much effort to remove that distortion, I find that the diameter is off again. Initially, it was about the size of an apple, but gradually it shrinks to the size of a strawberry. Even after persevering, it only becomes the size of a soybean. Even at the size of a soybean, I still can’t achieve a perfect circle. I’ve polished six glass balls of varying sizes since the New Year,」 he rambled on, leaving it unclear whether he was lying or telling the truth. 「Where are you polishing them so much?」 

「In the school’s laboratory, of course. I start polishing in the morning, take a short break for lunch, and then continue until it gets dark. It’s not easy at all.」

「So, when you say you’re busy every day, even on Sundays, it’s to polish those spheres, huh?」 

「Indeed, at the moment, I’m polishing spheres from morning till night.」 

「You’ve become a doctor of sphere-making, it seems. However, if they hear about your dedication, even Hanako would appreciate it a little. Actually, the other day, I had some business at the library, and on my way back, I happened to run into Oume-kun. I thought it was quite strange that he, after graduation, would be heading to the library, and when I remarked on how diligently he was studying, he made a peculiar face and said, “I didn’t come to read books; I just happened to pass by the gate and needed to relieve myself, so I stopped by.” I had a good laugh, but I’d like to include Oume-kun and you as contrasting examples in the new selection of Mongol writings.」 Meitei added his usual lengthy commentary. The master became a bit serious and asked, 「It’s fine for you to polish spheres every day, but when do you plan to finish?」 

「At this rate, it looks like it will take about ten years,」 Kangetsu replied, appearing more carefree than the master. 「Ten years?

You should polish them up a bit faster.」 

「Ten years is on the quicker side; it might take as long as twenty years, depending on the circumstances.」 

「That’s quite a long time; it won’t be easy to become a doctor then.」 

「Yes, I want to finish as soon as possible to put everyone’s mind at ease, but I must polish the spheres first to conduct the crucial experiments…」 

Kangetsu paused for a moment and said, 「No need to worry so much. Even Kaneda is well aware that I’m just polishing spheres. In fact, a few days ago when I went there, I explained the situation well.」 

At this, the wife, who had been listening to the three of them without understanding much, asked suspiciously, 「But Mr. Kaneda and his family have all gone to Oiso since last month, haven’t they?」 

Kangetsu seemed a bit taken aback by this but replied, 「That’s strange; I wonder what happened.」 

In such moments, Meitei was quite handy, as he would always jump in at the right time, whether the conversation had stalled, was awkward, or someone felt sleepy or troubled. 「It’s quite mystical to meet someone who went to Oiso last month just a few days ago in Tokyo. It’s what you call a spiritual exchange. Such phenomena often occur when feelings of mutual longing are strong. It may sound like a dream, but it’s a dream more certain than reality. For someone like you, who has no particular feelings for Kangetsu, it’s understandable to be suspicious…」 

「Oh, on what evidence do you say such things? You’re being quite contemptuous,」 the wife suddenly cut in at Meitei. 「You don’t seem to have ever experienced love troubles yourself, do you?」 the master also came to the wife’s aid. 「Well, my romantic affairs, if any, have all happened more than seventy-five days ago, so you may not remember them, but… actually, it’s the result of a broken heart that I’ve remained single until this age,」 he said, glancing around the room at everyone’s faces. 「Ho ho ho, how amusing,」 the wife remarked, while the master turned toward the garden and said, 「Don’t be ridiculous.」 Only Kangetsu remained, saying, 「I would like to hear that nostalgic story for the sake of my studies.」 He continued to grin as usual. 「My story is quite mysterious as well, and when I mentioned it to the late Mr. Koizumi Yakumo, he found it very engaging. Unfortunately, he has passed away, so there’s really no one to share it with, but since I’m at it, I’ll reveal it to you. However, you must listen attentively until the end," he insisted as he finally began the main narrative. "Looking back, it was—let’s see—how many years ago was it? It’s a hassle, so let’s say about fifteen or sixteen years ago."

"Don’t be ridiculous," the master snorted through his nose. "You have a terrible memory," his wife teased.

Only Kangetsu kept his promise, remaining silent, eager to hear what came next. "It was during a winter in a certain year when I was passing through the Kumamoto District in Echigo, heading towards the Takozubo Pass, and was about to enter the Aizu territory."

"What a strange place," the master interrupted again. "Please be quiet and listen. It’s interesting," his wife admonished. "However, the sun was setting, I lost my way, and I was hungry. With no other choice, I knocked on a house in the middle of the pass and explained my situation, asking them to let me stay. They said it was no trouble at all, and as I looked at the girl who held a bare candle up to my face, I trembled. It was then that I became acutely aware of the magic of love," he continued. "Oh dear, is there really a beautiful person even in such a mountain area?" 

"Whether in the mountains or the sea, my dear, I wanted to show you that girl at least once. She had her hair styled in a bun with a decorative comb," he replied. "Really?" his wife was taken aback. "When I entered, I found a large irori (hearth) in the middle of an eight-tatami room, and there sat the girl, her grandfather, her grandmother, and I, four of us in total. They asked if I was hungry, and I requested anything they had to eat quickly. The grandfather then said that since I was such a valued guest, he would prepare snake rice for me. Now, this is where the story takes a turn towards heartbreak, so brace yourself and listen closely."

"While I will listen closely, no matter how much it is Echigo in winter, surely there are no snakes around," the master interjected. "Well, that is indeed a reasonable question. However, when it comes to such a poetic tale, one cannot be too concerned with logic. In Kinka’s novels, crabs emerge from the snow, don’t they?" Upon hearing this, Kangetsu simply said, "I see," and returned to his attentive demeanor.

At that time, I was quite the glutton, having grown tired of locusts, slugs, and red frogs, so snake rice was a delicacy. I promptly replied to the old man that I would partake. Thereupon, the old man placed a pot over the hearth, added rice, and began to boil it. Strangely, I noticed that the lid of the pot had about ten holes of various sizes. Steam was puffing out from those holes, and I thought it was quite a clever contraption, impressive for a rural setting. While I was observing, the old man suddenly stood up and went somewhere, but after a while, he returned, cradling a large sieve under his arm. Casually, he placed it next to the hearth, and when I peered inside, there they were. Long ones, all coiled together for warmth, as it was cold. “Enough of that story. It’s disgusting,” his wife said, knitting her brows. “How can I stop when this is the very source of heartbreak? It’s not so easy to let it go.” The old man then took the lid in his left hand, casually grabbed one of those long, coiled creatures with his right, and suddenly tossed it into the pot, quickly covering it with the lid. Even I, at that moment, felt as if my breath had been cut off. “Please stop. It’s creepy,” his wife said, clearly frightened. “Just a little longer, and you’ll see the heartbreak unfold. Then, not a minute later, a head popped out from one of the holes in the lid, which startled me. ‘Ah, it’s out,’ I thought, and another head peeked out from the neighboring hole. One after another, they emerged. Soon, the pot was filled with snake heads. “Why are they sticking their heads out like that?” 

“It’s hot inside the pot, so they’re desperately trying to escape. Eventually, the old man said, ‘That should be enough; pull them out,’ and the old woman replied with a sigh. The daughter greeted them, and each took hold of a snake’s head and pulled. The meat remained in the pot, but the bones cleanly separated, and as they pulled, the long bodies amusingly slipped out. “Snake bone extraction, huh?” Kangetsu laughed as he asked. “Indeed, it’s a complete bone extraction. Quite a skill, wouldn’t you say? Then he removed the lid and, using a ladle, mixed the rice and meat together, saying, ‘Now, dig in!’”

“Did you eat it?” the master asked coldly. His wife made a bitter face and replied, “Please stop. I feel sick just thinking about it, and I can’t eat anything.”

“Since you won’t eat the snake rice, you say such things, but just try it once; that flavor is something you’ll never forget in your lifetime.”

“Oh, no way! Who would eat that?”

“Well, I had my fill, forgot the cold, and could gaze at the daughter’s face without hesitation.

I thought there was nothing more to desire when they said, ‘Good night,’ and considering the fatigue of travel, I obediently lay down, and, regrettably, I fell asleep without a care.”

“What happened next?” his wife prompted this time. “Then, the next morning, when I woke up, that was the heartbreak.”

“What happened?”

“Oh, nothing in particular. But when I got up and was smoking a rolled cigarette while looking out the back window, I saw a kettle head washing its face by the bamboo fountain.”

“Was it the old man or the old woman?” the master asked. “Well, I couldn’t tell at first, so I kept watching, and when the kettle turned to face me, I was shocked. It was the daughter from the night of my first love.”

“But you said earlier that the daughter had her hair in a shimada style.”

“Last night, it was in a shimada style, and a splendid one at that. But the next morning, it was a round kettle.”

“You’re making a fool of me,” the master said, as usual, casting his gaze toward the ceiling. I, too, was filled with a sense of wonder and a bit of fear, so I continued to observe from a distance. The kettle finally finished washing its face, carelessly put on the high shimada wig that had been resting on a nearby stone, and entered the house with an air of composure. I thought to myself, ‘Indeed,’ but from that moment on, I became a victim of the relentless fate of heartbreak. “What a trivial heartbreak that was. Hey, Kangetsu, that’s why, even with heartbreak, I’m so cheerful and full of energy,” the master remarked, evaluating Meitei’s heartbreak. Kangetsu replied, “But if that daughter, instead of being a round kettle, had happily returned to Tokyo with you, perhaps you would be even more lively. In any case, it’s a pity that such a lovely girl turned out to be bald. How could such a young woman lose her hair?”

“I’ve thought about that too, and I truly believe it must be due to eating too much snake rice. That snake rice can make one dizzy, you know.”

“However, you seem to be perfectly fine.”

“I managed to avoid becoming bald, but instead, I became nearsighted from that time on,” he said, taking off his gold-rimmed glasses and carefully wiping them with a handkerchief. After a moment, the master, as if recalling something, asked, “What’s so mysterious about it?”

“The mystery lies in where that wig came from—whether it was bought or found; I still can’t figure it out,” Meitei said, placing his glasses back on his nose. “It sounds just like listening to a storyteller,” was his wife’s critique. With that, Meitei’s rambling came to a pause, but it seemed that as long as he wasn’t gagged, he couldn’t help but speak, and he began to chatter on about the next matter.

"My heartbreak is a bitter experience, but receiving that kettle without knowing it would become a lifelong nuisance, so one must think carefully; it is a perilous matter. Marriage, you see, can reveal hidden wounds at the last moment. Even someone like Kangetsu, who yearns so much, should not fret alone; rather, he ought to calm himself and polish the jewel," I said, expressing a rather peculiar opinion. Kangetsu replied, "Yes, I would like to just polish the jewel as much as possible, but they won't let me do that over there, which is quite distressing." He put on an exaggeratedly weary expression. "Indeed, you find the other party making a fuss, but there are some absurdities among them. Take that old Ume, who came to urinate at the library; that's quite a curious case," I continued. "What did he do?" the master inquired, getting into the spirit of the conversation. "Well, here's the story. Once, the teacher stayed at the Tōzai-kan in Shizuoka. — Just for one night, mind you — and that very night, he proposed marriage to a maid there. I may be quite carefree, but I haven't evolved to that extent. Of course, at that time, there was a famous beauty named Onatsu at that inn, who happened to be in Ume's room, so it's not surprising," I explained. "Not surprising at all; it's just like your 'something or other pass,'" the master remarked. "There's a slight resemblance, to be honest. Ume and I aren't so different. In any case, after proposing to Onatsu, he became suddenly hungry for watermelon, you see."

"What?!" the master exclaimed, looking puzzled. It wasn't just him; both the mistress and Kangetsu tilted their heads in unison, pondering the matter. Meitei, undeterred, continued with his tale. "When he called for Onatsu to ask if there were any watermelons in Shizuoka, she replied, 'No matter how much Shizuoka is, there are certainly watermelons.' She then brought a mountain of watermelon on a tray. Ume devoured the entire mountain of watermelon while waiting for Onatsu's response, but before he could get an answer, he started to have a stomachache, groaning and moaning without relief. So he called for Onatsu again, this time asking if there were any doctors in Shizuoka. Onatsu replied, 'No matter how much Shizuoka is, there are certainly doctors,' and brought in a doctor with a name that sounded like a stolen phrase from some ancient text. The next morning, feeling grateful that the stomach pain had subsided thanks to the doctor, just fifteen minutes before his departure, he called for Onatsu to inquire about the response to his marriage proposal. Onatsu laughed and said, 'There are watermelons in Shizuoka, and there are doctors, but there are no brides made in one night,' and she left without showing her face again.

After that, Ume, like me, ended up with a broken heart and only returned to the library to urinate."

As I reflected on this, the master took it upon himself to agree, "That's truly the case. The other day, while reading a script by Musset, one of the characters quoted a Roman poet and said this: — 'The lightest thing is dust. Lighter than dust is wind. Lighter than wind is woman. Lighter than woman is nothing.' — Quite insightful, isn't it? Women are just like that."

Hearing this, the mistress disagreed. "You say it's the lightness of women that's the problem, but isn't it the heaviness of men that causes issues?"

"Heaviness? What do you mean by that?" the master asked. "It means you are heavy, just like you," she replied, and thus began a peculiar debate. Meitei listened with amusement, but soon opened his mouth to say, "The way you both turn red and attack each other with arguments is the true essence of marriage. It seems that marriages of old were utterly meaningless."

He made a vague remark that could either be teasing or commendatory, but instead of stopping there, he continued in his usual manner, stating:

"They say that in the past, no woman ever answered back to her husband, but if that's the case, having a mute wife is the same, and I find that utterly ungrateful. I would like to be told something like, 'You are heavy, just like you are.' If I have to have a wife, I might as well have a quarrel or two; otherwise, it would be dreadfully boring. My mother, for instance, would only say 'yes' and 'yes' in front of my father. And after twenty years together, she had never gone out except to visit the temple, which is quite pitiful. At least, thanks to that, she has memorized all the ancestral posthumous names. Even in relationships between men and women, back in my childhood, it was impossible to do things like play music with someone you liked or engage in spiritual exchanges like Kangetsu does; those things were utterly out of reach."

"How unfortunate," Kangetsu said, bowing his head. "Indeed, it is unfortunate. Moreover, the women of that time were not necessarily more virtuous than those of today. Nowadays, people complain about the moral decline of female students, but it was much worse back then."

"Is that so?" the mistress asked seriously. "Indeed, it's not nonsense; I have proof. Kushami, you might remember, but until we were about five or six years old, girls were carried in baskets like eggplants and sold on a yoke, you know?" 

"I don't recall such a thing," Kushami replied. "I don't know how it was in your country, but in Shizuoka, it was certainly the case."

"Surely not," the mistress murmured softly, while Kangetsu looked at me with a skeptical expression.

"Indeed. My father once put a price on something. At that time, I must have been around six years old. When we went out for a walk from Aburacho to Tsuromachi, a girl was shouting loudly, 'Is that girl good? Is that girl good?' As we reached the corner of the second block, we ran into a man in front of a kimono shop called Isegen. Isegen is a prominent kimono shop in Shizuoka, with a ten-ken (about 18 meters) frontage and five storehouses in front. You should go see it when you get the chance. It still stands there, quite distinctly. It’s a splendid establishment. The shopkeeper, named Jinbei, always has a face that looks like he just lost his mother three days ago, standing at the counter. Next to Jinbei is a young fellow named Hatsushi, around twenty-four or twenty-five, who has a pale face as if he had been fasting on soba broth for thirty-seven days. Next to Hatsushi is a man named Nagadon, who looks as if he had just been driven out by a fire yesterday, leaning despondently against the abacus. Alongside Nagadon..."

"Are you talking about the kimono shop or about human trafficking?"

"Ah, yes, I was talking about human trafficking. In fact, there is quite an extraordinary tale regarding Isegen, but I will omit that for now and focus solely on the human trafficking."

"You might as well stop that too."

"Why would I stop? This provides significant material for comparing the character of women today in the twentieth century with that of women in the early Meiji era, so it cannot be so easily dismissed—when I reached Isegen with my father, the usual trafficker saw my father and said, 'Sir, how about this girl’s handiwork? I’ll give you a discount, so please buy her.' As he spoke, he lowered his weighing pole and wiped the sweat from his brow. Inside the basket, there were two girls, one in front and one in back, both around two years old. My father asked the man if he would buy them if they were cheap, but he wanted to know if this was the last of them. The man replied, 'Unfortunately, today we’ve sold out and only have these two left. Please take whichever you like,' and he presented the girls to my father, holding them with both hands as if they were eggplants or something similar, right in front of my father’s nose. My father patted their heads and said, 'Ah, that’s quite a sound.' Then the negotiations began in earnest, and after much haggling, my father asked if the goods were reliable. The man replied, 'Yes, the one in front has been watched all the time, so there’s no mistake. But the one in back, well, she has no eyes, so there might be a crack in her. If you take this one, I’ll lower the price.' I still remember this exchange, and at that time, in my childish mind, I thought that women were indeed something to be wary of.

—However, today, in the year 1905, there is no one foolish enough to sell girls like that, nor do I hear anyone saying that the one in back is dangerous because she has no eyes. Therefore, I conclude that, thanks to Western civilization, the conduct of women has surely progressed significantly. What do you think, Kangetsu?"

Before responding, Kangetsu cleared his throat with a grandiose cough, then deliberately spoke in a calm, low voice, offering this observation: "These days, women walk around selling themselves, saying things like, 'Please buy this,' or 'Oh, really?' on their way to and from school, at concerts, charity events, and garden parties, so there is no need to hire those leftover peddlers to shout about how good the girls are. When human independence develops, it naturally leads to this kind of situation. Old men worry unnecessarily, saying this and that, but the truth is, this is the trend of civilization, and I secretly express my joy at this phenomenon. No one buying asks if the goods are reliable or not, so there is peace of mind in that regard. Besides, in this complex world, if one were to go through such trouble, there would be no end to it. Even at fifty or sixty, one cannot get married or go off to become a bride."

Kangetsu, being a youth of the twentieth century, presented a modern view, then puffed out a cloud of Shikishima smoke towards Meitei’s face. Meitei was not a man to be put off by mere smoke. "As you say, today’s female students and young ladies are so imbued with self-respect and confidence that they are made of bone, flesh, and skin, and they are admirable in every way, not losing to men. The girls from the school near my house are something else. They wear tunics and hang from the horizontal bar, which is impressive. Every time I witness their gymnastics from my second-floor window, I reminisce about the women of ancient Greece."

"More Greek references," the master said with a sneer. "Well, it can’t be helped, as most things that evoke beauty originate from Greece. Aesthetics and Greece are inextricably linked. —Especially when I see those dark-skinned female students exercising with such single-mindedness, I always think of the tale of Agnodice," he continued, speaking with a knowing air. "Another difficult name has come up," Kangetsu remarked, still smirking. "Agnodice was a remarkable woman; I was truly impressed. At that time, Athenian law prohibited women from practicing as midwives. Quite inconvenient. Agnodice must have felt that inconvenience as well, don’t you think?"

"What’s that—what’s the name again?"

"It’s a woman’s name. She thought to herself that it was truly pitiful and extremely inconvenient for women not to be able to become midwives.

She pondered for three days and nights about how she could become one. Just at dawn on the third day, she heard a baby crying next door and suddenly had an epiphany. She quickly cut her long hair, dressed in men’s clothing, and went to attend Hierophilus’s lectures. After successfully finishing the lectures, she was ready to open her midwifery practice. However, there was a boom in births; babies were crying everywhere, and all of them were under Agnodice’s care, so she made a fortune. But as the saying goes, 'life is full of ups and downs,' and eventually, her secret was revealed, and she was about to face severe punishment for breaking the law."

"It sounds like a lecture," someone remarked. "Quite a good one, isn’t it? However, the women of Athens all signed a petition, and the magistrate at the time, unable to respond with the usual wooden politeness, ultimately declared her innocent. From then on, it was decreed that even women could freely practice midwifery, and thus it was happily resolved."

"You certainly know a lot of things; I’m impressed."

"Well, I know most things. The only thing I don’t know is my own foolishness, but even that I have a vague awareness of."

"Haha, how amusing..." As she laughed, the sound of the bell at the lattice door rang out, just like it had when it was first installed. "Oh, another customer," she said, retreating to the tea room. Just as she left, someone entered the room, and it turned out to be none other than Tofu.

If only Tofu were to arrive here, I would not say that every eccentric who comes and goes at my master's house would be accounted for, but at the very least, I must admit that there would be enough of them to alleviate my boredom. To complain of any deficiency would be a waste. It is unfortunate that if I were to be kept by another household, I might die without ever realizing that there were such esteemed gentlemen among humans. Fortunately, having become a cat under Mr. Kushami’s tutelage, I am able to serve daily before the tiger skin, and it is indeed a rare honor for me to witness the actions of such extraordinary heroes as Mr. Meitei, Mr. Kangetsu, and even Tofu, in this vast Tokyo, where such figures are hardly common. Thanks to this, I can forget the difficulty of being wrapped in my fur coat in this heat and spend half the day amusingly passing the time, for which I am deeply grateful. After all, with this many gathered, it cannot be an ordinary affair. I respectfully observe from behind the sliding door, anticipating that something will arise.

"How long it has been since we last met!" Upon bowing, I saw Tofu's face, which, as on the previous occasion, was shining beautifully. If judged solely by his head, he might resemble a stage actor, but the way he awkwardly wore his white Ogura-style hakama made him look like a disciple of Sakakibara Kenkichi. Therefore, the only part of Tofu's body that resembled an ordinary human was from his shoulders to his waist. "Well, despite the heat, you’ve come out quite well. Please, come this way," Mr. Meitei greeted him as if it were his own home. "It has been quite a while since I last saw you, sir." 

"Indeed, it was surely at the reading session this spring. Speaking of reading sessions, they seem to be quite popular these days. Have you not been to the shrine since then? That was delightful. I applauded greatly; did you notice?" 

"Thanks to you, I gathered quite a bit of courage and managed to make it to the end." 

"When will the next event be held?" the master interjected. "I plan to take a break for seven or eight months and would like to do something lively in September. Do you have any interesting ideas?" 

"Indeed," the master replied nonchalantly. "Tofu, why not let me do one of my creations?" Mr. Kangetsu then engaged him. "Your creations must be interesting, but what exactly is it?" 

"A script," Mr. Kangetsu insisted, trying to push his point. As expected, the three of them were slightly taken aback and looked at him in unison. "A script sounds grand. Is it a comedy or a tragedy?" Tofu asked as he took a step forward, while Mr. Kangetsu remained composed and replied, "Neither comedy nor tragedy. These days, with all the noise about old and new dramas, I thought I would introduce a new concept and create something called haigeki (play-drama)." 

"What is haigeki?" 

"It’s a drama distilled from the essence of haiku," he explained, and both the master and Mr. Meitei were somewhat perplexed. "And what is this concept?" Tofu was the one to ask. "Since it stems from haiku, I thought it best not to make it too lengthy or tedious, so I kept it as a one-act play." 

"I see." 

"First, let’s discuss the set. It should be extremely simple. In the center of the stage, we plant a large willow tree. Then, from the trunk of that willow, we extend a branch to the right, and on that branch, we have a crow perched." 

"It would be fine as long as the crow stays still," the master muttered, as if to himself, worried. "There’s no problem; we’ll tie the crow’s feet to the branch with string. Below it, we’ll place a basin for washing, and a beautiful woman will be facing sideways, using a towel." 

"That sounds a bit decadent. First of all, who will play that woman?" Mr. Meitei inquired. "That can be arranged easily.

We can hire a model from an art school." 

"That sounds like it might attract the attention of the police," the master fretted again. "Well, as long as it’s not a commercial performance, it shouldn’t matter. If they start complaining about that, then no one could ever do life drawing at school." 

"However, that’s for practice, so it’s a bit different from just watching," Mr. Kangetsu argued. "If the teachers were to say such things, Japan would still be in a poor state. Painting and theater are both forms of art," Mr. Kangetsu asserted with great fervor. "Well, enough of the debate; what happens next?" Tofu seemed eager to understand the plot. "Then, from the hanamichi (flower path), the haiku poet Takahama Kyoshi appears, holding a cane, wearing a white hat with a wick, dressed in a transparent haori and half-boots with Satsuma patterns. Although the attire looks like it was made for the army, being a poet, he must carry himself with a certain nonchalance while being deeply engrossed in his poetic thoughts. As Kyoshi walks down the hanamichi and finally reaches the main stage, he suddenly looks up and sees a large willow tree, and in the shadow of the willow, a beautiful woman is bathing. Startled, he looks up and sees a crow perched on a long branch, watching the woman bathe. At that moment, Kyoshi is deeply moved by the poetic essence and, after about fifty seconds of contemplation, he loudly recites a verse about the crow falling in love with the bathing woman, signaling the sound of the clapper and drawing the curtain." 

"What do you think? Isn’t this an interesting concept? Wouldn’t you prefer to be Kyoshi rather than a mere shrine?" Tofu, with a somewhat unsatisfied expression, replied, "It seems a bit too abrupt. I feel it could use a bit more human emotion in the events." 

Mr. Meitei, who had been relatively quiet until now, was not the type to remain silent for long. "That alone makes the haigeki quite formidable. According to Ueda Bin, the concepts of haiku and humor are negative and sound like the death knell of a nation, but he certainly made a good point. If you try to put on such a trivial performance, you’ll only be laughed at by Ueda. First of all, whether it’s a drama or a farce, it’s too vague and unclear. Excuse me, but Mr. Kangetsu, you’d be better off polishing pearls in a laboratory. No matter how many haigeki you create, they’ll still be the death knell of a nation." 

Mr. Kangetsu, somewhat indignant, replied, "Is it really that negative? I consider myself quite positive." 

"Kyoshi, you see, Kyoshi reciting a verse about the crow falling in love with the woman is quite a positive notion, I believe." 

"That’s a new theory.

I’d love to hear your explanation." 

"From a scientific perspective, it’s unreasonable for a crow to fall in love with a woman." 

"That’s true." 

"The fact that such an unreasonable idea is expressed so casually doesn’t sound forced at all." 

"Is that so?" the master interjected skeptically, but Mr. Kangetsu paid no mind. "The reason it doesn’t sound forced is that, psychologically speaking, it can be well explained. To be honest, the feelings of love or lack thereof reside within the haiku poet himself and have nothing to do with the crow. When the crow feels that it is in love, it’s not about the crow itself; ultimately, it’s because the poet is in love. The moment Kyoshi sees the beautiful woman bathing, he must have been struck by a sudden realization and fell in love. Seeing the crow, which he perceives as gazing down at the woman from the branch without moving, he mistakenly thinks, 'Ah, that creature is also smitten like me.' It’s certainly a misunderstanding, but that’s what makes it literary and, moreover, positive. The act of extending one’s own feelings onto the crow without any hesitation and pretending as if nothing is amiss is quite a positive approach, don’t you think, sir?" 

"Indeed, that’s a brilliant argument. If Kyoshi were to hear it, he would surely be astonished. While the explanation is positive, if that play were actually performed, the audience would undoubtedly be passive, wouldn’t they, Tofu?" 

"Yes, I do think it seems a bit too passive," he replied with a serious expression. The master seemed to want to shift the conversation's direction and asked, "So, Tofu, have you produced any masterpieces recently?" 

Tofu replied, "No, I haven’t created anything particularly noteworthy, but I’m thinking of publishing a poetry collection soon—I've fortunately brought the manuscript, so I would appreciate your critique." He took out a purple fukusa (silk wrapping cloth) from his pocket and pulled out a notebook containing about fifty or sixty sheets of manuscript paper, placing it before the master. With a serious expression, the master looked at it and saw on the first page:

"Unlike the people of the world, you appear so delicately."  
"Dedicated to Miss Tomiko."

It is written in two lines. The master, with a somewhat mysterious expression, gazes silently at a page for a while, prompting Meitei to lean in and say, "What is it, a new-style poem?" He peers closer and exclaims, "Ah, you dedicated it! Tofu, it was brave of you to dedicate it to Miss Tomiko." The master, still looking puzzled, asks, "Tofu, is this Tomiko really a woman who exists?" "Indeed, she is one of the women we invited to the reading session with Meitei the other day. She lives just in this neighborhood. In fact, I came by to show you the poetry collection, but unfortunately, she has been away on vacation in Oiso since last month," Tofu replies, speaking earnestly. "Kushami, this is the twentieth century. Don’t make that face; hurry up and read a masterpiece or something. But Tofu, this dedication could have been done better. What do you think the elegant term 'aeka' means?" "I think it means weak or delicate," comes the response. "Well, that interpretation isn't entirely off, but the original meaning refers to something precarious. So I wouldn’t have written it that way." "How would you write it to make it more poetic?" "I would write it like this: 'To the lady Tomiko, who appears delicate unlike the people of this world, I dedicate this.' It’s just a matter of three characters, but having a nose or not makes a significant difference in feeling." "I see," Tofu said, struggling to comprehend but forcing himself to agree. The master, still silent, finally turns the page and begins to read the first chapter. In the fragrant haze of weariness, my dear,
Is it your spirit that lingers like smoke of longing? Oh, I, ah, I, in this bitter world,
Sweetly received that fervent kiss. "This is a bit beyond my understanding," the master sighs as he hands it to Meitei. "This is a bit too much," Meitei says as he passes it to Kangetsu. Kangetsu replies, "Indeed," and returns it to Tofu. "Of course, it’s understandable that you don’t grasp it, as the poetry world has developed remarkably over the past decade. Nowadays, poetry is read while lying down or at train stations, making it nearly impossible to comprehend, and even the authors themselves often struggle to answer questions about their work. They write purely from inspiration, and poets bear no other responsibility. Annotations and interpretations are the work of scholars, and we pay them no mind. Recently, a friend of mine named Sōseki wrote a short piece called 'One Night,' but anyone who reads it finds it vague and incoherent. When I met him to clarify his intentions, he simply said he didn’t know what he was talking about.

Truly, that seems to be a characteristic of poets." "He may be a poet, but he’s quite a peculiar man," the master comments, to which Meitei simply replies, "He’s a fool."

Tofu feels he hasn’t sufficiently defended himself. "Sōseki may be an oddity among our group, but I hope you will read my poetry with that spirit in mind. Particularly, I would like you to pay attention to the contrast between the bitter world and the sweet kiss, as that was my struggle." "It certainly shows signs of considerable effort," Meitei observes. "The way you juxtapose sweet and bitter is quite interesting, like a blend of seventeen spices in chili pepper. It’s truly a unique technique of yours, Tofu, and I am deeply impressed."
