The master, having thought something over, suddenly stands and heads toward the study, soon returning with a sheet of paper. "Having seen your work, Tofu, now I would like to read a short piece of mine and request your critiques," he says, somewhat seriously. "I’ve already heard the epitaph of the Naturalist several times," someone remarks. "Well, be quiet. Tofu, this is certainly not my best work, but it’s just for amusement, so please listen." "We would love to hear it." "Kangetsu, you should listen too." "I’ll listen even if it’s not a special occasion. It’s not a long piece, is it?" "Just over sixty characters," Mr. Kushami begins to read his self-composed masterpiece. "With a shout of 'Yamato spirit!' the Japanese coughs like one afflicted with tuberculosis."

"That’s quite abrupt," Kangetsu praises. "‘Yamato spirit!’ says the newspaper man. ‘Yamato spirit!’ says the pickpocket. The Yamato spirit leaps across the sea. In England, they speak of the Yamato spirit. In Germany, they perform plays of the Yamato spirit."

"Indeed, this is a work surpassing even the Naturalist," Meitei says, leaning back to appreciate it. "General Togo possesses the Yamato spirit. Even Gin-san from the fish shop possesses the Yamato spirit. Swindlers, fortune-tellers, and murderers all possess the Yamato spirit."

"Please add that Kangetsu possesses it too," someone interjects. "When asked what the Yamato spirit is, they replied, 'It is the Yamato spirit,' and walked away. After going a few paces, a cough was heard."

"That line is excellent. You certainly have a way with words. Now, what’s the next line?" 

"Is the Yamato spirit something triangular, or is it something square? The Yamato spirit is, as the name suggests, a spirit. Because it is a spirit, it is always wandering."

"That’s quite amusing, but don’t you think there’s a bit too much of the Yamato spirit?" Tofu cautions. "I agree," Meitei adds. "Though no one speaks of it, no one has seen it. Many have heard of it, but no one has encountered it.

Is the Yamato spirit akin to a tengu?"

The master finishes reading, intending to conclude with a vague sense of mystery, but even such a renowned piece is too short, and its intention unclear, so the three of them wait, thinking there must be more to come. No matter how long they wait, there is no sound, so finally Kangetsu asks, "Is that all?" The master lightly replies, "Yes." The "yes" feels a bit too casual. Strangely, Meitei did not engage in his usual chatter about this renowned piece, but soon turned back and said, "Why don’t you gather your short pieces into a volume and dedicate it to someone?" The master casually replied, "Shall I dedicate it to you?" To which Meitei responded, "That’s quite sincere," and then continued to trim his nails with the scissors he had shown his wife earlier. Kangetsu turned to Tofu and asked, "Do you know that Miss Kaneda?" "Since she invited us to the reading session this spring, we’ve become quite friendly and have been in contact ever since. Whenever I’m in front of her, I feel a certain inspiration, and for a while, I can write poetry or compose songs with great delight. I believe the many love poems in this collection are entirely due to the inspiration I receive from such a friend of the opposite sex. Therefore, I must sincerely express my gratitude to her, and I decided to dedicate my collection to her. It is said that no one has written great poetry without a close female friend." "Is that so?" Kangetsu replied, smiling inwardly. It seems that no matter how much chatterers gather, such conversations cannot last long, and the fire of discussion has begun to dwindle. I, too, am not obliged to listen to their unchanging chatter all day, so I excused myself and went out to search for a mantis in the garden. Through the green foliage of the paulownia trees, the sun slants westward, casting dappled light, while cicadas cry desperately from the trunks. It may rain tonight. **Chapter 1**

I have recently taken up exercise. While some may dismiss the idea of a cat exercising as absurd, I would like to remind them that not so long ago, those same humans were ignorant of what exercise truly entailed, believing that eating and sleeping were their divine calling. They would praise the notion of "living in peace" while lounging on their cushions, too lazy to lift their rotting behinds from the floor, all in the name of their master's honor and their own indulgence. It is only in recent years, as a result of a contagion from the West, that they have begun to bombard us with ridiculous demands to exercise, drink milk, bathe in cold water, jump into the sea, and retreat to the mountains in summer to live on mist for a while. This trend can be likened to a plague, akin to the pestilence, tuberculosis, or neuroses.

To be fair, I was born only last year, and being just one year old this year, I cannot recall the state of affairs when humans first began to suffer from such ailments. Moreover, it is likely that those early days were not even wafting through the winds of this world. However, it is said that one cat year is equivalent to ten human years. Despite our lifespan being two or three times shorter than that of humans, if one considers the full development of a cat within that brief span, it is a gross error to calculate human years and cat years on the same scale. After all, even I, at just a little over one year old, possess this level of understanding. Take my master’s third daughter, for instance; she is said to be three years old by human counting, yet in terms of intellectual development, she is quite dull. She knows nothing beyond crying, wetting herself, and nursing. Compared to my concerns about the world and my frustrations with time, she is utterly trivial. Thus, it should come as no surprise that I have been able to condense the history of exercise, sea bathing, and the benefits of changing environments into a mere few thoughts. If anyone were to be astonished by such matters, it would only be those humans who are lacking in two legs. Humans have always been deficient in this regard. That is why, in recent times, they have gradually begun to extol the virtues of exercise and speak of the benefits of sea bathing as if they were grand inventions. I, on the other hand, have known these things long before I was born. First of all, if one were to ask why seawater is medicinal, it becomes immediately clear with just a visit to the coast. One cannot fathom how many fish inhabit such a vast expanse, yet none of those fish have ever fallen ill or sought the help of a doctor. They all swim healthily. Should they fall ill, their bodies would cease to function. If they die, they will surely float. That is why we speak of the passing of fish as a "departure" and the demise of birds as a "fall," while lamenting the extinction of humans. If you were to ask someone who has traveled abroad and crossed the Indian Ocean whether they have ever seen a fish die, they would invariably respond with a no. And rightly so. No matter how many times they have traveled back and forth, no one has ever witnessed a single fish taking its last breath upon the waves—though, for fish, we must say it "took its last tide." Given that no fish has ever been seen floating after death, one can conclude that fish must be remarkably resilient. So why are fish so robust? The answer will only be known after humans have waited long enough, and it is quite simple. It is evident: they continuously bathe in seawater. The benefits of sea bathing are thus apparent for fish.

If they are evident for fish, they must also be evident for humans. When Dr. Richard Russell jumped into the seawater at Brighton in 1750 and exaggeratedly advertised that he cured four hundred and four diseases instantly, one could laugh at how late he was to the game. Even cats, when the right time comes, intend to head out to Kamakura. However, now is not the time. There is a time for everything. Just as the Japanese before the Meiji Restoration could not experience the benefits of sea bathing and died, today’s cats have yet to encounter the opportunity to leap into the sea in their nakedness. Haste makes waste; until the cats that have been sent to Tsukiji return home safely, we cannot recklessly jump in. Until the laws of evolution allow us cats to develop an appropriate resistance to the raging tides—until the phrase "the cat has risen" becomes commonly used instead of "the cat has died"—we cannot easily indulge in sea bathing.

I decided to postpone my trip to the beach and settled for some exercise in the meantime. It seems rather impoverished in this twentieth century to not engage in physical activity; it gives a bad impression. It is not that I refuse to exercise, but rather that I cannot do so — I have no time for it, no leisure. In the past, those who exercised were laughed at like fools, but now those who do not exercise are considered inferior. Our evaluations change according to time and circumstance, much like the pupils of my eyes, which merely grow smaller or larger. However, when it comes to human character, it can flip upside down entirely. Even if it flips, it does not matter. Everything has two sides, two ends. The ability to strike both ends and create a change of black and white on the same object is where human adaptability lies. There is charm in seeing a small space turned upside down into a larger one. Peering at Amanohashidate from between my legs reveals a particularly exquisite view. Shakespeare, too, would be tiresome if he were always the same. Occasionally, someone must look at Hamlet from between their legs and say, "This is no good," or else the literary world will not progress. Thus, it is not surprising that those who once spoke ill of exercise suddenly find themselves wanting to engage in it, with even women walking around with rackets in hand. As long as no one laughs at a cat exercising, it is all well and good. Now, some may wonder what kind of exercise I engage in, so I shall explain. Unfortunately, as you know, I do not possess any machinery. Therefore, I struggle with balls and bats. Next, I have no money to purchase them. From these two sources, I believe the exercise I have chosen can be classified as one that requires neither money nor equipment. You might think I simply stroll about or dash off with a piece of tuna in my mouth, but merely moving my four legs mechanically along the ground under the influence of gravity is rather simplistic and lacks interest. No matter what it is called, the kind of exercise my master occasionally engages in — the kind that reads as it is written — seems to tarnish the sanctity of exercise. Of course, even simple exercise can be stimulating under certain conditions. Competitions for bonito flakes or salmon hunting are quite enjoyable, but these require specific targets, and without them, they become dull and uninteresting. If there are no exciting incentives, I wish to try some artistic form of exercise. I have thought of various activities. One is to leap from the kitchen eaves to the roof, standing on the plum-shaped tiles at the peak with my four legs. Crossing the laundry pole — this is utterly impossible, as the bamboo is too slippery, and my claws cannot grip.

Suddenly pouncing on a child from behind — this is indeed an interesting form of exercise, but if done too often, it leads to terrible consequences, so I attempt it only about three times a month at most. Putting a paper bag over my head — this is not only painful but also a method lacking in interest. Particularly, it cannot succeed without a human opponent. Next, scratching the covers of books — this not only risks being scolded by my master but also engages only my dexterous paws without exercising my entire body. These are what I call old-fashioned exercises. Among the new styles, there are some that are quite intriguing. First, there is mantis hunting. While not as grand as rat hunting, it carries far less danger. It is the most superior pastime to engage in from mid-summer to early autumn. To describe the method, one first goes out to the garden and searches for a mantis. If the season is right, finding one or two is no trouble at all. Upon discovering a mantis, I dash towards it, cutting through the air. The mantis then assumes a defensive posture, raising its sickle-like head. The mantis is quite brave, intending to resist until it knows the strength of its opponent, which makes it amusing. I gently tap the raised head with my right front paw. The soft head bends sideways. The expression on the mantis's face at this moment adds considerable interest. There is a sense of surprise. Then, I leap behind it and lightly scratch its wings from the back. Those wings, usually carefully folded, become disheveled if scratched too fiercely, revealing a delicate, light-colored underlayer like Yoshino paper. Even in summer, it is quite a sight, as it is layered with two sheets. At this moment, the mantis’s long neck invariably turns back. Sometimes it faces me, but in most cases, it merely raises its head, waiting for me to make a move. If it maintains this posture for too long, it will not be an exercise at all, so if it drags on, I give it another gentle tap. If I do this much, an observant mantis will certainly flee. If it approaches me without care, it is a rather uneducated, barbaric mantis. If my opponent exhibits such barbaric behavior, I will wait for it to approach and then pounce on it mercilessly. Usually, it gets thrown two or three feet away. However, if the opponent advances calmly from behind, I feel pity and circle around the garden's trees a few times. The mantis has only escaped about five or six inches. Now that it knows my strength, it lacks the courage to resist. It merely scurries about in confusion. However, as I chase it, it sometimes becomes desperate and attempts a grand display of flapping its wings.

Originally, the mantis's wings are designed to harmonize with its neck, elongated and slender, but upon inquiry, I hear they are purely for decoration and serve no practical purpose, much like the English, French, or German languages to humans. Thus, when it attempts a grand display with its useless wings, it can hardly function against me. Though it is called a grand display, in reality, it merely drags itself along the ground. At this point, I feel a bit sorry for it, but it is for the sake of exercise, so there is no helping it. I apologize and dash forward. It cannot make a sharp turn due to inertia, so it has no choice but to advance. I strike its nose. At this moment, the mantis invariably falls with its wings spread. I press down on it with my front paws and take a little rest. Then I release it. I let it go and press down again. I attack it with the strategy of the famous general Zhuge Liang, capturing it and releasing it repeatedly. After about thirty minutes of this routine, when it can no longer move, I take it in my mouth and give it a shake. Then I spit it out. This time, it lies on the ground, motionless, so I poke it with my paw, and as it attempts to leap, I press down on it again. Eventually, when it becomes tiresome, I resort to the final measure and devour it. By the way, for those who have never eaten a mantis, I must say that it is not particularly delicious. Moreover, it seems to lack substantial nourishment. Following mantis hunting, I engage in cicada catching. Simply saying "cicada" does not refer to the same kind of creature. Just as there are oil cicadas, min-min cicadas, and oshiitsukutsuku cicadas among humans, there are also oil cicadas, min-min cicadas, and oshiitsukutsuku cicadas among cicadas. The oil cicada is persistent and difficult to catch. The min-min cicada is troublesome in crosswinds. However, the most enjoyable to catch is the oshiitsukutsuku cicada. This one only appears at the end of summer. When the autumn winds begin to blow, and I feel a chill that makes me sneeze, it begins to raise its tail and sing. It is a good singer, and from my perspective, it seems to have no other calling than to sing and be caught by a cat. I catch these at the beginning of autumn, which I refer to as cicada catching exercise. I must mention to you that as long as it is called a cicada, it does not lie on the ground. Anything that falls to the ground is sure to be covered with ants. I do not catch those that lie in the realm of the ants. Instead, I capture those that perch on high branches, singing their oshiitsukutsuku songs. Additionally, I would like to ask knowledgeable humans whether they sing "oshiitsukutsuku" or "tsukutsukuoshi," as the interpretation may have considerable relevance in cicada studies.

The superiority of humans over cats lies in such matters, and since this is a point of pride for humans, it would be wise to ponder it if you cannot answer immediately. However, in cicada catching, it does not matter either way. I simply climb the tree, guided by their voices, and catch them while they are lost in their singing. This appears to be the simplest form of exercise, yet it is quite labor-intensive. I possess four legs, so I do not think I am inferior to other animals when it comes to traversing the earth. At the very least, judging from the mathematical knowledge of two legs versus four, I do not intend to lose to humans. However, when it comes to climbing trees, there are certainly some who are more adept than I. Aside from professional monkeys, there are also humans who should not be underestimated. Originally, it is a challenging endeavor to defy gravity, so I do not consider it a disgrace if I cannot do it, but it does present considerable inconvenience in cicada catching. Fortunately, I have claws, which allow me to climb somewhat, but it is not as easy as it appears from the outside. Moreover, cicadas can fly. Unlike the mantis, once they take flight, my hard-earned tree climbing may lead to a tragic fate of not being able to climb at all. Lastly, there is the risk of being urinated on by cicadas. That urine seems to aim for my eyes. I have no choice but to flee, so I hope they do not urinate on me. What psychological state leads to such behavior just before they fly away? Perhaps it is due to overwhelming anxiety, or maybe it is a tactic to create a moment of escape from a sudden enemy. In that case, it would fall into the same category as squids spitting ink or the kind of tricks that humans play with their languages. This is also a matter that cannot be overlooked in cicada studies. With sufficient research, this alone could certainly hold the value of a doctoral thesis. But that is a side issue, so let us return to the main topic. The most concentrated gathering of cicadas — if "concentrated" sounds odd, then "gathering" is too cliché, so I will stick with "concentrated" — occurs on the blue paulownia tree. It is said to be called "wutong" in Chinese. However, this blue paulownia has an abundance of leaves, and those leaves are as large as fans, so when they overlap, the branches become nearly invisible. This greatly hinders cicada catching. The saying "You can hear their voices, but you cannot see their forms" seems to have been created especially for me. I have no choice but to go by sound. About a span below, the wutong tree forks as ordered, so I take a rest here and search for the cicadas from beneath the leaves. However, on my way up, there are some who rustle and fly away in a hurry. Once one flies, it is all over.

In terms of imitation, cicadas are as foolish as humans. One after another, they take flight. By the time I arrive at the fork, the tree may be completely silent, with not a single voice remaining. Having climbed this far, I look around, but no matter how I tilt my ears, there are no cicadas, and since it is troublesome to turn back, I decide to rest for a while at the fork, waiting for a second opportunity. Before I know it, I become drowsy and end up playing in the black sweet countryside. When I wake up, I find myself having fallen from the fork onto the garden stones below. However, I usually manage to catch at least one each time I climb. The only problem is that when I catch one up in the tree, I must swallow it there. Therefore, when I bring it down and spit it out, it is mostly dead. No matter how much I play with it or scratch it, there is no definite response. The charm of cicada catching lies in stealthily approaching and capturing the oshiitsukutsuku cicada while it is earnestly extending and retracting its tail. At that moment, the cicada lets out a cry, flapping its thin, transparent wings in every direction. Its speed and grace are beyond words, truly a magnificent sight in the cicada world. Each time I capture an oshiitsukutsuku cicada, I always request it to show me this artistic performance. When I grow tired of it, I apologize and stuff it into my mouth. Some cicadas continue their performance even after entering my mouth. The next exercise I engage in is sliding down pine trees. There is no need for lengthy explanation here, so I will briefly mention it. When one hears "sliding down pine trees," one might think it means sliding on the pine itself, but that is not the case; it is still a form of climbing. While cicada catching involves climbing to catch cicadas, sliding down pine trees is climbing for the sake of climbing. That is the difference between the two. Originally, since the pine has been serving as a feast since the time of the Tokugawa shogunate, it has become rather rough. Therefore, nothing is as slippery as a pine trunk. There are no good handholds. There are no good footholds — in other words, there are no good claw holds. I dash up the trunk in one go. Once I reach the top, I come back down. There are two methods for coming down. One is to turn upside down and descend with my head facing the ground. The other is to maintain my position while keeping my tail down as I descend. Humans might ask which is more difficult. In their shallow understanding, they might think that since I am coming down anyway, it is easier to descend headfirst. That is a mistake. You only know that Yoshitsune leaped down from Hiyodorigoe, and since even Yoshitsune descended headfirst, you think a cat can certainly do the same.

It is not something to be taken lightly. Do you think a cat's claws grow in any direction? They all curve backward. Therefore, while I can pull things toward me like a grappling hook, I cannot exert force to push them away. Now, let us say I have climbed the pine tree vigorously. Since I am originally a creature of the ground, nature dictates that I cannot remain atop the pine tree for long; if left alone, I will surely fall. However, if I fall freely, it is too fast. Thus, I must find some means to ease this natural tendency. This is what it means to descend. Falling and descending may seem vastly different, but in reality, it is not as significant as one might think. If you slow down your fall, you are descending; if you speed up your descent, you are falling. Falling and descending are merely slight differences. I dislike falling from the pine tree, so I must slow my fall to descend. In other words, I must resist the speed of my fall with something. Since, as mentioned earlier, all my claws point backward, if I stand with my head up and dig in my claws, I can utilize their strength against the force of gravity. Thus, falling transforms into descending. It is indeed an easily understandable principle. However, if I were to turn myself upside down and attempt to leap down from the pine tree like Yoshitsune, my claws would be of no use. I would slide down, unable to counterbalance my own weight. Here, the one who intended to descend would instead fall. This is how difficult it is to leap down from Hiyodorigoe. Among cats, I am likely the only one capable of this feat. That is why I refer to this exercise as sliding down pine trees. Lastly, I will say a word about fence running. My master's garden is enclosed with a bamboo fence in a square shape. One side parallel to the eaves stretches about eight or nine ken (a traditional Japanese unit of length). The other two sides are each only four ken long. The exercise I mentioned, fence running, involves making a complete circuit atop this fence without falling off. While it is sometimes easy to mess up, if I succeed, it is quite satisfying. Particularly, there are places where burnt roots stand, providing convenient spots for a little rest. Today, I performed well, attempting it three times from morning until noon, and I improved with each attempt. The more I improve, the more enjoyable it becomes. Finally, on my fourth attempt, halfway through, three crows flew in from the neighboring roof and landed in a row about one ken away. This was a troublesome situation. They were obstructing my exercise, and I thought it was outrageous for crows, with no known affiliations, to perch on someone else's fence. So I called out, "Hey, move along!" The leading crow looked at me and grinned.

The second one gazed at my master's garden. The third was wiping its beak on the bamboo fence. It must have eaten something. I stood on the fence, giving them three minutes to respond. The crows are said to be called Kanzaemon, and indeed, they are Kanzaemon. No matter how long I waited, they did not greet me or take flight. I had no choice but to begin walking slowly. Then, the leading Kanzaemon slightly spread its wings. I thought it was finally scared of my presence and was about to flee, but it merely changed its posture from right to left. This rascal! If it were on the ground, I would have left it behind, but alas, I have no leisure to deal with Kanzaemon while traversing this already arduous path. Moreover, waiting for the three crows to vacate would be tiresome. First of all, if I wait too long, my legs will tire. The crows, being creatures with wings, can perch here for as long as they like. If they are comfortable, they will linger indefinitely. Meanwhile, I am already on my fourth attempt and quite fatigued. Let alone performing a feat that rivals tightrope walking, I cannot guarantee that I will not fall even without any obstacles, so having three of these black-clad creatures blocking my path is quite inconvenient. If it comes to that, I will have no choice but to cease my exercise and descend from the fence. It is troublesome, so I might as well just do that. After all, they are a large group, and besides, they are unfamiliar beings in this area. Their beaks are pointed like those of a teng

Turning left at the alley, I saw something tall and bamboo-like standing ahead, emitting thin smoke from its top. This, indeed, was the bathhouse. I quietly snuck in through the back door. Some may call sneaking in through the back door cowardly or sentimental, but that is merely a repetitive complaint from those who cannot visit unless they come through the front, fueled by half jealousy. Since ancient times, clever people have always been known to strike unexpectedly from the back door. It is said that this is mentioned on page five of the second volume, first chapter of "The Gentleman’s Training." The next page states that the back door is the testament of a gentleman and the gateway to personal virtue. As a cat of the twentieth century, I possess this level of education. One should not look down on it too much. Now, upon sneaking in, I found to my left a pile of split pine logs stacked up like a mountain, and beside it, coal heaped up like a hill. Some may wonder why the pine logs are like a mountain while the coal is like a hill, but there is no particular meaning to it; it is merely a choice of words. It is unfortunate that humans, after consuming rice, birds, fish, and various other delicacies, have fallen so low as to even eat coal. As I looked around, I noticed an entrance about the size of a room wide open, and peering inside, it was eerily quiet. On the other side, I could hear the persistent voices of humans. Concluding that this so-called bathhouse must be where the voices were coming from, I made my way through the valley formed between the pine logs and coal, turned left, and moved forward. To my right, there was a glass window, outside of which were round small tubs stacked in a triangular, pyramid-like formation. I secretly sympathized with the small tubs, thinking how unfortunate it must be for round objects to be stacked in such a way. On the southern side of the small tubs, there was a space of four or five shaku (about 1.2 to 1.5 meters) of board left over, appearing as if it were welcoming me. The height of the board was about one meter off the ground, making it just right for me to leap up. "Very well," I thought, and with a graceful jump, the so-called bathhouse dangled right before my nose, beneath my eyes, and in front of my face. There is nothing more delightful in the world than to eat what has not yet been eaten and to see what has not yet been seen. If only you could spend about thirty to forty minutes in this bathhouse realm three times a week like my master, that would be splendid. However, if you have never seen a bath like I have, you should hurry to see it. You need not witness the death of your parents, but this is something you must definitely experience. What is this spectacle?

What is this spectacle that I hesitate to speak of? Within this glass window, there are humans bustling about, all completely nude. They are like the indigenous people of Taiwan. They are the Adam of the twentieth century. If we were to delve into the history of clothing—though it is a long story, so I shall leave that to dear old Teufelsdreck and refrain from elaborating—humans are entirely defined by their clothing. Back in the eighteenth century, when the British Bath in Bath established strict regulations, both men and women were required to cover themselves from shoulder to toe in the bathhouse. Sixty years ago, there was an incident in the departing capital of Britain where a design school was established. Since it was a design school, they had acquired and displayed nude paintings, nude sculptures, and models everywhere, which was fine, but when it came time to hold the opening ceremony, the officials and school staff found themselves in great trouble. If they were to hold the ceremony, they would have to invite the city’s ladies. However, according to the thinking of the noblewomen of that time, humans were considered dressing animals. They did not think of themselves as mere subordinates of a skin-clad monkey. To appear as a human without clothing was akin to being without an elephant's trunk, being without students, or lacking the courage of a soldier; it was to lose one's very essence. If one has lost their essence, they cannot be considered human; they are beasts. Even if it is a model or a sculpture, associating with naked humans would degrade your dignity. Thus, they declared their refusal to attend. The staff thought they were dealing with an uncommunicative bunch, but after all, women are a kind of ornament in both Eastern and Western countries. They cannot be rice pounders or soldiers, but they are indispensable decorative tools for the opening ceremony. Therefore, they had no choice but to go to a kimono shop and buy thirty-five yards of black cloth to dress all those naked humans in kimonos. They took great care to ensure there were no oversights, even going so far as to cover their faces with clothing. In this way, they finally managed to hold the ceremony without any issues. Such is the importance of clothing to humans. Recently, there are teachers who insist on nudity, proclaiming it repeatedly, but that is a mistake. From my perspective, having never been nude even for a single day since birth, I must say it is entirely incorrect. Nudity became fashionable after the influences of the Greek and Roman legacies were seduced by the lascivious winds of the Renaissance. The Greeks and Romans must have regarded nudity as commonplace, and thus they likely never considered it to have any moral implications.

However, Northern Europe is a cold place. If one cannot even imagine traveling naked in Japan, then one would surely perish in Germany or England. Since dying would be rather dull, one wears clothing. When everyone wears clothing, humans become dressing animals. Once they have become dressing animals, if they suddenly encounter a naked animal, they do not recognize it as human; they see it as a beast. Therefore, Europeans, particularly those from Northern Europe, can treat nude paintings and sculptures as beasts. They can be deemed inferior to cats. Beautiful? It does not matter if they are beautiful; they can simply be regarded as beautiful beasts. Some may ask if I have seen Western women's formal attire, but as a cat, I have never had the pleasure of viewing such garments. I have heard that they expose their chests, shoulders, and arms, calling this their formal attire. It is quite outrageous. Until the fourteenth century, their attire was not so ridiculous; they wore what ordinary humans wore. The reasons for their transformation into such lowly, circus-like figures are too tedious to explain. Those who know, know, and those who do not can simply pretend not to know. Regardless of history, they have such an odd appearance that, although they may feel proud at night, when the sun rises, they hunch their shoulders, conceal their chests, wrap their arms, and hide everything, even considering it a great shame to show a single toenail. From this, it is clear that their so-called formal attire is the result of a kind of nonsensical collaboration between fools. If they are embarrassed, they should try exposing their shoulders, chests, and arms even during the day. Even the nudists would agree. If nudity is such a wonderful thing, then they should let their daughters go naked and, while they are at it, stroll through Ueno Park in the nude themselves. But they cannot? It is not that they cannot; it is simply that Westerners do not do it, so they do not either. Yet, they strut around in this utterly unreasonable formal attire, going to places like the Imperial Hotel. When asked about the reason for this, there is none. It is simply because Westerners wear it, so they wear it too. Westerners are strong, so even if it is absurd, they feel compelled to imitate them. "Go with the long, bendable things, yield to the strong, and be pressed by the heavy," they say, but isn’t that rather dull? If it cannot be helped, then I will excuse them, but one should not think too highly of the Japanese. Even in the realm of scholarship, this holds true, but since it does not relate to clothing, I shall omit further discussion.

Clothing is, in this manner, an important thing for humans as well. It is such a crucial condition that one might say it is as if humans are clothing, or clothing is humans. I would go so far as to assert that human history is not a history of flesh, nor a history of bones, nor a history of blood, but simply a history of clothing. Therefore, when I see a human without clothing, it does not feel human at all. It is as if I have encountered a monster. If all monsters were to agree to become monsters together, then the so-called monsters would cease to exist, which would not matter; however, that would leave humans in a great predicament. In ancient times, nature manufactured humans as equals and cast them into the world. Thus, every human is born naked. If the true nature of humans is something to be content with equally, then it would be appropriate for them to grow up in this naked state. However, one naked individual claims that if everyone is the same, there is no point in studying. The results of hard work are not visible. Somehow, I want to make it evident that I am I, and anyone who sees me will recognize me as such. Regarding this, I wish to adorn myself with something that will make people gasp in astonishment. After pondering for ten years, I finally invented the fundoshi (a traditional Japanese loincloth) and immediately put it on, strutting about proudly, thinking, “How impressive I must be!” This is the ancestor of today’s rickshaw pullers. It is somewhat strange that it took ten long years to invent such a simple fundoshi, but that conclusion is drawn from a determination placed in the world of ignorance from ancient times, and at that time, there was no such significant invention. It is said that Descartes took many years to come up with the truth that even triplets could understand: “I think, therefore I am.” Everything that is thought out is a laborious endeavor, so one must not say that spending ten years on the invention of the fundoshi is excessive for the wisdom of a rickshaw puller. Now that the fundoshi has been created, it is only the rickshaw pullers who can walk with confidence in the world. Disliking the sight of rickshaw pullers parading about in their fundoshi, a competitive monster spent six years inventing the haori (a traditional jacket), a useless long garment. As a result, the influence of the fundoshi quickly waned, and the era of the haori became dominant. The vegetable vendors, herbal medicine sellers, and kimono merchants are all descendants of this great inventor. Following the fundoshi period and the haori period comes the hakama (traditional trousers) period. This was conceived by a monster who became irritated, saying, “What is this?

It’s a haori!” and now all samurai of old and current officials belong to this category. In this way, these monsters, each trying to outdo one another and compete in novelty, eventually gave rise to grotesque forms resembling the tail of a swallow. However, upon retreating to consider their origins, it is clear that these are not facts that arose from force, absurdity, chance, or carelessness. They are all manifestations of a fierce desire to win, transformed into various new shapes, worn as a means to say, “I am not like you.” From this psychological perspective, a significant discovery can be made. It is none other than the fact that, just as nature abhors a vacuum, humans dislike equality. In a time when humans are compelled to wear clothing as if it were flesh and bone, to cast aside these garments, which are a part of this essence, and return to the original era of fairness is the act of a madman. Even if one were to accept the name of madman, it is utterly impossible to return. Those who have returned would be seen as monsters in the eyes of enlightened individuals. Even if one were to drag down billions of people into the realm of monsters, claiming that this is equality, that everyone is a monster and thus there is nothing to be ashamed of, it would still not suffice. The day after the world becomes populated by monsters, the competition among monsters would begin anew. If competition cannot be conducted while wearing clothing, then the competition would occur among monsters. Nakedness, in its nakedness, will always establish distinctions. From this perspective, clothing has become something that cannot be removed at all. Yet, now I see before me a group of humans who have put aside their indispensable fundoshi, haori, and hakama, exposing their original madness to the gaze of the public without any shame, and casually engaging in conversation. What I referred to earlier as a grand spectacle is this. I have the honor of introducing this generality for the gentlemen of civilization.

It’s all rather chaotic, and I don’t know where to begin my description. There’s no discipline in the actions of these creatures, so it’s quite a task to provide an orderly account. Let’s start with the bath. I’m not entirely sure if it’s a bath or something else, but I can only assume it’s a bath. It’s about three shaku wide and perhaps one and a half ken long, divided into two sections, one of which contains white water. They call it a medicinal bath, and it’s murky with a color reminiscent of dissolved lime. However, it’s not merely murky; it’s thick and heavy with a certain opacity. Upon closer inspection, it doesn’t seem surprising that it looks rotten, as they say they only change the water once a week. Next to it is the ordinary bath, which is also transparent, but I wouldn’t dare call it clear or brilliant. Its color reflects the value of having stirred a rainwater bucket. Now comes the description of the creatures, which is quite a challenge. Standing by the rainwater bucket are two young fellows. They’re facing each other, pouring water over their bellies with a splashing sound. What a delightful sight! Both are remarkably developed in their dark spots. As I observe these creatures, one of them starts rubbing his chest with a towel and asks, “Kin-san, it really hurts here, what could it be?” To which Kin-san replies, “That’s your stomach; you know, the stomach can take your life. You must be careful, or it could be dangerous.” “But it’s on my left side,” he points to the left lung. “That’s where the stomach is. The left is the stomach, and the right is the lung.” “Is that so? I thought my stomach was around here,” he says, patting his waist, and Kin-san responds, “That’s just colic.” 

At that moment, a man with a thin beard, about twenty-five or twenty-six, jumps in with a splash. The soap clinging to his body rises to the surface along with the dirt, sparkling as if seen through iron-rich water. Next to him, an old man with a bald head is capturing a five-minute haircut and is saying something. Both of them are just floating their heads above the water. “You know, getting old like this isn’t good. Humans can’t compete with the young ones once they’ve aged. But if the bath isn’t hot, it makes me feel unwell.” “You’re a sturdy one, aren’t you? If you have that much energy, that’s great.” “I’m not energetic; I just don’t get sick. As long as a person doesn’t do bad things, they can live up to one hundred and twenty.” “Really? Can people live that long?” “Of course, I can guarantee they can live up to one hundred and twenty.

Before the Restoration, there was a samurai named Kurubuchi in Ushigome, and one of his servants lived to be one hundred and thirty.” “That’s quite a long life.” “Yes, he lived so long that he eventually forgot his own age. He remembered up to one hundred, but after that, he forgot. I knew him when he was one hundred thirty, but he didn’t die then. I don’t know what happened after that. He might still be alive.” 

As he says this, he rises from the bath. The bearded man is scattering something like mica around him while chuckling to himself. The next fellow who jumps in is different from the usual creatures; he has a pattern etched on his back. It looks like Iwami Jutaro is brandishing a sword to slay a python, but unfortunately, he hasn’t yet succeeded, so the python is nowhere to be seen. Consequently, Jutaro seems a bit deflated. As he jumps in, he exclaims, “This water is too warm!” Then another person follows him in, grimacing as if he’s enduring the heat, and greets Jutaro with, “Hey, boss.” Jutaro replies, “Hey,” and then asks, “What happened to Min-san?” “What happened? He just loves to splash around.” “It’s not just splashing…” “Is that so? That guy isn’t easy to deal with. He’s not well-liked—what is it about him that people don’t trust? A craftsman shouldn’t be like that.” “That’s right. Min-san isn’t humble; he’s arrogant. That’s why people don’t trust him.” “It’s true. He thinks he’s quite skilled, but in the end, it’s his own loss.” “An old man from Shiragane-cho has passed away, and now it’s just the former barrel maker and the brick maker left around here. I was born here, but I don’t know where Min-san came from.” “That’s true. But he’s made quite a name for himself.” “Yes. There’s something about him that people don’t like. He doesn’t socialize with others.” 

Let’s leave the rainwater bucket for now and look at the white bath, which is extraordinarily crowded. It would be more accurate to say that the water is entering the people rather than the people entering the water. Moreover, they are remarkably relaxed, as there have been some who have entered, but none have come out. If they stay in like this for a week, the water is bound to get dirty, I thought, as I looked around the bath. In the left corner, Mr. Kushami is crammed in, turning bright red. Poor fellow, someone should clear a path for him to get out, but no one seems inclined to move, and the master shows no sign of wanting to leave either. He just remains still, growing redder. This is quite a struggle. Perhaps it’s due to the spirit of wanting to make the most of the two sen and five rin bath fee that he’s turning so red, but I, thinking that he should get out soon lest he steam himself, felt quite worried from my perch on the window shelf.

Then, the man floating next to the master, while forming an eight with his arms, says, “This seems a bit too much; something hot is bubbling up from my back.” He subtly seeks sympathy from the other creatures present. “Oh, this is just right. The medicinal bath won’t work unless it’s this hot. In my country, we enter water that’s twice as hot.” Someone, with a face resembling a thin cucumber, boasts about this. “What does this bath cure?” asks a man, folding his towel and scratching his uneven head. “It cures all sorts of things. Anything will do, really. Quite impressive,” he replies. If it’s such a curative bath, one would expect it to make people look a bit healthier. “It’s best to enter the bath on the third or fourth day after the medicine is added. Today is just the right time to enter,” he states with an air of knowledge, and he is a rather bloated man. He’s probably just a dirt-fat fellow. “Can we drink it too?” someone asks from somewhere, with a yellow voice. “If you drink it after it cools down, you won’t need to get up to urinate, so give it a try,” comes a reply, though I couldn’t tell whose voice it was.

As I turned my gaze from the bathtub to the wooden floor, I saw a row of unremarkable Adams lined up, each in their own haphazard postures, washing whatever parts of themselves they deemed fit. Among them, the most astonishing were two Adams: one lying on his back, gazing up at the high skylight, and the other, propped on his stomach, peering into a drain. They appeared to be particularly idle Adams. A monk squatted facing the stone wall, while a young acolyte kept tapping him on the shoulder. This was likely due to the hierarchical relationship between teacher and student, with the young one serving as a proxy for the elder. The real three-year-old was also present. He seemed to have caught a cold, for despite the heat, he wore a padded jacket and poured hot water from an oval tub onto the shoulders of a gentleman. Looking at his right foot, I noticed he had a scrubber wedged between his big toe and the next. Nearby, a man greedily clutched three small buckets, engaged in a lengthy conversation with the person next to him about the use of soap. Curious, I leaned in to listen, and he was saying something like this: “Guns came from abroad, you know. In the old days, it was all about sword fighting. The foreigners are cowardly, and that’s how such things came to be. It doesn’t seem to be from China; it really looks like it’s from abroad. There was none of that during the Wataru period. Wataru was indeed the Seiwa Genji. There’s a story that when Yoshitsune crossed over from Ezo to Manchuria, a very learned man from Ezo accompanied him. Then, that Yoshitsune’s son attacked the Ming dynasty, but since that was troublesome, he sent a messenger to the third shogun asking for three thousand soldiers. The third shogun kept him there and wouldn’t let him go. — What was it called again? — It was some kind of messenger. — So, they kept that messenger for two years and finally showed him a courtesan in Nagasaki. The child born from that courtesan was Wataru. When he returned to his country, he found that the Ming had been destroyed by traitors.…” I couldn’t make heads or tails of what he was saying. Behind him stood a man of about twenty-five or six, with a gloomy face, absentmindedly washing his groin with white water. He seemed to be suffering from some sort of ailment. Next to him was a young man, perhaps seventeen or eighteen, chattering away with an air of arrogance, likely a student from the neighborhood. Further along, I spotted a peculiar back. The vertebrae jutted out as if bamboo had been shoved up his backside. On either side of him were four orderly rows of shapes resembling sixteen musashi. Some of these sixteen musashi were red and festering, surrounded by pus.

As I continued to write, I realized there was far too much to describe, and I could hardly manage to depict even a fraction of it. Just as I began to feel a bit overwhelmed by this troublesome task, an old monk in a light yellow cotton kimono suddenly appeared at the entrance. The monk respectfully bowed to these naked monstrosities and said, “Ah, thank you all for your continued patronage every day. It’s a bit chilly today, so please take your time — feel free to come in and out of the hot water and warm yourselves leisurely. — Head clerk, please be sure to check the water temperature.” The head clerk replied, “Hey!” Wataru remarked, “What a charming fellow! Without him, business wouldn’t thrive,” greatly praising the old man. I was a bit surprised to suddenly encounter this unusual elder, so I decided to keep my observations focused on him for a while. The old man soon spotted a little boy of about four and extended his hand, saying, “Come here, little boy.” The child, seeing the old man who looked like he had stepped on a large rice cake, must have thought it was quite a sight, for he let out a loud scream and began to cry. The old man, somewhat taken aback, exclaimed, “Oh dear, why are you crying? Am I scary? Oh dear, oh dear!” With no other option, he quickly shifted his attention to the boy’s parent. “Ah, Mr. Minamoto! It’s a bit chilly today, isn’t it? That thief who broke into Omi-ya last night was such a foolish fellow. He cut a square hole in the door to sneak in. And yet, he didn’t take anything with him. Perhaps he was spotted by the patrol or the night watch.” He laughed heartily at the thief’s recklessness, then turned to another person, saying, “Yes, yes, it’s cold. You young folks probably don’t feel it as much.” Only the old man seemed to be feeling the chill.

For a while, I was so absorbed in the old man that I completely forgot about the other creatures. Not only that, but even the master, who had been crouching in pain, vanished from my memory. Suddenly, from between the sink and the wooden floor, a loud voice erupted. It was unmistakably Mr. Kushami. His voice, far greater than the master's, and its muddy, grating quality were not new, but given the circumstances, I was somewhat taken aback. I instantly deduced that he must have lost his temper from being immersed in hot water for too long. If it were merely due to illness, there would be no fault to find, but it was clear that even in his rage, he retained his true feelings, as one could easily understand the reason behind his outrageous bellowing. He had started a senseless quarrel with a rather cheeky student. "Get back! You’re splashing dirty water into my tub!" he shouted, of course, the master. Since things can be interpreted in various ways, there is no need to judge this outburst solely as a result of his anger. Perhaps one out of a hundred might interpret it as akin to Takayama Hikokuro scolding bandits. The man himself might have intended it as such, but since his opponent was not a bandit, the expected outcome was bound to be absent. The student turned around and calmly replied, "I was here from the beginning." This was a perfectly ordinary response, merely indicating that he had no intention of leaving, which did not align with the master's wishes. Given his demeanor and words, it was not something that warranted a retort worthy of a bandit, even if the master was in a fit of rage. However, the master's outburst was not merely a complaint about the student's presence; it seemed he was genuinely upset because these two had been discussing, in a manner unbecoming of their youth, all sorts of arrogant and pretentious things. Having been subjected to this for some time, the master appeared to be thoroughly irritated by it. Therefore, even when greeted politely, he would not step onto the wooden floor in silence. This time he shouted, "What the hell, you fool! Is there anyone who splashes dirty water into someone else's tub?" 

I had also found this young lad somewhat detestable, so I felt a slight sense of satisfaction at that moment, but I thought it was rather inappropriate behavior for a schoolteacher. The master was originally far too rigid. He was as dry and hard as coal ash. Once, when Hannibal crossed the Alps, there was a large rock in the middle of the road that made it impossible for his army to pass. So, Hannibal poured vinegar on the rock and set fire to it, softening it, and then sawed it into pieces like kamaboko (fish cake) to allow his troops to pass without obstruction.

I believe that a man who, like the master, immerses himself in such a beneficial medicinal bath without any effect should be treated with vinegar and fire. Otherwise, with hundreds of such students emerging over decades, the master's stubbornness will never be cured. Those floating in the bath, those rolling around in the sink, are a group of creatures shedding the clothing necessary for civilized humans, so they cannot be governed by ordinary rules and norms. They can do whatever they please. The stomach may occupy the place of the lungs, and the Heike clan may become the Minamoto, and it may not matter if the common folk are untrustworthy. However, once they step out of the sink and onto the wooden floor, they are no longer creatures. They have entered the realm of ordinary humanity, where they must don the clothing necessary for civilization. Therefore, they should behave like human beings. The place where the master is standing is the threshold. It is the boundary between the sink and the wooden floor, and he is on the verge of returning to a world of joy and ease. If he is this stubborn even at that moment, then this stubbornness must be a disease that he cannot escape. If it is a disease, it cannot be easily corrected. According to my foolish thoughts, there is only one way to cure this illness: to ask the principal to dismiss him. If he were dismissed, given the master's inflexibility, he would surely end up wandering the streets. The result of wandering the streets would mean dying in misery. In other words, dismissal would be the distant cause of death for the master. He enjoys being ill but detests dying. He wants to indulge in a kind of luxury called illness, as long as it does not lead to death. Therefore, if I were to threaten him with death for being so ill, he would surely tremble in fear. I think that at that moment of trembling, the illness would beautifully fall away. If it does not, then that is that. No matter how foolish or ill he may be, the master remains unchanged. There is a poet who says that even a cat does not forget its master’s circumstances. Feeling a surge of sympathy, I became distracted and neglected to observe the sink. Suddenly, I heard voices cursing towards the white tub. Was there a quarrel breaking out here as well? When I turned around, I saw that the narrow pomegranate entrance was so crowded with creatures that there was hardly any room to spare, their furry shins and hairless thighs intertwined and moving about. Just then, the early autumn sun was about to set, and the steam from the sink filled the room up to the ceiling. The sight of those creatures writhing together was vaguely visible through the haze. The cries of "Hot! Hot!" pierced my ears, swirling around in my head.

There were yellows, blues, reds, and blacks in those voices, overlapping to create a sound that was indescribable within the bathhouse. It was merely a voice suitable for describing confusion and chaos, serving no other purpose. I stood there, transfixed by this scene, momentarily paralyzed. Soon, the cacophony reached a peak of confusion, stretched to the point where no one could move another step. Suddenly, from the midst of the crowd that was pushing and shoving, a tall figure emerged. When I looked at his height, he was indeed about three inches taller than the other gentlemen. Moreover, with a face that was either covered in a beard or had a face hidden within the beard, he threw back his head and let out a voice like a bell ringing in the midday sun, shouting, "Make way! Make way! Hot! Hot!" This voice and this face stood out high above the tangled mass of the crowd, to the point that, in that moment, it seemed as if the entire bathhouse belonged to this man alone. A superhuman. The so-called Übermensch of Nietzsche. The great king among the creatures. The head of the monsters. As I watched, someone responded from behind the tub with a call of "Hey!" When I turned my gaze that way, I saw, in the dimness where I could not discern anything, the familiar figure of San-suke in his traditional garb, throwing a lump of coal into the stove. As the lump passed through the stove lid and crackled, half of San-suke's face lit up. Simultaneously, the brick wall behind him glowed as if it were burning through the darkness. Feeling a bit overwhelmed, I quickly jumped out of the window and returned home. As I walked back, I pondered. In the midst of shedding my haori, my fundoshi, and my hakama, striving for equality, there emerged another naked hero who overwhelmed the other small groups. Equality cannot be achieved simply by stripping down. **Chapter 1**

When I returned home, the world was at peace, and my master, with a face glowing from his bath, was eating dinner. Upon seeing me come up from the porch, he remarked, "What a carefree cat! I wonder where he has been wandering around at this hour." Looking at the table, I noticed that despite having no money, he had laid out two or three dishes. Among them was a grilled fish. I do not know what kind of fish it was, but it must have been caught around Odaiba yesterday. I had previously explained that fish are robust creatures, but no matter how sturdy they may be, being grilled or boiled like this is intolerable. It would be much better to be afflicted with many ailments and maintain a lingering breath. With this thought in mind, I sat beside the table, pretending to look around as if I were not watching, hoping to snag a morsel when the opportunity arose.

Those who do not know how to feign such indifference must resign themselves to never tasting the fish. My master poked at the fish a little, but then put down his chopsticks with a face that said it was not good. His wife, sitting opposite him, silently moved her chopsticks up and down, intently studying the rhythm of his jaw as he chewed. "Hey, give that cat's head a little tap," my master suddenly requested of his wife. "What will happen if I tap it?" 

"Just tap it a little; it doesn't matter what happens."

"Is this how you want me to do it?" she asked, and then lightly slapped my head with her palm. It did not hurt at all. "Why isn't he meowing?" 

"Yes."

"Try it again."

"Whatever I do, it will be the same, won't it?" she said, and again she gave me a light slap. Since it still did not hurt, I remained still. However, the reason for this was quite difficult for a wise cat like myself to comprehend. If I could understand it, there might be some method to it, but since it was merely "just tap it," both my wife and I were at a loss. My master, finding it not going as he wished even after two attempts, grew a bit impatient and said, "Hey, try tapping him so he meows."

His wife, looking annoyed, asked, "What good will it do to make him meow?" and then gave me another slap. Once I understood the other party's intention, it was clear that if I meowed, I could satisfy my master. My master, being such a foolish creature, was tiresome. If all it took was to meow, then I could do it right away without needing to go through two or three unnecessary efforts, and I would not have to repeat it multiple times. The command to just tap should not be used unless the act of tapping itself is the goal. Tapping is their business; meowing is ours. To assume that my meowing, which should be voluntary, is included in the command to merely tap is exceedingly disrespectful. It shows a lack of regard for another's personality. It is an insult to cats. My master, who despises Kaneda like a snake or a scorpion, might do such a thing, but for a man who prides himself on being straightforward, it is exceedingly base. However, in truth, my master is not such a stingy man. Therefore, I believe this command of his did not stem from cunning. Rather, it seems to have arisen from a lack of wisdom. When one eats, the stomach fills up. When one cuts, blood flows. When one kills, death ensues. Thus, he hastily concluded that tapping would lead to a meow. However, that is unfortunate, as it does not quite align with logic. Following that reasoning, if one falls into a river, one must surely die. If one eats tempura, one must inevitably have diarrhea. If one receives a salary, one must certainly show up for work. If one reads books, one must surely become accomplished.

If everything must be so, it would create some troublesome people. If tapping must inevitably lead to a meow, it would be a nuisance for me. If I am to be treated like the bell of Mejiro, then there is no point in being born a cat. So, I first thoroughly mocked my master in my mind and then, as requested, let out a meow. Then my master turned to his wife and asked, "Did you hear that? Was that meow an interjection or an adverb, do you know?"

His wife, taken aback by the sudden question, said nothing. To be honest, I thought it was probably because the effects of the hot bath had not yet worn off. Originally, my master is a well-known eccentric in the neighborhood, and some have even gone so far as to assert that he is indeed a neurotic. However, my master is quite confident, insisting that he is not neurotic, but rather that everyone else in the world is. When the neighbors call him "dog," he insists on maintaining fairness by calling them "pigs." In fact, it seems my master intends to uphold fairness to the utmost. It is quite troublesome. For a man like this to pose such a strange question to his wife might be a minor incident for him before breakfast, but from the listener's perspective, it sounds like something a person close to being neurotic might say. Thus, his wife, feeling somewhat bewildered, said nothing. Naturally, I had no answer to give. Then my master suddenly called out loudly, "Hey."

His wife, startled, replied, "Yes?"

"Is that 'yes' an interjection or an adverb? Which is it?"

"Which is it? Such a silly question doesn’t matter at all, does it?"

"It does matter; this is a significant issue that currently governs the minds of linguists."

"Oh dear, are we talking about a cat's meow? How unpleasant."

"That's exactly it. That is the difficult question."

"Is that so?" His wife, being clever, decided not to engage with such a foolish question. "So, did you figure out which it is?"

"It's an important question, so I can't figure it out right away," he said, munching on the same fish. Then he casually ate the pork and sweet potato dish next to it. "This is pork," he said. "Yes, it is pork." "Hmph," he swallowed with a tone of great disdain. "I’ll have another drink," he said, reaching for the cup. "Tonight, you’re really getting into it. Your face is already quite red."

"I will drink—do you know the longest word in the world?"

"Yes, it’s the name of the former regent, the Daijōdaijin."

"That’s a name. Do you know the longest word?"

"Is it a foreign word?"

"Yes."

"I don’t know—enough with the drinking. Let’s have dinner now, shall we?"

"No, I’m still drinking.

I’ll tell you the longest word."

"Yes, then it’s time for dinner."

"It’s Archaiomelesidonophrunicherata."

"That’s nonsense."

"It’s not nonsense; it’s Greek."

"What does it mean in Japanese?"

"I don’t know the meaning; I only know how to spell it. When written out, it takes about six inches and three minutes."

It is quite a spectacle to hear someone say such things soberly, things that should be said over drinks. Tonight, however, he has been drinking recklessly. Normally, he limits himself to two cups, but he has already had four. Given that even two cups would make him quite red, having doubled that has made his face as hot as a burning stick, and he looks quite pained. Yet he still does not stop. "One more cup," he insists. His wife, overwhelmed, says with a bitter expression, "It would be good if you stopped now; it’s just painful."

"Even if it’s painful, I still have a little practice to do. Oomachi Keigetsu said to drink."

"What is Keigetsu?" Even Keigetsu, when faced with his wife, is worth no more than a single coin. "Keigetsu is a leading critic nowadays. Since he said to drink, it must be the best thing to do."

"Don’t be foolish. Whether it’s Keigetsu or Umegetsu, it’s unnecessary to suffer through drinking."

"Isn't that terrible? A person like that is a first-rate critic. How absurd! To recommend a hobby to someone with a wife and children..."

"Hobbies are fine. Even if Katsuge didn't recommend them, if one has the money, they might indulge anyway."

"Thank goodness I don't have any. If I were to start a hobby now, it would be a disaster."

"If you say it's a disaster, then I'll refrain from it. In exchange, you should take better care of your husband and serve me more lavish meals in the evening."

"This is the best I can do."

"Is that so? Then let's postpone the hobby until money comes in, and for tonight, let's call it a day," he said, putting away his rice bowl. It seemed he had eaten three bowls of chazuke (rice soaked in tea). That night, I was treated to three pieces of pork and a grilled fish head. ---

When I explained the exercise known as "fence-walking," I intended to briefly mention the bamboo fence that surrounds my master's garden, but it would be a misunderstanding to think that the area outside this fence is immediately adjacent to the next house, namely the home of Jiro-chan to the south. The rent is low, but that is Mr. Kushami's residence. There is no close relationship with those who are referred to as "chan" like Yocchan and Jiro-chan, separated by a flimsy single fence. Beyond this fence lies an empty space of five or six ken (about ten to twelve meters), at the end of which stand five or six towering cypress trees. From the porch, looking out, one sees a dense forest beyond, and it gives the impression that the master, residing here, is a recluse in the wilderness, spending his days and nights with an unnamed cat as his companion. However, the branches of the cypress trees are not as densely packed as one might think, allowing the roof of a shabby inn called Gunkaku to be seen without hesitation, making it quite a challenge to imagine the master in such a setting. Nevertheless, if this inn is indeed Gunkaku, then the value of the master's dwelling is certainly akin to that of a dragon's cave. Since names are not taxed, we can freely assign grand titles, and this empty space, measuring about five or six ken, runs east to west alongside the bamboo fence for approximately ten ken, then suddenly bends at a right angle, encircling the northern side of the dragon's cave. This northern side is the source of commotion. Originally, the empty space could have been proudly claimed as a thoroughfare, but the master of the dragon's cave, and even I, the spiritual cat within, find this empty space troublesome. Just as the cypress trees dominate the southern side, there are seven or eight paulownia trees lined up on the northern side.

They have grown to about a foot in height, so if a sandal maker were to come, they could fetch a good price, but the tragedy of renting means that no matter how much one notices, action cannot be taken. I feel sorry for the master as well. The other day, the school janitor came and cut off a branch, and when he returned, he was wearing a brand new pair of wooden sandals, boasting that they were made from the branch he had cut, without even being asked. What a sly fellow! The paulownia trees exist, but they are of no value to me or the master's family. There is an old saying that goes, "To hold a jewel and be guilty," which seems fitting here, as it could be said that having a paulownia tree without money is a case of treasure going to waste. The foolish ones are neither the master nor I, but the landlord, Denbei. "Is there no sandal maker? Is there no sandal maker?" he seems to be urging from the direction of the paulownia trees, while he comes to collect the rent with a blank expression. I bear no grudge against Denbei, so I will leave my criticisms at that and return to the main topic, introducing the curious tale that this empty space is the source of commotion, but I must not tell the master. This is all I will say. The primary inconvenience regarding this empty space is that there is no fence. It is an open area, free for passage, a place where one can walk without restriction under clear skies. To say there is one would be a lie. To tell the truth, there was one. However, the story must trace back to the past to understand its origins. Without understanding the origins, even a doctor would struggle with a prescription. Therefore, I will begin the story from the time we moved here. The open space is quite refreshing in the summer, and it feels pleasant; there should be no theft in a place where there is no money. Thus, all manner of walls, fences, or even haphazard stakes are entirely unnecessary for the master's house. However, I believe this issue is determined by the nature of the humans or animals residing on the other side of the empty space. Therefore, to resolve this issue, it is necessary to clarify the character of the gentlemen stationed on the other side. It may seem premature to call them gentlemen before knowing whether they are humans or animals, but they are likely gentlemen nonetheless. In a world where even a thief is referred to as a gentleman, as in the saying "gentlemen on the beams," it is important to note that these gentlemen are not the kind who would trouble the police. Instead, they seem to be numerous, plentiful. There is a private middle school called Rakugunkan—charging a monthly fee of two yen to train eight hundred gentlemen into even more refined gentlemen.

One might think that since it is called Rakugunkan, it would be filled with cultured gentlemen, but that would be a fundamental misunderstanding. The unreliability of this is akin to the cranes not descending at Gunkaku, or cats being present at the dragon's cave. Once one learns of the eccentricities of those who call themselves scholars or teachers, like Mr. Kushami, it becomes clear that not all gentlemen at Rakugunkan are cultured. If one cannot comprehend this, they should come and stay at the master's house for about three days to see for themselves.

As I mentioned earlier, at the time of our move here, there was no fence around the vacant lot, so the gentlemen of Rakugunkan, like Kuro the rickshaw man's cat, lazily wandered into the paulownia field to chat, eat their bento, and lie down on the grass — they engaged in various activities. After that, it seemed they began to discard the remains of their bento, namely bamboo leaves, old newspapers, or even old sandals and geta, things that could be described as "old." The indifferent master appeared surprisingly unfazed, and it was unclear whether he was unaware of it or simply intended not to complain. However, as these gentlemen received their education at school, they gradually seemed to become more gentlemanly and began to scheme to encroach from the north side towards the south side. If the term "encroach" seems inappropriate for gentlemen, it can be omitted, but there is no other word for it. They moved like desert dwellers changing their homes in pursuit of aquatic plants, leaving the paulownia trees to advance towards the cypress. The place where the cypress stood was directly in front of the sitting room. Only a very bold gentleman would dare to act in such a manner. After a day or two, their boldness increased even further, becoming exceedingly audacious. There is nothing more terrifying than the results of education. They not only encroached upon the front of the sitting room but also began to sing songs there. I have forgotten what the song was, but it was certainly not of the thirty-one syllable variety; it was more lively and easier on the ears of the common folk. It was not only the master who was astonished; even I found myself captivated by the talents of these gentlemen, unable to help but lend an ear. However, as the reader may know, admiration and annoyance can sometimes coexist. The unfortunate coincidence of these two sentiments merging into one at this moment is, upon reflection, quite regrettable. The master must have felt the same way, as he had no choice but to rush out of his study, declaring that this was not a place for them to enter and that they should leave, having chased them out two or three times. However, being educated gentlemen, they could not be expected to acquiesce to such treatment. If they were chased out, they would immediately return. Upon entering, they would sing their lively songs and engage in animated conversations. Moreover, since it was the discourse of gentlemen, it had a certain flair, using phrases like "you" and "I don’t know." Such expressions, it seems, belonged to the specialized knowledge of the likes of Orisuke, Unosuke, and Sansuke before the Meiji Restoration, but since the twentieth century, they have become the sole language learned by educated gentlemen.

Some have explained that this phenomenon, which was once looked down upon by the general public, has now become welcomed in such a manner. The master, again rushing out of his study, caught one of the gentlemen who was most proficient in this gentlemanly speech and questioned him as to why he had entered. The gentleman immediately forgot his refined words of "you" and "I don’t know" and answered in a rather vulgar manner, "I thought this was the school’s botanical garden." The master, foreseeing the future, let him go. Though it seemed amusing to let him go like a turtle's child, in reality, he had grasped the gentleman's sleeve to negotiate. The master thought that after making such a fuss, it should suffice. However, in reality, it was different from what he had anticipated since the time of the lady, and he failed once more. This time, they crossed the estate from the north side and burst through the front gate, which swung open, leading the master to think it was a guest. Then, from the direction of the paulownia field, laughter could be heard. The situation was becoming increasingly unstable. The fruits of education were becoming more and more evident. The unfortunate master thought that this was beyond his capacity, and thereafter barricaded himself in his study, respectfully submitting a letter to the principal of Rakugunkan, pleading for some regulation. The principal also sent a courteous reply to the master, saying they would put up a fence, so please wait. After a while, two or three craftsmen arrived, and within half a day, a fence about three feet high was completed between the master's estate and Rakugunkan. The master rejoiced, thinking he could finally feel at ease. The master is a foolish man. Such a minor matter would not change the behavior of gentlemen.

It is quite amusing to tease others. Even a cat like me occasionally plays around by teasing the young lady of this household, so it is entirely reasonable for the gentlemen of Rakugunkan to tease Mr. Kushami, who lacks any wit. The only ones who might complain about this are likely the ones being teased. If we dissect the psychology behind teasing, we can identify two elements. First, the person being teased must not remain indifferent. Second, the teaser must be stronger than the target in terms of power and numbers. Recently, my master returned from the zoo, greatly impressed by what he had seen. Upon inquiry, he recounted witnessing a fight between a camel and a puppy. The puppy would dart around the camel like a whirlwind, barking incessantly, while the camel stood there, oblivious, with its hump still raised. No matter how much the puppy barked or went wild, the camel paid no attention, and eventually, the puppy lost interest and stopped. My master laughed, saying that the camel was utterly insensitive, and this serves as a perfect example in this case. No matter how adept the teaser may be, if the target is like a camel, the teasing will not succeed. On the other hand, if the opponent is too strong, like a lion or a tiger, it would be disastrous; one could be torn to shreds before even starting to tease. There is much amusement in the moment when the target bares its teeth in anger, for while it may be furious, there is a comforting realization that it cannot do anything about it. The reason this is amusing is manifold. First, it is suitable for passing the time. In moments of boredom, one might even find themselves counting the number of whiskers. There is a tale of a prisoner once thrown into a cell who, out of sheer ennui, spent his days drawing triangles on the walls to pass the time. There is nothing more intolerable in this world than boredom; without some stimulating event, living becomes a struggle. Teasing, in essence, is a form of entertainment that creates such stimulation. However, it must provoke some irritation, annoyance, or weakness in the target to be truly stimulating. Thus, those who indulge in the pastime of teasing are often either dull-witted lords who know nothing of others' feelings or immature youths whose minds are not yet developed and who have no outlet for their energy. Next, it is the simplest method to demonstrate one's superiority in practice. One can prove their superiority by killing, injuring, or deceiving others, but these actions are rather means to an end when the goal is to harm. The superiority one seeks is merely a phenomenon that arises as a consequence of carrying out such means.

Therefore, when one wishes to demonstrate their superiority without causing harm to others, teasing becomes the most fitting approach. One cannot prove their greatness without causing at least some harm to others. If it does not manifest in reality, even if one feels secure in their mind, the pleasure derived from it is surprisingly thin. Humans rely on their own strength; even in difficult situations, they wish to rely on something. Thus, one cannot feel satisfied without practically applying their sense of superiority to others. Moreover, those who are unable to grasp such reasoning or who feel insecure about their own strength will seize every opportunity to hold onto this proof of superiority. It is akin to a judo practitioner who sometimes feels the urge to throw someone, wishing to encounter a weaker opponent, even if just once, to demonstrate their skill, which is a rather dangerous mindset. There are various other reasons, but I shall refrain from elaborating too long. If you wish to know more, bring a piece of dried bonito, and I will gladly teach you anytime.
