Based on the above reasoning, I believe that the monkeys in the mountains and the school teachers are the most suitable targets for teasing. It would be a waste to compare a school teacher to the monkeys in the mountains. — Not that it would be a waste to the monkeys, but rather to the teachers. However, they are so similar that it cannot be helped; as you know, the monkeys in the mountains are chained. No matter how much they bare their teeth or screech, there is no worry of being scratched. The teachers, on the other hand, are not chained but are bound by their salaries. No matter how much they are teased, they are safe; they will not resign and beat the students. If they had the courage to resign, they would not have taken up teaching in the first place, nor would they have been responsible for the students' well-being. My master is a teacher. Although he is not a teacher at Rakugunkan, he is still a teacher, without a doubt. He is exceedingly suitable, straightforward, and completely safe to tease. The students at Rakugunkan are boys. They consider teasing as a means to elevate their own status, believing it to be a rightful claim as a result of their education. Moreover, if they do not tease, they are left to squander their energetic bodies and minds during their ample free time, which is quite troubling. With these conditions in place, the master will inevitably be teased, and the students will naturally do the teasing; it is a situation that is entirely reasonable from any perspective. A master who gets angry in such a situation is the epitome of foolishness, the height of absurdity.

From here on, I shall detail how the students of Rakugunkan teased my master and how he exhibited the utmost foolishness in response. You all know what a four-eyed fence is, do you not? It is a breezy, simple fence. I can freely come and go through it. Whether it is constructed or not makes no difference. However, the principal of Rakugunkan did not build the four-eyed fence for the sake of cats; he had the craftsmen come in to weave it so that the gentlemen he trains could not slip through. Indeed, no matter how well-ventilated it may be, it seems impossible for humans to pass through. Even the four-inch square holes made with this bamboo would be difficult for the renowned Chinese magician Zhang Shizun to navigate. Thus, it is certain that the fence serves its purpose well for humans. It is no wonder that my master was pleased when he saw it completed, thinking it would suffice. However, there is a significant flaw in my master's logic. There exists a much larger hole than this fence—a hole large enough to let fish slip through. He operates under the assumption that a fence should not be something that can be crossed. He presumes that as long as it bears the name of a fence, even if it is a crude one, and as long as the boundary is clearly defined, there is no worry of intrusion. Next, he temporarily dismantles that assumption, concluding that even if someone were to intrude, it would be fine. He hastily determines that no boy, no matter how small, could possibly slip through the holes of the four-eyed fence, thus there is no risk of intrusion. Indeed, as long as they are not cats, it is unlikely they will come through this square opening, and even if they wanted to, they could not. However, jumping over or climbing over is no issue at all. In fact, it could even be amusing exercise.

From the day after the fence was built, they continued to leap into the vacant lot on the north side just as they had before the fence was erected. However, they did not venture too close to the front of the house. If they were to be chased, they would have a little time to escape, so they played in a place where there was no danger of being caught, taking into account the time needed to flee. Naturally, the master in the eastern annex could not see what they were doing. The only way to observe their activities in the northern vacant lot was to open the gate and peek around the corner or to gaze over the fence from the back window. When looking from the window, one could see clearly where everything was, but even if one spotted a few enemies, there was no way to catch them. All one could do was scold them through the window's lattice. If one were to try to circumvent the gate and charge into enemy territory, the sound of footsteps would alert them, and they would quickly retreat to the other side before being caught. It was like a poaching boat heading towards a basking turtle. Of course, the master was not on watch in the back room. That said, he was also not prepared to spring into action the moment he heard a noise from the gate. If he were to do such a thing, he would have to resign from his teaching position and specialize in that line of work, for he would never keep up otherwise. Speaking of the master's disadvantage, from the study, he could only hear the enemy's voices without seeing them, while from the window, he could see their figures but could not reach them. The enemy, having discerned this disadvantage, devised such a strategy. When they suspected that the master was holed up in the study, they would make as much noise as possible, shouting and clamoring. Among their ruckus, they would make comments meant to tease the master, while keeping the source of their voices deliberately ambiguous. At first glance, it would be difficult to determine whether the commotion was coming from inside the fence or from the other side. If the master were to come out, they would either flee or pretend to be on the other side all along. Furthermore, when the master would cross over to the back room—though I do not take any particular pride in repeatedly using the filthy term "back room," it is utterly bothersome, but necessary for describing this war—when the master would see that he had entered the back room, they would certainly loiter near the paulownia tree, deliberately making themselves visible to him. If the master were to raise a loud uproar from the back room, the enemies would retreat to their base without a hint of fluster. When this strategy was employed, the master found himself in quite a predicament.

Just when he thought he had caught them and stepped out with his cane, the place would be utterly silent, with no one in sight. If he peered out the window, he would invariably spot one or two of them sneaking in. The master would go around to the back to check, peek from the back room, and look again from the back room, going around to the back once more. It was the same thing repeated over and over, and this is what it meant to be exhausted from running around. It had become so maddening that one could hardly tell whether teaching was his profession or if waging war was his main duty. It was at the peak of this frenzy that the following incident occurred.

Incidents generally arise from a state of agitation. Agitation, as the characters suggest, is akin to being turned upside down; in this regard, even Gehlen, Paracelsus, and the old-fashioned Bianque would not dispute. The question, however, lies in where one is turned upside down and what exactly is turned upside down. According to ancient European legends, it is said that within our bodies, four types of fluids circulate. The first is what one might call the fluid of anger. When this fluid is turned upside down, one becomes enraged. The second is known as the dull fluid. When this fluid is turned upside down, one’s nerves become dull. Next is the fluid of sorrow, which casts a gloom over humanity. Lastly, there is the blood, which invigorates the limbs. As humanity has progressed, the dull fluid, the anger fluid, and the sorrow fluid have gradually disappeared, leaving only the blood to circulate as it once did. Therefore, if one is to become agitated, it seems there is no fluid other than blood involved. However, the quantity of this blood is precisely determined by the individual. There may be slight variations depending on one’s temperament, but on average, it amounts to five shō and five go per person (approximately 18.5 liters). Thus, when this five shō and five go is turned upside down, the area that rises becomes intensely active, while other parts feel a deficiency and grow cold. It is akin to the time when all the police officers gathered at the station during the burning of the police box, leaving the town devoid of any presence. From a medical standpoint, that was a case of police agitation. To remedy this agitation, the blood must be evenly distributed throughout the body as it once was. To achieve this, one must bring down that which has been turned upside down. There are various methods for this. My late master, for instance, would place a wet towel on his head while sitting by the kotatsu (a heated table). The principle of keeping the head cool and the feet warm is a sign of longevity and is mentioned in the treatise on cold illnesses; the wet towel is an indispensable element in the practice of longevity. If that does not suffice, one might try the methods commonly used by monks. It is said that wandering monks, who do not have a fixed abode, must find shelter under trees or on stones. This practice is not for the sake of enduring hardship, but rather a secret method devised by the Sixth Patriarch while he pounded rice to alleviate dizziness. Try sitting on a stone, and it is only natural that your backside will grow cold. A cold backside means that the dizziness subsides; this is also a natural order, and there is no room for doubt.

Various methods have been devised to alleviate dizziness, yet it is regrettable that no effective means to induce it has been discovered. Generally speaking, dizziness is a phenomenon that brings more harm than good, but there are cases where one cannot hastily conclude that. Depending on one’s profession, agitation can be quite essential, and there are instances where one cannot accomplish anything without it. Among all, the poet values agitation the most. For a poet, agitation is as indispensable as coal is to a steamship; if this supply is interrupted even for a day, they become mere ordinary people who can do nothing but sit idle and eat. However, agitation is often synonymous with madness, and if one cannot maintain their livelihood without becoming mad, it would be detrimental to their reputation. Therefore, among their peers, they do not refer to agitation by its true name. They have agreed to call it inspiration, treating it as something precious. This name is a fabrication to deceive the world, for in reality, it is precisely agitation. Plato supported them, calling this type of agitation a sacred madness, but no matter how sacred, madness is not something people will engage with. It is better for them to stick with the newly invented name of inspiration, akin to a patent medicine. However, just as the ingredient of kamaboko (fish cake) is yam, the statue of Kannon is made from decayed wood measuring one shaku and eight sun, the materials for duck nanban (a noodle dish) are crow, and the beef hot pot at a boarding house is made from horse meat, inspiration is, in fact, agitation. When viewed as agitation, it is merely a temporary madness. The reason one does not need to be hospitalized in Sugamo is simply that it is a temporary madness. However, producing this temporary madness is quite difficult. It is easier to create a lifelong madman than to induce madness only while one is writing. Even the most skilled gods would find it quite challenging to manage this, and it is not easily achieved. Since the gods do not create it, one must rely on their own efforts. Thus, from ancient times to the present, the art of inducing agitation has troubled the minds of scholars just as much as the art of dispelling it. Some individuals have eaten twelve persimmons daily to gain inspiration. This is based on the theory that eating persimmons causes constipation, and constipation inevitably leads to agitation. Others have jumped into a hot bath with a sake bottle, believing that drinking alcohol in the water would induce agitation. According to this person’s theory, if this does not succeed, they firmly believed that boiling wine in the bath would work in one go.

However, lacking the funds, they ultimately could not carry it out and died, which is unfortunate. Lastly, there were those who thought that imitating the ancients would induce inspiration. This was based on the theory that mimicking someone’s demeanor would also reflect their mental state. If one behaves like a drunkard, they will unconsciously adopt the mindset of a drinker; if one practices zazen (seated meditation) and endures the burning of a single incense stick, they will inevitably feel somewhat like a monk. Therefore, it is certain that if one imitates the actions of famous masters who have received inspiration, they will surely experience agitation. It is said that Hugo lay on a fast-moving ship to contemplate his literary themes, so if one lies on a boat and gazes at the blue sky, they will surely find inspiration. Stevenson reportedly wrote novels while lying on his stomach, so if one takes up the pen while lying flat, the blood will surely rise. Many have thought of various ways to induce agitation, yet no one has succeeded. For now, it seems that artificial agitation is impossible. It is regrettable, but it cannot be helped. There is no doubt that the time will come when one can induce inspiration at will, and I earnestly hope for the arrival of that day for the sake of humanity. I believe this explanation of agitation is sufficient, so I shall now proceed to the events at hand. However, before every major incident, there are always minor incidents that occur. To recount only the major incidents while neglecting the minor ones is a common pitfall that historians have fallen into since ancient times. My master’s agitation, too, intensified with each minor incident, ultimately leading to a major event. Therefore, to describe its development somewhat chronologically is necessary to understand how agitated my master truly was. If it is unclear, my master’s agitation may be dismissed as mere empty notoriety, and people might underestimate its significance. Even if one is agitated, if it is not recognized as a splendid agitation by others, it would be rather disheartening. The events I am about to describe, regardless of their size, are not honorable for my master. If the event itself is dishonorable, then at least it is agitated, and I want to clarify that it is a genuine agitation, certainly not inferior to that of others. My master does not possess any particular qualities that would warrant boasting to others. Without boasting about agitation, there is no material to write about.

The enemy forces surrounding Rakugunkan have recently invented a type of dum-dum bullet, and during their ample breaks or after school, they fiercely bombard the northern vacant lot. This dum-dum bullet is commonly referred to as a ball, and it is launched into the enemy ranks using a large pestle. No matter how dum-dum it may be, since it is fired from the playground of Rakugunkan, there is no concern of it hitting the master who is holed up in his study. Even though the enemy is aware that the trajectory is far too distant, that is the essence of military strategy. It is said that during the war at Port Arthur, the navy achieved great success through indirect fire; thus, even a ball rolling into the vacant lot could yield a significant result. Moreover, each time they launch a shot, the entire army combines to produce a loud, intimidating noise. As a result, the master is left in a state of embarrassment, with the blood vessels in his limbs constricting involuntarily. The blood, tormented to the extreme, must surely rise up in rebellion. One could say that the enemy's plan is quite clever. There was once a writer in ancient Greece named Ischylus. It is said that this man possessed a common trait shared by scholarly writers. The common trait I refer to among so-called scholarly writers is baldness. The reason for baldness, I believe, is due to a lack of nourishment for the head, resulting in insufficient vitality for hair growth. Scholars and writers are those who use their heads the most, and as a rule, they end up impoverished. Therefore, the heads of scholarly writers are all undernourished and bald. Now, since Ischylus was also a writer, it follows that he must have been bald by nature. He had a shiny, bald head like a kumquat. However, one day, the good doctor—his head, which is usually devoid of any formal or casual attire, is simply referred to as "the usual head"—was strutting about in the sunlight, shaking his head. This was the source of his misfortune. When a bald head is exposed to the sun and viewed from a distance, it shines quite brilliantly. The wind blows through the tall trees, and something must strike that shining head. At that moment, a hawk was soaring above Ischylus's head, clutching a turtle it had captured somewhere. Turtles, along with soft-shelled turtles, are undoubtedly delicious, but they have hard shells that have existed since the days of ancient Greece. No matter how tasty they may be, there is nothing to be done with a shelled creature. While there are grilled shrimp with their shells, there are no turtle shell stews even today, so it is certain that none existed back then. Just as the hawk was somewhat at a loss, it spotted something shining far below. The hawk thought it had hit the jackpot.

If it dropped the turtle onto that shining object, the shell would surely shatter. After the shell was broken, it could swoop down and enjoy the contents without any trouble. So, with that thought in mind, it aimed carefully and dropped the turtle onto the top of Ischylus's head without so much as a greeting. Unfortunately, the writer's head was softer than the turtle's shell, and thus, the bald head was smashed to pieces, leading the famous Ischylus to meet a tragic end. That aside, what is puzzling is the hawk's reasoning. Did it know that it was a writer's head and drop the turtle, or did it mistake it for a bald rock? Depending on how one resolves this, one could compare the enemies of Rakugunkan to this hawk, or one could not. The master's head does not shine like that of Ischylus or the other renowned scholars. However, whether it is in a six-tatami room or a modest study, as long as he dozes off while casting his face over difficult books, he must be considered a member of the scholarly writers. Thus, the fact that the master's head is not bald means that he has not yet qualified to be bald, and it is likely that he will eventually become so; it is a fate that will soon befall him. Therefore, it must be said that the students of Rakugunkan aiming their dum-dum balls at this head are acting in perfect timing. If the enemy continues this action for two weeks, the master's head will surely complain of a lack of nourishment due to fear and anxiety, and it will transform into a kumquat, a kettle, or a copper pot. After two weeks of bombardment, the kumquat will undoubtedly be crushed. The kettle will surely leak. The copper pot will certainly crack. Without foreseeing these obvious outcomes, only Mr. Kushami, the master himself, is struggling to continue the battle against the enemy. One afternoon, as usual, I went out to the porch to take a nap and dreamt I had become a tiger. When I commanded the master to bring me chicken, he timidly brought it out, saying, "Yes, sir." When Meitei arrived, I told him I wanted to eat wild goose and to go to the goose hot pot to have it prepared. He replied that he would enjoy it with pickled turnips and salted rice crackers, saying that would enhance the flavor of the goose. As usual, I opened my mouth wide and growled to frighten him, causing Meitei to turn pale and say that the goose hot pot at Yamashita had gone out of business; what should be done? I then said that I would settle for beef, so he should hurry to Nishikawa and bring back a pound of roast. I warned him that if he didn't hurry, I would eat him instead. Meitei dashed off in a hurry.

I suddenly grew large, sprawled across the porch, waiting for Meitei's return when a loud voice echoed throughout the house, waking me from my dream before I could even eat the beef. Then, unexpectedly, the master, who had been bowing before me in fear, suddenly leaped out from behind the chair and kicked me hard in the side. While I was taken aback, he quickly slipped on his geta and ran around the gate toward Rakugunkan. I had shrunk back from a tiger to a cat in an instant, feeling both awkward and amused, but the pain from the master's kick made me forget about the tiger right away. At the same time, I thought it was amusing that the master was now going out to battle the enemy, so I endured the pain and followed him out the back door. Simultaneously, I heard the master's voice shouting, "Thief!" Looking, I saw a stubborn young man, around eighteen or nineteen, wearing a cap, climbing over the four-panel fence. Just as I thought it was too late, that young man, in a running posture, dashed away toward his base. The master, having had great success in catching the thief, shouted again, "Thief!" while chasing after him. However, in order to catch that enemy, the master would have to leap over the fence himself. If he went too far, he would surely become a thief himself. As I mentioned earlier, the master is a remarkable hothead. It seems that in his eagerness to chase the thief, he intended to become a thief himself, showing no signs of turning back as he advanced to the base of the fence. Just as he was about to step into the thief's territory, a thin-bearded officer emerged from among the enemy ranks. The two were negotiating something across the fence. Upon listening, it turned out to be a rather trivial discussion. "That is a student from our school."
"What kind of student trespasses into another's residence?"
"No, the ball just happened to fly over."
"Why didn't you call out and come to retrieve it?"
"I will be more careful from now on."
"Then, that is fine."

What was expected to be a grand spectacle of a fierce negotiation concluded swiftly and peacefully with such mundane dialogue. The master's bravado was merely a matter of spirit. When it came down to it, this is how it always ends. It was as if I had suddenly returned from a tiger's dream to being a cat. This small incident is precisely what it is. After recounting this small incident, it is only proper to discuss a significant event. **Chapter 1**

My master opened the shoji screen in the tatami room and lay down on his stomach, seemingly deep in thought. He was likely devising some defensive strategy against an enemy. The Rakugunkan school appeared to be in session, as the playground was surprisingly quiet.

I could distinctly hear a lecture on ethics being delivered in one of the classrooms. The voice was resonant and eloquent, reminiscent of a general who had just emerged from enemy territory to engage in negotiations. “...Thus, public virtue is of utmost importance. If you go abroad, whether to France, Germany, or England, you will find no country where public virtue is not upheld. Moreover, there is no one, no matter how lowly, who does not respect this public virtue. Alas, in our Japan, we are still unable to compete with foreign nations in this regard. Some of you may think that when we speak of public virtue, it is something newly imported from abroad, but that is a grave error. The ancients spoke of the Way of the Master, which is to uphold loyalty and compassion. This compassion is, after all, the very source of public virtue. As a human, there are times when I feel the urge to sing loudly. However, when I hear someone in the next room singing freely while I am studying, it is in my nature to be unable to concentrate on my reading. Therefore, even when I feel that reciting a Tang poem aloud might lift my spirits, I cannot help but think of the person next door who might be disturbed by my noise. In such moments, I always refrain. For this reason, I urge you all to uphold public virtue and to never engage in actions that might disturb others...”

My master listened attentively to this discourse, but at this point, he broke into a smile. It is necessary to explain the meaning behind this smile. A cynic might think that beneath this smile lay a critical disposition. However, my master was certainly not a man of such ill nature. Rather, he was simply not a man of such developed intellect. The reason he smiled was that he was genuinely pleased. The fact that an ethics teacher could deliver such a poignant admonition assured him that he would be spared from the incessant barrage of troubles that lay ahead. For the time being, he would be free from baldness, and though his irritability might not vanish immediately, it would gradually improve with time. He felt confident that even without a warm towel or a kotatsu, he could manage without having to sleep under trees or on stones, which made him smile. It was only natural that a master who honestly believed in repaying debts would listen seriously to such a lecture in this twentieth century. Before long, it seemed the time had come, and the lecture abruptly ceased. The lessons in the other classrooms also concluded simultaneously. Then, the eight hundred students, who had been sealed within the room until now, erupted with a cheer and burst out of the building. The force of their exit was akin to knocking down a beehive about a foot in size.
Buzzing and barking, they rushed out through the windows, doorways, and any openings, without a hint of restraint, as if they were competing to escape. This was the beginning of a great event.

First, let me explain the formation of the bees. To say that there is no formation in such a war is a mistake. Ordinary people, when they hear the word "war," think only of places like Shakhe, Fengtian, or Port Arthur, as if there were no other wars to speak of. Those who become a bit poetic and barbaric might imagine Achilles dragging Hector's corpse around the walls of Troy, or Yan Ping and Zhang Fei blocking Cao Cao's million-man army at Changban Bridge, conjuring up only exaggerated tales. While such associations are at the discretion of the individual, it is inconvenient to assume that there are no other forms of war. Perhaps such foolish wars occurred only in the dark ages of antiquity; however, in today's peaceful era, such barbaric actions in the heart of the imperial capital of Japan belong to the realm of the miraculous. No matter how much commotion arises, there is no concern beyond the burning of the police box. In this light, the war between Mr. Kushami, the master of the Garyō Cave, and the valiant youths behind the Rakuunkan should rightly be counted as one of the great wars since the founding of Tokyo. When Sima Qian recorded the Battle of Yanling, he began by describing the enemy's formation. It has been a general rule since ancient times that those skilled in narration employ this method. Thus, it would not be out of place for me to discuss the formation of the bees in detail. So, as I observe the formation of the bees, I see a group arranged in a vertical line outside the four-legged fence. These seem to be the ones tasked with luring the master into the combat zone. "Are you going to surrender?" "No way!" "Not a chance!" "Come out!" "You won't fall, will you?" "You must fall!" "Bark and see!" "Woof, woof!" "Woof, woof, woof, woof!" From here on, the entire line joins in a shout. Slightly to the right, away from the line, in the direction of the playground, the artillery is occupying the advantageous ground and setting up their positions. Facing the Garyō Cave, one officer stands ready with a large pestle. Standing about five or six paces away, another stands opposite, and behind the pestle, yet another stands, facing the Garyō Cave. Thus, they are lined up in a straight line, facing each other, the gunners. According to some, this is merely baseball practice and not preparation for battle at all. I, being an illiterate cat, do not understand what baseball is. However, I have heard that this game was imported from America and is among the most popular sports practiced in schools of junior high level and above today. Since America is a country that comes up with all sorts of bizarre ideas, it is only fitting that they would mistakenly teach a noisy game to the Japanese, perhaps out of kindness.

Moreover, Americans likely regard this as a genuine form of physical exercise. However, even if it is purely a game, if it possesses the capacity to astonish the neighbors to such an extent, it can certainly serve the purpose of artillery. From my observations, it seems they are attempting to utilize this sport to achieve the effects of cannon fire. Things can be interpreted in various ways. Given that there are those who commit fraud under the guise of charity and delight in their madness under the name of inspiration, it is not impossible that they might wage war under the guise of a game called baseball. Some explanations may refer to the general concept of baseball. However, the baseball I am describing now is limited to this specific instance, namely, siege artillery. Next, I will introduce the method of launching dum-dum bullets. One among the straight line of gunners, holding a dum-dum bullet in his right hand, throws it at the owner of the pestle. What the dum-dum bullet is made of is unknown to outsiders. It is something like a hard, round stone ball wrapped in skin and sewn together. As I mentioned earlier, when this bullet leaves the hand of one of the gunners and cuts through the air, the person standing opposite finally swings the pestle to strike it back. Occasionally, a bullet may miss and go astray, but generally, it rebounds with a loud bang. The force is quite fierce; it could easily crush the head of my nervous, gastrically weak master. This is sufficient for the gunners, but around them, there is a crowd of onlookers and auxiliary troops, swarming like clouds. As soon as the pestle strikes the dum-dum bullet, there is a chorus of shouts, claps, and exclamations of "Wow!" and "Did it hit?" "Is that not impressive?" "Are you scared yet?" "Are you going to surrender?" This alone would be enough, but the rebounded bullet inevitably rolls into the Garyō Cave three times out of ten. If it does not roll in, the purpose of the attack cannot be achieved. Dum-dum bullets are produced in various places recently, but they are quite expensive, so even in war, one cannot expect a sufficient supply. Typically, there is one or two per squad of gunners. They cannot afford to waste these precious bullets every time they fire. Therefore, they have established a unit called the "dumb pickers" to retrieve the fallen bullets. If the landing spot is favorable, it is not too difficult to pick them up, but if they fly into a grassy field or someone’s residence, it is not so easy to retrieve them. Thus, under normal circumstances, they would aim to drop them in places that are easy to collect, but in this case, the opposite occurs.

The objective is not to play a game but to wage war, so they intentionally drop the dum-dum bullets into the master's residence. Once they fall inside, they must enter the residence to retrieve them. The simplest way to enter the residence is to climb over the four-legged fence. If they cause a commotion inside the fence, the master is bound to get angry. Otherwise, they must take off their helmets and surrender. They must also be troubled enough that their heads gradually become bald.

Just now, a bullet fired from the enemy's forces struck true, passing over the four-sided fence and shaking down the lower leaves of the paulownia tree, hitting the second wall, namely the bamboo fence. It made quite a loud noise. According to Newton's first law of motion, if no other force is applied, a body in motion will continue to move in a straight line at a constant speed. If the motion of a body were governed solely by this law, my master's head would have shared the same fate as that of Iskander at this moment. Fortunately, Newton established the second law at the same time, allowing my master's head to narrowly escape disaster. The second law states that the change in motion is proportional to the force applied, and occurs in the direction of that force. This is a bit difficult to comprehend, but considering that the dumdum bullet did not pierce through the bamboo fence and destroy my master's head, it must surely be thanks to Newton. After a while, as expected, the enemy made their way into the estate, and I could hear sounds of them striking the bamboo leaves with sticks, saying things like, "Is it here?" and "More to the left?" Whenever the enemy enters my master's estate to collect dumdum bullets, they always make a particularly loud noise. They cannot achieve their main objective by sneaking in quietly and picking them up. While dumdum bullets may be precious, it is far more important to mock my master than to collect them. At such times, the location of the bullets is clear from a distance. I know the sound of them hitting the bamboo fence. I know where they struck, and I am aware of the ground where they fell. Therefore, if they behave quietly, they could pick them up without any trouble. According to Leibniz's definition, space is the order of possible coexisting phenomena. The syllables of the Japanese alphabet always appear in the same order. There is always a loach under the willow. The evening moon is always accompanied by bats. A ball may seem out of place in a fence. However, the space that someone who throws a ball into another's estate sees is certainly accustomed to this arrangement. It is immediately apparent upon a glance. To make such a fuss about it is ultimately a strategy to challenge my master to war. In such a situation, even my master, who is generally passive, must respond. Just a moment ago, he was sitting in the tatami room, grinning while listening to a lecture on ethics, but now he stood up with determination. He dashed out furiously and captured one of the enemy. For my master, this was quite an achievement. It was indeed a significant accomplishment, but upon closer inspection, it turned out to be a boy of about fourteen or fifteen.

As an enemy of my master, he seemed somewhat mismatched given my master's beard. However, my master must have thought this was enough. He forcibly dragged the boy, who was apologizing, to the front of the porch. Here, it is necessary to say a word about the enemy's strategy. The enemy surmised that my master, having seen the banner of authority yesterday, would surely come out himself today. If by any chance he were to miss and get caught by a big monk, it would become a troublesome matter. It was better to send a first or second-year student to pick up the balls and avoid danger. Even if my master were to capture the boy and drag him around, it would not affect the honor of the Drop Cloud Pavilion; it would only serve as a disgrace for my master to deal with such a trivial matter. This was the enemy's thinking. This is a perfectly reasonable thought for an ordinary human. However, the enemy forgot to take into account that my master was not an ordinary human. If my master had this much common sense, he would not have rushed out yesterday either. A frenzy draws ordinary people and elevates them beyond their usual limits, bestowing the ordinary with the extraordinary. As long as they distinguish between women, children, rickshaw pullers, and horse boys, they are not worthy of boasting about their frenzy. To capture a middle school first-year student, like my master, as a hostage in a war requires a mindset that surpasses that of a mere frenzied individual. The pitiful one is the captive. Simply following the orders of upperclassmen, he performed the role of a foot soldier picking up balls, and unfortunately, he was cornered by the enemy general, a genius of frenzy, and was brought before the garden, barely managing to leap over the fence. In this situation, the enemy forces could not afford to watch their comrade's disgrace in peace. One after another, they leaped over the four-sided fence and rushed into the garden through the gate. There were about a dozen of them, lined up in front of my master. Most of them were not even wearing jackets. Some rolled up their white shirt sleeves and crossed their arms. Others wore a simple cotton flannel shirt draped over their backs. There were also some fashionable ones with black-edged white cotton shirts, adorned with embroidered characters in the same color on their chests. They all appeared to be fierce warriors, as if they had just arrived from the bamboo mountains of Tanba the night before, their muscles dark and robust. It seemed a waste to have them studying in middle school; they would surely be of greater service to the nation as fishermen or boatmen. They stood before my master, barefoot and with their trousers rolled up high, looking as if they were about to assist with a nearby fire.

They remained silent, not uttering a word. My master also did not speak. For a while, both sides stared at each other, and a slight tension filled the air. "Are you thieves?" my master interrogated. The atmosphere was tense. The anger bubbling up inside him made his nostrils flare, as if the anger had transformed into flames escaping through his nose. The nose of the Echigo lion must have been modeled after the expression of a human when angry. Otherwise, it could not have been made to look so fearsome. "No, we are not thieves. We are students of the Drop Cloud Pavilion."

"Don't lie. Is there anyone from the Drop Cloud Pavilion who would invade another's garden without permission?"

"But look, I am wearing a hat with the school emblem."

"That must be a fake. If you are a student of the Drop Cloud Pavilion, why did you invade recklessly?"

"The ball flew in."

"Why did you throw the ball in?"

"It just happened to come in."

"You are a suspicious bunch."

"We will be more careful from now on, so please forgive us this time."

"Do you think I would easily forgive someone who has crossed over the fence and invaded my estate without knowing who they are?"

"Still, we must be students of the Drop Cloud Pavilion."

"If you are a student of the Drop Cloud Pavilion, what year are you in?"

"I am in the third year."

"Is that so?"

"Yes."

My master looked back toward the inner room and called out, "Hey, come here."

Osan, born in Saitama, opened the sliding door and peeked in. "Go to the Drop Cloud Pavilion and bring someone back."

"Who should I bring?"

"Anyone will do, just bring someone."

The maid replied, "Yes," but the strange scene before her and the unclear nature of the task, combined with the absurdity of the unfolding events, left her neither standing nor sitting, just grinning. My master was convinced he was engaged in a great war. He believed he was wielding his frenzied prowess. However, his own servant, who should have been on his side, was not only approaching the matter with a serious attitude but was also laughing while listening to his orders. This only fueled my master's frenzy further. "I told you to bring anyone, but you don't understand? The principal, the secretary, or the vice-principal…"

"That principal…" The maid only knew the word "principal."

"I said the principal, the secretary, or the vice-principal. Don't you understand?"

"If no one is available, would it be alright to bring a little servant?"

"Don't be foolish. What would a little servant know?"

At this point, the maid seemed to have resigned herself to the situation, saying, "Well then," as she left. I still could not grasp the intention of the messenger. Just as I was worrying whether she might not bring the assistant, lo and behold, the ethics teacher arrived, entering through the front gate. The master, who had been waiting calmly for him to take his seat, immediately began negotiations. "Just now, these fellows have intruded into the premises..." he used an old-fashioned phrase reminiscent of the loyal retainers' tale, but then added somewhat sarcastically, "Are they really your students?"

The ethics teacher, showing no particular surprise, casually surveyed the brave souls lined up in the garden. After a moment, he turned his gaze back to the master and replied as follows:

"Indeed, they are all students from the school. I constantly admonish them to avoid such behavior... but it is quite troublesome... Why do you fellows insist on climbing over the fence?"

As expected, the students remained silent, perhaps not daring to speak to the ethics teacher, and they huddled quietly in a corner of the garden, resembling a flock of sheep encountering snow. "It is understandable for Maru to come in. Living right next to the school, it is only natural that a ball might occasionally fly over. However... it is rather reckless. Even if you must climb over the fence, if you were to do so quietly, picking up the ball gently, I could still overlook it..."

"That is quite right, and I will certainly pay attention to it, but with so many of them... I must be more vigilant from now on. If a ball flies over, you must go around to the front and ask for permission to retrieve it. Understand? — Since it is a large school, it is quite troublesome. However, exercise is necessary for education, so I cannot prohibit it outright. If I allow this, it could lead to further inconveniences, and I sincerely hope for your understanding. In exchange, I will ensure that from now on, they will definitely go around to the front and ask for permission before retrieving any balls."

"Well, if you understand that, then that is good. You may throw as many balls as you like. Just come around and ask for permission, and that will be fine. Now, I will hand over this student to you, so please take him back. I apologize for having summoned you all the way here," the master said, as was his custom, with a long-winded greeting. The ethics teacher took the students and left through the front gate, heading back to the Dropping Cloud Pavilion. Thus, my so-called great incident came to a temporary resolution. If you laugh and ask what makes it a great incident, then laugh away. For those people, it might not be a great incident at all.

I have merely reflected my master's great incident, not recorded theirs. If anyone were to speak ill of me, saying that I am merely a tail cut off from a strong bow's final force, I would like them to remember that this is a characteristic of my master. It is also this characteristic that allows my master to become material for humorous writing. If one says it is foolish to deal with children of fourteen or fifteen, then I must agree that I am foolish as well. Therefore, Oomachi Keigetsu has remarked that my master still has not escaped his childishness. Having already narrated a small incident and now concluded a great incident, I intend to depict the aftereffects that arise following the great incident, thereby providing a conclusion to the entire narrative. Some readers may think that my writing is merely a haphazard collection of words, but I assure you, I am no careless cat. Behind every word lies a profound philosophy of the universe, and each word, when layered and interconnected, reflects a coherent narrative that, if read carelessly as trivial chatter, suddenly transforms into a profound discourse. Therefore, do not act disrespectfully by lounging about or reading it all at once in a lazy manner. It is said that Yanagisawa Sojun would cleanse his hands with rosewater every time he read Han Taizhi's writings, so I hope that at the very least, you will not commit the impropriety of borrowing a friend's magazine to get by, but instead purchase one for yourself. What I am about to describe, which I call the aftereffects, may seem trivial, and you might think it unnecessary to read, but you will surely regret it if you think so. You must read it thoroughly until the end. The day after the great incident, I felt like taking a little walk, so I went outside. Just as I was about to turn the corner to the side street, I saw Kaneda and Suzuki Tojuro standing together, engaged in conversation. Kaneda was on his way home in a rickshaw, while Suzuki had visited Kaneda's house and was on his way back when the two unexpectedly ran into each other. Recently, Kaneda's residence had become quite familiar to me, so I had not ventured in that direction often, but seeing them like this felt somewhat nostalgic. It had been a while since I last saw Suzuki, so I thought I would take the opportunity to greet him. With this decision made, I sauntered closer to where the two gentlemen were standing, and naturally, their conversation reached my ears. This was not my fault; it was their talking that was to blame. Kaneda, being a man of good conscience who even hired a detective to keep tabs on his master's movements, would not mind if I happened to overhear their conversation. If he were to be angry, it would mean he did not understand the meaning of fairness.

In any case, I listened to their conversation. I did not listen out of desire; their discussion simply flew into my ears uninvited. "I just visited your house, and it was perfect timing to run into you," Suzuki said, bobbing his head politely. "Ah, is that so? Actually, I have been wanting to see you for a while now. This is fortunate," Kaneda replied. "Well, that is quite convenient. Is there something you need?"

"Well, it’s nothing serious. It’s just something that can only be done by you."

"If it is something I can do, I will gladly help. What is it?"

"Um, let me think..." Kaneda pondered. "How about I come back at a more convenient time? When would be good for you?"

"Oh, it’s nothing that important. — Well, since we’re at it, I might as well ask you."

"Please, do not hesitate..."

"That strange fellow, you know, your old friend. What was his name? Kushami or something like that?"

"Ah, what about Kushami?"

"Well, it’s nothing in particular, but ever since that incident, I’ve been feeling quite ill at ease."

"That’s quite true; Kushami is indeed arrogant... He should consider his social standing a bit, but he acts as if he is the only one in the world."

"Exactly. He won’t bow to money, and he talks all sorts of cheeky nonsense about businessmen, so I thought I would show him what a businessman’s skills are like. I’ve been weakening him quite a bit lately, but he still holds on. He’s a stubborn fellow, I tell you."

"He really lacks a sense of profit and loss, so he stubbornly endures. He has always had that kind of habit, and he simply does not realize when he is causing himself harm; it’s quite hopeless."

"Ah, indeed, it’s truly hopeless. I’ve tried various means to make things easier for him, but in the end, I had the students from the school deal with him."

"That’s quite a clever plan. Did it yield any results?"

"Well, it seems he has been quite troubled by that. It won’t be long before he falls." 

"That’s splendid. No matter how much he boasts, he is outnumbered." 

"Exactly, he can’t do anything alone. It seems he has been quite weakened, but I thought I would send you to see how things are going."

"Ah, is that so? Well, there's no reason to delay. Let's go and see right away. I'll inform you of the details on my way back. It will be amusing to see that stubborn one in a state of dejection; it will surely be a sight worth watching."

"Ah, then I shall wait for you on your return."

"Then I beg your pardon."

Oh dear, here we go again with ulterior motives. Indeed, the power of businesspeople is something remarkable. To provoke a master who is like a burning coal, and to turn his head into a slippery slope of anguish, leading it to the same fate as Iskander, all of this is due to the influence of businesspeople. I do not know what causes the earth to revolve on its axis, but it is certain that money moves the world. Those who understand the power of this money and can freely exert its influence are none other than the businesspeople. The sun rises safely in the east and sets safely in the west, all thanks to the businesspeople. Until now, I have been nurtured in the house of the ignorant and have not known the benefits of businesspeople, which I now realize is a great oversight on my part. Nevertheless, even my obstinate master must come to some realization this time. If he insists on being obstinate, it could be dangerous. His most precious life is at stake. I wonder how he will greet Suzuki-kun. From that interaction, I will be able to discern how enlightened he is. I cannot afford to dawdle; as a cat, I am greatly concerned for my master. I will quickly slip past Suzuki-kun and return home. Suzuki-kun is still the same cheerful fellow. Today, he does not mention Kaneda at all and is busily engaging in harmless small talk. "You seem a bit pale today; is something the matter?"

"Not at all."

"But you look quite blue; you must be careful. The season is not good for health. Are you able to sleep well at night?"

"Yes."

"Is there something worrying you? If there's anything I can do, just let me know without hesitation."

"Worrying about what?"

"Well, I hope there isn't anything, but if there is, that's what I mean. Worry is the worst poison. It's better to live joyfully and amusingly in this world. You seem a bit too gloomy."

"Laughing can be poisonous too. If you laugh indiscriminately, it can lead to death."

"Don't joke about that. Good fortune comes to those who laugh."

"Once, there was a philosopher in Greece named Chrysippus, but you probably don't know him."

"I don't know him. What of it?"

"That man laughed so much that he died."

"Really? That's quite strange, but that was long ago..."

"Whether it was long ago or now, there's no difference. He saw a donkey eating figs from a silver bowl and found it so amusing that he couldn't stop laughing.

In the end, he laughed himself to death."

"Haha, but you don't have to laugh so uncontrollably. A little laughter—just enough—feels good."

As Suzuki-kun continues to study my master's movements, the front gate rattles open. I think a guest has arrived, but it turns out not to be so. "Excuse me, a ball has come in; may I retrieve it?"

The maid responds from the kitchen, "Yes." The student goes around to the back. Suzuki looks puzzled and asks what's going on. "The student from the back threw a ball into the garden."

"A student from the back? Is there a student back there?"

"At a school called Rakugunkan."

"Oh, I see, a school. It must be quite noisy."

"Noisy? It's unbearable. They can't study at all. If I were the Minister of Education, I would immediately order it to be closed."

"Haha, you're quite angry. Is there something bothering you?"

"Whether there is or not, it's been bothering me from morning till night."

"If it's bothering you that much, why not just move?"

"Who would move? That's utterly ridiculous."

"Getting angry at me won't help. After all, they're just children; you can just ignore them."

"You might be fine with that, but I'm not. Yesterday, I called the teacher and negotiated with him."

"That must have been interesting. He must have been quite intimidated."

"Yes."

At that moment, the gate opens again, and the voice calls out, "Excuse me, a ball has come in; may I retrieve it?"

"Wow, they're coming quite a lot, aren't they? Another ball, my friend."

"Yes, I made a contract for it to come from the front."

"I see, that's why they come so much. Ah, I understand now."

"What do you understand?"

"Well, the source of why they come to retrieve the ball."

"Today makes sixteen times."

"Isn't it annoying? You could just make it so they don't come."

"Even if I wanted to prevent them from coming, they will come regardless."

"Well, if that's the case, then so be it, but you don't have to be so stubborn. It's hard to roll through life with sharp edges. Round things can roll anywhere without difficulty, but square things not only struggle to roll but also get hurt every time they do. After all, this isn't a world for just oneself; people won't conform to your wishes. Well, what can be done? It's a losing battle to go against those with money. You only end up straining your nerves, your body deteriorates, and people won't praise you. They remain unfazed. They can just sit back and use others to get by. It's clear that against many, one is powerless. Stubbornness is fine, but if you insist on standing your ground, it will only hinder your studies and complicate your daily affairs, ultimately leading to a fruitless struggle."

"I beg your pardon.

A ball just flew in; may I go around to the back and retrieve it?"

"Here comes another one," Suzuki-kun laughs. "How rude," my master blushes with embarrassment. Suzuki-kun thinks he has fulfilled his visiting duty, so he says, "Then I shall take my leave," and departs. Replacing him is Dr. Amaki. It is rare for someone who identifies as a businessman to actually be one; when one realizes this, they have already passed the peak of their obstinacy. My master's obstinacy reached its peak during yesterday's major incident, but despite the negotiations being a tangled mess, somehow or another, things were settled. That evening, as he pondered in his study, he realized something felt a bit strange. There is ample room for doubt as to whether it is Rakugunkan that is strange or if he himself is strange, but in any case, it is certainly strange. No matter how close one resides to a middle school, it is odd to be perpetually irritable throughout the year. If it is indeed strange, then something must be done about it. But what can be done? There is no other way than to take the doctor's medicine and perhaps bribe the source of his irritability to soothe it. With this realization, he decided to invite his usual doctor, Dr. Amaki, for a consultation. Whether wise or foolish is a separate matter, but at the very least, he has shown the admirable intention of recognizing his own irritability. Dr. Amaki, as usual, is calm and cheerful, asking, "How are you?" Doctors usually ask this question to the utmost degree. I cannot bring myself to trust a doctor who does not ask, "How are you?"

"Doctor, it's really no good."

"What? Is there such a thing?"

"Isn't it true that a doctor's medicine works?"

Dr. Amaki was surprised, but being a mild-mannered gentleman, he did not show any particular agitation and replied gently, "It can work."

"My stomach ailment, no matter how much medicine I take, it remains the same."

"That is certainly not the case."

"Is it not? Will it get better at all?" I ask about my own stomach. "It won't heal all at once; it will gradually improve. Even now, it is already quite better."

"Is that so?"

"Do you still have irritability?"

「I do get angry, even in my dreams.」
「You should try to exercise a little.」
「Exercising only makes me angrier.」
Dr. Amaki seemed quite taken aback and began his examination, saying, “Well then, let’s see what we can do.” The master, unable to contain his impatience, suddenly raised his voice and asked, “Doctor, I read a book about hypnosis the other day that said it could be used to cure bad habits and various ailments.

Is that true?”  
“Yes, there are such therapies.”  
“Do they still practice it?”  
“Yes.”  
“Is it difficult to induce hypnosis?”  
“It’s not difficult at all; I can do it quite well.”  
“You can do it too?”  
“Yes, shall we give it a try? It’s something everyone should be able to do. If you’re willing, I’ll give it a shot.”  
“Now that sounds interesting! Please do it. I’ve always wanted to experience it myself. But what if I can’t wake up?”  
“Don’t worry, you’ll be fine. Let’s do it.”  
The decision was made in an instant, and the master was about to be hypnotized. I had never seen anything like this before, so I secretly rejoiced and watched the outcome from the corner of the room. The doctor began by focusing on the master’s eyes. As I observed the method, he stroked the master’s eyelids from top to bottom, and even though the master’s eyes were already closed, he persistently tried to impose a habit in the same direction. After a while, the doctor asked the master, “As I stroke your eyelids like this, don’t your eyes feel heavier?” The master replied, “Indeed, they do feel heavier.” The doctor continued to stroke downwards, saying, “They’re getting heavier and heavier, isn’t that right?” The master seemed to be getting into it, remaining silent. The same stroking continued for another three or four minutes. Finally, Dr. Amaki said, “Well, they won’t open anymore.” Poor master’s eyes had completely shut. “They won’t open anymore?” “No, they won’t open.” The master remained silent, his eyes still closed. I assumed the master had gone blind. After a while, the doctor said, “If you can open them, go ahead and try. They won’t open at all.” “Is that so?” Before he finished speaking, the master opened both eyes as usual. With a grin, he said, “I’m not under!” Dr. Amaki laughed in response, “No, you’re not.” The hypnosis ultimately failed. Dr. Amaki took his leave. The next visitor was—never before had so many guests come to the master’s home. It seemed almost unbelievable for someone with so few social connections. Yet, they had indeed come. Moreover, it was an unusual guest. My intention to describe this unusual guest is not merely because he is unusual; as I mentioned earlier, I am sketching the aftermath of a significant event. This unusual guest is indispensable material for portraying that aftermath. I do not know his name, but he was a man of about forty, with a long face and a beard like a goat. In contrast to Meitei, the aesthete, I intend to call this man a philosopher. The reason I call him a philosopher is not that he scatters ideas like Meitei, but because he appears quite philosophical when conversing with the master. They seemed to be old classmates, and their interaction was remarkably relaxed.

“Ah, Meitei, he floats around like a goldfish cracker in a pond. The other day, when he passed by the gate of a nobleman he had never met, he casually suggested stopping for tea, and they pulled him in. Quite carefree, isn’t he?”  
“And what happened then?”  
“I didn’t see what happened, but—well, he’s probably a natural eccentric. In exchange, he has no thoughts at all, just a complete goldfish cracker. Suzuki, is he coming? Oh, really? He’s a clever man in worldly matters, though I don’t understand his reasoning. He can wear a gold watch, but he lacks depth, so he’s restless and useless. They say he’s smooth and polished, but he doesn’t even understand what that means. If Meitei is a goldfish cracker, then he’s just a konjac tied with straw—smooth but merely quivering and shaking.”  
The master seemed greatly impressed by this peculiar metaphor and laughed heartily for the first time in a while. “Well then, what about you?”  
“As for me, I suppose I’m like a natural yam—long and buried in the mud.”  
“You seem to be calm and carefree all the time; I envy you.”  
“I’m just living like any ordinary person. There’s nothing particularly enviable about it. I’m just grateful that I don’t feel the urge to envy others, and that’s good enough.”  
“Is your financial situation doing well lately?”  
“It’s the same as always. It’s just enough to get by. But since I’m eating, I’m fine. No need to worry.”  
“I’m feeling unpleasant, and I can’t stand it. I find complaints everywhere I look.”  
“Complaining is fine. If you have complaints, just let them out, and for a while, you’ll feel better. People are different; you can’t expect others to be like you. You have to hold your chopsticks like everyone else to eat, but when it comes to cutting your own bread, it’s best to do it your own way. If you have a skilled tailor, they’ll bring you clothes that fit your body perfectly from the start. But if you go to a poor seamstress, you’ll have to endure it for a while. However, the world is well-made; while you wear them, the clothes will adjust to your body shape. If you’re born to good parents who know how to raise you well, that’s happiness. But if you’re poorly made, you’ll either have to endure not fitting into the world or wait until the world adjusts to you.”  
“But for someone like me, it seems I’ll never fit in, and that’s disheartening.”  
“If you force yourself into a suit that doesn’t fit, it will tear. That’s when fights break out, or people commit suicide, or disturbances occur. But you, you’re just bored, and of course, you won’t commit suicide, nor have you ever fought. You’re doing quite well.”  
“Yet I’m fighting every day. Even if the opponent doesn’t show up, if I’m angry, that’s a fight.”  
“I see, a one-sided fight. How amusing!

Go ahead and do it as much as you like.”  
“I’ve grown tired of that.”  
“Well then, stop it.”  
“Before you, it’s not so easy to free my heart.”  
“Well, what is it that you’re so dissatisfied about?”  
At this point, the master began to recount all his grievances, starting with the incident at Rakuenkan, the tanuki from Imado, Pinsuke, and Kishyago, and all other complaints, pouring them out before the philosopher. The philosopher listened quietly but eventually opened his mouth and began to explain to the master.

"Just ignore what Pinsuke and the others say. It’s all nonsense anyway. What value is there in concerning oneself with middle school students? It’s nothing but a nuisance. Even if you negotiate or argue, that nuisance won’t go away. When it comes to this point, I think the old Japanese were far superior to Westerners. The Western approach is all about being proactive, and that’s become quite fashionable lately, but it carries a significant flaw. First of all, the idea of being proactive is an endless discussion. No matter how long you push forward proactively, you can never reach a state of satisfaction or a realm of completeness. There’s a cypress tree in front of you, right? You remove it because it’s in the way, but then the boarding house beyond it becomes a nuisance. If you evict the boarding house, the next house will irritate you. It’s an endless cycle. This is the way of the Westerners. Not a single one of them, be it Napoleon or Alexander, was ever satisfied after winning. If someone is displeased, they fight; if the other party doesn’t back down, they take it to court; if they win in court, they think it’s settled. That’s a mistake. The peace of mind is something that can’t be resolved until death. Because of the shortcomings of oligarchic politics, they want to switch to a representative government. When that doesn’t work, they want to change it to something else. If the river is too arrogant, they build a bridge; if the mountain is bothersome, they dig a tunnel. They lay down railroads because transportation is troublesome. But none of this leads to permanent satisfaction. So, how far can humans go in asserting their will? Western civilization may be proactive and enterprising, but it’s essentially a civilization created by those who live in perpetual dissatisfaction. Japanese civilization, on the other hand, doesn’t seek satisfaction by changing the state of things outside oneself. The fundamental difference from the West is that it develops under the major assumption that the surrounding circumstances are not to be changed. If the relationship between parent and child is unsatisfactory, we don’t try to improve it like Europeans do; instead, we seek means of finding peace of mind under the existing relationship, which is unchangeable. The same goes for the relationships between husband and wife, lord and vassal, and the distinctions between samurai and townspeople. Observing nature follows the same principle. If there’s a mountain blocking the way to a neighboring country, instead of thinking of breaking it down, we devise ways to manage without going to that neighboring country. We cultivate a mindset that finds satisfaction without crossing the mountain. Therefore, look here.

Whether Zen or Confucian, they all grasp this fundamental problem. No matter how great one thinks oneself to be, the world will never conform to one’s wishes; one cannot turn back the setting sun or reverse the flow of the Kamo River. The only thing one can control is one’s own heart. If one practices to free the heart, then no matter how much noise the students of Rakuenkan make, it wouldn’t matter; one could even ignore the tanuki of Imado-yaki. If Pinsuke says something foolish, just treat him like a fool and it wouldn’t matter. There’s a story that says that in the old days, when a monk was attacked, he would say something witty like ‘I cut the spring breeze in the blink of an eye.’ When the training of the heart reaches the extreme of passivity, such a lively action can occur. I don’t understand such difficult matters, but in any case, it seems a bit mistaken to think that only Western-style proactivity is good. In reality, no matter how proactive you are, you can’t do anything about students coming to tease you. Unless you use your power to close that school, or if the other side does something bad enough to report to the police, it’s a different matter, but otherwise, no matter how proactive you are, you won’t win. If you were to be proactive, it would come down to money. It becomes a matter of numbers. In other words, it means you have to bow your head to the rich. You have to be afraid of the many children who rely on the crowd. The fact that you, a poor man, still want to fight proactively all alone is the very seed of your discontent. Do you understand now?"

The master listened without saying whether he understood or not. After the peculiar guest left, he crawled into his study and sat there, lost in thought without reading a single book. Suzuki Tojuro taught the master to follow money and the crowd. Dr. Amaki advised him to calm his nerves with hypnosis. The last peculiar guest preached that he should find peace through the cultivation of passivity. Which one the master would choose was entirely up to him. However, it was clear that he could not go on like this. ---

The master has a pockmarked face. It is said that before the Restoration, pockmarks were quite common, but from the perspective of the current Anglo-Japanese alliance, such a face seems somewhat out of date. The decline of pockmarks is a conclusion precisely drawn from medical statistics, which suggests that in the near future, they will completely disappear in proportion to the increase in population. Even a cat like me has no room to doubt this sound argument. I don’t know how many people on this earth still have pockmarked faces, but when I consider the area of my acquaintances, there isn’t a single cat with one.

Among humans, there is only one, and that one is the master. It’s quite unfortunate. Every time I see the master’s face, I wonder what kind of karma has led him to have such a peculiar face and to breathe the air of the twentieth century without a trace of shame. In the past, it might have had some significance, but now that all pockmarks have been ordered to retreat to the upper arms, the fact that they still stubbornly occupy the tip of the nose and the cheeks is not only nothing to boast about, but rather a matter concerning the dignity of pockmarks. If possible, it would seem better to remove them while there’s still time. The pockmarks themselves must feel insecure as well. Or perhaps, in times of political decline, they occupy the entire face with the determination that they will not rest until they have turned the setting sun back to the zenith. If that’s the case, then these pockmarks should not be viewed with contempt. They are a collection of timeless, unyielding holes that resist the tide of popular opinion and are worthy of our great respect. Their only flaw is that they are unclean. When the master was a child, there was a famous Chinese medicine doctor named Asada So-haku in Yotsuya’s Yamabukicho, who would always arrive in a palanquin when visiting patients. However, after So-haku passed away and his adopted son took over, the palanquin was quickly transformed into a rickshaw. So, if that adopted son dies and another takes over, perhaps the herbal medicine will turn into antipyrin. Even in So-haku’s time, it was not particularly respectable to be seen riding around Tokyo in a palanquin. The only ones who did so were the old-fashioned dead, pigs being loaded onto trains, and So-haku himself. The master’s pockmarks, in their lack of movement, are like So-haku’s palanquin; they appear pitiful from the outside, but the stubborn master, no less than a Chinese medicine doctor, continues to expose his pockmarked face to the world while teaching reading and writing every day. Standing at the lectern, with such a relic of the last century etched on his face, he must be imparting great lessons to his students beyond just the curriculum. He interprets the major issue of "the impact of pockmarks on the face" with ease, rather than repeating "the monkey has hands," quietly providing answers to his students. If a person like the master were to cease to exist as a teacher, those students would have to rush to libraries or museums to study this problem, expending as much effort as we do to conjure up the Egyptians through mummies. From this perspective, the master’s pockmarks are quietly bestowing a strange merit in the depths of the universe.

However, my master did not intentionally plant pockmarks all over his face to perform this merit. In truth, he did have pockmarks. Unfortunately, what he thought he had contracted on his arm had, before he knew it, spread to his face. At that time, being a child, he had no thoughts of beauty or anything of the sort, and while scratching his face in a fit of itchiness, he ended up ruining the face that his parents had given him. My master often tells his wife that before he had pockmarks, he was as beautiful as a boy made of jewels. He even boasts that he was so lovely that Westerners turned around to look at him at the Kannon Temple in Asakusa. Indeed, that may be true. It is just unfortunate that no one can vouch for it. No matter how much merit or admonition it may bring, a dirty person is still a dirty person. Since I became aware of such things, my master has been greatly troubled by his pockmarks, and he has tried every means to smooth over this disgrace. However, unlike the old man Souhaku, who, when he became fed up, could suddenly toss things aside, my master’s pockmarks have not disappeared so easily. They still remain quite evidently. It seems that this evident fact bothers him somewhat, as he counts the number of pockmarked faces he sees whenever he walks down the street. He records in his diary how many pockmarked individuals he encounters each day, whether they are men or women, and whether they are in the Kankōjō in Ogawamachi or Ueno Park. He is convinced that he will never yield to anyone in his knowledge regarding pockmarks. The other day, when a friend returned from a trip to the West, he even asked, “Do Westerners have pockmarks?” When his friend thought for a while and replied, “Well, not often,” my master pressed on, “But do they have any at all?” The friend, with an indifferent expression, answered, “If they do, they’re probably beggars or street performers. Educated people seem not to have them.” My master then remarked, “Is that so? It seems a bit different from Japan.”

Having reconsidered his quarrel with the Rakuunkan based on a philosopher’s opinion, my master has since locked himself in his study, pondering something incessantly. He may intend to cultivate a spiritually active mind in a passive manner through quiet meditation, but being inherently a timid person, it is unlikely that he will achieve any satisfactory results by merely sulking in such a gloomy manner. He has realized that it would be far better to sell some English books and learn a lively tune from a geisha, but being such a stubborn man, he has no intention of heeding the advice of a cat like me, so I left him alone for five or six days. Today marks exactly seven days since then.

In Zen practices, there are those who, within a span of seventeen days, demonstrate great enlightenment through intense meditation, so I wondered how my master was faring, whether he had died or lived, and if he had come to some resolution. I ambled from the porch to the entrance of the study to spy on the movements inside. The study is a south-facing six-tatami mat room, with a large desk set in a sunny spot. But it is not just any large desk; it is a grand piece, six feet long, three feet eight inches wide, and of a height to match. Of course, it was not a ready-made item. It was a rare piece made by negotiating with a local carpenter, designed to serve as both a bed and a desk. I cannot fathom why he would buy such a large desk, nor why he would think to lie down on it. Perhaps it was a momentary whim that led him to bring in such an unwieldy object, or maybe, as is often found in those with a certain kind of mental illness, he connected two unrelated ideas—desk and bed—in his mind. In any case, it is an eccentric thought. The only flaw is that while it is eccentric, it is also utterly useless. I once saw my master roll over while napping on this desk and tumble off onto the porch. Since then, it seems that this desk has never been used as a bed again. In front of the desk is a thin, flat merino cushion, with about three holes burned into it from a cigarette. The cotton visible inside is a dull black. Sitting backward on this cushion is my master. His mouse-colored obi, tied in a neat knot, hangs down loosely to his feet. Just the other day, I had the misfortune of getting my head caught in that very obi. It is not a thing one should approach lightly. I peered over his shoulder to see if he was still thinking, as there is a saying about foolish thoughts. On the desk, something was shining annoyingly bright. I blinked a few times in surprise, but then I realized that this brightness was coming from a mirror moving on the desk. But why would my master have a mirror in his study? Mirrors are typically found in bathrooms. Indeed, I had seen this very mirror in the bathroom that morning. I specify this mirror because it is the only one in my master's house. He uses it every morning after washing his face to part his hair. — Some might wonder if a man like him really parts his hair, but in truth, he is only meticulous about his hair while being negligent in other matters. Since I came to this household, he has never once had a buzz cut, regardless of how hot it has been. He always leaves it about two inches long, parting it grandly on the left side, while the right side is slightly flipped up for a tidy look. This may also be a sign of mental illness.

Such a pretentious way of parting hair does not harmonize at all with this desk, but since it does not harm anyone, no one says anything. He seems quite pleased with himself. Setting aside the highfalutin way he parts his hair, I wondered why he let it grow so long. The reason is that his pockmarks not only invade his face but have long since penetrated to the top of his head. Therefore, if he were to cut it short like an ordinary person, dozens of pockmarks would emerge from the roots of the short hair. No matter how much one strokes or rubs, those spots will not disappear. It might be charming, like releasing fireflies into a barren field, but it certainly does not please his wife. If he keeps his hair long, he can avoid revealing the truth, and it would be foolish to expose his flaws willingly. If possible, he would like to grow hair all the way down to his face to cover up those pockmarks, so there is no need for him to pay to have the hair he could grow for free cut, proclaiming, “I have been afflicted with smallpox all the way to my skull.” — This is the reason my master keeps his hair long, which leads to the way he parts it, and that, in turn, explains why he looks in the mirror, which is found in the bathroom, and thus, the fact that there is only one mirror in the house.

The mirror that ought to be in the bathroom, and which is the only one, has somehow found its way into the study. This can only mean that the mirror has been afflicted with a case of soul-separation, or that the master has brought it from the bathroom. If he did bring it, what could have been the reason? Perhaps it is a tool necessary for that well-known negative cultivation. Once, a certain scholar visited a monk who was polishing a brick with both sleeves rolled up. When asked what he was making, the monk replied, "I am trying my utmost to create a mirror." The scholar was astonished and said that no matter how great a monk he was, he could not turn a brick into a mirror. The monk laughed heartily and replied, "Oh, is that so? Then I shall stop. No matter how many books one reads, one cannot understand the way." It is possible that my master, having heard such a thing, has brought the mirror from the bathroom and is now waving it about with a self-satisfied expression. Things have become rather unsettling, and I watch quietly. The master, oblivious to all this, gazes intently at the mirror. A mirror is, after all, a rather eerie object. It takes a great deal of courage to peer into one alone in a large room at midnight with a candle lit. I remember the first time the young lady of the house pressed a mirror to my face; I was so startled that I ran around the estate three times. Even in broad daylight, when one stares at oneself as intently as my master is doing, it is only natural to find one's own face frightening. Just looking at it, it is not a particularly pleasant face. After a while, the master muttered, "Indeed, what a filthy face." To confess one's own ugliness is quite admirable. Judging by his demeanor, it is certainly the behavior of a madman, but the statement is true. If one were to take it a step further, one might become frightened of one's own hideousness. A person who has not deeply felt the fact that they are a terrible villain cannot be called a person of hardship. Without being a person of hardship, one cannot attain liberation. At this point, my master might even exclaim, "Oh, how frightening!" but he does not say it. After declaring, "Indeed, what a filthy face," he seems to have thought of something and puffed out his cheeks. Then he slapped his puffed cheeks two or three times with his palm. I cannot tell what sort of incantation this is. At that moment, I felt that there was something resembling that face. Upon closer inspection, it was Osan's face. Since I am at it, let me briefly introduce Osan's face; it is indeed quite puffed up. The other day, someone brought back a pufferfish lantern from Anamori Inari, and it is just like that pufferfish lantern, all puffed up.

The way it is puffed up is so cruel that both eyes have vanished. Of course, a pufferfish puffs up evenly into a perfect sphere, but as for Osan, her original bone structure is angular, and she puffs up according to that structure, resembling a hexagonal clock troubled by moisture. If Osan were to hear this, she would surely be angry, so I shall leave it at that and return to my master. With cheeks puffed out as much as possible, he continues to slap his cheeks while saying, "When the skin is this tense, even a blemish won't catch the eye," talking to himself again.
