Now he turns his face sideways and reflects the part illuminated by light in the mirror. "When viewed like this, it stands out quite a bit. Indeed, the side facing the light looks flat. How strange," he seems to be quite impressed. Then he stretches out his right hand and holds the mirror as far away as possible, gazing at it intently. "At this distance, it doesn't look so bad. It really is too close that causes the problem. — It's not just the face; everything is like that," he says as if he has come to a realization. Next, he suddenly turns the mirror sideways. Then, focusing on the bridge of his nose, he scrunches his eyes, forehead, and eyebrows all toward that center at once. I thought an unpleasant appearance had formed, and he seemed to realize it too, promptly stopping. "Why does my face look so poisonous?" he said, pulling the mirror closer, about three inches from his eyes, with a somewhat puzzled expression. He stroked his nostrils with his right index finger and pressed the tip of that finger onto the blotting paper on the desk. The absorbed nasal grease rounded up and floated on the paper. He performs various tricks. Then, my master turned the finger that had smeared the nasal grease and deftly flipped his lower eyelid, performing what is commonly known as a "bengankō." It is somewhat unclear whether he is studying blemishes or competing with the mirror in a staring contest. Given my master's capricious nature, it seems he will shift to various things as he watches. It is not just that. If one were to interpret it benevolently in a Socratic manner, my master might be engaging in various gestures before the mirror as a means of self-realization. All human research is, in essence, self-research. The earth and sky, mountains and rivers, sun and moon, stars and constellations are merely different names for oneself. There is no other subject to study outside of oneself. If a person could leap beyond themselves, the moment they did so, they would cease to exist. Moreover, no one else can study oneself. No matter how much one wishes to do so or how much one wants to receive it, it is an impossible consultation.

Therefore, throughout history, all great men have become great through their own efforts. If one could understand oneself through the help of others, one could simply feed beef to one's proxy and judge whether it is tough or tender. Listening to the law in the morning, seeking the way in the evening, and holding a book under the ginkgo tree at night are merely means to provoke this self-evidence. Among the laws expounded by others, the paths articulated by others, or even amidst the piles of decaying paper exceeding five vehicles, there is no reason for the existence of oneself. If there were, it would be the ghost of oneself. In certain circumstances, a ghost may be superior to a non-ghost. It is not impossible that chasing a shadow may lead one to encounter the body. Most shadows do not stray far from the body. In this sense, if my master is twisting the mirror, he is quite a talkative man. I think he is far better than those who blindly swallow Epictetus and pretend to be scholars. The mirror is both a brewing device for self-adoration and a disinfectant for boasting. When approached with a sense of vanity and superficiality, there is no tool more foolish than this to incite such folly. Throughout history, two-thirds of the deeds of arrogance that harm oneself and others are indeed the work of mirrors. Just as a curious doctor during the French Revolution invented a guillotine and caused a great deal of trouble, the first person to create a mirror must have had a very restless night. However, when one is on the verge of losing affection for oneself, there is no remedy quite like looking into a mirror. The beauty and ugliness are clear. One inevitably realizes how one has managed to live up to this point with such a face. The moment one becomes aware of this is the most precious time in a person's life. There is nothing more noble than being aware of one's own foolishness. Before this self-aware fool, all pretentious people must bow their heads in fear. Even if the person intends to look down on and ridicule me, from my perspective, that very arrogance becomes an act of bowing in fear. My master is not wise enough to realize his own foolishness by looking in the mirror. However, he is a man who can fairly read the marks of pockmarks imprinted on his face. Acknowledging the ugliness of one's face may serve as a stepping stone to understanding the baseness of one's heart. He is a reliable man. This may also be a result of being bested by philosophers.

As I contemplated this, observing the situation, my master, unaware of my scrutiny, after indulging in a hearty yawn, remarked, "It seems to be quite bloodshot. It must be chronic conjunctivitis," and began to rub his inflamed eyelids vigorously with the side of his index finger. He was likely feeling itchy, but one should not rub something that is already so red. Before long, it would surely rot like the eyes of a salted sea bream. Eventually, when he opened his eyes and faced the mirror, they appeared, as expected, cloudy and dull, resembling the overcast winter sky of the northern regions. To be fair, his eyes were not particularly bright even on ordinary days. If one were to use an exaggerated adjective, they were so vague that the distinction between the black and white of his eyes was indiscernible. Just as his mind seemed to be in a fog, lacking clarity and consistency, so too did his eyes drift aimlessly in the depths of their sockets. Some say this is due to the toxins from the womb, while others interpret it as a remnant of smallpox; it is said that in his youth, he had suffered considerably from willow caterpillars and red frogs. Yet, despite his mother's careful nurturing, he remained as dull as he was at birth. I secretly think that this condition is not due to toxins or smallpox at all. The reason his eyes wander in such a murky and muddled state is simply that his intellect is composed of an opaque substance, and its function has reached the depths of obscurity, naturally manifesting itself in his physical form, causing unnecessary worry for his oblivious mother. The murkiness of his eyes signifies the dullness of his mind, and since his mind is like a Tenpo coin with holes in it, his eyes too, like the Tenpo coin, must be largely ineffective. Now he began to twist his beard. It was originally a rather unruly beard, growing in all sorts of directions. No matter how much individualism is in vogue these days, one cannot help but feel for the owner when such a beard is allowed to run rampant in the town. Therefore, my master, taking this into consideration, has recently been training it diligently, striving to arrange it as systematically as possible. His earnest efforts have not been in vain, as it has finally begun to take on a somewhat orderly appearance. Until now, he had merely been growing a beard, but recently he has taken to boasting that he is cultivating one. Enthusiasm tends to be spurred by the degree of success, and seeing the promising future of his beard, my master, whenever he has a moment to spare, is sure to apply himself to the task of grooming it. His ambition is akin to that of His Imperial Majesty the German Emperor, as he nurtures a fervent desire for improvement in his beard.

Thus, whether the hair follicles are oriented sideways or downward, he pays little heed and grabs them all together, pulling them upward. The beard must surely find this quite troublesome, as even its owner sometimes experiences pain. But that is part of the training. Whether one likes it or not, it must be handled with care. To an outsider, it may seem like an incomprehensible pastime, but the person involved understands it to be entirely reasonable. It is akin to an educator whimsically bending the nature of a student and boasting of their own achievements; there is no reason to criticize such a thing. While my master was diligently grooming his beard with full fervor, Osan, the housekeeper, appeared from the kitchen, extending her red hand into the study, as usual, to announce that the mail had arrived. With his right hand grasping his beard and his left holding a mirror, my master turned to look at the entrance. Upon seeing his beard, which resembled a tail standing upright in an "8" shape, Osan suddenly withdrew back into the kitchen, bursting into laughter as she leaned against the lid of the pot. My master remained unfazed. Calmly, he lowered the mirror and picked up the mail. The first letter was printed in a rather imposing typeface. Upon reading it, it said:

"Dear Sir, I extend my heartfelt congratulations on your continued prosperity. Reflecting on the recent Russo-Japanese War, we have achieved victory after victory and are now heralding the restoration of peace. Our brave and valiant soldiers, now celebrated with cheers of 'Banzai,' have dedicated their lives to the nation, enduring the hardships of cold and heat in distant lands. Their unwavering loyalty must forever be remembered. The army's triumphant return is nearing completion this month. Therefore, we will hold a grand victory celebration on the 25th of this month, representing the citizens of this district to honor over a thousand officers and soldiers who have been dispatched. We also wish to provide comfort to the families of the soldiers. We sincerely hope for your support in this endeavor, and it would be a great honor for us if this celebration could be carried out with your cooperation. We earnestly request your enthusiastic participation. Sincerely yours."

The sender was a member of the nobility. After reading the letter silently, my master immediately rolled it up and pretended not to notice it. He was unlikely to contribute anything. Just the other day, he had donated two or three yen for relief efforts due to the poor harvest in the Tohoku region and had been boasting to everyone he met about how he had been asked for donations. Since it is called a donation, it is something one gives, not something one is taken from.

It is inappropriate to say he was taken from; he was not robbed. Nevertheless, my master seemed to think he had been treated as if he had suffered a theft. Whether it was a military welcome or an invitation from the nobility, he would not be swayed by a mere printed letter to part with his money. From my master's perspective, he would prefer to be welcomed himself before welcoming the army. After he has welcomed himself, he might be inclined to welcome most things, but as long as it interferes with his daily life, it seems he intends to leave the welcoming to the nobility. My master picked up the second letter, exclaiming, "Ah, this one is printed too."

"In this autumn chill, I hope this letter finds you and your family in ever-increasing prosperity. As you are aware, our school has been hindered by the ambitions of a few individuals since the year before last, reaching a critical point at one time. However, I believe this is all due to my own shortcomings as a needle maker, and I am deeply aware of this. Enduring hardships, I have finally devised a way to secure the funds necessary to build a new schoolhouse that meets my ideals. This is not for any other purpose but to publish a book titled 'Essential Techniques of Sewing,' which is based on the principles of craftsmanship that I have painstakingly researched over many years. Therefore, I humbly request that this book be purchased at cost, with a small profit added, to assist in the development of this craft while also accumulating a modest profit to be used for the construction of the schoolhouse. I am truly sorry to trouble you with this, but if you could consider making a donation towards the construction costs, I would be most grateful. I sincerely hope you will purchase a copy of this book and share it with your maidservants, thus expressing your support. I humbly request this."

The principal, Nuita Harisaku, signed off with nine bows. My master coldly crumpled this formal letter and tossed it into the wastebasket. It was unfortunate that Harisaku's nine bows and his enduring hardships had been of no use. Now, onto the third letter. The third letter radiated an exceptionally unusual brilliance. The envelope was adorned with a red-and-white striped pattern, and in the center, as splendid as a candy shop sign, was written in bold letters: "Kushami-sensei, Tiger Skin Underwear." I cannot guarantee whether a lady would emerge from within, but the exterior was indeed quite impressive.

若し我を以て天地を律すれば一口にして西江の水を吸いつくすべく、若し天地を以て我を律すれば我は則ち陌上の塵のみ。すべからく道え、天地と我と什麼の交渉かある。……始めて海鼠を食い出せる人は其胆力に於て敬すべく、始めて河豚を喫せる漢は其勇気に於て重んずべし。海鼠を食えるものは親鸞の再来にして、河豚を喫せるものは日蓮の分身なり。苦沙弥先生の如きに至っては只干瓢の酢味噌を知るのみ。干瓢の酢味噌を食って天下の士たるものは、われ未だ之を見ず。……

親友も汝を売るべし。父母も汝に私あるべし。愛人も汝を棄つべし。富貴は固より頼みがたかるべし。爵禄は一朝にして失うべし。汝の頭中に秘蔵する学問には黴が生えるべし。汝何を恃まんとするか。天地の裡に何をたのまんとするか。神？　神は人間の苦しまぎれに捏造せる土偶のみ。人間のせつな糞の凝結せる臭骸のみ。恃むまじきを恃んで安しと云う。咄々、酔漢漫りに胡乱の言辞を弄して、蹣跚として墓に向う。油尽きて灯自ら滅す。業尽きて何物をか遺す。苦沙弥先生よろしく御茶でも上がれ。……

人を人と思わざれば畏るる所なし。人を人と思わざるものが、吾を吾と思わざる世を憤るは如何。権貴栄達の士は人を人と思わざるに於て得たるが如し。只他の吾を吾と思わぬ時に於て怫然として色を作す。任意に色を作し来れ。馬鹿野郎。……

吾の人を人と思うとき、他の吾を吾と思わぬ時、不平家は発作的に天降る。此発作的活動を名づけて革命という。革命は不平家の所為にあらず。権貴栄達の士が好んで産する所なり。朝鮮に人参多し先生何が故に服せざる。

在巣鴨　　天道公平　再拝  
針作君は九拝であったが、この男は単に再拝だけである。寄附金の依頼でないだけに七拝ほど横風に構えている。寄附金の依頼ではないがその代りすこぶる分りにくいものだ。どこの雑誌へ出しても没書になる価値は充分あるのだから、頭脳の不透明をもって鳴る主人は必ず寸断寸断に引き裂いてしまうだろうと思のほか、打ち返し打ち返し読み直している。こんな手紙に意味があると考えて、あくまでその意味を究めようという決心かも知れない。およそ天地の間にわからんものは沢山あるが意味をつけてつかないものは一つもない。どんなむずかしい文章でも解釈しようとすれば容易に解釈の出来るものだ。人間は馬鹿であると云おうが、人間は利口であると云おうが手もなくわかる事だ。それどころではない。人間は犬であると云っても豚であると云っても別に苦しむほどの命題ではない。山は低いと云っても構わん、宇宙は狭いと云っても差し支えはない。烏が白くて小町が醜婦で苦沙弥先生が君子でも通らん事はない。だからこんな無意味な手紙でも何とか蚊とか理窟さえつければどうとも意味はとれる。ことに主人のように知らぬ英語を無理矢理にこじ附けて説明し通して来た男はなおさら意味をつけたがるのである。天気の悪るいのになぜグード・モーニングですかと生徒に問われて七日間考えたり、コロンバスと云う名は日本語で何と云いますかと聞かれて三日三晩かかって答を工夫するくらいな男には、干瓢の酢味噌が天下の士であろうと、朝鮮の仁参を食って革命を起そうと随意な意味は随処に湧き出る訳である。主人はしばらくしてグード・モーニング流にこの難解な言句を呑み込んだと見えて「なかなか意味深長だ。何でもよほど哲理を研究した人に違ない。天晴な見識だ」と大変賞賛した。この一言でも主人の愚なところはよく分るが、翻って考えて見るといささかもっともな点もある。主人は何に寄らずわからぬものをありがたがる癖を有している。これはあながち主人に限った事でもなかろう。分らぬところには馬鹿に出来ないものが潜伏して、測るべからざる辺には何だか気高い心持が起るものだ。それだから俗人はわからぬ事をわかったように吹聴するにも係らず、学者はわかった事をわからぬように講釈する。大学の講義でもわからん事を喋舌る人は評判がよくってわかる事を説明する者は人望がないのでもよく知れる。主人がこの手紙に敬服したのも意義が明瞭であるからではない。その主旨が那辺に存するかほとんど捕え難いからである。急に海鼠が出て来たり、せつな糞が出てくるからである。だから主人がこの文章を尊敬する唯一の理由は、道家で道徳経を尊敬し、儒家で易経を尊敬し、禅家で臨済録を尊敬すると一般で全く分らんからである。但し全然分らんでは気がすまんから勝手な註釈をつけてわかった顔だけはする。わからんものをわかったつもりで尊敬するのは昔から愉快なものである。――主人は恭しく八分体の名筆を巻き納めて、これを机上に置いたまま懐手をして冥想に沈んでいる。

ところへ「頼む頼む」と玄関から大きな声で案内を乞う者がある。声は迷亭のようだが、迷亭に似合わずしきりに案内を頼んでいる。主人は先から書斎のうちでその声を聞いているのだが懐手のまま毫も動こうとしない。取次に出るのは主人の役目でないという主義か、この主人は決して書斎から挨拶をした事がない。下女は先刻洗濯石鹸を買いに出た。細君は憚りである。すると取次に出べきものは吾輩だけになる。吾輩だって出るのはいやだ。すると客人は沓脱から敷台へ飛び上がって障子を開け放ってつかつか上り込んで来た。主人も主人だが客も客だ。座敷の方へ行ったなと思うと襖を二三度あけたり閉てたりして、今度は書斎の方へやってくる。

「おい冗談じゃない。何をしているんだ、御客さんだよ」
「おや君か」
「おや君かもないもんだ。そこにいるなら何とか云えばいいのに、まるで空家のようじゃないか」
「うん、ちと考え事があるもんだから」
「考えていたって通れくらいは云えるだろう」
「云えん事もないさ」
「相変らず度胸がいいね」
「せんだってから精神の修養を力めているんだもの」
「物好きだな。精神を修養して返事が出来なくなった日には来客は御難だね。そんなに落ちつかれちゃ困るんだぜ。実は僕一人来たんじゃないよ。大変な御客さんを連れて来たんだよ。ちょっと出て逢ってくれ給え」
「誰を連れて来たんだい」
「誰でもいいからちょっと出て逢ってくれたまえ。是非君に逢いたいと云うんだから」
「誰だい」
「誰でもいいから立ちたまえ」

主人は懐手のままぬっと立ちながら「また人を担ぐつもりだろう」と椽側へ出て何の気もつかずに客間へ這入り込んだ。すると六尺の床を正面に一個の老人が粛然と端坐して控えている。主人は思わず懐から両手を出してぺたりと唐紙の傍へ尻を片づけてしまった。これでは老人と同じく西向きであるから双方共挨拶のしようがない。昔堅気の人は礼義はやかましいものだ。

「さあどうぞあれへ」と床の間の方を指して主人を促がす。主人は両三年前までは座敷はどこへ坐っても構わんものと心得ていたのだが、

その後ある人から床の間の講釈を聞いて、あれは上段の間の変化したもので、上使が坐わる所だと悟って以来決して床の間へは寄りつかない男である。ことに見ず知らずの年長者が頑と構えているのだから上座どころではない。挨拶さえ碌には出来ない。一応頭をさげて「さあどうぞあれへ」と向うの云う通りを繰り返した。

「いやそれでは御挨拶が出来かねますから、どうぞあれへ」
「いえ、それでは……どうぞあれへ」と主人はいい加減に先方の口上を真似ている。

「Well, I must say, your modesty is quite overwhelming.

On the contrary, I am the one who feels humbled. Please, do not hold back, go ahead.」

“Your modesty… I am quite flustered… please…” The master turned bright red, mumbling his words. It seems that even mental cultivation has little effect on him. Meitei, laughing from behind the sliding door, thought it was about time and, while pushing the master from behind, insisted, “Come on out. If you stick to the fusuma, there will be no place for me to sit. Don’t hesitate, step forward.”

The master, having no choice, squeezed his way to the front. “Kushami, this is my uncle from Shizuoka, whom I often speak of. Uncle, this is Mr. Kushami.” 

“Ah, it is my first time meeting you. I have heard from Meitei that I often cause you trouble, and I had been meaning to visit and listen to your esteemed conversation. Fortunately, I happened to pass by today, so I came to express my gratitude. Please remember me, and I look forward to our future interactions,” he said, delivering an old-fashioned introduction without hesitation. The master, being a reserved man with few social connections, had rarely encountered such an antiquated gentleman, so he was somewhat taken aback from the start. Now, being bombarded with words, he completely forgot about the Korean ginseng and the candy bag, and could only respond awkwardly. “I too… I too… had intended to come and ask you something… if you would be so kind…” he finished, lifting his head slightly from the tatami mat to see that the old man was still bowing deeply, and he quickly lowered his head again in embarrassment. The old man, measuring his breath, raised his head and said, “I originally had a residence here and lived for a long time at your feet, but after the collapse, I went over there and have not returned since. Now that I come back, I hardly know the direction anymore—if I don’t have Meitei to accompany me, I can’t even run errands. Though times have changed, it has been three hundred years since your family came to power…” He began to speak, but Meitei, sensing the conversation was becoming tedious, interjected, “Uncle, while the shogunate may be admirable, the Meiji era is quite splendid as well. In the past, there was no such thing as the Red Cross.”

“That’s not true. There was absolutely nothing called the Red Cross. Especially, to see the face of the imperial family is something that could only be done in the Meiji era. Thanks to my long life, I can attend today’s general meeting and hear the voice of the prince; I could die content now.”

“Well, just seeing Tokyo after such a long time is a gain in itself. Mr. Kushami, my uncle came all the way from Shizuoka for the Red Cross general meeting, and today he went out to Ueno with me, but now he’s on his way back,” he pointed out.

Indeed, the old man was wearing a frock coat. Although he wore the frock coat, it did not fit him at all. The sleeves were too long, the collar was wide open, there was a gap in the back, and the underarms were pulled up. No matter how poorly it was made, it shouldn’t be so distorted. Moreover, the white shirt and white collar were separated, and when he looked up, he could see the Adam's apple peeking through. First, it was unclear whether the black collar ornament belonged to the collar or the shirt. The frock coat was still tolerable, but the old man’s topknot of white hair was quite a sight. Curious about the reputed iron fan, he glanced down to see it neatly tucked beside his knee. At this moment, the master finally returned to his true feelings and was somewhat surprised at how the results of his mental cultivation were fully applied to the old man’s attire. He thought it couldn’t possibly be as remarkable as Meitei’s story, but upon meeting him, he found it exceeded his expectations. If his own blemishes could be historical research material, then this old man’s topknot and iron fan certainly had even greater value. The master wanted to ask about the origin of this iron fan, but he couldn’t just blurt out a question, and he thought it would be rude to let the conversation drop, so he asked in a very ordinary manner, “There seem to be quite a few people out today.”

“No, there are quite a lot of people, and they all stare at me—people have become quite curious lately. It wasn’t like this in the past.” 

“Yes, indeed, it wasn’t like this in the past,” he replied, sounding like an old man. This was not because the master was trying to show off his knowledge; it was merely the words flowing out from his hazy mind. “And everyone is focusing on this iron fan.” 

“That iron fan must be quite heavy, I suppose.” 

“Mr. Kushami, why don’t you try holding it? It’s rather heavy. Uncle, let him try it.” 

The old man picked it up with some effort and said, “I apologize for the trouble,” as he handed it to the master. It was like a pilgrim receiving the sword of Renshōbō in Kurotani, Kyoto. Mr. Kushami held it for a moment and said, “Indeed,” before returning it to the old man. “Everyone calls this an iron fan, but this is actually called a kabuto-wari (helmet-splitter) and is entirely different from an iron fan…” 

“Really, what is it made for?” 

“It is used to split helmets—striking at the place where the enemy’s eyes are blinded. It seems to have been used since the time of Kusunoki Masashige…” 

“Uncle, is that Masashige’s kabuto-wari?” 

“No, I don’t know whose it is. But it is certainly from an ancient era. It might be from the Kenmu era.” 

“It might be from the Kenmu era, but Kangetsu was feeling weak. Mr.

Kushami, since it’s a good opportunity on your way back today, let’s pass through the university and stop by the science department to see the physics laboratory. When I was there, this kabuto-wari, being iron, caused the magnetic instruments to go haywire and made quite a fuss.” 

“No, that can’t be. This is iron from the Kenmu era, and it’s good iron, so there’s no way that could happen.” 

“No matter how good the iron is, it can’t be that simple. In fact, Kangetsu said so, so there’s no helping it.” 

“Kangetsu, is he the man polishing the glass spheres? It’s a pity for the young man. He should have something more to do.” 

“How unfortunate; he is doing research. If he polishes that sphere, he can become a fine scholar.” 

“If polishing a sphere can make one a fine scholar, then anyone can do it. I could do it. Even the owner of the glass shop could do it. Those who do such things are referred to as ‘gyokunin’ in China, and they are considered to be of very low status,” he said, turning to the master, implicitly seeking agreement. “Indeed,” the master replied, nodding. “Overall, the studies of today are all materialistic and seem somewhat fine, but when it comes down to it, they are of no use at all. In the past, it was different; samurai engaged in life-and-death business, so they practiced mental cultivation to avoid panicking in critical moments. You must know that polishing jewels or twisting wire is not something easy.” 

“Indeed,” the master again nodded. “Uncle, when you speak of mental cultivation, you mean sitting idle with your hands in your pockets, don’t you?” 

“That’s why it’s troublesome. It is certainly not something so simple. Confucius said, ‘Seek the lost heart,’ and Shao Kangjie taught about the necessity of releasing the heart. Moreover, in Buddhism, there is a monk named Chūhō who teaches about the concept of ‘non-retreating.’ It is not something easily understood.” 

“I can’t possibly understand it at all. What should one do?” 

“Have you ever read the ‘Record of the Mysterious Wisdom of the Unmoving Mind’ by Zen Master Sawamura?” 

“No, I have never even heard of it.”

"Where shall I place my heart? If I place my heart on the movements of the enemy, I am drawn into the movements of the enemy. If I place my heart on the enemy's sword, I am drawn into the enemy's sword. If I place my heart on the thought of cutting the enemy, I am drawn into the thought of cutting the enemy. If I place my heart on my own sword, I am drawn into my own sword. If I place my heart on the thought of not being cut, I am drawn into the thought of not being cut. If I place my heart on the schemes of others, I am drawn into the schemes of others. In any case, there is no place to put my heart."

"You've memorized that quite well. Uncle has a good memory too. It's quite long, isn't it? Did you understand, Kushami?"

"Indeed," I replied, once again merely acknowledging it. "Ah, you see, that's how it is. Where shall I place my heart? If I place my heart on the movements of the enemy, I am drawn into the movements of the enemy. If I place my heart on the enemy's sword..."

"Uncle, Kushami understands such things very well. Lately, he has been practicing mental discipline every day in his study. He is so absorbed that he doesn't even attend to guests, so he's quite alright."

"Ah, that's quite remarkable—perhaps you should join him for a bit."

"Hehe, I have no such leisure. Uncle thinks that since he is comfortable, others must be playing as well."

"Well, he is indeed playing."

"However, even in idleness, one can be busy."

"Yes, because of carelessness, one must practice, they say. There's a saying, 'In the midst of busyness, there is idleness,' but I've never heard of 'In the midst of idleness, there is busyness.' Right, Kushami?"

"Yes, it seems I've never heard of that."

"Hahaha, if that's the case, there's no winning. By the way, Uncle, how about it? Let's have some eel in Tokyo after a long time. I'll treat you to it at Takebaya. It's just a quick train ride away."

"Eel sounds good, but I have an appointment to go to Suihara today, so I must excuse myself."

"Oh, Suihara? That old man is doing well, isn't he?"

"It's not Sujihara, it's Suihara. You often make mistakes, which is troublesome. Confusing someone else's name is rude. You must be more careful."

"But it says Sujihara here."

"It is written Sujihara but read as Suihara."

"How strange."

"There's nothing strange about it. It's called 'name-reading' and has existed since ancient times. An earthworm is called 'mimizu' in Japanese. That's a name-reading based on not seeing. The same goes for calling a toad 'kairu.'"

"Wow, that's surprising."

"When you kill a toad, it turns over on its back. That's what is referred to as 'kairu' in name-reading. A透垣 is read as 'suigaki,' and a stalk is read as 'kukudate.' It's all the same.

To call Sujihara 'sugihara' is the language of country folk. Be careful, or people will laugh at you."

"Then, are you going to Suihara now? That's troublesome."

"Well, if you don't want to go, you don't have to. I'll go alone."

"Can you go by yourself?"

"It would be difficult on foot. I'll hire a rickshaw and ride from here."

The master, in a formal manner, immediately sends Osan to the rickshaw man. The old man gives a long greeting and puts on his top hat before leaving. Meitei remains behind. "Is that your uncle?"

"Yes, that's my uncle."

"I see," he said, sitting back down on the cushion, putting his hands in his sleeves, and pondering. "Hahaha, what a remarkable fellow. I'm fortunate to have an uncle like that. No matter where you take him, he's just like that. You must have been surprised," Meitei said, pleased with himself for having startled the master. "Well, it wasn't that surprising."

"If you weren't surprised by that, you must have a lot of courage."

"However, that uncle seems to have quite a bit of merit. His insistence on mental discipline is something to greatly admire."

"Is it really something to admire? You might find yourself becoming like that uncle when you reach sixty. So be careful. A person who is out of touch with the times is not very perceptive."

"You are overly concerned with being out of touch, but depending on the time and situation, being out of touch can be quite admirable. First of all, the current education system just keeps advancing, and no matter how far it goes, there is no end to it. You can never attain satisfaction. In contrast, Eastern learning is passive and has a lot of flavor. It focuses on the cultivation of the heart itself," he expounded, echoing what he had recently heard from a philosopher. "This is getting serious. You sound like Yagi Dokusen."

Hearing the name Yagi Dokusen, the master was taken aback. In truth, the philosopher who had recently visited the master and had left calmly after persuading him was none other than Yagi Dokusen, and the arguments the master was now presenting were entirely derived from Dokusen's teachings. Meitei, unaware, had inadvertently brought up the name of this teacher, which served to puncture the master's temporary facade. "Have you ever heard Dokusen's teachings?" the master asked, feeling a bit uneasy. "Whether I have or not, his teachings haven't changed at all since I was in school ten years ago."

"Truth doesn't change, so perhaps it's reassuring that it remains the same."

"Well, that's because of favoritism that Dokusen is able to carry on like that. First of all, the name Yagi is quite fitting. His beard is just like that of a goat. And he has looked that way since his days in the dormitory. The name Dokusen is also quite a show.

He once stayed at my place and discussed the usual passive cultivation. He kept repeating the same thing without stopping, so when I suggested that we should go to sleep, he insisted, 'No, I'm not sleepy,' and continued with his passive arguments, which was quite bothersome. I had no choice but to say, 'You may not be sleepy, but I am very sleepy, so please do go to sleep,' and I managed to get him to sleep, which was fine, but— that night a rat came out and bit the tip of Dokusen's nose. There was a great commotion in the middle of the night. He spoke as if he had gained some insight, but it seemed he still valued his life, and he was very worried. If the rat's poison spread throughout his body, it would be terrible, and he kept blaming me. I had no choice but to go to the kitchen and stick some rice grains onto a piece of paper to deceive him."

"How so?"

"This is an imported plaster, recently invented by a famous German doctor. It is used when bitten by poisonous snakes, and it works immediately, so as long as you put this on, you'll be fine," I told him. "You had quite the knack for deception even back then."

"...So, Dokusen, being such a good person, believed me completely and fell fast asleep. The next morning, when I woke up, I found threads hanging down from under the plaster, caught in his usual goat-like beard, which was quite comical."

"However, it seems he has become quite impressive since then."

"Have you seen him recently?"

"He came about a week ago and talked for a long time."

"That explains why he was so eager to present Dokusen's passive theories."

"Actually, I was very impressed at that time, so I am also quite determined to engage in cultivation."

"Determination is good, but if you take everything others say to heart, you'll end up looking foolish. You take everything people say too seriously. Dokusen may talk a good game, but when it comes down to it, he's just like everyone else. You remember the great earthquake nine years ago, right? He was the only one who jumped from the second floor of the dormitory and got injured."

"That one seems to have quite a theory, doesn't he?"  
"Indeed, according to him, it is something greatly appreciated. The essence of Zen is steeped in sharpness, and when it comes to the so-called 'flash of enlightenment,' it can respond to things with a speed that is almost frightening. While others are panicking, calling it an earthquake, he alone jumped down from the second-floor window, claiming it was a delightful manifestation of his training, all the while limping with joy. He is a man who holds onto his grudges tightly. Honestly, there is nothing more dubious than those who make a fuss about Zen or Buddhism."  
"Is that so?" Mr. Kushami's voice wavers slightly. "The other day, when he came, he mentioned something that sounded like the ramblings of a Zen monk in his sleep."  
"Yes, he taught me a verse that says something about cutting through the spring breeze with a flash of lightning."  
"That flash of lightning, you see, has been in the box for ten years, so it’s quite strange. Everyone in the boarding house knows about Master Mukaku's flash of lightning. Moreover, when he occasionally coughs, he mistakenly says 'cutting through the spring breeze with the flash of lightning' instead of the other way around, which is amusing. You should try it next time. While he is calmly explaining something over there, you should start contradicting him here. He will immediately turn it upside down and say something strange."  
"I can't stand meeting someone as mischievous as you."  
"Who is the mischievous one, I wonder? I absolutely detest Zen monks and those who claim to be enlightened. There is a temple nearby called Nanzoin, where there is an old man in his eighties. The other day, during the white rain, lightning struck the temple, splitting the pine tree in the old man's garden. However, the monk remained calm and unperturbed, so when I listened closely, it turned out he was deaf. That explains his calmness. Generally, that's how it is. Dokusen could be fine on his own, but he often lures others out, which is unfortunate. In fact, thanks to Dokusen, a couple of people have gone mad."  
"Who?"  
"Who, you ask? One is Rino Tōzen. Thanks to Dokusen, he became deeply entrenched in Zen studies and went off to Kamakura, ultimately losing his mind out there. You know there is a train crossing in front of Engaku-ji? He jumped into that crossing to sit in zazen on the tracks, intending to stop the train coming from the other side. Quite the audacious act! Fortunately, the train stopped for him, so he only narrowly escaped with his life.

But then he proclaimed that he had a body that could not be burned in fire or drowned in water, and he crawled into the temple's lotus pond, splashing around."  
"Did he die?"  
"At that time, luckily, a monk from the dojo happened to pass by and saved him. However, after returning to Tokyo, he ultimately died of peritonitis. While it was peritonitis that killed him, the cause of that peritonitis was the barley rice and pickled vegetables he ate at the monk's quarters, so in a way, it can be said that Dokusen indirectly killed him."  
"Being overly passionate has its pros and cons," the master said, making a slightly uneasy expression. "Indeed. There is another one among our classmates who has been affected by Dokusen."  
"That sounds dangerous. Who?"  
"It’s Tachimachiro Ume-kun. That man was completely incited by Dokusen, spouting nonsense about eels ascending to heaven, and eventually, he became the real deal."  
"What do you mean by 'the real deal'?"  
"Ultimately, the eels ascended to heaven, and the pig became an immortal."  
"What on earth does that mean?"  
"If Yagi is Dokusen, then Tachimachiro is the pig immortal. There has never been a man with such a voracious appetite, but with that appetite combined with the bad temperament of a Zen monk, he was doomed. At first, we didn’t notice, but looking back now, he strung together the strangest things. He would come to my house and ask if a cutlet would fly into that pine tree, saying that in my country, kamaboko swims on a board. He kept spouting these strange warnings. As long as he was just talking, it was fine, but when he suggested going to dig for gold in the ditch outside, I had to give up. A few days later, he finally became the pig immortal and was confined to Sugamo. Originally, pigs have no right to go mad, but it was entirely thanks to Dokusen that he ended up there. Dokusen's influence is quite formidable."  
"Oh, is he still in Sugamo?"  
"Of course he is. He is a self-important madman, puffing out grandiose statements. Recently, he has claimed that the name Tachimachiro Ume is too trivial, so he has taken on the name Tendō Kōhei, declaring himself an incarnation of the way of heaven. It’s quite something. You should go see for yourself."  
"Tendō Kōhei?"  
"Tendō Kōhei. For a madman, he has come up with quite a clever name. Sometimes he writes it as Kōhei. He claims that since the world is lost, he must save everyone, and he recklessly sends letters to friends and others. I received four or five letters, and some of them were quite long, resulting in me being taxed twice for insufficient taxes."  
"So the one that came to me also came from Ume?"  
"Did it come to you too? That’s strange. It must have been in a red envelope."  
"Yes, the center is red, and the sides are white.

It’s quite an unusual envelope."  
"I hear that it is specially ordered from China. It illustrates the saying of the pig immortal: 'The way of heaven is white, the way of earth is white, and man exists in between and is red...'"  
"That’s quite a fateful envelope."  
"Being mad, he has put a lot of thought into it. Even after going mad, it seems he still retains his appetite, as every letter invariably mentions food, which is quite strange. He must have said something to you as well."  
"Yes, it mentioned sea cucumbers."  
"Ume liked sea cucumbers, so that makes sense. What else?"  
"Then there was something about fugu and Korean ginseng or something like that."  
"The combination of fugu and Korean ginseng is delicious. I suppose he means to say that if you eat fugu and get sick, you should brew some Korean ginseng and drink it."  
"It doesn’t seem that way."  
"Even if it doesn’t, it doesn’t matter. After all, he’s mad. Is that all?"  
"There’s still more. There’s a line that says, 'Mr. Kushami, please come up for tea.'"  
"Ahahaha! 'Please come up for tea' is a bit too harsh. He must have thought he had you cornered. Quite a feat. Long live Tendō Kōhei!" Mr. Meitei said, laughing heartily. The master, upon realizing that the sender of the letter he had read with such enthusiasm and concern was a gilded madman, felt a mix of frustration and embarrassment, as if all his fervor and effort had been in vain. Finally, he began to wonder if he himself might not be a little unhinged, given how impressed he was by the madman's writing, leaving him with a restless expression that combined anger, shame, and worry. Just then, the front lattice was opened, and the sound of heavy shoes echoed as someone stepped in. "Excuse me, excuse me," came a loud voice. Contrary to the master’s heavy demeanor, Mr. Meitei was a remarkably lighthearted man, so without waiting for Osan’s introduction, he leaped over the partition and bounded into the entrance. While it might seem bothersome to enter someone’s house without asking for an introduction, once he was in, he performed the duties of a student, making it quite convenient. No matter how much Mr. Meitei might be, he was still a guest, and there was no way for the master, Mr. Kushami, to remain seated in the tatami room while his guest was at the entrance. Normally, a man would follow behind and join the fray, but that was Mr. Kushami for you. He calmly settled himself onto the cushion. However, there is a significant difference between being settled and being at ease; while their appearances may be quite similar, their essence is very different.

Meitei burst out into the entrance, fervently speaking about something, and soon turned to the back, calling out in a loud voice, "Hey, Master, I know it's a bit of a bother, but please come out. It won't do without you." The master, with no choice but to comply, shuffled out with his hands tucked into his sleeves. Upon looking, I saw that Meitei was crouching down, holding a business card, and greeting someone. His posture was remarkably lacking in dignity. The card read "Detective Constable Yoshida Torazo of the Metropolitan Police." Standing next to Torazo was a tall, dapper man in his mid-twenties, dressed in a stylish Western outfit. Strangely, this man, like the master, stood there silently with his hands tucked away. I thought I recognized his face and, upon closer inspection, realized it was no mere resemblance. This was the thief who had visited late at night the other day and made off with some mountain yam. Oh, now he had come openly in broad daylight through the entrance. "Hey, this gentleman here is Detective Constable who caught the thief the other day, and he has come specifically to ask you to come forward," Meitei explained. The master finally seemed to understand the reason for the detective's visit, bowing his head and politely nodding towards the thief. The thief, appearing more imposing than Torazo, likely caused the master to mistakenly assume he was the detective. The thief must have been surprised as well, but it seemed he couldn't very well deny being a thief, so he stood there composed, still with his hands tucked away. Of course, with handcuffs on, he had no intention of pulling them out even if he wanted to. Normally, one could discern the situation from such behavior, but the master, unlike contemporary people, had a peculiar habit of excessively revering officials and the police. He regarded the authority of the government as something tremendously fearsome. Although theoretically, he understood that they were merely hired guards paid for by the public, in practice, he was overly subservient. The master’s father had once been a village headman in a backwater, and perhaps this habit of bowing to superiors had been passed down to him as a consequence. Truly, it was a pitiable state of affairs. The constable seemed amused, grinning as he said, "Please come to the Nihonbashi police substation by 9 AM tomorrow. — What were the stolen items again?"

"I was about to say the stolen items were…" but unfortunately, the master had mostly forgotten. The only thing he remembered was the mountain yam from Tatara Sampei. He thought that the mountain yam didn’t really matter, but it was quite embarrassing to start saying the stolen items and then be unable to finish.

If someone else had been robbed, it would have been one thing, but having been robbed himself and not being able to provide a clear answer was proof he was not yet a full-fledged adult. He resolved to say, "The stolen items were… a box of mountain yam."

At this moment, the thief seemed to find it quite funny, lowering his head and tucking his chin into his collar. Meitei laughed heartily, saying, "It seems you were quite attached to that mountain yam." Only the constable remained unexpectedly serious. "It seems the mountain yam is unlikely to be recovered, but most of the other items have returned. — Well, you’ll understand when you come. And once you hand them over, you’ll receive a receipt, so don’t forget to bring your seal. — You must come by 9 AM. This is the Nihonbashi substation. — It’s under the jurisdiction of the Asakusa police station. — Well then, goodbye," he concluded, speaking to himself as he left. The thief followed him out the gate. Since he couldn’t reach out, he couldn’t close the gate, so he left it wide open. The master, feeling both intimidated and disgruntled, puffed out his cheeks and slammed the door shut. "Haha, you really respect the detective, don’t you? If only you could maintain such a humble attitude all the time, you’d be a fine man, but you’re only polite to the constable, which is troublesome."

"Well, he did come all the way to inform us."

"Even if he came to inform us, it’s still a business matter. It’s enough to treat him normally."

"But it’s not just any business."

"Of course, it’s not just any business. It’s the detestable profession of a detective. It’s inferior to ordinary business."

"If you keep saying things like that, you’ll find yourself in serious trouble."

"Haha, then let’s stop speaking ill of detectives. However, while it’s one thing to respect a detective, it’s quite another to respect a thief; that’s something to be astonished by."

"Who wants to respect a thief?"

"You do."

"Me? How could I possibly get close to a thief?"

"How could you not? You just bowed to one."

"When?"

"Just now, you bowed deeply."

"Don’t be ridiculous, that was the detective."

"Do detectives stand around like that?"

"Isn’t it because he’s a detective that he stands like that?"

"You’re stubborn."

"No, you’re the stubborn one."

"Well, first of all, does a detective come to someone’s house standing there with his hands tucked away?"

"Not all detectives must stand with their hands tucked away."

"Well, it’s intimidating when they come so forcefully. While you were bowing, he stood there the whole time."

"Perhaps it’s normal for a detective to act that way."

"You really are quite the self-assured one. No matter how much I say, you won’t listen."

"I won’t listen.

You’re just spouting off about thieves without having seen one enter anywhere. You’re just stubbornly holding onto your thoughts."

Seeing that Meitei had given up on the argument, he fell silent, which was unusual for him. The master felt quite pleased, thinking he had finally bested Meitei after a long time. From Meitei’s perspective, the master’s value had diminished simply by being stubborn, but from the master’s viewpoint, he had become superior to Meitei just by being obstinate. Such absurdities often occur in the world. While one may feel victorious by holding onto their stubbornness, their worth as a person may plummet significantly. Strangely, the stubborn individual may go to their grave believing they have maintained their dignity, never realizing that from that point onward, others will look down on them and no longer regard them. How fortunate they are. Such happiness is said to be akin to the happiness of a pig. "Anyway, are you planning to go tomorrow?"

"Of course, since they said to come by 9 AM, I’ll leave at 8."

"What about school?"

"I’ll skip it." The way he said this, as if throwing it away, was quite something. "That’s quite a bold statement. Is it really okay to skip?"

"Of course, my school pays by the month, so there’s no worry about deductions. I’m fine," he confessed straightforwardly. While being cunning is one thing, being simple-minded is another. "You, it’s fine to go, but do you know the way?"

"How would I know? If I get in a rickshaw, it won’t be a problem," he replied, sulking. "I’m amazed that you would boast of being a Tokyoite without having been passed down from your uncle in Shizuoka."

"You can be amazed all you want."

"Haha, the Nihonbashi substation is not just any place, you know. It’s Yoshiwara."

"What?"

"It’s Yoshiwara."

"That Yoshiwara with the pleasure quarters?"

"Yes, indeed. There’s only one Yoshiwara in Tokyo. So, what do you say? Are you interested in going to see it?" Meitei began to tease again. Upon hearing "Yoshiwara," the master hesitated slightly, but then quickly recalled, "Whether it’s Yoshiwara or a pleasure quarter, once I say I’ll go, I’ll definitely go," he declared, showing determination to go to a place he shouldn’t. Fools often take pride in such matters. Meitei simply said, "Well, it should be interesting; go and see for yourself." With that, the tumultuous detective incident was momentarily settled. Afterward, Meitei continued to chat idly, and as dusk approached, he said he would return home before his uncle got angry.

After Meitei returned home, he finished his dinner in a rather casual manner and retreated to his study once again, where he began to ponder with his arms crossed as follows:

"Mr. Dokusen, whom I greatly admire and aspire to emulate, seems, according to Meitei's account, to be a person not worthy of imitation in particular. Moreover, the doctrines he espouses appear somewhat nonsensical and, as Meitei suggests, may belong to a somewhat deranged category. Not to mention, he has two distinctly mad disciples under his wing. This is quite dangerous. If I were to approach him too closely, I might be dragged into the same category. The fact that I am astonished by his writings leads me to believe that he is undoubtedly a man of great insight, yet the truth is that Tendō Kōhei, who is reputedly a wise elder residing in Nakano, is nothing but a pure madman, currently living in a hospital in Sugamo. Even if Meitei's descriptions are mere ramblings, it is likely true that he enjoys a certain fame within the lunatic asylum and has appointed himself as its overseer. Perhaps I too might be a little mad in my own way. They say like attracts like, so if I am impressed by the theories of the mad—at least if I express sympathy for their words—I must also be someone closely related to madness. Even if I am not cast into the same mold, if I were to live next door to a madman, it would not be impossible for me to inadvertently find myself sharing a room with him, laughing and chatting away. This is quite alarming. Upon reflection, my brain has been functioning in a remarkably strange and peculiar manner lately, adding oddities to its already curious workings. The chemical changes in my brain are one thing, but the way my will manifests into action and transforms into words is filled with many points of wonder and imbalance. There is no dragon spring on my tongue, nor a refreshing breeze under my arms, yet there is a mad stench at the roots of my teeth and a lunatic flavor in my muscles. This is truly serious. Perhaps I have already become a fine patient. Fortunately, I have not yet harmed anyone or become a nuisance to society, so I continue to exist as a citizen of Tokyo without being expelled from the neighborhood. This is not a matter of passive versus active. First, I must examine my pulse. However, it seems there is no change there. Is my head hot? This does not seem to be a sign of madness either. Yet, I cannot help but worry."

"If I keep comparing myself only to the mad and tallying the similarities, I will never be able to escape the realm of madness. This method is flawed. It is because I am using the mad as a standard and interpreting myself in relation to them that I arrive at such conclusions.

If I were to consider a healthy person as the benchmark and place myself beside them, perhaps I would arrive at the opposite result. I must start with something nearby. First, what about that uncle in the frock coat who came today? Where should I place my thoughts... he seems a bit suspicious too. Second, what about Kangetsu? He spends all day polishing a ball while bringing his own bento. He is quite the odd one. Third, then... Meitei? He seems to take his frivolous antics as his vocation. He is undoubtedly a positive madman. Fourth, what about Mrs. Kaneda? Her venomous nature is completely outside the bounds of common sense. She is purely a mad type. Fifth is Mr. Kaneda's turn. I have not seen Mr. Kaneda, but judging by how he reverently presents his wife and harmonizes with the koto, it would not be unreasonable to consider him an extraordinary person. The extraordinary is synonymous with madness, so I can safely place him in the same category. And then—there are still others. The gentlemen of Rakugunkan, considering their age, are still budding, but in terms of mania, they are splendidly capable of wasting a whole generation. When I count them up like this, it seems that most of them belong to the same kind. Surprisingly, I am beginning to feel more secure. Perhaps society is merely a gathering of madmen. Madmen congregate, competing fiercely, grappling, quarreling, and cursing each other, and this entire collective, like cells, collapses and rises again, and this is what we call society. Within it, those who understand a bit of reason and possess discernment become a nuisance, which is why they create asylums to confine them and prevent their escape. Thus, those confined in asylums are the normal ones, while those rampaging outside are the true madmen. While a madman remains isolated, he will continue to be considered mad, but when he forms a group and gains strength, he may become a sound individual. There are not a few cases where great madmen, abusing their wealth and power, employ many lesser madmen to commit acts of violence, and they are praised as fine men by others. I have completely lost track of everything."

The above is a faithful depiction of the mental processes of the master as he pondered deeply under the flickering light of a solitary lamp that night. The opacity of his thoughts is strikingly evident here. Despite sporting a Kaiser-like mustache, he is of such a mediocre caliber that he cannot even distinguish between the mad and the sane. Moreover, he has presented this problem to himself and appealed to his own powers of thought, yet ultimately failed to reach any conclusion. In all matters, he is a man devoid of the capacity for thorough contemplation.

The vagueness of his conclusions, like the smoke of the morning sun bursting forth from his nostrils, is a fact that should be remembered as the sole characteristic of his arguments. I am a cat. Some may doubt how a cat could describe the master's inner thoughts with such precision, but this is nothing for a cat. I possess the art of mind-reading. When I learned it is an unnecessary question. In any case, I know it. While I sleep on a human's lap, I gently rub my soft fur against their belly. In doing so, a current of electricity arises, and the happenings within their belly vividly reflect in my mind's eye. Just the other day, the master was gently stroking my head when he suddenly had the ridiculous notion that if he were to skin this cat and make a warm coat out of it, it would surely be delightful. I sensed that thought immediately and was involuntarily startled. It is a frightening thing. The thoughts that arose in the master's mind that night, thanks to such a circumstance, I am fortunate to be able to report to you all. However, the master thought until he reached the point of "I have completely lost track of everything," and then fell sound asleep. By tomorrow, he will surely have forgotten everything he thought about. If he ever considers madness again, he will have to start over from scratch. I cannot guarantee that he will take such a path again and end up "losing track of everything" in this manner. However, no matter how many times he reconsiders or which path he takes, it is certain that he will ultimately "lose track of everything."

「You, it’s already seven o’clock,” said the mistress’s voice from beyond the sliding door. The master, whether awake or asleep, turned away without responding. Not responding is this man’s habit. When he must speak, he will grunt. This grunt does not come easily, either. While it is somewhat charming when a human becomes so lazy that they can’t even reply, such people have never been particularly favored by women. Even the mistress, who currently accompanies him, seems not to hold him in high regard, so it is safe to assume that the others are even less favorable. If he has been abandoned by his family and is not likely to be cherished by a beautiful stranger, it stands to reason that a master who cannot win the affection of his own wife would not be favored by women in general. There is no need to particularly expose the unpopularity of the master among the opposite sex at this time, but when he himself mistakenly believes that it is merely due to the passage of time that the mistress does not like him, I feel compelled, out of kindness, to add a little note that this is a source of confusion and might serve as a bit of self-awareness.

Even when the appointed time arrives and I remind him of it, if the other party disregards that reminder, and he does not even utter a grunt, it is clear that the mistress has determined that the fault lies with the husband, not the wife. With a posture that says she does not care if it gets late, she took her broom and dustpan and went off toward the study. Soon, the sound of her bustling about in the study could be heard, as she began her usual cleaning. The purpose of cleaning, whether for exercise or play, is not something I, who bear no responsibility for such duties, need to concern myself with. However, I must say that the way this mistress cleans is utterly meaningless. Why is it meaningless? Because she cleans simply for the sake of cleaning. She dusts the sliding doors and sweeps the tatami mats, interpreting that as the completion of her task. She bears not even the slightest responsibility for the source or results of the cleaning. As a result, while the clean places remain clean every day, the areas with dirt and dust are perpetually cluttered and dusty. There is a saying about the sheep that are not sheared, so perhaps this is better than doing nothing at all. However, even if she does clean, it does not particularly benefit the master. The fact that she diligently does this every single day is what makes her admirable. The mistress and cleaning have been linked in a mechanical association for many years, yet when it comes to the act of cleaning itself, it is as if she has not yet been born, as if the broom and dustpan had not yet been invented, and it is not at all improved. I believe the relationship between these two is akin to the terms in a formal logic proposition, combined regardless of their content. Unlike the master, I am naturally an early riser, so by this time I had already become hungry. It is not as if, even before the household members sit down for breakfast, I, as a cat, can expect to be fed. Yet, such is the pitiful nature of a cat that, when I think perhaps the fragrant steam of soup might be rising enticingly from the abalone shell, I can’t help but become restless. When one knows that something is fleeting and yet relies on it, it is wiser to keep that hope in one’s mind and remain still and calm. However, this is not how it goes for me, and I feel compelled to test whether my heart’s desire aligns with reality. Even though testing it will surely lead to disappointment, I cannot accept that reality until I have personally faced the final disappointment. Unable to bear it any longer, I crawled out to the kitchen.

First, I peeked into the abalone shell in the shadow of the hearth, and as expected, it lay empty, having been licked clean the previous evening, with a strange light shimmering in the autumn sunlight filtering through the window. Osan had already transferred the freshly cooked rice to the rice container and was now stirring the pot over the hibachi. Around the pot, the rice soup that had boiled over and flowed out was stuck in several places, looking as if it had been pasted with Yoshino paper. Since both the rice and soup were ready, it seemed reasonable to think I should be fed. At such a time, it is a trivial matter to hesitate; even if things do not go as I wish, I would not suffer any loss, so I resolved to boldly demand breakfast. No matter that I am merely a guest, hunger does not change. With this determination, I mewed in a way that seemed to plead, or perhaps to complain. Osan did not even glance my way. I know well that she is naturally indifferent to feelings, but it is my skill to evoke sympathy by crying out effectively. This time, I tried mewing more insistently. I believed my cries carried a tragic sound, sufficient to evoke the heartstrings of a wandering child. Osan remained oblivious. Perhaps this woman is deaf. While a deaf person could not serve as a maid, it might be that she is only deaf to the voice of a cat. There are color-blind people who, despite believing they have perfect vision, are told by doctors that they are impaired; perhaps Osan is voice-blind. A voice-blind person is surely impaired in some way. Despite her impairment, she is oddly stubborn. Even at night, no matter how much I plead to be let in, she never opens the door. When she does let me out, she never lets me back in. Even in summer, the night dew is poisonous. How much more so with frost! Standing under the eaves and waiting for dawn is a hardship that is beyond imagination. The last time I was shut out, I was nearly attacked by a stray dog, and I barely managed to climb onto the roof of the storage shed, trembling all night. All these troubles stem from Osan’s lack of compassion. There is no point in crying to someone like her, as there is no chance of eliciting a response. Yet, in times of hunger, one might as well pray to the gods, for even a thief in poverty can find love. So, I was willing to try anything. On the third meow, I made a particularly complex cry to attract her attention. I was convinced that it sounded as beautiful as a Beethoven symphony, but it seemed to have no effect on Osan. Suddenly, she knelt down, pushed aside a board, and pulled out a piece of charcoal about four inches long.

Then, she struck that long piece against the corner of the hibachi, breaking it into three pieces, and the surrounding area became covered in charcoal dust. It seemed some of it had even fallen into the soup. Osan was not the type to care about such things. Immediately, she pushed the three broken pieces of charcoal into the pot from the back of the hibachi. She was certainly not inclined to listen to my symphony. With no other choice, I turned back toward the tea room, feeling dejected, and as I passed by the bathroom, I saw three girls washing their faces, and it was quite a lively scene.

Even if one were to say they were washing their face, the two above are kindergarten students, and the third is so small that they cannot even follow their sister's behind. Therefore, it is impossible for them to properly wash their faces or skillfully apply makeup. The smallest one is dragging a wet rag out of a bucket and persistently rubbing it all over their face. Washing one's face with a rag must feel rather unpleasant, but since this child finds it amusing whenever an earthquake occurs, it is no surprise that they would do such a thing. Perhaps they are even more enlightened than Dokusen-kun. As expected of the eldest daughter, she takes it upon herself to look after her siblings, throwing the rinsing cup aside with a clatter and saying, "Little boy, that’s a rag," as she goes to retrieve it. The little boy, being quite self-assured, is not easily swayed by his sister’s words. "No, I won’t," he says, pulling the rag back. The term "babu" he uses, no one knows its meaning or origin. It is simply a word he occasionally uses when he is throwing a tantrum. At this moment, the rag is being tugged back and forth between his sister and him, causing drops of water to fall from the middle, mercilessly splattering onto the boy's feet. If it were just his feet, he could endure it, but his knees are getting thoroughly soaked. The boy is dressed in a garment called Genroku. When I inquired about what Genroku meant, I learned that any medium-patterned fabric is considered Genroku. It is unclear who taught him this. "Little boy, stop it, your Genroku is getting wet," his sister says in a playful manner. Yet, this same sister had only recently confused Genroku with a board game. Since I was reminded of Genroku, I cannot help but continue to speak. The child's mispronunciations are numerous, and they occasionally make ridiculous mistakes that seem to mock others. They say things like "Mushrooms flew in during a fire," or "I went to a girls' school for tea and miso," or mix up "Ebisu" and "kitchen." At one point, the child exclaimed, "I’m not a straw shop kid," but upon careful inquiry, it turned out they were confusing "uraten" (back shop) with "waraten" (straw shop). The master laughs every time he hears such mistakes, but when he goes to school to teach English, he must present even more ridiculous errors with a serious demeanor to his students. The little boy—who does not refer to himself as such, but always as "baba"—saw that his Genroku was wet and cried out, "Where is my Genroku wet?" It would be a disaster if the Genroku were cold, so Osan rushed out from the kitchen, took the rag, and wiped his clothes. During this commotion, the second daughter, Sunko, remained relatively quiet.

Sunko was facing away, having opened a jar of face powder that had rolled off the shelf, and was diligently applying makeup. First, she poked her finger into the jar and dabbed it on the tip of her nose, leaving a white line that made her nose slightly more defined. Next, she turned her finger and rubbed it on her cheek, creating another white patch. Just as she was finishing her adornments, a maid entered and wiped the little boy's clothes, inadvertently wiping Sunko's face as well. Sunko appeared somewhat dissatisfied. I observed this scene from the side and, sneaking a glance from the tea room to the master’s bedroom, wondered if he was already awake, but I could not see his head anywhere. Instead, a high-footed blanket was protruding from beneath the bedding. He must have burrowed in like that to avoid being disturbed when he woke up. He is a man like a turtle. Just then, my master’s wife, who had finished cleaning the study, came in with a broom and dustpan. As before, she stood at the entrance of the sliding door and called out, "Are you still not awake?" After a moment, she stared at the blanket that concealed his neck. Again, there was no response. She took a couple of steps forward from the entrance, poked the broom, and asked again, "Are you still not up, dear?" At this point, the master was already awake. Since he was awake, he had buried his head in the bedding in preparation for his wife’s onslaught. He thought that if he kept his head hidden, perhaps she would overlook him, and he lay there relying on this trivial hope, but it seemed she would not let him off so easily. However, the first call had at least a one-room distance from the threshold, so he felt somewhat relieved. Just as he was thinking this, the broom poked him from about three feet away, which startled him a bit. Moreover, the second "Are you still not up, dear?" reached him with more force and volume than before, penetrating the bedding, and he braced himself for the worst, responding in a small voice. "You’re supposed to be up by nine. If you don’t hurry, you won’t make it."

"It’s strange to say that when I’m just about to get up," he replied from the sleeve of his nightwear. His wife always took this as a sign that he would get up, but when he fell back asleep, she could not afford to be careless and urged him, "Come on, get up." It was displeasing to be told to get up when one was already in the process of doing so. For a selfish man like the master, it was even more displeasing. At this point, he threw off the nightwear that had been covering his head all at once. Upon looking, both of his large eyes were wide open. "What’s all this noise?

If I say I’m getting up, then I am."

"Even if you say you’re getting up, you’re not actually getting up, are you?"

"Who said such a lie?"

"Always, that’s who."

"Don’t be foolish."

"You can’t tell which of us is the fool," his wife retorted, standing bravely with the broom at his bedside. At that moment, the child from the rickshaw man, Hatchan, suddenly began to cry loudly. Hatchan is commanded by the rickshaw man’s wife to cry whenever the master gets angry. The wife thinks that every time the master gets angry, Hatchan’s crying might earn her some pocket money, but for Hatchan, it is a great inconvenience. Having such a mother means he must cry from morning till night. If only the master could be a little more considerate of the situation, Hatchan’s life might be extended a bit, but no matter how much Kaneda-kun has asked him, it would be reasonable to conclude that he is more severe than the impartial heavens. If Hatchan only had to cry whenever the master got angry, there would still be some leeway, but every time Kaneda-kun hires local ruffians to set fire to the Imado kiln, Hatchan must cry. Even before it is clear whether the master is angry or not, Hatchan anticipates that he will be and begins to cry in advance. At this point, it becomes unclear whether the master is Hatchan or Hatchan is the master. It is not difficult to provoke the master; a little jab at Hatchan will easily result in a slap to the master’s face. In the past, when criminals were punished in the West, if the person fled beyond the borders and could not be captured, they would create an effigy and burn it in place of the person. It seems that among them, there were military strategists well-versed in Western customs, who devised clever plans. The rickshaw man’s child and the rickshaw man’s wife must surely be a source of great difficulty for the inept master. There are various other difficulties as well. Perhaps the entire neighborhood is a source of trouble, but for now, it is unrelated, so I will gradually introduce them as necessary.

Hatchan's cries reached the master, and it seemed he was in quite a temper from early morning, as he suddenly sat up in bed. At this point, all notions of spiritual cultivation and even Dokusen were out the window. As he sat up, he scratched his head vigorously with both hands, to the point of flaking the skin. The dandruff that had accumulated over the month flew without restraint onto his neck and the collar of his nightgown. It was quite a sight. When he checked his beard, it was astonishing to see it standing upright. Perhaps it thought that it couldn't remain calm while its owner was angry, as each hair seemed to flare up in a fit of rage, charging off in any direction with great force. This too was quite a spectacle. Yesterday, in front of the mirror, he had obediently mimicked the posture of Emperor Doku, standing in formation, but after a night’s sleep, all training was forgotten, and he returned to his original state, resuming his usual disheveled appearance. It was as if the master's one-night endeavor in spiritual cultivation had vanished overnight, revealing his innate wild boar-like nature in full display. When I think about how such a rough man with such a wild beard has managed to remain a teacher without being dismissed, I begin to understand the vastness of Japan. It is precisely because of this vastness that Kaneda and his dog can pass as humans. As long as they can pass as humans, it seems the master has no reason to fear dismissal. If it came to that, he could always send a note to Sugamo and consult with Mr. Tendō Kōhei, and it would be clear in no time. At this moment, the master was intently watching the chaotic eyes of ancient times that I had introduced yesterday, firmly gazing at the cupboard across the room. It was a cupboard divided horizontally with two sliding doors on both the upper and lower sections. The lower cupboard was positioned just above the edge of the futon, so when the master opened his eyes, his gaze naturally fell upon it. Upon looking, he saw that the patterned paper was torn in several places, revealing strange intestines. There were various types of intestines. Some were printed, while others were handwritten. Some were upside down, and others were reversed. As the master looked at these intestines, he suddenly felt a desire to read what was written on them. It seemed strange that the master, who had been so furious that he wanted to rub the nose of the rickshaw man's wife against a pine tree, would suddenly want to read this scrap of paper, but such is not uncommon for someone with a fiery temperament. It is like a child who, when given a toy while crying, immediately bursts into laughter.

When the master used to stay at a temple where several nuns were separated by a sliding door, it seemed that one of the nuns, who are generally the most spiteful of women, had seen through the master's nature. While banging on her cooking pot, she sang in rhythm, “The crow that cried just now has already laughed,” and it is said that this was when the master began to despise nuns. Regardless of whether he disliked them, it was undoubtedly true. The master cried, laughed, felt joy, and felt sorrow more than anyone else, but none of these feelings lasted long. One could say he was unattached and that his moods shifted aimlessly, but to put it more simply in colloquial terms, he was a shallow, thin-skinned child who was only strong in his tantrums. Given that he was already a spoiled child, it is only natural that he suddenly shifted gears and began to read the intestines of the sliding door with a fighting spirit. The first thing that caught his eye was a reversed document from Itō Hirobumi. Looking up, he saw it was dated September 28, 1878. It seemed that even the Governor-General of Korea was chasing after the tail of the government decree from this era. I wonder what the general was doing at that time, he thought, as he strained to read what seemed illegible, and found the title of Minister of Finance. Indeed, what a remarkable thing; no matter how reversed it was, it was still the Minister of Finance. A little to the left, he saw the Minister of Finance lying down for a nap. Naturally. One cannot maintain a reversed position for too long. At the bottom, he could only see the two characters for “Thou art,” and he wanted to see more, but unfortunately, it was not exposed. The next line only had the two characters for “quickly.” He wanted to read that too, but it was cut off, leaving him with no clues. If the master had been a detective from the police department, he might have torn it off regardless of whose it was. Detectives, lacking higher education, would do anything to gather facts. They are quite troublesome. I wish they would show a bit more restraint. If they don’t, it would be wise to ensure that facts are never brought to light. I have heard that they even frame innocent citizens with fabricated evidence. It would be quite a feat for a citizen who pays to hire someone to turn against their employer. Next, he turned his gaze to the center and saw Ōita Prefecture doing a somersault. Since even Itō Hirobumi could be reversed, it was only natural for Ōita Prefecture to be doing a somersault. The master read up to this point, clenched his fists, and thrust them high towards the ceiling. He was preparing to yawn.

This yawn was quite an extraordinary sound, reminiscent of a whale’s distant call, but when it signaled the end of a chapter, the master slowly changed his clothes and headed to the bath to wash his face. His long-awaited wife suddenly threw back the futon, folded his nightgown, and began her usual cleaning routine. Just as her cleaning was as usual, the master’s method of washing his face was as consistent as it had been for the past ten years. As I mentioned the other day, he continued to make a raucous noise, “Gah-gah, geh-geh.” Eventually, having finished parting his hair, he draped a Western-style towel over his shoulder and made his way to the tea room, where he nonchalantly took a seat beside the long hibachi. Speaking of the long hibachi, it might be made of zelkova or copper, and some of you may envision the hairdresser standing on her knees, banging a long pipe against the edge of a black persimmon. However, my Mr. Kushami’s long hibachi is certainly not of such spirited craftsmanship; it is an object so antiquated that even an amateur could not guess what it was made from. The long hibachi is supposed to shine brightly from being polished, but this one, whether made of zelkova, cherry, or paulownia, is originally unclear, and it has hardly ever been covered with a cloth, making it exceedingly dull and unremarkable. When I ask where such a thing was bought, it seems he has no recollection of having purchased it. When I inquire if it was a gift, he says no one has ever given it to him. So, when I question whether he stole it, he seems uncertain about that too. Long ago, there was a relative who had retired, and when that relative passed away, he was asked to watch over the place for a while. However, when he later established his own household and vacated the retirement home, he casually took the hibachi he had been using as if it were his own without a second thought. It seems a bit questionable. When I think about it, it does seem questionable, but I believe such things often happen in the world. It is said that bankers, while handling other people's money every day, begin to see other people's money as their own. Officials are servants of the people. They are like agents entrusted with certain powers to carry out tasks. However, when they handle the delegated power daily, they begin to think that this power belongs to them, and that the people have no reason to voice any objections to it. As long as there are such people in the world, one cannot conclude that the master has a thief's mentality simply because of the long hibachi incident. If the master has a thief's mentality, then it seems everyone in the world does.

Positioned beside the long hibachi, the master sat at the dining table, with three young girls already gathered and eating breakfast: the boy, who had just washed his face with a rag, Tonko, who was going to school to learn about tea and miso, and Sunko, who had thrust her fingers into a jar of face powder. The master glanced fairly at the faces of these three girls. Tonko's face had a contour resembling the tsuba (guard) of a Nanban iron sword. Sunko, being the younger sister, bore some resemblance to her older sister and could be likened to a lacquered red tray from Ryukyu. However, the boy stood out distinctly, with a long face. While it is not uncommon for faces to be long vertically, this child's was long horizontally. No matter how fashion trends may change, a horizontally long face is unlikely to become popular. The master, despite being his own child, found himself pondering deeply. This child must grow up. Not only must he grow, but the speed of his growth is akin to bamboo shoots in a Zen temple transforming into young bamboo. Each time the master thought about how much he had grown, he felt a chill as if he were being pursued from behind. Even the most indifferent of masters understands that these three young ladies are female. Being female, it is understood that they must somehow be managed. He is aware that simply understanding this does not equip him with the skill to manage them. Thus, he finds himself somewhat at a loss, despite being their father. If he were to be at a loss, it would have been better not to have produced them, but therein lies the essence of being human. To define humanity, one could say that it is merely those who fabricate troubles for themselves by creating things that ought not to exist, and that would suffice. Children are indeed remarkable. Unaware of how their father is struggling to manage them, they eat their meals joyfully. However, the one who is truly unmanageable is the boy. At three years old, the boy is given small chopsticks and a bowl by his mother, who is being considerate, but he absolutely refuses to accept them. He invariably snatches his sister's bowl and grabs her chopsticks, clumsily handling them as if they were his own. Looking at the world, it seems that the most incompetent and talentless little people are the ones who wish to rise to positions of authority that do not suit them, and this nature is entirely budding from the boy's age. The roots of this behavior run deep, and it is best to give up early on the notion that education or guidance can remedy it. The boy, having seized the grand bowl and long chopsticks from next door, is continuously exerting his tyrannical will. Since he is trying to use things he cannot handle, he is inevitably compelled to act with great force.

The boy first gripped both chopsticks at their base and plunged them into the bottom of the bowl. The bowl was filled eight-tenths with rice, and on top of that, miso soup was brimming. As the force of the chopsticks was transmitted to the bowl, what had been balanced until now was suddenly attacked and tilted about thirty degrees. At the same time, the miso soup spilled mercilessly onto his chest. The boy was not one to be deterred by such trivialities. He was a tyrant. This time, he forcefully flicked the chopsticks up from the bottom of the bowl.
