Simultaneously, he brought his small mouth to the edge and caught the rice grains that had been flung up into his mouth. The grains that missed their target splattered against his nose, cheeks, and chin, making a mess. The rice that fell onto the tatami was beyond calculation. It was a remarkably reckless way of eating. I humbly advise the renowned Kaneda and the powerful figures of the world: if you handle matters as you would handle the boy's bowl and chopsticks, the rice grains that fly into your mouths will be exceedingly few. They do not enter with a natural force; they stumble in. I kindly ask you to reconsider. Such behavior is unbecoming of a shrewd and capable person. Sister Tonko, having had her chopsticks and bowl snatched by the boy, had been enduring with the small ones that were far too inadequate for her. Even if she thought she had a full bowl, it would only amount to three bites. Thus, her hand frequently reached for the serving bowl. After four servings, she was now on her fifth. Tonko opened the lid of the serving bowl and picked up a large ladle, gazing at it for a moment. It seemed she was contemplating whether to eat or serve, but ultimately, she appeared to have made up her mind. She carefully scooped a portion from the part that looked least burnt, but when she flipped it over and poured it into her bowl, the rice that could not fit rolled onto the tatami. Tonko, without a hint of surprise, began to pick up the spilled rice. When she pondered what to do with it, she placed it all back into the serving bowl. It seemed a bit unsightly. Just as the boy attempted a grand display by flicking up his chopsticks, Tonko had just finished serving her rice. As expected, being the older sister, she could not bear to see the boy's face in such disarray and said, "Oh, Boy, what a mess! Your face is covered in rice grains!" and immediately set about cleaning his face. First, she removed the grains that had congregated on his nose. To her surprise, instead of discarding them, she promptly put them into her own mouth. Then she moved to his cheeks, where there were quite a few, perhaps about twenty grains in total.

The sister meticulously picked them one by one and ate them, until she had consumed every last grain on her sister's face. At that moment, Sunko, who had been quietly nibbling on pickled daikon, suddenly fished out a piece of sweet potato that had fallen into the miso soup and boldly tossed it into her mouth. As you may know, there is nothing that feels as hot in the mouth as sweet potato that has been boiled in soup. Even adults can burn themselves if they are not careful. Naturally, for someone like Sunko, who had little experience with sweet potatoes, it was a cause for panic. Sunko cried out and spat the sweet potato onto the dining table. For some reason, a few pieces slid right in front of the boy, stopping at just the right distance. The boy, of course, loved sweet potatoes. Since his beloved sweet potatoes had flown right in front of him, he immediately threw down his chopsticks and, using his hands, gobbled them up.

The master, who had been witnessing this spectacle for some time, said not a word, engrossed in his own meal, sipping his soup, and at that moment was already in the midst of using a toothpick. It seems he intends to adopt an absolutely hands-off approach to his daughter's education. Even if the three of them were to become like Ebichan Shikibu or Nezumi Shikibu, and all three conspired to take lovers and run away, he would still be calmly eating his meal and sipping his soup, observing the situation. It is a matter of idleness. However, when I see those who claim to be industrious in this world, they appear to know nothing beyond telling lies to ensnare others, preemptively gouging out the eyes of horses, posturing to intimidate, and setting traps to ensnare people. Even the boys in middle school, imitating what they see, mistakenly believe that they must act in such a way to gain influence, and they carry out actions that should make them blush with shame, all the while thinking they are becoming gentlemen of the future. This cannot be called industriousness; it is merely the behavior of ruffians. Being a cat in Japan, I possess a certain degree of patriotism. Every time I see such workers, I feel an urge to strike them. If even one of these creatures multiplies, the nation will decline accordingly. A school with such students is a disgrace to the school, and a nation with such people is a disgrace to the nation. Despite this disgrace, it is hard to comprehend how they continue to roam about without care. It seems that the people of Japan lack even the spirit of a cat. It is a pitiful thing. Compared to such ruffians, I must say the master is a far superior human being. It is precisely his lack of spirit that makes him superior. His incompetence makes him superior. His lack of cleverness makes him superior. With this idle way of eating, the master finished his breakfast without incident and soon dressed in Western clothes before heading out to the police station at Nihonbashi. When he opened the lattice, he asked the rickshaw man if he knew where Nihonbashi was, and the rickshaw man chuckled. It was somewhat amusing when he emphasized that it was near the Yoshiwara district where the brothels are located. After the master had uncharacteristically left the house by rickshaw, his wife, as usual, finished her meal and urged, "Come on, it's time for school. You'll be late," but the child, unfazed, replied, "Oh, but today is a holiday," showing no signs of preparation.

"It's not a holiday; hurry up," she admonished, but the sister remained unmoved, saying, "But yesterday, the teacher said it was a holiday." At this point, the wife seemed to find it a bit strange, so she took out the calendar from the cupboard and checked it again, confirming that it indeed stated in red letters that it was a holiday. The master must have submitted a notice of absence to the school without knowing it was a holiday. The wife must have unknowingly dropped it into the mailbox as well. However, whether Meitei genuinely did not know or was pretending not to know is somewhat questionable. The wife, surprised by this revelation, decided that everyone should quietly play and, as usual, took out her sewing box to get to work. For the next thirty minutes, the household was peaceful, and no events occurred that would serve as material for me, but suddenly, a strange person came to visit. It was a girl of seventeen or eighteen, wearing shoes with bent heels and dragging a purple hakama, her hair puffed up like abacus beads, coming in through the back door without asking for guidance. This was the master's niece. She was a student at the school, and she often came on Sundays, frequently quarreling with her uncle before leaving. Her name was Yukie, a beautiful name, though her face was not as lovely as her name suggested; she was the kind of person one would inevitably encounter after stepping outside for a couple of blocks. "Good morning, Aunt," she said, striding into the tea room and plopping down beside the sewing box. "Oh, you're up early today..."

"Today is a big holiday, so I thought I’d drop by in the morning. I left home around eight-thirty and hurried over."

"Oh, do you have something to do?"

"No, I just came because I hadn't visited in a while."

"You're welcome to stay longer; take your time. Uncle will be back soon."

"Where has Uncle gone? That's unusual."

"Well, today he went to a strange place... to the police station, isn't that odd?"

"Oh, why's that?"

"Apparently, the thief who broke in this spring has been caught."

"Is he being called in for that? What a hassle."

"Not at all; the items are being returned. Since the stolen goods have turned up, they asked him to come and collect them. The officer came by yesterday specifically for that."

"Oh, I see. Otherwise, Uncle wouldn't have left so early. Normally, he would still be sleeping at this time."

"Uncle is the biggest late sleeper... and when you wake him, he gets furious. This morning, he insisted on being woken by seven o'clock, so I woke him. But then he just burrowed back into his bedding and didn't respond at all. I was worried, so I woke him again, and he muttered something from under the covers. It was truly exasperating."

"Why is he so sleepy?

He must be suffering from nervous exhaustion."

"What do you mean?"

"He's really quite irritable. How can he manage at school like that?"

"Well, they say he's calm at school."

"That makes it even worse. He's like a konjac demon."

"Why is that?"

"Why, indeed, he is like a konjac demon! Doesn't he seem like one?"

"He's not just angry; if someone says right, he says left, and if someone says left, he says right. He never does what anyone says—he's quite stubborn."

"He's like a celestial maiden. Uncle enjoys that. So, if you want him to do something, just say the opposite, and he'll do what you want. The other day, when I wanted him to buy a bat umbrella, I said I didn't want it on purpose, and he immediately bought it, saying, 'How could you not want it?'"

"Haha, that's clever! I should do that too."

"Do that! Otherwise, you'll miss out."

"The other day, a man from the insurance company came and insisted that I should join, explaining various benefits for over an hour, but I absolutely refused. We don't have any savings, and with three children, it would be much more reassuring if we could at least get insurance, but I just don’t care about that at all."

"That's true; it would be worrisome if something were to happen," she said, sounding rather domestic for a girl of seventeen or eighteen. "Listening to that negotiation from the shadows was truly amusing. I certainly don't deny the necessity of insurance. It must exist because it is needed. However, as long as I don't die, there's no need to get insurance, right? He was being stubborn about that."

"Uncle said that?"

"Yes, and then the insurance man said, 'Of course, you don't need insurance unless you die. But human life, while it seems sturdy, is actually fragile, and you never know when danger might strike.' Uncle replied, 'No worries; I've made up my mind not to die,' which was quite outrageous."

"Making up his mind won't prevent death. I was determined to pass, but I ended up failing."

"The insurance agents say that too. One cannot control their lifespan. If one could live longer by mere determination, no one would die."

"The insurance company is right."

"Indeed, they are. But he doesn't understand that. No, he insists he will never die, swearing he won't."

"How strange."

「It is indeed strange, very strange. Rather than paying insurance premiums, it would be far better to save money in a bank, and yet they maintain their composure about it.」
「Do you have any savings?」
「Do I? Not a chance. I have no thoughts about what happens after I die.」
「That’s truly concerning. I wonder why it is that none of the people who come here are like your uncle.」
「Are there any? Not a single one. They are quite rare.」
「You should ask Suzuki-san for his opinion.

It would be much easier with someone as calm as him.」
「However, Suzuki-san has a bad reputation in our house.」
「Everyone seems to think the opposite. Then, that person would be good—look at that calm demeanor—」
「Yagi-san?」
「Yes.」
「I’ve been quite at a loss with Yagi-san. Yesterday, Meitei-san came and spoke ill of him, so he may not be as effective as I thought.」
「But isn’t that fine? If he’s that magnanimous and calm—he gave a speech at school the other day.」
「Yagi-san did?」
「Yes.」
「Yagi-san is Yukie-san’s teacher, isn’t he?」
「No, he’s not a teacher, but he was invited to speak at the Shukutoku Women’s Association.」
「Was it interesting?」
「Well, it wasn’t particularly interesting. But that teacher has such a long face, and with a beard like a deity, everyone listened with great interest.」
「What kind of story did he tell?」 As the wife began to ask, the voices of Yukie-san could be heard from the porch, and three children burst into the tea room. They must have been playing outside the bamboo fence until now. 「Oh, Yukie-san has come!」 the two older sisters exclaimed joyfully. The wife said, 「Don’t make so much noise; everyone sit quietly. Yukie-san is about to tell an interesting story.」 She put her work aside. 「Yukie-san, what story are you going to tell? I love stories!」 said Tonko, while Sunko asked, 「Is it the story of the Kachikachi Yama?」 The youngest daughter, who began to speak, pushed her knees forward between her sisters. However, this was not to say she wanted to hear the story; it meant she wanted to tell a story herself. 「Oh, another story from the little one,」 laughed the older sister, while the wife coaxed, 「Let the little one wait. We’ll listen to Yukie-san’s story first.」 The little one seemed reluctant to comply. 「No, I don’t want to, bubu,」 she shouted loudly. 「Oh, alright, let’s start with the little one. What do you have to say?」 Yukie-san humbly asked. 「Well, you see. Little boy, little boy, where are you going?」
「That’s funny. And then?」
「We’re going to the rice fields to harvest rice.」
「That’s right, you know that well.」
「If you eat it, it will be a nuisance.」
「Oh, it’s not eat; it’s come, you know,」 Tonko interjected. The little one immediately shouted, 「Bubu,」 and promptly annoyed her sister. However, since she had been interrupted, she forgot the continuation and could not proceed. 「Is that all, little one?」 Yukie-san asked. 「Well, you see. After that, no more farts, please. Puu, puupuu.」
「Hohoho, how dreadful! Who taught you such things?」
「Osan.」
「Bad Osan, teaching such things,」 the wife said with a wry smile, but then added, 「Now it’s Yukie-san’s turn. The little boy will listen quietly.」 It seemed that even the little tyrant was satisfied with this, and for the time being, silence fell.

「Yagi-sensei’s speech goes like this,」 Yukie-san finally spoke up. 「Once, in the middle of a crossroads, there was a large stone Jizo. However, since it was in a very busy place where horses and carriages passed, it became a nuisance, and so the townspeople gathered to discuss how to move the stone Jizo to a corner.」
「Was that a true story?」
「What do you think? I can’t say for certain. So, when everyone discussed it, the strongest man in the town said, “It’s no problem; I’ll definitely move it,” and he went to the crossroads alone, rolled up his sleeves, sweated, and pulled, but it wouldn’t budge.」
「That stone Jizo must be quite heavy.」
「Yes, and so that man got tired and went home to sleep, and the townspeople consulted again. Then the smartest man in the town said, “Leave it to me; I’ll do it best,” and he filled a bento box with sweet rice cakes and came in front of the Jizo, saying, “Come here, look at this,” thinking the Jizo would be tempted by the rice cakes, but it didn’t move at all. The smart man thought this wouldn’t do, so he filled a gourd with sake, hung it from one hand, held a cup in the other, and came in front of the Jizo, saying, “Don’t you want to drink? If you want to, come here,” and teased him for about three hours, but still, it didn’t budge.」
「Yukie-san, doesn’t the Jizo get hungry?」 Tonko asked, while Sunko said, 「I want to eat rice cakes.」
「The smart man failed twice, so next he made a lot of counterfeit money and said, “You want this, don’t you? If you want it, come and get it,” showing and hiding the bills, but that didn’t help at all. That Jizo must be quite stubborn.」
「That’s right. He’s a bit like your uncle.」
「Yes, just like your uncle. In the end, the smart man got fed up and gave up. Then a big blusterer came along, saying, “Don’t worry; I’ll definitely move it for you,” as if it were an easy task.」
「What did that blusterer do?」
「That’s the interesting part. At first, he wore a policeman’s uniform, put on a false beard, and came in front of the Jizo, saying, “Hey, hey, if you don’t move, it won’t be good for you; I’ll leave you to the police,” trying to act tough. In this day and age, no one would listen to a policeman’s fake voice.」
「That’s true. So, did the Jizo move?」
「Of course not; he’s your uncle.」
「But your uncle is very afraid of the police.」
「Oh really? With that face? Then it can’t be that scary. However, the Jizo wouldn’t move; he remained calm. So the blusterer got very angry, took off the policeman’s uniform, threw the false beard into the trash, and this time came out dressed like a wealthy man. In modern terms, he would have looked like Baron Iwasaki. Isn’t that funny?」
「What kind of face is like Iwasaki’s?」
「Just a big face, you know.

And without doing anything or saying anything, he walked around the Jizo, puffing on a big roll of tobacco.」
「What good does that do?」
「He envelops the Jizo in smoke.」
「It sounds just like a storyteller’s joke. Did he manage to envelop him in smoke?」
「No, it didn’t work; the opponent was a stone. If you’re going to deceive, you should do it properly. Then he transformed into a prince. What a fool!」
「Oh, were there princes back then?」
「There must have been. Yagi-sensei said so. He certainly transformed into a prince, which is quite a daring thing to do, but he did it—first of all, isn’t it disrespectful for a blusterer to do that?」
「Which prince are you talking about?」
「Which prince? It’s disrespectful no matter which prince you mention.」

"Well then,"  
"Even His Highness wouldn't be able to do anything about it. It seems that the man gave up, saying that with my skills, there was nothing I could do about that Jizō."  
"Serves him right."  
"Yes, they should have just sent him to prison along with it. — But the people in the neighborhood were quite worried and held another meeting, yet it seems no one was willing to take it on, so they were at a loss."  
"And that was the end of it?"  
"Not quite. In the end, they hired a lot of rickshaw men and ruffians to make a racket around the Jizō. They said they should just bully the Jizō until it couldn't take it anymore, and they would make noise day and night in shifts."  
"How troublesome."  
"Still, they didn't pay any mind to it. The Jizō was quite stubborn as well."  
"And then what happened?" Tonko asked eagerly. "Then, you see, no matter how much they made noise every single day, they didn't see any results, so everyone started to get quite fed up. But the rickshaw men and ruffians were happy to make noise for as many days as they could because they were getting paid."  
"Yukie, what's 'getting paid'?" Sunko asked. "'Getting paid' means money."  
"What do you do with the money?"  
"You get money and... Hohoho, you are a troublesome one, Sunko. — So, Auntie, they were making a racket every day and night. At that time, there was a fool in the neighborhood called Bakadake, who knew nothing and was ignored by everyone. When that fool saw this commotion, he said, 'Why are you making such a fuss? Can't you move a single Jizō even after all these years? How pitiful!' —"  
"He's a fool, yet he speaks grandly."  
"He's quite the impressive fool. Everyone listened to what Bakadake said, thinking it was worth a try even if it would probably fail, so they decided to let him handle it. Bakadake readily accepted, telling them to keep quiet and not make such a ruckus, and he calmly went in front of the Jizō."  
"Yukie, what does 'calmly' mean? Is Bakadake a friend of yours?" Tonko asked, throwing a curious question at just the right moment, causing the ladies and Yukie to burst into laughter. "No, he's not a friend."  
"Then what is he?"  
"'Calmly' means... — I can't quite explain it."  
"'Calmly' means you can't explain it?"  
"That's not it. 'Calmly' means —"  
"Yes?"  
"Well, you know Tatara Sampei, right?"  
"Yes, the one who gave us mountain yams."  
"That's the kind of thing I'm talking about."  
"Tatara is calm?"  
"Yes, in a way.

— So, when Bakadake came in front of the Jizō and put his hands in his pockets, he said, 'Jizō, the people in the neighborhood want you to move, so please do so.' The Jizō immediately replied, 'Oh, if that's the case, you should have said so earlier,' and started to move."  
"What a strange Jizō."  
"Then came the speech."  
"There's more?"  
"Yes, then Mr. Yagi said, 'Today we have the Ladies' Association, and the reason I am telling you this story is that I have a little thought on my mind. It may be rude to say this, but women often do not take the direct route when it comes to doing things; instead, they tend to take roundabout and convoluted methods. Of course, this is not limited to women. In the Meiji era, even men have become somewhat feminine due to the influence of civilization, and many seem to misunderstand that spending unnecessary effort and labor is the proper way for gentlemen to conduct themselves. These are merely deformed children bound by the works of enlightenment. There is no need to discuss this further. However, for the ladies, I hope you will remember the old story I just mentioned, and in times of need, please handle matters with the honest perspective of Bakadake. If you all become like Bakadake, I am certain that one-third of the dreadful conflicts that arise between husbands and wives, and between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law, will surely be reduced. The more ulterior motives a person has, the more those motives will bring misfortune, and many women are indeed more unfortunate than average men because they have too many ulterior motives. So please, become like Bakadake.' That was the speech."  
"Wow, so Yukie is planning to become like Bakadake?"  
"Oh no, I don't want to be a Bakadake. I wouldn't want to be something like that. Mrs. Kaneda would be furious if she heard."  
"Mrs. Kaneda, the one from the street over?"  
"Yes, that fashionable lady."  
"Does she go to Yukie's school?"  
"No, she just came to listen because it's the Ladies' Association. She's really fashionable. It's quite surprising."  
"But they say she's very beautiful."  
"She's average. Not as much as she boasts. Anyone would look good with that much makeup."  
"Then if Yukie were to wear makeup like that, she'd be twice as beautiful as Mrs. Kaneda."  
"Oh, don't say that. I wouldn't know. But that lady really overdoes it. No matter how much money she has—"  
"Isn't it better to have money even if you overdo it?"  
"That's true, but—she really should become a little more like Bakadake. She boasts so much. The other day, some poet dedicated a collection of new-style poetry to her, and she was bragging about it to everyone."  
"That must be Tofu."  
"Oh, was it him? That's quite the oddity."  
"But Tofu is very serious.

He thinks it's only natural to do such things."  
"That's the problem. — And there's something even more interesting. The other day, someone sent him a love letter."  
"Oh dear, how scandalous. Who would do such a thing?"  
"They say they don't know who it was."  
"No name?"  
"The name is written clearly, but it's someone they've never heard of, and the letter is a long one, about a room's length. It has all sorts of strange things written in it. It says, 'My love for you is like a religious person's longing for God, and for you, I would gladly be a lamb sacrificed on the altar. The shape of my heart is triangular, and in the center of that triangle stands Cupid's arrow. If it were a blow dart, it would hit the mark...'"  
"Is that serious?"  
"Apparently, it is. In fact, three of my friends have seen that letter."  
"What a dreadful person to flaunt such a thing. That person intends to marry Kangetsu, so it would be a problem if that got out."  
"Not a problem at all; it's quite the achievement. When Kangetsu comes, it would be good to let him know. Kangetsu probably has no idea."  
"How could he? He's busy polishing balls at school, so he probably doesn't know."  
"Does Kangetsu really intend to marry that person? How unfortunate."  
"Why? They have money, and they can be of help when needed. Isn't that good?"  
"Auntie, you keep talking about money; it sounds so vulgar. Isn't love more important than money? Without love, the relationship between husband and wife cannot be established."  
"Well then, where do you think Yukie will marry?"  
"How would I know? There's nothing in particular."

As Yukie and Aunt were passionately debating the marriage incident, Tonko, who had been listening attentively despite not fully understanding, suddenly opened her mouth and said, “I want to get married too.” This reckless hope, filled with the spirit of youth, momentarily disarmed even Yukie, who usually would have sympathized greatly. However, Aunt remained relatively composed and, laughing, asked, “Where do you want to go?”

“Well, you see, I really want to go to the Shokon Shrine to get married, but I’m hesitant about crossing the Suidobashi (the bridge over the water), so I’m wondering what to do.”

Upon hearing this brilliant response, both Aunt and Yukie were so taken aback that they lost the courage to ask any further questions and burst into laughter. At that moment, the younger sister, Sunko, approached her sister with a similar proposal. “Sister, do you like the Shokon Shrine too? I love it! Let’s go to the Shokon Shrine together to get married, okay? No? If you don’t want to, that’s fine. I’ll just hop into a rickshaw and go by myself.”

“Even the boy wants to go,” and thus it was decided that even the boy would get married at the Shokon Shrine. If the three of them could go together to the Shokon Shrine, it would surely be a relief for the master. Just then, the sound of a rickshaw came rattling to a stop in front of the gate, followed by a cheerful voice announcing, “I’m back!” It seemed the master had returned from the Nipponzutsumi police station. The rickshaw man handed a large furoshiki (wrapped bundle) to the maid, and the master entered the tea room with an air of leisure. “Ah, you’re here,” he greeted Yukie, casually tossing aside a sake flask he had brought along, right next to the famous long hibachi. The sake flask, of course, was not a pure sake flask but rather a peculiar piece of pottery that could not even be mistaken for a flower vase, which is why I had to refer to it as such for the time being. “What a strange sake flask! You received something like that from the police?” Yukie asked as she helped the fallen object back up. The uncle, looking at Yukie’s face, boasted, “What do you think? Doesn’t it look good?”

“Looks good? Really? It doesn’t look that great, does it? Why on earth did you bring back an oil flask?”

“It’s not an oil flask. It’s troublesome when you say things that lack taste.”

“Then what is it?”

“A flower vase.”

“For a flower vase, the opening is too small, and the body is oddly bulging.”

“That’s what makes it interesting. You’re so unrefined. You’re just like Aunt; there’s no difference between you two. It’s a troublesome matter,” he said, picking up the oil flask and gazing towards the shoji (sliding door). “Anyway, it’s unrefined. I can’t pretend to bring back an oil flask from the police.

Right, Aunt?” Aunt was too preoccupied with unwrapping the furoshiki, her eyes wide as she examined the stolen goods. “Oh, how surprising! Thieves have become more sophisticated. Everything is unwrapped and washed clean. Hey, wait a moment, you!”

“Who would bring back an oil flask from the police? I was bored waiting, so while I was strolling around, I dug this up. You wouldn’t understand, but it’s still a rare item.”

“Too rare. Where exactly did you go for a stroll?”

“Where? Around Nipponzutsumi. I even went into Yoshiwara. It’s quite a lively place. Have you ever seen that iron gate? I bet you haven’t.”

“Who would go there? I have no reason to go to Yoshiwara, where the courtesans are. You, being a teacher, how could you go to such a place? I’m truly astonished. Right, Aunt?”

“Indeed, it seems there aren’t enough items. I wonder if everything has returned.”

“The only thing that hasn’t returned is the mountain yam. Originally, they told us to report by nine, yet we had to wait until eleven. This is why the Japanese police are no good.”

“The Japanese police are no good? Going for a stroll in Yoshiwara is even worse. If that gets out, you’ll be dismissed. Right, Aunt?”

“Indeed, that would happen. By the way, one side of my obi is missing. I thought something was off.”

“Just give up on one side of the obi. I’ve been made to wait three hours, wasting half a day of precious time,” he said, changing into his Japanese clothes and leaning casually against the hibachi while gazing at the oil flask. Aunt, seeing there was no other option, resigned herself and put the returned items away in the cupboard before returning to her seat. “Aunt, this oil flask is a rare item, they say. It’s filthy, isn’t it?”

“Did you buy that in Yoshiwara? My, my.”

“What do you mean, ‘my, my’? You don’t even understand.”

“Even so, if it’s such a flask, you could find one anywhere without going to Yoshiwara.”

“However, you can’t find it just anywhere. It’s not something you come across often.”

“Uncle, you’re quite the stone-headed fellow.”

“You’re just a child, yet you’re so cheeky. The girls these days have such foul mouths; it’s terrible. You should read a little from a women’s university.”

“You don’t like insurance, do you? Which do you dislike more, women’s universities or insurance?”

“I don’t dislike insurance. It’s a necessary thing. Anyone with foresight should get it. Women’s universities are useless.”

“Even if they’re useless, they’re still good. You haven’t even entered insurance.”

“I plan to enter next month.”

“Really?”

“Absolutely.”

“Stop it with the insurance. You’d be better off buying something with that money instead. Right, Aunt?” Aunt was grinning.

The master became serious and said, “You’re saying such carefree things because you think you’ll live a hundred or two hundred years, but if you develop a little more reason, it’s only natural to feel the need for insurance. I must enter next month.”

“Well, if that’s the case, there’s no helping it. But if you have money to buy a bat umbrella like last time, it might be better to enter insurance instead. You insist on buying something when I say I don’t want it.”

“Was it that unnecessary?”

“Indeed, I didn’t want a bat umbrella at all.”

“Then return it. Tonko has been wanting one, so I’ll pass it on to her. Did you bring it today?”

“Oh, that’s too much! It’s cruel to say return it after you’ve gone through the trouble of buying it for me.”

“I’m saying return it because you said you didn’t want it. It’s not cruel at all.”

“I don’t want it, but it’s still cruel.”

“You’re saying something nonsensical. I’m saying return it because you said you didn’t want it; how is that cruel?”

“But—”

“But what?”

“But it’s cruel.”

“You’re foolish, repeating the same thing over and over.”

“You’re repeating the same thing too, Uncle.”

“It’s because you’re repeating it that it can’t be helped. You did say you didn’t want it, didn’t you?”

“I did say that. I don’t want it, but I don’t want to return it either.”

“How surprising! You’re stubborn without understanding. Don’t they teach logic at your school?”

“Fine, it’s okay. I’m uneducated anyway, so say whatever you want. No one would say to return someone else’s belongings; even others wouldn’t say such unkind things. Just act a little like a bamboo shoot.”

“What kind of act?”

“I’m saying to be a little honest and simple.”

“You’re a stubborn fool, and that’s why you’ll fail.”

“Even if I fail, I won’t be getting any school funds from you.”

Yukie, upon reaching this point, seemed unable to contain her emotions, and tears fell from her eyes onto her purple hakama. The master, in a daze, stared at the tears as if studying the psychological workings behind them, gazing at both the hakama and Yukie's downcast face. At that moment, Osan appeared from the kitchen, her red hands neatly arranged at the threshold, and announced, "A guest has arrived." "Who is it?" the master asked, to which Osan replied, casting a sidelong glance at Yukie's tear-streaked face, "It's a student from school." The master went out to the guest room. I, too, followed the master quietly to the porch, both to observe and to conduct my own study of humans. One must choose a time of turmoil to truly understand humans; otherwise, no results will emerge. Generally, most people are just ordinary, and observing them is so mundane that it hardly stirs any interest. However, when the moment arises, this ordinariness suddenly swells with mysterious and profound significance, giving rise to strange, bizarre, and curious occurrences that, from a cat's perspective, provide invaluable lessons. Yukie's tears are indeed one such phenomenon. Though Yukie appeared to possess a mind that was unfathomable and mysterious, I had not thought much of it while she conversed with her husband. But as soon as the master returned and threw down the oil jar, she suddenly erupted with a depth of emotion that was intricate, exquisite, and extraordinary, as if someone had poured steam into a dragon's mouth. That beauty she displayed was a quality common to all women in the world. It is regrettable, however, that it does not easily manifest. No, it is constantly present, but it does not appear so prominently and unabashedly. Fortunately, there was a peculiar man like the master, who often liked to stroke my fur in the opposite direction, allowing me to witness such a performance. Wherever I follow the master, the actors on stage will unknowingly move. Having an interesting man as my master, I can gather quite a bit of experience in my short cat life. I am grateful for that. I wonder who this new guest is. Looking closely, he appeared to be around seventeen or eighteen, a student who was chasing after Yukie. His large head was shaved so closely that it seemed to blend with the ground, and he had a round nose that dominated the center of his face, sitting quietly in the corner of the room. He had no particularly distinguishing features, but his skull was exceptionally large. Even with his head shaved like a monk, it looked quite big; if he were to grow it long like the master, he would surely attract attention. The master had long held the belief that such a face could not possibly belong to someone who excels in studies.

While this may be true, at a glance, he bore a striking resemblance to Napoleon, exuding an impressive aura. His clothing was typical of a student, whether it was Satsuma kasuri, Kurume kasuri, or Iyo kasuri, I could not tell, but he wore a short-sleeved, lined garment that was unmistakably kasuri. It seemed he had neither an undershirt nor a juban beneath it. While it is said that a simple garment and bare feet are spirited, this man gave off a rather shabby impression. In particular, the three distinct prints of his bare toes on the tatami mats were undoubtedly the fault of his lack of footwear. He sat squarely on top of the fourth footprint, appearing quite uncomfortable and stiff. It is not particularly concerning when something that ought to be humble behaves itself, but it was somewhat discordant to see a bald-headed ruffian like him acting so timidly. It is a source of pride for such individuals to not even bow when encountering a teacher, yet they must find it difficult to sit still like ordinary people for even thirty minutes. Yet here he was, posturing as if he were a humble gentleman of virtue, a paragon of propriety, which, despite his discomfort, appeared quite amusing from the outside. How could someone who is so boisterous in the classroom or on the playground possess such self-restraint? It is both pitiable and comical. As I observed them face to face, I felt that even my foolish master held some weight in the presence of a student. The master must surely have felt proud. As the saying goes, "Even dust can accumulate to form a mountain," so even a single student, when gathered with many, can become a formidable group that might engage in protests or strikes. This phenomenon is akin to a coward becoming bold after drinking. To rely on the crowd to stir up trouble is to acknowledge that one has lost their sanity in the intoxication of others. Otherwise, it would be more fitting to say that he was so intimidated that he pressed himself against the sliding door, unable to look down on the Satsuma kasuri that, despite its age, could not afford to belittle a master simply because he was called a teacher. There is no way to dismiss him. The master pushed a cushion toward him, saying, "Now, please sit down," but the monk remained stiff and replied, "Yes," without moving. Behind him, a worn cushion lay silently, as if saying, "Please take a seat," while a living head sat awkwardly atop it. The cushion was not brought in for the sake of staring at it; it was meant to be sat upon, and if it were not, it would indeed suffer a loss of honor, and the master who suggested it would also lose some face. The monk, who was staring down at the cushion as if to crush the master's face, was not necessarily averse to the cushion itself.

In truth, he had hardly ever sat formally since birth, except perhaps during his grandfather's memorial service, and he had already begun to feel numbness creeping into his legs, which were now protesting slightly. Yet, he still would not sit down. Even though the cushion sat idly waiting, he would not take his place. Despite the master's urging to sit down, he remained obstinate. What a troublesome monk he was! If he were to show such restraint, he ought to do so more often when many people gathered, or at school, or even at the boarding house. He was overly considerate in inappropriate situations and lacked humility when it was needed; rather, he was quite unruly. What a troublesome monk indeed. Just then, the sliding door behind him opened quietly, and Yukie respectfully offered a bowl of tea to the monk. Normally, I would tease him, saying, "Look, it's savage tea," but even toward the master alone, he seemed to be in great distress, especially when a young woman, with a refined gesture learned from school, presented the tea bowl to him. The monk appeared to be in considerable agony. As Yukie closed the door, she smiled slyly from behind. It seemed that even among peers, she was quite remarkable. Compared to the monk, she displayed far more composure. Particularly, given the single drop of red tear she had shed earlier, this smile stood out even more. After Yukie left, both parties remained silent for a while, but realizing that this was akin to performing a task, the master finally opened his mouth. "What did you say your name was?" 

"Furui..." 

"Furui? Furui something, right? Your full name?" 

"Furui Buemon." 

"Furui Buemon—indeed, that is quite a long name. It’s not a modern name, but an old one. You’re in the fourth year, right?" 

"No." 

"Third year then?" 

"No, I’m in the second year." 

"Are you in the A class?" 

"No, I’m in the B class."

"Well then, that would be my supervisor, wouldn't it? I see," the master said, impressed. In truth, this large head had been in the master's sight since the time of enrollment, so it was certainly not something he could forget. Moreover, it was a head that had made such an impression that he sometimes dreamt of it. However, the easygoing master could not connect this head with this old-fashioned name, nor could he link that connection to the second-year乙 class. Therefore, upon hearing that this head, which had impressed him to the point of dreaming, was a student under his supervision, he couldn't help but clap his hands in his heart. Yet, he could not fathom why this large-headed, old-named student of his was coming around at this time. Given the master's generally unlikable nature, students hardly ever visited, whether it was New Year's or the end of the year. The only exception was Furui Buemon, who could be considered a rare guest, but the master seemed quite perplexed as to the purpose of that visit. It was unlikely that anyone would come just to play at the house of such a dull person, and if it were a resignation notice, one would expect a more assertive demeanor. Furthermore, it was hard to believe that Buemon would come with personal matters to discuss, so the master was at a loss. Judging by Buemon's demeanor, it was possible that even he himself did not clearly understand why he had come this far. With no other option, the master finally asked outright. "Did you come to play?"

"That's not it."

"Then is it business?"

"Yes."

"Is it about school?"

"Yes, I thought I might talk a little..."

"Well then, what is it? Go ahead and speak," the master said, but Buemon only looked down and said nothing. Normally, Buemon was quite articulate for a second-year middle school student; despite his large head, his intellect was not particularly developed, but he was quite loquacious. In fact, it was this very Buemon who had recently caused the master great trouble by asking him to teach the Japanese translation of Columbus. That loquacious student was now fidgeting like a shy princess, which surely meant there was something significant to discuss. It could not simply be a matter of hesitation. The master felt a bit suspicious. "If you have something to say, why not just say it quickly?"

"It's a bit difficult to talk about..."

"Difficult?" the master said while looking at Buemon's face, but he remained downcast, making it impossible to gauge the situation. Reluctantly, the master changed his tone slightly and added, "It's fine. You can talk about anything. No one else is listening. I won't tell anyone either."

"Is it alright if I talk?" Buemon was still hesitating. "Of course," the master made a hasty judgment.

"Then I will speak," Buemon began, lifting his chestnut-shaped head slightly to glance at the master with a somewhat dazed look. His eyes were triangular. The master puffed out his cheeks and blew out the morning smoke while turning slightly away. "Actually, it’s that... I’ve gotten into a bit of trouble..."

"What kind of trouble?"

"What kind? It's quite troublesome, so I came."

"Then what is the trouble?"

"I hadn't planned on doing such a thing, but Hamada kept insisting..."

"Hamada, you mean Heisuke Hamada?"

"Yes."

"Did you borrow some lodging fee from Hamada?"

"Not anything like that."

"Then what did you borrow?"

"I borrowed my name."

"Hamada borrowed your name for what purpose?"

"He sent a love letter."

"What did he send?"

"Well, he said that without a name, he couldn't mail it, so he told me to use yours, and I thought mine was dull. He said Furui Buemon would be better—so in the end, I let him borrow my name."

"So, do you know that girl? Are you in contact with her?"

"I have no relationship at all. I've never even seen her face."

"That's reckless. How could you send a love letter to someone whose face you don't even know? What kind of reasoning is that?"

"Everyone says she's arrogant and full of herself, so I thought I’d tease her."

"That's even more reckless. So you openly wrote your name and sent it?"

"Yes, the letter was written by Hamada. I lent him my name, and Endo went to her house at night to mail it."

"So the three of you collaborated on this?"

"Yes, but afterward, I thought that if it came to light and I got expelled, it would be terrible, so I worried a lot and couldn't sleep for a few days, and somehow I became all dazed."

"That’s quite a foolish thing to do. Did you write 'Furui Buemon, second-year student at Bunmei Middle School'?"

"No, I didn’t write the name of the school."

"At least it’s good you didn’t write the name of the school. Just imagine if the name of the school came out; that would concern the honor of Bunmei Middle School."

"Do you think I might get expelled?"

"Well..."

"Teacher, my father is a very strict man, and my mother is a stepmother, so if I were to get expelled, I would be in big trouble. Will I really get expelled?"

"Then you should avoid doing anything reckless."

"I didn't mean to do it, but it just happened. Is there no way to avoid expulsion?" Buemon pleaded, his voice on the verge of tears. Behind the sliding door, the master's wife and Yukie had been giggling for some time. The master continued to feign seriousness, repeating, "Well..." It was quite amusing.

When I say I am interesting, there may be some who ask what is so interesting about me. Such inquiries are quite reasonable. Whether human or animal, knowing oneself is a significant matter throughout one’s life. If one can truly understand oneself, then a human may rightly receive more respect than a cat. At that point, I would feel it a pity to continue writing such mischief and would promptly cease. However, just as one cannot discern the height of one’s own nose, it seems that one’s own essence is difficult to grasp, and it is perhaps because of this that even those who usually look down on cats would pose such questions. Humans, though they may appear arrogant, are still somewhat lacking in understanding. They wander about, claiming to be the spirits of all things, yet they cannot comprehend such a simple fact. Moreover, when they reach a state of serene indifference, it almost makes one want to laugh. They carry the spirits of all things upon their backs, clamoring for someone to tell them where their noses are. Yet, when one considers resigning from being the spirits of all things, they seem unwilling to let go, no matter what. If one can remain so openly contradictory and yet be unbothered, it becomes rather charming. However, to replace charm with such foolishness is a price one must pay.

吾輩がこの際武右衛門君と、主人と、細君及雪江嬢を面白がるのは、単に外部の事件が鉢合せをして、その鉢合せが波動を乙なところに伝えるからではない。実はその鉢合の反響が人間の心に個々別々の音色を起すからである。第一主人はこの事件に対してむしろ冷淡である。武右衛門君のおやじさんがいかにやかましくって、おっかさんがいかに君を継子あつかいにしようとも、あんまり驚ろかない。驚ろくはずがない。武右衛門君が退校になるのは、自分が免職になるのとは大に趣が違う。千人近くの生徒がみんな退校になったら、教師も衣食の途に窮するかも知れないが、古井武右衛門君一人の運命がどう変化しようと、主人の朝夕にはほとんど関係がない。関係の薄いところには同情も自から薄い訳である。見ず知らずの人のために眉をひそめたり、鼻をかんだり、嘆息をするのは、決して自然の傾向ではない。人間がそんなに情深い、思いやりのある動物であるとははなはだ受け取りにくい。ただ世の中に生れて来た賦税として、時々交際のために涙を流して見たり、気の毒な顔を作って見せたりするばかりである。云わばごまかし性表情で、実を云うと大分骨が折れる芸術である。このごまかしをうまくやるものを芸術的良心の強い人と云って、これは世間から大変珍重される。だから人から珍重される人間ほど怪しいものはない。試して見ればすぐ分る。この点において主人はむしろ拙な部類に属すると云ってよろしい。拙だから珍重されない。珍重されないから、内部の冷淡を存外隠すところもなく発表している。彼が武右衛門君に対して「そうさな」を繰り返しているのでも這裏の消息はよく分る。諸君は冷淡だからと云って、けっして主人のような善人を嫌ってはいけない。冷淡は人間の本来の性質であって、その性質をかくそうと力めないのは正直な人である。もし諸君がかかる際に冷淡以上を望んだら、それこそ人間を買い被ったと云わなければならない。正直ですら払底な世にそれ以上を予期するのは、馬琴の小説から志乃や小文吾が抜けだして、向う三軒両隣へ八犬伝が引き越した時でなくては、あてにならない無理な注文である。主人はまずこのくらいにして、次には茶の間で笑ってる女連に取りかかるが、これは主人の冷淡を一歩向へ跨いで、滑稽の領分に躍り込んで嬉しがっている。この女連には武右衛門君が頭痛に病んでいる艶書事件が、仏陀の福音のごとくありがたく思われる。理由はないただありがたい。強いて解剖すれば武右衛門君が困るのがありがたいのである。諸君女に向って聞いて御覧、「あなたは人が困るのを面白がって笑いますか」と。聞かれた人はこの問を呈出した者を馬鹿と云うだろう、馬鹿と云わなければ、わざとこんな問をかけて淑女の品性を侮辱したと云うだろう。侮辱したと思うのは事実かも知れないが、人の困るのを笑うのも事実である。であるとすれば、これから私の品性を侮辱するような事を自分でしてお目にかけますから、何とか云っちゃいやよと断わるのと一般である。僕は泥棒をする。しかしけっして不道徳と云ってはならん。もし不道徳だなどと云えば僕の顔へ泥を塗ったものである。僕を侮辱したものである。と主張するようなものだ。女はなかなか利口だ、考えに筋道が立っている。いやしくも人間に生れる以上は踏んだり、蹴ったり、どやされたりして、しかも人が振りむきもせぬ時、平気でいる覚悟が必用であるのみならず、唾を吐きかけられ、糞をたれかけられた上に、大きな声で笑われるのを快よく思わなくてはならない。それでなくてはかように利口な女と名のつくものと交際は出来ない。武右衛門先生もちょっとしたはずみから、とんだ間違をして大に恐れ入ってはいるようなものの、かように恐れ入ってるものを蔭で笑うのは失敬だとくらいは思うかも知れないが、それは年が行かない稚気というもので、人が失礼をした時に怒るのを気が小さいと先方では名づけるそうだから、そう云われるのがいやならおとなしくするがよろしい。最後に武右衛門君の心行きをちょっと紹介する。君は心配の権化である。かの偉大なる頭脳はナポレオンのそれが功名心をもって充満せるがごとく、まさに心配をもってはちきれんとしている。時々その団子っ鼻がぴくぴく動くのは心配が顔面神経に伝って、反射作用のごとく無意識に活動するのである。彼は大きな鉄砲丸を飲み下したごとく、腹の中にいかんともすべからざる塊まりを抱いて、この両三日処置に窮している。その切なさの余り、別に分別の出所もないから監督と名のつく先生のところへ出向いたら、どうか助けてくれるだろうと思って、いやな人の家へ大きな頭を下げにまかり越したのである。彼は平生学校で主人にからかったり、同級生を煽動して、主人を困らしたりした事はまるで忘れている。いかにからかおうとも困らせようとも監督と名のつく以上は心配してくれるに相違ないと信じているらしい。随分単純なものだ。監督は主人が好んでなった役ではない。校長の命によってやむを得ずいただいている、云わば迷亭の叔父さんの山高帽子の種類である。ただ名前である。ただ名前だけではどうする事も出来ない。名前がいざと云う場合に役に立つなら雪江さんは名前だけで見合が出来る訳だ。武右衛門君はただに我儘なるのみならず、他人は己れに向って必ず親切でなくてはならんと云う、人間を買い被った仮定から出立している。笑われるなどとは思も寄らなかったろう。武右衛門君は監督の家へ来て、きっと人間について、一の真理を発明したに相違ない。彼はこの真理のために将来ますます本当の人間になるだろう。人の心配には冷淡になるだろう、人の困る時には大きな声で笑うだろう。かくのごとくにして天下は未来の武右衛門君をもって充たされるであろう。金田君及び金田令夫人をもって充たされるであろう。吾輩は切に武右衛門君のために瞬時も早く自覚して真人間になられん事を希望するのである。しからずんばいかに心配するとも、いかに後悔するとも、いかに善に移るの心が切実なりとも、とうてい金田君のごとき成功は得られんのである。いな社会は遠からずして君を人間の居住地以外に放逐するであろう。文明中学の退校どころではない。

かように考えて面白いなと思っていると、格子ががらがらとあいて、玄関の障子の蔭から顔が半分ぬうと出た。
「先生」
主人は武右衛門君に「そうさな」を繰り返していたところへ、先生と玄関から呼ばれたので、誰だろうとそっちを見ると半分ほど筋違に障子から食み出している顔はまさしく寒月君である。「おい、御這入り」と云ったぎり坐っている。
「御客ですか」と寒月君はやはり顔半分で聞き返している。
「なに構わん、まあ御上がり」
「実はちょっと先生を誘いに来たんですがね」
「どこへ行くんだい。また赤坂かい。あの方面はもう御免だ。

せんだっては無闇にあるかせられて、足が棒のようになった」
「今日は大丈夫です。久し振りに出ませんか」
「どこへ出るんだい。まあ御上がり」

Kangetsu, thinking that it was impossible to negotiate from such a distance, took off his shoes and slowly made his way inside. As usual, he was wearing mouse-colored trousers that were patched at the rear, but this was not due to the times or the weight of his backside; according to his own explanation, he had recently begun practicing on a bicycle, which caused relatively more friction in that area. Unaware that he was being observed by the future lady of his affections, he casually greeted Mr. Furui with a light nod and settled down near the porch. "Isn't it pointless to hear a tiger's roar?" 

"Well, not at all. We’re going for a stroll around eleven o'clock tonight, heading to Ueno."

"Oh, I see."

"Then the old trees in the park will be quite imposing, won't they?"

"Yes, they will be a bit lonely compared to the daytime."

"So, if we choose to walk in places where the trees are thick and where no one passes even during the day, before long, we’ll forget we live in a bustling city and feel as if we've wandered into the mountains."

"What good does that feeling do?"

"Well, if we linger in that state for a while, suddenly we’ll hear the tiger roaring in the zoo."

"Does it really roar that well?"

"Absolutely, it does. That roar can be heard even during the day at the university, so at midnight, when it’s eerily quiet and there’s no one around, it’s bound to pierce the air like a ghostly presence..."

"What do you mean by 'piercing the air like a ghostly presence'?"

"Don’t say such things when it’s scary."

"Is that so? It seems I don’t hear it much. So?"

"And then the tiger will roar with such force that it shakes the old cedar leaves in Ueno. It’s quite terrifying."

"That would indeed be terrifying."

"How about going on an adventure? I think it would be quite delightful. I believe one must hear the tiger's roar at night to truly say they’ve heard it."

"That’s true," the master replied, showing indifference to Mr. Furui's pleas, as well as to Kangetsu's exploration. Until this moment, Mr. Furui had been silently listening to the tiger tales with envy, but upon hearing the master’s "that’s true," he seemed to recall his own situation and asked again, "Sir, I’m worried. What should I do?" Kangetsu looked at his large head with a puzzled expression. I thought it best to excuse myself for a moment and slipped into the tea room. In the tea room, Mrs. Kaneda was giggling as she poured bancha into a Kyoto-style tea bowl and placed it on an antimony tea tray. "Yukie, please bring that out."

"I don’t want to."

"Why not?" Mrs. Kaneda asked, a bit surprised, stopping her laughter. "Just because," Yukie replied, putting on a sulky face and dropping her gaze onto the Yomiuri newspaper nearby. Mrs. Kaneda began negotiating again.

"Oh, what a strange person. It’s Kangetsu, you know. It doesn’t matter."

"But I really don’t want to," she insisted, not taking her eyes off the newspaper. At such a moment, she wouldn’t be able to read a single word, but if she were found out for not reading it, she would likely start crying again. "There’s nothing to be embarrassed about," Mrs. Kaneda said, laughing as she deliberately pushed the tea bowl onto the newspaper. Yukie exclaimed, "Oh, how mean!" and as she tried to pull the newspaper from under the bowl, the tea tray caught on it, causing the bancha to flow freely onto the tatami mat. "See, look at that," Mrs. Kaneda said, and Yukie dashed into the kitchen, likely to fetch a cloth. I found this little scene quite amusing. Unaware of this commotion, Kangetsu was discussing odd matters in the parlor. "Sir, the shoji have been well replaced, haven’t they? Who did it?"

"A woman did it. It’s quite well done, don’t you think?"

"Yes, it’s rather good. Did that young lady who sometimes visits do it?"

"Yes, she helped with it. They say if you can put up shoji like this, you’re qualified to get married."

"Oh, I see," Kangetsu said, gazing at the shoji. "This side is flat, but the right edge has some excess paper that’s created a wave."

"That’s where it was just put up, and it was done at a time when there was little experience."

"I see, the workmanship is a bit lacking there. That surface has an extraordinarily curved line that cannot be represented by any ordinary function," he said, speaking in a complicated manner as a scientist would, to which the master replied with a casual, "That’s true."

With this exchange, Mr. Furui, feeling that there was no hope of persuading them any longer, suddenly pressed his great skull against the tatami mat, silently expressing his intent to part ways. The master asked, "Are you leaving?" Mr. Furui, dejected, dragged his Satsuma geta and exited through the gate. Poor fellow. If left to his own devices, he might just write a poem on a cliff and leap into the Kegon Falls. To trace it back, this all stemmed from the fashionable and audacious nature of the Kaneda daughter. If Mr. Furui were to die, he could come back as a ghost and take revenge on her. The world wouldn’t be any worse off with one or two of such people gone. Kangetsu would do better to find someone more suitable. "Sir, is that a student?"

"Yes."

"That’s quite a large head. Can he study?"

"Despite the size of his head, he doesn’t do well, but he does ask strange questions from time to time. Just the other day, he asked me to translate Columbus, which really put me in a bind."

"Indeed, having such a large head must lead to unnecessary questions. What did you say, sir?"

"Oh?

I just said something vague and translated it for him."

"Still, you did translate it? That’s impressive."

"Children won’t trust you unless you translate everything for them."

"You’ve become quite a politician, sir. But from what I see now, he doesn’t seem very lively and doesn’t appear to be troubling you much."

"Today, he’s a bit weak. He’s a foolish lad."

"What happened? I just saw him and felt quite sorry for him. What’s going on?"

"Oh, it’s a foolish thing. I sent a love letter to the Kaneda daughter."

"What? That big-headed fellow? The students these days are quite something. I’m really surprised."

"You’re worried too, I suppose..."

"Not at all. In fact, it’s quite amusing. No matter how many love letters come in, it’ll be fine."

"Well, as long as you’re not worried, that’s fine..."

"I’m not worried at all. But it is a bit surprising that that big head wrote a love letter."

"Well, you see, it was a joke. Since that girl is fashionable and audacious, we thought we’d tease her, and the three of us collaborated..."

"Three of you sent a single letter to the Kaneda daughter? That’s even more bizarre. It’s like three people sharing one Western meal."

"However, there was a division of labor. One wrote the letter, one mailed it, and one borrowed a name. The one who just came is the one who borrowed the name. He’s the biggest fool of all. Moreover, he claims he’s never even seen the Kaneda daughter’s face. How could he do something so absurd?"

"That’s quite a recent phenomenon. A masterpiece, indeed. It’s amusing to think that that big head would write to a girl."

"That would be quite a blunder."

"Whatever happens, it doesn’t matter; it’s the Kaneda family."

"But you might be the one to receive it." 

"It doesn’t matter if I might receive it. Kaneda is nothing to me." 

"Even if you don’t mind..."

「It doesn’t matter if it’s Kaneda; it’s all right.」
「Well, if that’s the case, the person in question suddenly became overwhelmed by guilt later on and, feeling terrified, came to consult me at my house.」
「Oh, so that’s why he looks so dejected. He seems like a timid boy. Surely you said something to reassure him, didn’t you?」
「He’s most worried about whether he’ll be expelled from school.」
「Why would he be expelled?」
「Because he did something so wicked and immoral.」
「It’s not really immoral to that extent. It’s nothing to worry about. I’m sure Kaneda takes pride in it and is boasting about it.」
「No way.」
「In any case, it’s pitiful. Even if what he did was wrong, to make him worry so much could kill a young man. He has a big head, but his features aren’t that bad. His nose twitches adorably.」
「You’re quite carefree, just like Meitei.」
「What? This is the spirit of the times.

You’re too old-fashioned, so you interpret everything too seriously.」
「But isn’t it foolish to send a love letter to someone you don’t even know? That’s just lacking common sense.」
「Foolishness often lacks common sense. You should save him. It would be a good deed. With that appearance, he’s bound to head for the Kegon Falls.」
「That’s true.」
「So, how about going to Ueno to hear the tiger’s roar?」
「A tiger?」
「Yes, let’s go hear it. Actually, I have to return to my country in a few days for some business, so I won’t be able to accompany you anywhere for a while. That’s why I thought we should definitely take a walk together today.」
「Oh, you’re going back? Do you have some business?」
「Yes, I have a little matter to attend to. — In any case, let’s go out.」
「Right. Then let’s go.」
「Come on, let’s go. Today, I’ll treat you to dinner, and after that, if we exercise a bit, we’ll reach Ueno just in time.」 As he kept urging, the master also got in the mood and went out with him. Later, the mistress and Yukie were laughing heartily without any reservations. ---

In front of the alcove, Meitei and Dokusen were seated across from each other at a go board. 「No free games. The loser has to treat the winner to something. Understand?」 Meitei emphasized, and Dokusen, as usual, tugged at his goat beard and replied,
「If you do that, you’ll ruin the purity of the game. It’s not interesting to be distracted by stakes. Only when you play with a heart free from such concerns, like a white cloud drifting naturally from the mountain, can you truly savor the essence of the game.」
「Here we go again. Dealing with such a sage is a bit too much work. You’re like a character from a celestial tale.」
「Playing the unstrung zither.」
「Unable to send a wireless telegram.」
「In any case, let’s play.」
「Are you taking white?」
「It doesn’t matter which.」
「As expected of a sage, you’re so easygoing. If you’re white, then by natural order, I’ll take black. Now, come on. Play from wherever you like.」
「The rule is to play from black.」
「I see. Then I’ll humbly start from this point in the established moves.」
「There’s no such move in the established play.」
「Even if there isn’t, it’s fine. It’s a novel invention of a move.」
I, having a narrow view of the world, had only recently seen a go board for the first time, but the more I thought about it, the more peculiar it seemed. A small square board, divided into cramped squares, with a dizzying array of black and white stones scattered about. And then they fuss over who won or lost, who lived or died, sweating profusely. It’s just a space of about one shaku (about 30 cm) square. If a cat were to scatter it with its paws, it would be a complete mess. If you pull it together, it becomes a grass hut; if you let it go, it returns to the original field.

It’s a pointless distraction. It’s far more comfortable to stand back and observe the board with my hands in my pockets. The first thirty or forty moves might not be too bothersome in terms of how the stones are placed, but when it comes to the crucial moment of deciding the game, oh dear, what a pitiful sight it is. The black and white stones are pushing against each other, threatening to spill off the board, both sides grunting in exertion. It’s cramped, and I can’t ask the fellow next to me to move, nor do I have the right to demand the teacher in front to leave, so I resign myself to fate, remaining still and frozen, unable to do anything else. The one who invented go was human, and if human preferences are reflected in the game, then the fate of the cramped go stones can be said to represent the petty nature of humanity. If we can deduce human nature from the fate of the go stones, then I must assert that humans like to carve out their territory in a world as vast as the sky and sea, shrinking it down to their own two feet, and they enjoy marking their domain with fine craftsmanship. Humans are, one might say, creatures that seek out suffering. The carefree Meitei and the zen-like Dokusen, for some reason, decided to drag out an old go board from the cupboard today and began this sweltering distraction. As expected of both of them, at first, they each acted freely, and the white and black stones danced across the board with ease, but the board has its limits, and as the rows and columns filled with each move, it was only natural that, no matter how carefree or zen-like they were, it would become uncomfortable. 「Meitei, your go is reckless. There’s no way to enter such a place.」
「There may not be such a way in the go of a Zen monk, but in the style of Honinbo, it can’t be helped.」
「But it’s going to lead to death.」
「I would not shy away from death; let alone shoulder the burden of it, I would go this way.」
「If you’re going to do that, very well. A fragrant breeze comes from the south, bringing a coolness to the palace. If you set it up like this, it should be all right.」
「Oh, you set it up well. I thought you wouldn’t bother to do so. If you set it up like this, what will happen?」
「What will happen or not happen? Leaning on my sword, it’s cold — ah, what a hassle. Just cut it off.」
「Oh dear, oh dear. If you cut there, I’ll die. Hey, this isn’t a joke. Wait a moment.」
「That’s why I’ve been saying from the start that you can’t enter a situation like this.」
「I apologize for entering. Just take this white stone for me.」
「Are you going to wait for that too?」
「While you’re at it, please lift that one next to it as well.」
「You’re so shameless.」
「Do you see the boy? — What? We’re not strangers. Don’t be so formal; just lift it for me.

It’s a matter of life or death. Just a moment, just a moment, I’m about to dash out from the flower path.」
「I don’t know anything about that.」
「It’s fine if you don’t know; just move it a bit.」
「You’ve already asked me to wait six times, haven’t you?」

"What a man with a good memory! From now on, I shall double my patience. So, I ask you to step aside a bit, you see. You are quite stubborn yourself. If you were to practice zazen, you might be able to manage a little better."

"However, if I don't kill this stone, I might end up losing a bit..."

"You're not the type to mind losing from the start, are you?"

"I don't mind losing, but I don't want you to win."

"What a ridiculous philosophy! You're still cutting through the spring breeze like a flash of lightning."

"Not a spring breeze, but a flash of lightning. Yours is reversed."

"Hahaha! I thought it was about time for everything to be reversed, but there is still some certainty in it. Well then, I suppose I have no choice but to give up."

"Life and death are of great importance, and impermanence is swift; I shall give up."

"Amen," Mr. Meitei said, this time throwing a stone into a completely unrelated area. As Mr. Meitei and Mr. Dokusen were earnestly competing in their game of go in front of the alcove, Mr. Kangetsu and Mr. Tofu stood side by side at the entrance of the tatami room, while their host sat nearby with a yellow face. "Isn't it bonito flakes?"

"Yes, it's a specialty from my hometown."

"Well, try eating it."

"That's why I said I was worried if I didn't bring it quickly."

"Don't worry, it won't harm you to nibble on that much."

"What a careless mouse! Living on a ship, does it lose its discernment?" the host said, still gazing at the bonito flakes, as if no one could understand him.
