"I can't sleep holding the violin because it's too big, but..." he began to say when—

"What? You slept holding the violin? That's quite refined. There’s a phrase about the heavy biwa being held in the departing spring, but that’s a distant matter. A Meiji genius must sleep holding a violin if he is to surpass the ancients. How about 'guarding the long night with a violin'? Mr. Tofu, can you say such a thing in new-style poetry?" Mr. Meitei called out loudly, connecting the conversation from afar. Mr. Tofu, serious, replied, "New-style poetry, unlike haiku, cannot be created so quickly. However, when it is finally done, it will produce a more delicate sound that touches upon the subtleties of the living spirit."

"Is that so? I thought the living spirit was something to be welcomed by burning incense, but can it really come through the power of new-style poetry?" Mr. Meitei continued to tease, still neglecting the game of go. "If you keep babbling nonsense like that, you'll lose again," the host warned Mr. Meitei. Unfazed, Mr. Meitei replied, "Whether I want to win or lose, my opponent is like an octopus in the pot, unable to move a hand or foot, so I have no choice but to entertain myself with the violin."

Mr. Dokusen, in a somewhat heated tone, said, "Now it's your turn. We're waiting over here."

"What? Have you already played?"

"I have indeed, a long time ago."

"Where?"

"I extended this white stone."

"Ah, I see. By extending this white stone, you've lost, huh? Then what about this—this—this—oh dear, I have no good moves left. I'll let you play again, so go ahead and make a move wherever you like."

"Is there such a game?"

"If there isn't, then let's play. —Well then, shall I place this stone a little crookedly on the corner? —Mr. Kangetsu, your violin is so cheap that the mouse looks down on it and bites it. You should splurge a little and buy a better one. Shall I order you an ancient piece from Italy that’s three hundred years old?"

"Please do.

And while you’re at it, I’d like to ask for an exorcism too."

"Will such an old thing be of any use?" the host, who knew nothing, retorted sharply, putting Mr. Meitei in his place. "You are equating human antiques with violin antiques, aren't you? Even among human antiques, there are things like Kaneda that are still in fashion, so when it comes to violins, the older, the better. —Now, Mr. Dokusen, please make your move quickly. As they say, autumn days grow short."

"It’s painful to play go with a man as fidgety as you. There’s no time to think. I have no choice but to place a stone here and keep an eye on it."

"Oh dear, I’ve let you live. What a pity! I thought you wouldn't play there, so I was just chatting a bit to distract you, but it seems I was wrong."

"Of course. Yours is not about playing; it's about deceiving."

"That’s the Honinbo style, the Kaneda style, the modern gentleman's style. —Hey, Mr. Kushami, as expected, Mr. Dokusen, having eaten pickled vegetables in Kamakura, is unflappable. I truly respect that. His go may be poor, but his composure is solid."

"That's why a man without your composure should try to imitate a little," the host replied without turning around, and just then, Mr. Meitei stuck out his long, red tongue. Mr. Dokusen, as if completely unconcerned, urged, "Now it’s your turn."

"When did you start playing the violin? I was thinking of learning a bit too, but I've heard it’s quite difficult," Mr. Tofu was asking Mr. Kangetsu. "Well, anyone can do it if they just give it a try."

"Since it's the same art, those with a taste for poetry should also improve quickly in music, I secretly hope. What do you think?"

"That should be fine. You’ll surely become skilled."

"When did you start?"

"During my high school days. —Have I ever told you the story of how I started learning the violin?"

"No, you haven't told me yet."

"Did you start learning when you were a teacher too?"

"Oh, there was no teacher involved. It was self-taught."

"Truly a genius!"

"One might say that genius is not limited to self-study," said Kangetsu with a huff. It seems that only Kangetsu reacts with such indignation when called a genius. "Well, that doesn't matter much, but do tell me how you went about your self-study. I’d like to take some notes."

"I can share that. Shall I tell you, Mr. Kushami?"

"Yes, do go ahead."

"Nowadays, young people walk around with their violins slung over their shoulders, but back in my day, there were hardly any high school students dabbling in Western music. Especially at my school, which was so rural that it was said we didn’t even have straw sandals; it was a very simple place. Naturally, there wasn’t a single student who played the violin."

"It seems an interesting story has begun over there. Dokusen, let’s wrap this up."

"There are still a couple of points that need addressing."

"Even if there are, that’s fine. If it’s just general information, I’ll gladly accept it."

"Even so, I can’t just take it."

"You’re a rather meticulous man for a Zen scholar. Then let’s do it all at once. — Kangetsu, it sounds rather amusing, doesn’t it? — That high school, I hear the students go barefoot to school…"

"That’s not true."

"But they all do their military-style exercises barefoot, and I’ve heard that their feet get quite tough from it."

"Surely not. Who said such a thing?"

"Anyone will do. They say they bring a grand rice ball for lunch, hanging it from their waist like a summer orange, and they eat it. Rather than eating, they seem to gnaw at it. And then, from the center, a pickled plum pops out. They say they eagerly devour the saltless exterior, anticipating the arrival of that plum. Indeed, they’re quite vigorous, aren’t they? Dokusen, you might find this story to your liking."

"It reflects a simple, robust spirit."

"There’s even more to it. I hear there’s no ash scoop there. When my friend went to work there, he set out to buy an ash scoop marked with the seal of Tsugetsu Peak, but to his surprise, there wasn’t a single thing that could be called an ash scoop. When he inquired, he was told that anyone could just go to the back thicket and cut one for themselves, so there was no need to sell them. This too is a beautiful tale that illustrates the simple and robust spirit, wouldn’t you agree, Dokusen?"

"Well, that’s fine, but we must insert a 'but' here."

"Very well. But, but, but. That settles it. — I was truly surprised to hear that you self-studied the violin in such a place. As it says in the Chuci, 'Alone and unmatched,' Kangetsu, you are indeed the Qu Yuan of the Meiji era."

"I’d rather not be compared to Qu Yuan."

"Then how about being the Werther of this century? — What, you want to calculate with stones? You have a rather serious disposition.

It’s certain I’m already losing without needing to calculate."

"However, it doesn’t add up…"

"Then you go ahead and do it. I’m not the accountant. I must hear the story of how the great genius Werther began to learn the violin, or I’ll feel I’ve done a disservice to my ancestors," and with that, I slipped away towards Kangetsu. Dokusen was carefully picking up white stones to fill the white holes, and black stones to fill the black holes, continuously calculating in his mouth. Kangetsu continued his tale. "Given the local character, my countrymen are also quite stubborn, so if there’s even a hint of weakness, they impose strict punishments on the students from other prefectures, which made things quite troublesome."

"Your country’s students are truly hard to talk to. Why on earth do they wear plain navy hakama? That alone is quite odd. And perhaps due to the salt wind, they seem rather dark in complexion. It’s fine for men, but for women, that must be quite a predicament," Meitei interjected, causing the essential conversation to veer off somewhere. "The women are just as dark."

"And yet they still find suitors?"

"Well, it can’t be helped since the whole country is dark."

"Such is fate, isn’t it? Hey, Kushami."

"Being dark is better. If they were fair, they would be vain every time they looked in the mirror. Women are truly a troublesome matter," the master sighed heavily. "But if the whole country is dark, wouldn’t they be vain about being dark?" Tofu posed a reasonable question. "Nevertheless, women are entirely unnecessary," the master stated, to which

"Be careful saying such things, or your wife will be in a bad mood later," Meitei warned with a laugh. "Not at all, it’s fine."

"Is she not here?"

"She went out with the child a little while ago."

"That’s why it’s so quiet. Where did they go?"

"I don’t know. They just go out as they please."

"And they come back as they please?"

"Well, yes. You’re lucky to be single," Tofu remarked, showing a hint of discontent. Kangetsu chuckled. Meitei said,

"Once you have a wife, everyone feels that way. Don’t you agree, Dokusen? You must have your own troubles with your wife."

"Eh? Just a moment. Four, six, twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven. If it feels narrow, is there a forty-sixth? I thought I had a bigger lead, but upon checking, it’s only an eighteen-point difference. — What’s that?"

"I was saying you must have your own troubles with your wife."

"Ahahaha, it’s not particularly troublesome. My wife loves me as I am."

"That’s a bit presumptuous. That’s just like you, Dokusen."

"It’s not just Dokusen. There are plenty of such cases," Kangetsu interjected, defending wives everywhere. "I agree with Kangetsu.

In my view, there are only two paths to reach the absolute realm: one is through art, and the other is through love. The love between husband and wife represents one of these paths, so I believe that one must marry and fulfill this happiness, or else they go against the will of heaven. — What do you think, sir?" Tofu turned seriously to Meitei. "That’s a noble theory. I, for one, feel I could never reach the absolute realm."

"If you marry, you certainly won’t get there," the master said with a serious expression. "Nevertheless, we unmarried youths must touch the spirit of art and carve out a path of improvement, or we won’t understand the meaning of life. So, I thought I’d start by learning the violin, which is why I’ve been listening to Kangetsu’s experiences."

"Yes, yes, I was supposed to hear the story of Werther and the violin. Now, do tell. I won’t interrupt anymore," Meitei finally settled down. "The path of improvement cannot be opened by something like the violin. It would be a disaster if one could grasp the truths of the universe through such trifles. To understand the news here, one must have the courage to reach out to the precipice and be reborn from the depths," Dokusen proclaimed grandly, giving a lecture that was well-intentioned but lost on Tofu, who knew nothing of Zen and showed no sign of being impressed. "Well, that may be true, but I still believe that art represents the pinnacle of human yearning, so I cannot simply abandon it."

"If you can’t abandon it, then as you wish, I will share my violin story. So, as I mentioned, I had quite a struggle before I began practicing the violin. First of all, I had trouble buying one, you see, sir."

"Indeed, in a place without straw sandals, there’s no way there could be a violin."

「No, there is indeed something. I have saved up money beforehand, so there is no problem, but somehow I cannot buy it.」
「Why not?」
「Because the land is narrow, if I were to buy it, it would be found out immediately. If it is discovered, I would be reprimanded for being too presumptuous.」
「Geniuses have always been persecuted, you know,」 Tofu expressed great sympathy. 「Another genius, I would prefer to be spared from being called a genius. You see, every day when I take a walk and pass by the shop with violins, I think how wonderful it would be if I could buy one, what it would feel like to hold it in my arms, oh how I want it, oh how I want it—there hasn’t been a single day when I haven’t thought that.」
「That makes sense,」 Meitei remarked, while the master, unable to comprehend, said, 「It’s quite peculiar, isn’t it?」 Tofu, on the other hand, admired, 「You are indeed a genius.」 Only Dokusen remained aloof, twisting his beard.

「You might wonder why there is a violin in such a place, but upon reflection, it is quite natural. The reason is that there is a girls' school in this area, and the students must practice the violin every day as part of their curriculum, so there must be some. Of course, they are not good ones. They are barely worthy of the name "violin." Therefore, the shop does not place much importance on them, hanging two or three together in the storefront. However, sometimes when I walk by, the wind blows or a boy's hand brushes against them, and they produce sound. When I hear that sound, my heart suddenly feels like it might burst, and I can’t help but be restless.」
「That’s dangerous. There are various kinds of epilepsy, but yours is a Werther-like violin epilepsy,」 Meitei teased. 「Well, if one doesn’t have such a keen sensitivity, one cannot become a true artist. You must be a genius,」 Tofu continued to express his admiration. 「Yes, it may indeed be epilepsy, but that sound is extraordinary. Since then, I have heard it many times, but never has such a beautiful sound emerged. How can I describe it? It is utterly indescribable.」
「It rings like the sound of fine jade,」 Dokusen brought up a difficult term, but no one paid him any mind, which was unfortunate. 「As I walked by the storefront every day, I finally heard this miraculous sound three times. By the third time, I resolved that I must buy it no matter what. Even if I were reprimanded by the authorities, looked down upon by others from different prefectures—yes, even if I were to die from a beating—if I were to mistakenly receive expulsion from school—this was something I could not refrain from buying.」
「That is genius. If it weren’t for genius, one wouldn’t be able to be so committed. I envy you. I have long wished to feel such a fierce sensation, but somehow I cannot. I go to concerts and listen as attentively as I can, but I just can’t get that excited,」 Tofu lamented repeatedly. 「It’s better not to get too excited. What I can speak of so casually now, the suffering I experienced at that time is not something you can easily imagine. —And then, the teacher finally splurged and bought it.」
「Oh? How did that happen?」
「It was just the night before the November Emperor’s Birthday. Everyone from the country went on an overnight trip to the hot springs, so no one was around. I pretended to be sick and took the day off school to stay in bed. That night, I thought to myself that I would finally go out and acquire the long-desired violin, and I kept thinking about it while lying in bed.」
「So you faked an illness to skip school?」
「Indeed, that’s exactly what I did.」
「Well, that’s a bit genius, isn’t it?」 Meitei seemed somewhat impressed. 「As I poked my head out from under the bedding, I could hardly wait for dusk.

I had no choice but to burrow back under and try to sleep, but it didn’t work. When I poked my head out again, the fierce autumn sun was shining directly on the six-foot shoji, and it was blazing hot, which made me irritable. I noticed a long, thin shadow gathering above, swaying occasionally in the autumn breeze.」
「What’s that long shadow?」
「It was the skin of astringent persimmons that I had peeled and hung out to dry.」
「Hmm, and then?」
「I had no choice but to get out of bed, open the shoji, step outside, and grab one of the dried persimmons to eat.」
「Was it good?」 the master asked, sounding like a child. 「It was delicious; the persimmons from that area are something you can’t find the same flavor of in Tokyo.」
「The persimmons are good, but what happened next?」 Tofu asked this time. 「Then I burrowed back under and closed my eyes, secretly praying to the gods that night would come quickly. After about three or four hours, I thought it was finally time, so I poked my head out again, and to my surprise, the fierce autumn sun was still shining on the six-foot shoji, and the long shadow was still gathering and swaying.」
「I’ve heard that before.」
「There’s more to it. Then I got out of bed, opened the shoji, stepped outside, and ate another dried persimmon, and then I crawled back into bed, praying secretly that night would come quickly.」
「You’re back to where you started.」
「Please, teacher, don’t rush me. After enduring about three or four hours in the bedding, I thought this time it must be alright, so I poked my head out again, and the fierce autumn sun was still shining on the six-foot shoji, and the long shadow was still gathering and swaying.」
「It’s the same thing no matter how long you go on.」
「Then I got out of bed, opened the shoji, stepped outside, and ate another dried persimmon…」
「You ate another persimmon? It seems like you’re just going to keep eating persimmons forever.」
「I was getting impatient myself.」
「It’s far more frustrating for me to listen to you.」
「You are too impatient, teacher, which makes it difficult for me to speak.」
「It’s a bit troublesome for the listener too,」 Tofu also subtly expressed his dissatisfaction. 「Since you all are troubled, there’s no helping it. Let’s wrap this up. In short, I ate the dried persimmons, burrowed, and kept eating until I finally finished all that were hung out on the eaves.」
「If you ate them all, it must have gotten dark.」
「However, it didn’t go that way. After I finished the last dried persimmon, I thought it must be alright to poke my head out again, and still, the fierce autumn sun was shining on the six-foot shoji…」
「I can’t take it anymore. It’s endless.」
「I’m getting tired of talking too.」
「But if you have that much patience, you can accomplish most endeavors.

If you stay silent, the autumn sun will keep blazing until tomorrow morning. When do you plan to buy the violin, anyway?」 Even Meitei seemed to be losing his patience. Only Dokusen remained calm, indifferent to whether the autumn sun blazed on until tomorrow morning or the morning after that. Kangetsu also appeared to be quite composed.

"You ask when I intend to buy it, but as soon as evening falls, I plan to head out to make the purchase. Unfortunately, every time I stick my head out to take a look, the autumn sun is blazing down—oh, the suffering I endured at that moment is beyond what you can imagine! Even after eating the last of my sweet dried persimmons, I found myself weeping at the sight of the sun refusing to set. Tofu, I truly cried out of sheer pity for myself."

"Indeed, artists are inherently sentimental and prone to grievances, so I sympathize with your tears, but I would prefer to move the story along more swiftly," Tofu said, his good-natured demeanor making his earnest yet comical remarks all the more amusing. "I wish I could move it along, but the sun simply refuses to set, and that’s what troubles me."

"Well, if the sun doesn’t set, it’s troublesome for the listeners too, so let’s stop this," the master finally said, unable to contain his impatience any longer. "Please don’t stop! We’re just about to enter the climax of the tale."

"Then let’s say the sun has set, and we can proceed."

"Well, it’s a bit of a stretch, but since it’s you, sir, I’ll bend the rules and say that the sun has set."

"That works out nicely," Dokusen remarked with a composed expression, prompting everyone to burst into laughter. "Now that night has truly fallen, I took a deep breath of relief and left my lodgings in Kurakake Village. I naturally dislike noisy places, so I deliberately avoided the convenience of the city and settled in a remote farmer's house in a quiet village for a while, creating a snail's retreat..."

"To say it was a remote place is a bit of an exaggeration," the master protested, to which Meitei added, "A snail's retreat sounds grand. It would be more picturesque and interesting to describe it as a four-and-a-half tatami mat room without a tokonoma."

Tofu alone praised, "The poetic quality of the language is what matters, regardless of the facts." Dokusen, with a serious expression, asked, "Living in such a place must make it difficult to attend school. How far is it?"

"It's only about four or five blocks to school. The school itself is located in the village..."

"Then students must be lodging around there," Dokusen insisted, not easily convinced. "Yes, in most farmer's houses, there is at least one or two."

"And that’s why it’s remote?" he pressed with a direct attack. "Yes, without the school, it would truly be deserted... As for my attire that night, I wore a handwoven cotton padded jacket over a uniform coat with gold buttons, pulling the hood of the coat over my head to avoid drawing attention. It was the season of falling persimmon leaves, and the path from my lodging to the Nango Highway was covered in leaves.

With every step I took, the rustling made me uneasy, as if someone might be following me. When I turned to look, the forest of Tōreiji loomed darkly, casting shadows in the night. This Tōreiji is the family temple of the Matsudaira clan, located at the foot of Mount Kōshin, only about a block away from my lodging, a remarkably secluded temple. Above the forest, the starry night sky stretched endlessly, and the Milky Way crossed the Nagase River at an angle, flowing—yes, flowing toward Hawaii..."

"Hawaii is quite a leap," Meitei remarked. "I walked two blocks along the Nango Highway, entered the city from Takadai Town, passed through Kojō Town, turned at Sengoku Town, glanced at Kuidate Town, and passed through the first, second, and third blocks of Tōmachi, then on to Owari Town, Nagoya Town, Shachihoko Town, and Kamaboko Town..."

"You don’t need to list all those towns. The question is whether you bought the violin or not," the master asked, sounding rather impatient. "The store with the instruments is Kanzen, or Kaneko Zenbei's place, so it’s still quite a distance."

"Even if it’s a distance, hurry up and buy it."

"Understood. When I arrived at Kanzen, the store was brightly lit..."

"Another bright light? Your bright lights never seem to end, making it quite a hassle," Meitei interjected, setting up a precautionary remark. "No, this time the brightness was just a brief flash from the street, so there’s no need for concern... When I looked through the light, the violin reflected the soft glow of autumn, its hollow body shimmering with a cold light. Only a part of the tightly strung strings sparkled white in my eyes..."

"That’s quite a vivid description," Tofu complimented. "When I thought, 'That’s it, that violin,' my heart raced, and my legs felt unsteady..."

"Hmph," Dokusen snickered. "I rushed in without thinking, pulled out my hidden pouch, and took out two five-yen bills from inside..."

"Did you finally buy it?" the master asked. "I intended to buy it, but wait a moment; this is the crucial part. I mustn’t act rashly and make a mistake. I decided to hold off at the last moment."

"What? You still haven’t bought it? A violin can really draw people in."

"It’s not that it draws me in, but I simply can’t buy it yet."

"Why not?"

"Why? Because it’s still early evening, and there are many people passing by."

"It doesn’t matter; even if two hundred or three hundred people pass, you’re quite the peculiar fellow," the master huffed. "Ordinary people wouldn’t matter if there were a thousand or two thousand, but the students from school are out there, rolling up their sleeves and wandering about with large canes, making it difficult to make a move.

Some of them even call themselves the Sediment Party, happily lingering at the bottom of the class. Those are the ones who are particularly strong in judo. They rarely meddle with violins. I can’t predict what might happen. I certainly want a violin, but I value my life even more. It’s easier to live without being killed while playing a violin."

"So, in the end, you didn’t buy it," the master pressed. "No, I did buy it."

"You’re such a frustrating man. If you’re going to buy it, just buy it quickly. If you don’t want to, then just say so, but it would be better to settle it quickly."

"Hehehe, things in this world don’t always go as we wish," Kangetsu said coolly as he lit a cigarette. The master, seeming to grow weary of the conversation, stood up and went into the study. He soon returned with an old Western book, lying down on his stomach to read. Dokusen had quietly retreated to the front of the tokonoma, arranging go stones and playing a solitary game. The lengthy tale had dragged on so long that the audience dwindled, leaving only the artistically devoted Tofu and the ever-patient Meitei. Kangetsu, puffing out long clouds of smoke without reservation, resumed his conversation at the same pace as before. "Tofu, at that moment, I thought to myself, 'This early evening won’t do at all. If I wait until midnight, Kanzen will be asleep, and that would be even worse. I must time my arrival for when the students have returned from their stroll, and Kanzen is still awake; otherwise, my carefully laid plans will go to waste. However, timing it just right is quite difficult.'"

"Indeed, that sounds quite challenging," Tofu replied.

"Well, I estimated that time to be around ten o'clock. So, I had to find a place to spend the time until about ten o'clock. It would be quite a hassle to go home and come back again. Going to a friend's house to chat felt somewhat burdensome and uninteresting, so I decided to take a stroll around the city until a reasonable amount of time had passed. However, on a normal day, two or three hours would pass by in a flash while I wandered about, but that night, time seemed to drag on endlessly. I felt as if I were experiencing what the poet meant by the longing of a thousand autumns," I said, turning deliberately toward Mr. Meitei as if to emphasize my sentiment. "There is a saying that waiting for an old friend is as painful as sitting by a kotatsu (a heated table) in winter. It is also said that the one who waits suffers more than the one being waited for. The violin hanging from the eaves must have felt the same way, but you, wandering aimlessly like a detective without a clue, must be suffering even more. You are like a dog from a grieving household. In fact, nothing is more pitiful than a dog without a home."

"Dogs are cruel, aren't they? I have never been compared to a dog before."

"Whenever I hear you speak, I can't help but feel sympathy, as if I were reading the tales of artists from long ago. The comparison to a dog was merely a joke from you, so please continue with your story," Tofu reassured. Of course, Kangetsu intended to continue his tale regardless of any consolation. "Then, I walked from Tatemachi through Hyakukicho, out to Ryogaemachi, counted the number of withered willows in front of the prefectural office, calculated the lights in the hospital windows, smoked two rolled cigarettes on the Konya Bridge, and then checked the time..."

"Is it ten o'clock yet?"

"Not quite yet. — After crossing the Konya Bridge and heading east along the riverbank, I encountered three massage therapists. And the dogs kept barking, Mr. Meitei..."

"Hearing dogs howl along the riverbank on an autumn night feels a bit theatrical, doesn't it? You are like a fugitive."

"Have I done something wrong?"

"That's what I am about to do."

"Poor thing, it’s not wrong to buy a violin; all the students at the music school are sinners."

"If one does something that is not recognized by others, then no matter how good it is, it is a sin. Therefore, nothing is more unreliable than a sinner in this world. Even Jesus would be a sinner if born into such a world. Even the handsome Kangetsu would be a sinner if he bought a violin in such a place."

"Then I shall accept being a sinner. Sinners are fine, but it is troubling that it is still not ten o'clock."

"I will count the names of the towns once more. If that is not enough, I will make the autumn day blaze on.

If that still does not suffice, I will eat three dozen of those dried persimmons. I will keep talking until it is ten o'clock."

Kangetsu smiled slyly. "Having been overtaken like that, I have no choice but to concede. Let us leap ahead to ten o'clock. When the promised ten o'clock arrived and I reached the front of Kinzen, it was a chilly night, and as expected, even in the bustling Ryogaemachi, the streets were nearly deserted, and the sound of geta (wooden sandals) approaching felt lonely. Kinzen had already closed its large doors, leaving only a small sliding door open. I felt somewhat uneasy, as if I were being followed by a dog, as I opened the sliding door and entered..."

At that moment, the master glanced away from the messy book and asked, "Hey, have you bought the violin yet?" When Tofu replied, "I am about to buy it," the master muttered, "Still not bought? It’s taking quite a while," and resumed reading his book. Dokusen remained silent, having filled most of the go board with black and white stones. "I must boldly dive in and ask for a violin while still wearing my hood," I said. The four or five young boys gathered around the hibachi were startled and looked at my face as if they had agreed upon it. I instinctively raised my right hand and pulled my hood forward. When I asked for a violin a second time, the boy who was peering closely at my face replied hesitantly and stood up to retrieve three or four violins that were hanging at the shopfront. When I asked how much they cost, he said five yen and twenty sen..."

"Is there such a cheap violin? It must be a toy."

"When I asked if they were all the same price, he replied, 'Yes, they are all the same. They are all sturdy and well made.' So, I pulled out a five-yen bill and twenty sen in silver from my frog purse, took out a large wrapping cloth, and wrapped the violin. During this time, the shopkeeper had stopped talking and was staring intently at my face. Although my face was hidden by the hood, I felt anxious and wanted to get out into the street as quickly as possible. Finally, I managed to slip the wrapped violin under my coat, and as I left the shop, the clerk called out in unison, 'Thank you!' in a loud voice, which startled me. When I stepped out onto the street and looked around, fortunately, it seemed that no one was around, but from a distance, two or three people were reciting poetry loudly, echoing throughout the neighborhood. This was quite a predicament, so I turned west at the corner of Kinzen, headed along the moat to Yakuoshido, and finally made my way back to my lodging from Hanokimura to the foot of Kōshinzan. When I returned to my lodging, it was already ten minutes to two."

"It felt like I had been walking all night," Tofu said sympathetically. "I finally made it.

What a long journey it has been, like a game of sugoroku," Mr. Meitei sighed with relief. "Now comes the interesting part. Until now, it has merely been the prologue."

"Is there more? This is not an easy matter. Most things lose their patience when they meet you."

"Patience aside, if I stop here, it would be like making a Buddha and not putting in a soul, so I will talk a little more."

"Of course, talking is entirely up to you. I will listen."

"How about you, Mr. Kushami? I have already bought the violin. Yes, sir."

"Now you are going to sell the violin? I don't need to hear about where you are selling it."

"I'm not selling it yet."

"Then I don't need to hear about it."

"This is quite troublesome, Tofu. You are the only one who is listening earnestly. It takes away some of the excitement, but it can't be helped; I will just summarize the story."

"Please don't summarize; take your time and tell it leisurely. It is very interesting."

"I finally managed to get my hands on the violin, but the first problem I faced was where to keep it. Since many people come to visit me, if I hang it or lean it in a careless place, it will be discovered immediately. Digging a hole and burying it would be a hassle."

"Then did you hide it in the attic?" Tofu said casually. "There is no attic. It’s a farmer's house."

"That must have been a problem. Where do you want to put it?"

"Where do you think I put it?"

"I have no idea. In the door pocket?"

"No."

"Did you wrap it in bedding and put it in the cupboard?"

"No."

While Tofu and Kangetsu were engaged in this back-and-forth about the hiding place of the violin, the master and Mr. Meitei were also conversing about something. "What does this say?" the master asked. "What do you mean?"

"These two lines."

"What? Quid aliud est mulier nisi amiciti inimica... This is Latin, isn't it?"

"I understand Latin, but how do you read it?"

"But you said you could read Latin fluently," Mr. Meitei observed, sensing danger, and took a slight step back. "Of course, I can read it. I can read it, but what does it say?"

「I can read it, but what is this? It’s quite a mess.」
「Just translate it into English, whatever it is.」
「“Look” is a bit intense, isn’t it? It’s as if I were a servant.」
「Even if I were a servant, what of it?」
「Well, let’s set aside the Latin for now and listen to a bit of Mr. Kangetsu’s esteemed discourse. It’s quite a critical moment. We are at a point of crisis, teetering on the edge of revelation. — Hey, Kangetsu, what do you want to do next?」 Suddenly, he became enthusiastic and joined in with the violin again. The master was left behind, feeling rather pitiful. Mr. Kangetsu, encouraged by this, began to explain the hiding place. 「In the end, I hid it in an old chest.

This chest was a farewell gift from my grandmother when I left the country, and it seems she brought it with her when she got married.」
「That’s quite an antique. It doesn’t seem to harmonize with the violin at all. What do you think, Tofu?」
「Yes, it doesn’t harmonize much.」
「Even the attic doesn’t harmonize, does it?」 Mr. Kangetsu countered, putting Tofu in his place. 「It may not harmonize, but it can still make a verse, so don’t worry. How about this: “In the autumn, lonely, hidden in a chest, a violin.” What do you think, both of you?」
「You’ve made quite a haiku today, sir.」
「It’s not just today. I can make them any time in my mind. If you were to speak of my knowledge of haiku, even the late Shiki would be astonished.」
「Sir, did you have a relationship with Shiki?」 The honest Tofu asked with a straightforward question. 「What relationship? We were always in touch through wireless telegraphy, sharing our thoughts, you see,」 he said nonsensically, leaving Tofu speechless in astonishment. Mr. Kangetsu laughed and continued. 「So, I managed to find a hiding place, but now I’m troubled about how to bring it out. It’s not impossible to sneak a glance at it, but merely glancing won’t do any good. If I don’t play it, it won’t serve any purpose. If I play it, sound will come out. If sound comes out, it will be immediately revealed. It’s quite dangerous since the leader of the sediment group is lodging right next door, separated only by a hibiscus hedge.」
「That’s a predicament, isn’t it?」 Tofu chimed in sympathetically. 「Indeed, this is a problem. As they say, the proof is in the sound, and the young lord’s chamber failed because of this. If it were about stealing food or counterfeiting money, it would be easier to handle, but music cannot be hidden from others.」
「If only there were no sound, I could manage somehow…」
「Hold on a moment. You say if there were no sound, but there are things that can’t be hidden even if there’s no sound. Back when we were cooking for ourselves at the temple in Koishikawa, there was a man named Mr. Suzuki, who had a great fondness for mirin. He would buy mirin in a beer flask and enjoy drinking it all by himself. One day, after Mr. Suzuki went out for a walk, for no good reason, Mr. Kushami stole a bit and drank it…」
「I would never drink Suzuki’s mirin; it was you who drank it,」 the master suddenly raised his voice. 「Oh, I thought you were engrossed in your book, but you were indeed listening. You’re a man who can’t be caught off guard. With ears as sharp as a hawk and eyes as keen as a hawk, that’s you. Now that you mention it, I did drink it. There’s no doubt I drank it, but it was you who got caught. — Now, both of you, listen. Mr. Kushami originally cannot drink alcohol.

However, thinking it was mirin belonging to someone else, he drank it with all his might, and oh dear, his face turned bright red. He was in such a state that he could hardly be looked at again…」
「Be quiet. You can’t even read Latin.」
「Hahaha! So when Mr. Suzuki returned and shook the beer flask, more than half was missing. He thought someone must have drunk it, and when he looked around, there was the master, stiff as a clay figure in the corner…」

The three of them burst into laughter without restraint. The master, too, chuckled quietly while reading his book. Only Dokusen seemed to have played too much with the pieces and appeared somewhat fatigued, leaning over the go board, and before long, he was sound asleep. 「There was a time when I was revealed without any sound. I once stayed at a hot spring in Ubako, sharing a room with an old man. He was supposedly a retired kimono merchant from Tokyo. Well, since we were sharing a room, it didn’t matter whether he was a kimono merchant or an old-clothes dealer, but there was one troublesome thing that arose. You see, on the third day after arriving at Ubako, I ran out of tobacco. As you all know, Ubako is a remote place in the mountains, where you can only bathe in the hot spring and eat, and there’s no other way to manage. So running out of tobacco was quite a hassle. When you lack something, you tend to want it even more, and as soon as I thought about not having tobacco, I suddenly craved it desperately. To make matters worse, that old man had brought a whole bundle of tobacco with him, wrapped in a furoshiki, and he would take it out little by little, smoking it right in front of me as if to say, “You’d like to smoke this, wouldn’t you?” He would puff away. Just puffing would have been bearable, but eventually, he started blowing smoke in rings, then vertically, horizontally, or even in reverse like a dream of Handan, and sometimes blowing through his nose like a lion entering and exiting a cave. In short, he was flaunting it…」
「What do you mean by flaunting?」
「If it were clothing or props, one would show them off, but since it’s tobacco, one flaunts it.」
「Well, rather than suffering like that, wouldn’t it be better to just ask for some?」
「But I didn’t ask. I’m a man too.」
「Oh, so you can’t ask?」
「I might be able to, but I didn’t.」
「So what did you do?」
「I didn’t ask; I stole some.」
「Oh dear.」
「The old man went out to the bath with a towel hanging, so I thought if I were to smoke, this was the time, and I smoked it continuously, lost in joy, and before I knew it, the sliding door opened with a creak, and there was the owner of the tobacco.」
「Did he not enter the bath?」
「I intended to, but I realized I had forgotten my pouch and turned back from the hallway.

If I had just gone to get my pouch, that would have been the end of it, but first, that was rude.」
「That’s quite something to say about the tobacco.」
「Hahaha! The old man had quite the discernment. Regardless of the pouch, when he opened the sliding door, the smoke from two days’ worth of tobacco consumption filled the room, and it was indeed true what they say: bad deeds travel far. It was immediately revealed.」
「What did the old man say?」
「As expected of his age, he said nothing, but wrapped fifty or sixty pieces of rolled tobacco in a thin paper and said, “Excuse me, but if you wouldn’t mind this coarse leaf, please enjoy it,” and then he went back down to the hot spring.」
「Is that what they call Edo taste?」
「Whether it’s Edo taste or kimono merchant taste, I don’t know, but after that, I had a delightful two-week stay with the old man, sharing our thoughts.」
「So the tobacco was on the old man’s tab for those two weeks?」
「Well, something like that.」
「Have you finished with the violin yet?」 The master finally closed his book and stood up, surrendering at last. 「Not yet. This is where it gets interesting, so please listen. It’s just the right time. And I’d like Mr. Dokusen, who is napping on the go board, to hear it too — what was his name again? Ah, Mr. Dokusen. — It’s not good for your health to sleep so much. It’s fine to wake him up now.」
「Hey, Dokusen, wake up, wake up. There’s an interesting story. Get up. Sleeping like that is bad for you. Your wife is worried.」

「Eh?」 said Dokusen, lifting his face, as a long strand of drool flowed down his goat-like beard, glistening like the trail of a snail. “Ah, I was so sleepy. The white clouds on the mountain resemble my laziness. Ah, I had such a pleasant sleep.”

“Everyone acknowledges that you slept, but how about waking up for a bit?”

“Well, I suppose I can wake up now. Is there something interesting to talk about?”

“From now on, we’re going to play the violin—what was it we were going to do, Mr. Kushami?”

“I have no idea what we’re going to do.”

“We’re about to play it now.”

“We’re about to play the violin. Come over here and listen.”

“Still the violin? This is troubling.”

“You’re part of the group that plays the stringless koto, so you’re not the one to be troubled. But Mr. Kangetsu’s playing can be heard squeaking and screeching all the way to the neighbors, so he’s in quite a predicament.”

“Is that so? Don’t you know how to play the violin so that Mr. Kangetsu’s sound doesn’t reach the neighbors?”

“I don’t know; if there is such a way, I’d like to hear about it.”

“You should be able to tell just by looking at the white cow in the alley,” I said, sensing that he was speaking nonsense. I figured Mr.

Kangetsu must be half-asleep to be using such strange words, so I deliberately ignored him and continued the conversation. “I finally came up with a plan. The next day was the Emperor’s birthday, so I stayed home all morning, taking the lid off the box, putting it back on, and fidgeting about all day. But as evening fell, and the bug in the bottom of the box started chirping, I boldly took out the violin and bow.”

“Finally, it’s out,” said Tofu, and Meitei warned, “It’s dangerous to play too often.”

“First, I took the bow and examined it from the tip to the guard…”

“You’re not a poor swordsmith,” Meitei remarked coldly. “Indeed, when I think of this as my soul, it feels like a samurai drawing his finely honed sword in the shadow of a long night’s lamp. I trembled with the bow in my hand.”

“Truly a genius,” Tofu said, to which Meitei added, “Truly an epileptic.” The master said, “It would be better to play quickly.” Dokusen looked troubled. “Fortunately, the bow is safe. Now, I pulled the violin close to the lamp and examined both sides carefully. Imagine this took about five minutes, during which the bug in the bottom of the box kept chirping…”

“Think whatever you like; just play comfortably.”

“I’m not playing yet. Fortunately, the violin has no damage. Now I can stand up confidently…”

“Are you going somewhere?”

“Please be quiet and listen. It’s impossible to have a conversation when I’m interrupted every other sentence…”

“Hey, everyone, be quiet, will you? Shh, shh.”

“You’re the only one talking.”

“Ah, I see, my apologies. Please listen attentively.”

I tucked the violin under my arm and stepped out a few paces, still wearing my sandals, but then I paused…

“Look who’s here. I thought for sure there would be a power outage somewhere.”

“There’s no sweet-dried persimmon left if you go back now.”

“I regret that all of you have mixed in, but there’s no helping it; it’s better than just dealing with Tofu alone. Now, listen, Tofu, I took a few steps out but turned back again, putting on the red blanket I bought for three yen and twenty sen when I left the country, and when I suddenly extinguished the lamp, it became pitch dark, and I couldn’t tell where my sandals were.”

“Where on earth are you going?”

“Just listen. Finally finding my sandals, I stepped outside, and under the starry night, with fallen persimmon leaves and the red blanket, I headed right, right, toward Kōshin Mountain. As I approached, the bell of Tōrei Temple rang out, resonating through the blanket, through my ears, and into my head. Do you know what time it was?”

“I don’t know.”

“It was nine o’clock. From here, I was to climb the mountain path for eight miles to a place called Ōhira.

Normally, being the timid person I am, I would be terrified, but when I became single-minded, it was strange; whether I was scared or not, such thoughts didn’t arise in my mind at all. I was just filled with the desire to play the violin. This place called Ōhira is on the southern side of Kōshin Mountain, and on a clear day, you can see the castle town from among the red pines, offering a breathtaking view—a flat area about a hundred tsubo in size, with a single rock about eight tatami mats in the center, and to the north, there’s a pond called U no numa, surrounded by camphor trees that are three embraces wide. Since it’s in the mountains, the only place where people live is a small hut for camphor extraction, and the area near the pond isn’t very pleasant even during the day. Fortunately, the engineers had cleared a path for drills, so it wasn’t too hard to climb. Finally reaching the rock, I spread out my blanket and sat down on it. It was my first time climbing on such a cold night, and as I settled on the rock, the loneliness of the surroundings gradually seeped into my gut. In such a situation, the only thing that disturbs one’s heart is the feeling of fear, so once that feeling is drawn out, what remains is only the pure, clear air of the sky. After sitting in a daze for about twenty minutes, I felt as if I were the only one living in a palace made of crystal. Moreover, my body—not just my body, but my heart and soul—felt as if they had all been made of agar or something, strangely transparent, and I couldn’t tell if I was in the crystal palace or if the crystal palace was inside me…”

“What a strange situation you’ve gotten into,” Meitei teased seriously, and Dokusen seemed a bit impressed, saying, “What an interesting boundary.”

“If this state continued for long, I might have sat on that rock until morning without ever playing my precious violin…”

“Is there a fox around?” Tofu asked. “In such a state, with no distinction between self and others, not knowing if I was alive or dead, suddenly from the depths of the old pond behind me came a cry…”

“Finally, it’s out.”

“That voice echoed far and crossed the autumn treetops of the mountains, and just as I thought it had passed with the wild wind, I suddenly returned to myself…”

“Finally relieved,” Meitei pretended to pat his chest in relief. “Great death brings forth a new universe,” Dokusen winked. Mr. Kangetsu didn’t understand at all.

Then, coming to my senses and looking around, I found that the whole of Kōshinzan was silent, not even the sound of raindrops could be heard. I wondered what that sound was. It was too sharp to be a human voice, too loud to be a bird's call, and as for a monkey's voice—surely there are no monkeys around here. What could it be? As the question of "What is it?" arose in my mind, those who had been silent until now began to stir, as if they were in a frenzy reminiscent of the people of the capital welcoming Prince Connaught. In the midst of this, all the pores of my body suddenly opened, and like a shank of meat splashed with shōchū, my courage, boldness, discernment, and composure evaporated into thin air. My heart began to dance beneath my ribs. My legs started to tremble like a paper kite. This was unbearable. Suddenly, I threw a blanket over my head, tucked a violin under my arm, and wobbled down a sheer rock face, racing down the mountain path towards the foot of the hill, where I returned to the inn, wrapped myself in a futon, and fell asleep. Even now, I cannot think of anything more eerie than that, Tofu-kun. "And then?"

"That's all there is to it."

"Aren't you going to play the violin?"

"Even if I wanted to, I can't. It's too frightening. You wouldn't be able to play either."

"I feel like your story is somewhat unsatisfying."

"Even if you feel that way, it's the truth. What do you think, Mr. Kushami?" Kangetsu looked around the group, appearing quite pleased with himself. "Hahaha, this is quite good. It must have taken considerable effort to get it to that point. I thought I was listening to a serious lecture on the appearance of the male Sandra Belloni in the land of the Eastern Gentleman, and until now, I had been listening earnestly," said Meitei, who, upon realizing that no one was asking questions about Sandra Belloni, continued, "When Sandra Belloni plays the harp under the moon and sings an Italian-style song in the woods, it is a similar yet different piece to your climbing Kōshinzan with a violin. Unfortunately, while she astonishes the moon's Chang'e, you were startled by the ancient pond's monstrous tanuki, resulting in a stark contrast between the ridiculous and the sublime. It must be quite regrettable."

"Not so regrettable," Kangetsu replied, surprisingly unfazed. "After all, trying to play the violin on a mountain is a bit too fashionable, which is why you were startled," the master added with harsh criticism. "A brave man makes a living in this den of demons. What a pity," Dokusen sighed. Everything Dokusen said was never understood by Kangetsu. Not just Kangetsu, but probably by anyone. "By the way, Kangetsu-kun, are you still polishing pearls at school these days?" Meitei shifted the topic after a while.

"No, I just returned home from the country recently, so I've temporarily stopped. I've grown tired of polishing pearls, and I'm actually thinking of giving it up."

"But if you can't polish pearls, you won't become a doctor," the master frowned slightly, but Kangetsu seemed surprisingly relaxed. "A doctor? Hehehe. I don't need to become one anymore."

"But delaying marriage will cause trouble for both parties."

"Whose marriage are you talking about?"

"Yours."

"Who am I marrying?"

"Kaneda's daughter."

"Oh?"

"Oh, but there was such a promise made, wasn't there?"

"There was no promise. Don't spread such rumors; it's their own business."

"This is a bit reckless. Hey, Meitei, you know about that incident too, right?"

"That incident? The nose incident? If it's that incident, it's not just you and I who know about it; it's a public secret known throughout the world. In fact, people come to me asking when the photos of the bride and groom will be published under the title 'Flower Groom and Bride' in the Morning News. Tofu-kun has already composed a grand epic called 'The Mandarin Duck Song' and has been waiting for three months, but since Kangetsu hasn't become a doctor, it seems that this splendid work might end up being a wasted treasure, and he's worried sick about it. Right, Tofu-kun?"

"I'm not handling it with enough concern yet, but in any case, I intend to publish a work filled with sympathetic feelings."

"See, whether you become a doctor or not, the influence spreads in all directions. Please take it a bit more seriously and polish those pearls."

"Hehehe, I'm sorry for causing you various worries, but I no longer need to become a doctor."

"Why not?"

"Because I already have a clearly defined wife."

"Wow, that's quite something. When did you have a secret marriage? It's a world that can't be trusted. Mr. Kushami, as you just heard, Kangetsu-kun already has a wife and child."

"I don't have a child yet. It's only been less than a month since the marriage, so if a child were to be born, that would be something."

"When and where did you get married?" the master asked, as if he were a preliminary judge. "When? When I returned to the country, she was waiting for me at home. The bonito flakes I brought to you today were a wedding gift from my relatives."

"Only three sticks? That's stingy."

"Well, I brought only three from a large batch."

"So she's from your country, huh? I suppose she's quite dark-skinned."

"Yes, she's very dark. Just right for me."

"And what about Kaneda's side?"

"I have no plans regarding that."

"That's a bit inconsiderate, don't you think? Hey, Meitei."

"Not really. If you send her elsewhere, it's the same thing. After all, marriage is like two people bumping into each other in the dark.

Essentially, it's unnecessary to bump into each other, yet they go out of their way to do so. If it's unnecessary, it doesn't matter whose pots bump into each other. The only one who might feel sorry is Tofu-kun, who composed the Mandarin Duck Song."

"Well, the Mandarin Duck Song can be easily directed this way depending on the circumstances. I'll compose another for Kaneda's wedding."

"As expected of a poet, you're quite flexible."

"Have you informed Kaneda?" the master still seemed concerned about Kaneda. "No, I have no reason to inform him. I haven't asked for her hand, nor have I expressed a desire to take her. If I remain silent, that's enough. — Oh, it's enough to remain silent. Nowadays, detectives are everywhere, ten or twenty of them, knowing everything from start to finish."

Upon hearing the word "detective," the master suddenly made a bitter face and said, "Hmph, then just keep quiet," but it seemed he was still unsatisfied, as he continued to expound on detectives as if it were a grand debate. "Picking someone's pocket at an unguarded moment is a thief, and drawing someone’s heart at an unguarded moment is a detective. Removing a sliding door without anyone knowing to steal someone's belongings is a burglar, and slipping up and reading someone's mind without them knowing is a detective. Forcing someone's money by stabbing a dagger into the tatami is robbery, and coercing someone's will with threats is a detective. Therefore, a detective is a kind of family of thieves, burglars, and robbers and cannot be placed above others. Listening to such a person will become a habit. Never give in."

"Don't worry, I'm not afraid of a thousand or two thousand detectives attacking me in formation. I'm the pearl-polishing master, the physicist, Mizushima Kangetsu."

"How impressive. As expected of a newlywed scholar, you are full of vigor. But Mr. Kushami, if detectives are akin to thieves, burglars, and robbers, what kind of kindred is Kaneda-kun, who employs such detectives?"

"Probably something like Kumazaka Nagaharu."

"Kumasaka is doing well, isn't he? They say that what appeared to be one long-range shot has now become two, but a greedy fellow like that, who has built his fortune on crow gold in the alley, has no fear of losing it no matter how old he gets. If you get caught by someone like him, it's karma. You'll be haunted for life, so be careful, Kangetsu."

"Oh, it's fine. That thief is quite something. He must already know the tricks of the trade. And yet, he still dares to break in again. I'll make sure he has a terrible time," Kangetsu replied calmly, puffing out his chest in the style of the Hōshū school. "When it comes to detectives, it seems that people of the twentieth century tend to act like detectives, but I wonder why that is," Dokusen posed a detached question, as was his habit, unrelated to the current issues. "It's probably because of the high prices," Kangetsu answered. "Because they don't understand the appreciation of art," Tofu chimed in. "It's because humans have developed horns of civilization, becoming as irritable as sugar and rice," Meitei added. Now it was the master's turn. He began this discussion in a grandiose tone, as if he had given it considerable thought. "This is something I've pondered quite a bit. According to my interpretation, the detective-like tendencies of contemporary people stem from an excessively strong sense of self-awareness. What I call self-awareness is not the kind of enlightenment that Dokusen refers to when he speaks of seeing one's true nature and attaining Buddhahood, or the idea that the self is one with the universe..."

"Oh, it seems to have gotten rather complicated. Mr. Kushami, if you are going to toy with such grand discussions, then I, too, shall boldly express my grievances about modern civilization," Meitei interjected. "Feel free to say what you like, even if it’s nothing of consequence."

"However, there is something to be said. There is indeed something. Just the other day, you revered the detective inspector as if he were a god, and today you compare detectives to thieves, which is quite a contradiction. But I, for my part, have remained consistent from before my parents were born until now, never once changing my views."

"Detectives are detectives. Thieves are thieves. Just because they were thieves yesterday doesn't mean they are today. Not changing one's views is proof of stagnation. The saying that fools do not change is about you..."

"That's harsh. Detectives, when they come at you straightforwardly, can be rather endearing."

"I am a detective."

"Just because you are not a detective doesn't mean you are honest. Enough of this quarrel.

Now, let us listen to the continuation of this grand debate."

"What I mean by the modern person's sense of self-awareness is that they are overly aware of the stark divide between their own interests and those of others. This self-awareness becomes sharper day by day as civilization progresses, to the point where one can no longer act naturally in any gesture or movement. A man named Henley once remarked about Stevenson that he was the kind of person who could not help but see his own reflection every time he passed a mirror in a room with mirrors, which aptly describes the current trend. Whether I am asleep or awake, I am always surrounded by this self, which makes human actions and words artificially contrived, only tightening the noose around oneself, making the world increasingly difficult, much like how young couples must navigate their feelings from morning till night. Words like 'calm' and 'composed' become meaningless. In this regard, modern people are detective-like. They are thief-like. Detectives are in the business of cleverly stealing the eyes of others to benefit themselves, so they must have a strong sense of self-awareness. Thieves, too, cannot escape the worry of being caught or discovered, which forces them to have a strong sense of self-awareness. Today's people are constantly thinking about how to benefit or lose, whether asleep or awake, thus inevitably developing a strong sense of self-awareness akin to that of detectives and thieves. They are always on edge, sneaking around, never finding a moment's peace until they are buried in the grave. This is the heart of modern people. The curse of civilization. Absurd."

"That is indeed an interesting interpretation," Dokusen remarked. When it comes to such issues, he is not one to back down easily. "Mr. Kushami's explanation resonates with my own thoughts. People of the past taught us to forget ourselves. Today's people teach us not to forget ourselves, which is entirely different. They are filled with a consciousness of self at all times. Because of this, there is never a moment of peace. It is always a hell of burning heat. There is nothing better than forgetting oneself in this world. The phrase 'entering the state of no self under the moon at midnight' captures this ultimate state. Today's people, even when being kind, are acting unnaturally. The English, boasting of their niceness, seem to be overly self-aware. When the English emperor visited India and dined with the local royalty, one of the royals, forgetting himself, took a potato with his hands from the plate, only to feel embarrassed afterward. The emperor, however, remained unfazed and took the potato with two fingers..."

"Is that what you call English taste?" This was Kangetsu's question.

"I heard a story like this," the master continued. "There was a time in an English barracks when a group of officers treated a lower-ranking officer to a meal. After the feast, when they brought out water in a glass bowl for handwashing, the lower-ranking officer, not accustomed to such banquets, drank the water straight from the bowl. At that moment, the commanding officer, suddenly raising a toast to the health of the lower-ranking officer, also downed the water from the finger bowl in one gulp. Then, all the officers, not wanting to be outdone, raised their cups to toast the health of the lower-ranking officer."

"I have another story," Meitei, who disliked remaining silent, interjected. "When Carlyle first met the Empress, being unfamiliar with court etiquette, he suddenly asked, 'How about this?' and plopped down into a chair. However, the many attendants and ladies-in-waiting standing behind the empress all burst into giggles—not that they laughed outright, but they were about to. Then the empress turned around and, with a slight gesture, had all the attendants and ladies-in-waiting sit down, so Carlyle did not lose face, but what a thoughtful kindness that was."

"If it were about Carlyle, he might have been fine even if everyone stood," Kangetsu ventured a brief commentary. "The self-awareness of kindness is all well and good," Dokusen continued. "But having self-awareness makes being kind a laborious task. It's a pity. People commonly say that as civilization progresses, the atmosphere of brutality diminishes, and interactions between individuals become more gentle, but that is a gross misunderstanding. With such strong self-awareness, how can things become gentle? Indeed, at a glance, it may seem very quiet and peaceful, but the interactions between individuals are extremely painful. It's like two sumo wrestlers locked in a stalemate in the center of the ring. To an outsider, it appears perfectly calm, but inside, their bellies are churning."

"Fights of the past were violent and oppressive, so they were less sinful, but nowadays, they have become quite clever, which only increases self-awareness," Meitei's thoughts circled back to him. "Bacon once said that only by following the forces of nature can one win against nature. Today's fights are indeed structured according to Bacon's maxim, which is quite strange. It's much like jujitsu, where one thinks of using the enemy's strength to defeat them..."

「Or it’s like hydroelectric power, isn’t it? Instead of resisting the force of water, we convert it into electricity and make it serve a grand purpose…」 As Kangetsu began to speak, Dokusen immediately took over.

“Thus, in times of poverty, one is bound by poverty; in times of wealth, one is bound by wealth; in times of sorrow, one is bound by sorrow; and in times of joy, one is bound by joy. The talented perish by their talent, the wise are defeated by their wisdom, and those with a temper like Mr. Kushami can easily fall prey to their own outbursts…”
“Ha ha!” Meitei clapped his hands, and Mr. Kushami, grinning, replied, “It doesn’t quite work that easily, you know,” prompting everyone to burst into laughter at once. “By the way, how does someone like Kaneda perish?”
“The wife perishes by her nose, the master by his karma, and the subordinate by his detective work, perhaps?”
“What about the daughter?”
“The daughter—well, I’ve never seen one, so I can’t say for sure—but she would likely perish from either overdressing, overeating, or perhaps from drunkenness. Surely, she wouldn’t perish from love. It’s possible she might end up like the legendary Komachi, dying in the streets.”
“That’s a bit harsh,” Tofu interjected, having just recited a new-style poem. “Therefore, the phrase ‘be without abode and give rise to your mind’ is an important saying; one must reach such a state to avoid the pains of life,” Dokusen said, as if he had come to a profound realization. “Don’t be so arrogant. You might just end up doing a backflip in the shadow of lightning,” Meitei retorted. “Anyway, I don’t want to live in a time when civilization progresses at this rate,” the master declared. “No need to hold back; you’ll die,” Meitei bluntly stated. “I’d rather not die,” the master insisted stubbornly. “When one is born, no one considers it deeply, but when one dies, it seems everyone is troubled by it,” Kangetsu offered a distant proverb. “It’s the same as borrowing money; one borrows without a care, but when it comes time to repay, everyone worries,” Meitei was quick to respond in such moments. “Those who do not think about repaying borrowed money are happy, just as those who do not worry about dying are happy,” Dokusen remarked, detached and worldly. “When you say that, it means you’re rather thick-skinned,” Meitei replied. “Indeed, there’s a Zen saying about the iron bull’s face and the iron bull’s heart, and the ox’s iron face and the ox’s iron heart.”
“So you’re saying you’re that specimen?”
“Not quite. However, the concern about dying arose only after the disease known as nervous breakdown was invented.”
“I see; you seem to be a person from before the age of nervous breakdown.”
As Meitei and Dokusen engaged in their peculiar banter, the master continued to express his grievances about civilization to Kangetsu and Tofu. “The real issue is how to avoid repaying borrowed money.”
“There’s no such issue. What’s borrowed must be repaid.”
“True enough.

But listen quietly, for this is a debate. Just as the question of how to avoid repaying borrowed money is an issue, so too is the question of how to avoid dying. In fact, it was an issue. This is alchemy. All alchemy has failed. It has become clear that humans must inevitably die.”
“That was clear even before alchemy.”
“True, but this is a debate, so just listen. You see, when it becomes clear that one must inevitably die, a second question arises.”
“Oh?”
“If one must die, how should one die? This is the second question. The suicide club is destined to arise alongside this second question.”
“I see.”
“Dying is painful; however, if one cannot die, it is even more painful. For the citizens of the land of nervous breakdown, living is a far greater torment than death. Hence, they suffer over death. It is not that they suffer because they dislike dying, but rather they worry about how to die in the best way. Most people, lacking wisdom, leave it to nature, allowing the world to bully them to death. However, those with a peculiar disposition will not be satisfied with being bullied to death by the world. They will surely, after various considerations regarding how to die, present innovative and unique methods of departure. Therefore, the trend of the world will be an increase in suicides, and those suicides will all leave this world in their own creative ways.”
“That sounds rather alarming.”
“It will be. It certainly will. In a script written by someone named Arthur Jones, there is a philosopher who repeatedly advocates for suicide…”
“Will he commit suicide?”
“Unfortunately, he does not. However, in a thousand years, everyone will surely put it into practice. After ten thousand years, death will come to be thought of as nothing but suicide.”
“That will be quite something.”
“It will be, without a doubt. When that happens, suicide will be thoroughly studied and become a respectable science, and in middle schools like Rakugunkan, they will teach the science of suicide as a formal subject instead of ethics.”
“How peculiar! I’d love to attend such a lecture. Meitei, did you hear Mr. Kushami’s brilliant discourse?”
“I did. By that time, the ethics teacher at Rakugunkan will say this: ‘You must not cling to the barbaric remnants of public virtue. As the youth of the world, your foremost duty is to commit suicide. Moreover, what you prefer, you may bestow upon others; thus, it is permissible to expand suicide into homicide. Especially someone like the illustrious Mr. Kushami, who seems to suffer greatly from living, it is your duty to kill him as soon as possible. However, unlike in the past, today is an enlightened era, so do not engage in cowardly acts using spears, halberds, or firearms.

“Indeed, that sounds like an interesting lecture.”
“There’s even more that’s interesting. In modern times, the police’s primary purpose is to protect the lives and property of the people. However, by that time, the police will walk around beating the citizens to death with clubs like dog killers…”
