“Why? Because today, people value life, and the police protect it, but in those days, citizens will find living to be a pain, so the police will mercifully beat them to death. Of course, those with a bit of wit will generally have committed suicide, so those who get beaten to death by the police will be the utterly spineless or the idiots and invalids who lack the ability to take their own lives. Thus, those who wish to be killed will post signs at their door. Just put up a sign saying, ‘There are men or women who wish to be killed,’ and the police will conveniently come by at the right time and fulfill their wishes. As for the corpses, the police will still be the ones to haul them away. There’s even more fun to come…”
“Your jokes truly know no bounds,” Tofu remarked, greatly impressed. Just then, Dokusen, as usual, began to speak while fussing with his goat-like beard. “While it may be a joke, it could also be a prophecy. Those who do not penetrate the truth tend to be bound by the phenomena of the world before their eyes, mistaking ephemeral dreams for eternal realities, so when one says something slightly out of the ordinary, they immediately dismiss it as a joke.”
“‘How can the sparrow know the ambitions of the great roc?’” Kangetsu interjected, impressed, and Dokusen continued, as if to say, “Exactly.”
“Long ago, there was a place in Spain called Cordova…”
“Isn’t it still there?”

"There may be such a thing. Regardless of the issues of the past and present, it is customary for the bell at the temple to ring at dusk, and all the women from the houses come out and enter the river to swim…"
"Do they do this in winter as well?"
"I can't say for sure, but in any case, regardless of social status or age, they jump into the river. However, not a single man joins them; they only watch from a distance. From afar, in the twilight, the white skin of the women appears to move indistinctly on the waves…"
"How poetic. It sounds like a new-style poem. What a place to describe," Tofu said, leaning forward at the mention of nudity. "Cordova, you see. There, the local young men, unable to swim with the women, lament their inability to even clearly see their figures from afar, and so they played a little prank…"
"Oh? What kind of prank?" Meitei asked, delighted at the mention of mischief. "They bribed the temple bell ringer to ring the bell an hour early as a signal for sunset. The women, being rather simple-minded, thought the bell had rung, and each gathered at the riverbank in their half-jackets and half-pants, plunging into the water. Although they jumped in, unlike usual, the sun did not set."
"Wasn't the fierce autumn sun blazing down?"
"Looking from the bridge, many men stood watching. It was embarrassing, but there was nothing they could do. They were said to have turned very red."
"And then?"
"And then, you see, people are easily misled by the customs before their eyes, forgetting the fundamental principles, so one must be careful."
"Indeed, that's a valuable sermon. Speaking of being misled by the customs before one's eyes, let me share a little story. The other day, I read a novel about a con artist. Suppose I were to open an art and antiques shop here. I would display fine pieces by famous artists and renowned craftsmen. Of course, they would not be fakes; I would have only genuine, high-quality items on display. Since they are high-quality, they would naturally be expensive. Then a curious customer comes in and asks, 'How much for this piece by Motonobu?' If I say six hundred yen, the customer, wanting it but lacking the funds, would regretfully say they cannot afford it."
"Is that how it goes?" the master said, still with his usual lack of theatricality. Meitei, with a serious face, continued,
"Well, it's a novel, after all. Just putting it out there. So I would say, 'I don't mind what you pay, if you like it, take it.' The customer hesitates, saying they can't just do that. 'Then let's do it on installment,' I would say, 'with small, long payments, since you will surely become a regular patron from now on—oh no, there's no need to hold back. How about ten yen a month?

If you prefer, I can even make it five yen a month.' I would say this very generously. After a few exchanges between the customer and me, I would sell the piece by Kano Motonobu for six hundred yen, with the condition of ten yen monthly payments."
"You sound like you've read the Times Encyclopedia."
"The Times is indeed accurate, but my method is quite dubious. Now, here comes the truly clever part of the con. Listen carefully: if it's ten yen a month for six hundred yen, how many years do you think it will take to pay it off, Kangetsu?"
"Of course, five years."
"Indeed, five years. Now, do you think five years is long or short, Dokusen?"
"One thought can last a thousand years; a thousand years can be but one thought. It is both short and long."
"What kind of nonsense is that? A nonsensical proverb without common sense. So, since you will be paying ten yen each month for five years, that means the other party only has to pay sixty times. However, that's where the terror of habit comes in. After repeating the same thing sixty times each month, you will inevitably feel compelled to pay ten yen on the sixty-first time as well. You will feel the same for the sixty-second time. As the months go on, you will find that when the due date comes, you simply cannot feel at ease without paying that ten yen. Humans may seem clever, but they have this great weakness of being misled by habits and forgetting the fundamentals. I will profit ten yen each month, time and again, by exploiting that weakness."
"Hahaha, surely people can't be that forgetful," Kangetsu laughed, but the master, somewhat serious, said,
"No, such things do indeed happen. I once had my university loan payments rejected because I didn't keep track of them."
"See, there are indeed people like that right here. So those who laugh at my earlier mention of the future of civilization as a joke are the same ones who think it's perfectly reasonable to pay installments for life after sixty payments. Especially young fellows like Kangetsu and Tofu, who lack experience, must listen carefully to what we say and not be deceived."
"I understand. I will make sure that installments are limited to sixty payments."
"Though it sounds like a joke, it's actually a story worth considering, Kangetsu," Dokusen turned to Kangetsu. "For example, if Mr. Kushami or Meitei were to advise you that your secret marriage was inappropriate and that you should apologize to someone named Kaneda, what would you do?"
"I would prefer not to apologize. If they apologize, that would be different; I have no desire for such a thing."
"What if the police ordered you to apologize?"
"I would still prefer not to."
"What if it were a minister or a noble?"
"Then I would absolutely prefer not to."
"See there?

People have changed that much from the past to the present. In the past, the authority of the government could accomplish anything. Then came a time when there were things that could not be done even with the authority of the government. In today's world, no matter how high-ranking someone is, they cannot impose themselves on an individual’s character beyond a certain degree. To put it bluntly, the more power one has, the more the person on the receiving end feels discomfort and resists. Thus, unlike the past, the present is a time when new phenomena arise, where one cannot do things simply because of the authority of the government. In a world where things that seem almost inconceivable from the perspective of the past are perfectly reasonable, the changes in human emotions and societal conditions are truly mysterious. Even if Meitei's future predictions are dismissed as mere jokes, if they explain that sort of situation, they are quite interesting, aren't they?"

"When such acquaintances emerge, I inevitably feel compelled to continue my chronicle of the future. As Mr. Dokusen suggests, in this present age, some take refuge under the majesty of the government and, relying on a few hundred bamboo spears, attempt to force their way through with unreasonable demands. They are like outdated, stubborn creatures trying to race a train while riding in a basket—well, they are about as clueless as the likes of Mr. Kurokin, the long-winded scholar. It would be best to silently observe their efforts. However, my chronicle of the future is not a mere trivial matter of the moment. It concerns the social phenomena related to the fate of humanity as a whole. Reflecting on the current trends of civilization, I foresee that marriage will become impossible. Do not be alarmed—impossible marriage. The reason is this: as I have mentioned before, the present world is centered around individuality. In times when a household was represented by its master, a district by its magistrate, and a nation by its lord, there was practically no personality outside of these representatives. Even if it existed, it was not recognized. But as this has dramatically changed, every living being now insists on asserting their individuality, creating an atmosphere where everyone seems to say, "You are you, and I am I." When two people meet on the street, they pass each other while secretly vying for recognition, thinking, "If you are human, then I am human too." 

Thus, the individual has become stronger. Because individuals have become equally strong, they have also become equally weak. While it has become more difficult for people to harm one another, it is evident that, in terms of intervening in another's affairs, they have become weaker than before. While it is delightful to grow stronger, no one appreciates becoming weaker. Therefore, in their desire to avoid being infringed upon in any way, they stubbornly cling to their strengths while simultaneously feeling compelled to encroach upon others, even in their weaker aspects. As a result, the space between people has diminished, making life feel constricted. They stretch themselves as tightly as possible, puffing up to the point of bursting, suffering in their existence. Because of this suffering, they seek various ways to create some leeway between individuals. Thus, humanity suffers from its own making, and the first solution they devise in their desperation is the separation of parents and children. If you venture into the mountains of Japan, you will see families all huddled together in one house. There is no individuality to assert, and even if there were, it is not asserted, which is why it works.

However, in civilized societies, even between parents and children, if they do not assert their whims, they feel they are at a loss, thus necessitating separation to ensure the safety of both parties. In Europe, civilization has progressed, so this system has been established there earlier than in Japan. Even when parents and children live together, the son may borrow interest-bearing money from his father or pay rent like a stranger. This beautiful custom exists because parents recognize their children's individuality and show them respect. This custom must inevitably be imported to Japan soon. Relatives are particularly distanced, and parents and children are separated today, barely managing to coexist. The development of individuality and the boundless respect for it will continue to grow, making it impossible to enjoy life without separation. However, in today's world, with parents and siblings already distanced, there is nothing left to separate, leading to the final solution: the separation of couples. In the current mindset, people believe that being together makes them a couple. That is a significant misunderstanding. To be together, there must be sufficient compatibility in their individualities. In the past, there were no complaints; they would say, "Different bodies, same heart," and while they appeared as a couple, in reality, they were one entity. Thus, they would call it "growing old together in the same grave," transforming into a single raccoon after death. How barbaric! But that is no longer feasible. The husband remains a husband, and the wife remains a wife. The wife, having donned her school uniform and cultivated her individuality, enters the household with her hair tied up, making it impossible for her to conform to her husband's wishes. Moreover, if a wife were to conform to her husband's desires, she would be nothing more than a doll. The more intelligent the wife becomes, the more her individuality develops. The more it develops, the less compatible she becomes with her husband. If they are incompatible, they will naturally clash. Therefore, as long as she is called a wise wife, she will be in conflict with her husband from morning till night. It is indeed a splendid thing, but the more one welcomes a wise wife, the greater the degree of suffering for both parties. Like oil and water, there is a distinct barrier between husband and wife. If that barrier were calm and maintained a level horizon, it would be manageable, but since both sides are actively working against each other, the household resembles a great earthquake, rising and falling. Here, it gradually becomes clear to humanity that cohabitation is detrimental to both parties. . . ."

"Is that why couples separate?" Mr. Kangetsu inquired with concern.

"They will separate. Surely, they will separate. All couples in the world will eventually part. Until now, those who lived together were considered a couple, but henceforth, those who cohabit will be regarded as lacking the qualifications of a couple."

"Then I suppose I will be incorporated into a disqualified group," Mr. Kangetsu remarked, playfully flirting at a delicate moment. "How fortunate to be born in the Meiji era! As one who creates chronicles of the future, my intellect is a step or two ahead of the times, so I am quite content to remain single from now on. People make a fuss about the results of unrequited love, but the perspective of shortsighted individuals is truly pitifully shallow. Nevertheless, to continue the chronicle of the future, let me say this: At that time, a philosopher will descend from the heavens to proclaim a groundbreaking truth. His doctrine will state that humans are creatures of individuality. To extinguish individuality is to extinguish humanity itself. To fully realize the significance of humanity, we must preserve and develop this individuality at any cost. To be constrained by outdated customs and reluctantly engage in marriage is a barbaric practice that goes against the natural tendencies of humanity. In an age of civilization, it is utterly absurd to remain trapped in such a folly without reflecting on it. In this era of enlightenment, there should be no reason for two individualities to be connected with an intimacy beyond the ordinary. Despite the obviousness of this reasoning, uneducated young men and women, driven by momentary passions, engage in hasty unions, which is a profoundly immoral act. For the sake of humanity, for civilization, and for the protection of the individuality of these young men and women, we must resist this barbaric trend with all our might..."

"I completely oppose that doctrine," Mr. Tofu interjected boldly, slapping his knee with determination. "In my view, nothing in this world is as precious as love and beauty. It is entirely due to these two that we find solace, completeness, and happiness. They refine our emotions, elevate our character, and cultivate our compassion. Therefore, no matter when or where we are born, we can never forget these two things. When these two manifest in the real world, love takes the form of marriage, while beauty is expressed through poetry and music. "If it doesn't exist, that's fine, but as the philosopher said, it will surely perish, so there's no helping it. What is art? Art ultimately leads to the same fate as marriage. The development of individuality means the freedom of individuality, doesn't it? The meaning of the freedom of individuality is that I am I, and you are you. There’s no way such art can exist. Art flourishes because there is a harmony of individuality between the artist and the audience. No matter how much you insist you are a new-style poet, if there isn't a single person who finds your poetry interesting, your new-style poetry will be unfortunate, and there will be no readers other than yourself. Even if you create a few pieces of love poetry, it won't get anywhere. Fortunately, born in the Meiji era, the world seems to read it with great enthusiasm, but..."

"No, it's not that much," came the reply. "If it’s not that much even now, then when the developed humanities of the future, that is, when that great philosopher emerges and advocates for the theory of non-marriage, there will be no readers at all. There’s a reason for that. Such works are not interesting unless read by someone with a similar individuality. If what you write is incomprehensible to me, and what I write is incomprehensible to you, then there’s no art or anything else between you and me."

"That's true, but I just don't intuitively feel that way," replied Kangetsu. "If you don't intuitively feel that way, then I will think of it in a more twisted way," I said. And it’s no wonder; in the past, when there was one great person, the world would gather under their banner, which was delightful. If such delight were to manifest in reality, there would be no need for someone like Nietzsche to express it through the power of pen and paper. Thus, whether it’s Homer or Chévy Chase, even if they reflect superhuman characteristics, the feeling is entirely different. It’s cheerful. It’s written cheerfully. There are delightful facts, and since this delightful fact was transcribed onto paper, there should be no bitterness. In Nietzsche's time, that was not the case. No heroes emerged. Even if they did, no one would elevate them as heroes. In the past, there was only Confucius, so he had influence, but now there are many Confuciuses. Perhaps the whole world is made up of Confuciuses. Therefore, even if I boast that I am Confucius, it doesn’t carry weight. It doesn’t carry weight, so there is discontent. Discontent leads to the idea of the Übermensch being swung around only in books. We desire freedom and have gained freedom. As a result of gaining freedom, we feel unfree and are troubled. Therefore, Western civilization may seem good at first glance, but in essence, it is worthless. In contrast, the East has been practicing the cultivation of the heart since ancient times. That is the correct path. Look, as a result of the development of individuality, everyone becomes neurotic, and when it becomes unmanageable, we will first discover the value of the phrase, 'The king's subjects are numerous.' We will realize the significance of the phrase 'to act without action and transform.' However, even if we realize it, by that time, it will be too late. "Your theories seem quite pessimistic, gentlemen, but I find it strange. No matter how much I hear, I feel nothing. What is it like?" Kangetsu asked. "The teacher must have thought about it in a barrel."

"Pythagoras said there are three terrible things in the world: fire, water, and women."

"That's enough, teacher. I have no complaints after hearing that much slander about my foolish wife."

"There are still four or five pages left, so why not listen to the rest?"

“Let’s call it a day. It must be about time for the lady to return,” Mr. Meitei teased, and from the tea room came the voice of the mistress calling for the maid, “Kiyo, Kiyo.”

“I want to cultivate a spirit of tranquility, you see. How about you all? Have you ever been fishing? It’s quite enjoyable. “Well, with tobacco, for instance, you can’t get by smoking Asahi or Shikishima,” he said, pulling out a cigarette made of Egyptian tobacco adorned with gold leaf, and began to smoke it.

“Do you have money for such luxuries?”

“I have some money, but it will be alright eventually. Smoking this tobacco makes a big difference in how people regard you.”

“It’s easier to gain trust with this than polishing jewels, and it doesn’t take much effort. It’s convenient trust,” Mr. Meitei said to Kangetsu, who remained silent. “Are you Mr. Kangetsu? Aren’t you going to become a doctor? Since you won’t become a doctor, I’ve decided to take her for myself.”

“Take her?”

“No, the daughter of the Kaneda family. To be honest, I felt a bit sorry for her. However, they insisted that I take her, so I finally decided to do so, sir. But I’m worried that it might be unfair to Mr. Kangetsu.”

“Please don’t hesitate,” Kangetsu said, and the master replied ambiguously, “If you want to take her, then go ahead.”

“That’s quite a fortunate story. So, no matter what kind of daughter you have, you won’t have to worry. After all, as I said earlier, a splendid gentleman like this has come to be your son-in-law. Tofu, you’ve got the makings of a new-style poem. Get right to it,” Mr. Meitei encouraged, and Sampei said,

“Are you Mr. Tofu? Could you compose something for my wedding? I’ll have it printed and distributed everywhere. Even to the sun.”

“Sure, I’ll compose something. When do you need it?”

“Anytime is fine. Even something you’ve already composed will do. In return, I’ll invite you to the reception and treat you. I’ll serve champagne. Have you ever had champagne? It’s delicious. — I plan to hire a band for the reception, but how about arranging your composition for them to play?”

“Do as you like.”

“Sir, could you arrange it for me?”

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

“Is there anyone here who can play music?”

“The failed candidate, Kangetsu, is a master of the violin. Be sure to ask him. But I doubt he’d agree for just champagne.”

“About the champagne, it shouldn’t be one that costs four or five yen a bottle. What I’ll treat you to isn’t that cheap, but could you compose a score for me?”

“Sure, I can compose it, even if it’s for champagne that costs twenty sen a bottle. If you want, I’ll do it for free.”

“I won’t ask for it for free; I’ll show my gratitude. If you don’t want champagne, how about this as a token of gratitude?” he said, pulling out seven or eight photographs from his inner coat pocket and scattering them across the tatami. There were half-body shots, full-body shots, some standing, some sitting, some in hakama, some in furisode, and some with high hairstyles—all of them depicting young women of charming age. “Sir, we have this many candidates. Mr. Kangetsu and Mr. Tofu can choose any of these as a token of gratitude. How about this one?” he presented one to Kangetsu. “That looks good.

I’d like to request a match.”

“Is this one okay?” he presented another. “That one looks good too. Please arrange it.”

“Which one?”

“Any of them will do.”

“You’re quite the romantic, aren’t you? Sir, this one is the doctor’s niece.”

“Is that so?”

“This lady has an excellent disposition. She’s young too. She’s seventeen. — With her, there’s a dowry of a thousand yen. — This one is the governor’s daughter,” he explained eagerly. “You can’t expect to take them all, can you?”

“All of them? That’s a bit greedy. Are you a proponent of polygamy?”

“I’m not a proponent of polygamy, but I’m a carnivore.”

“Whatever it is, you should put those away quickly,” the master said, scolding him, and Sampei, while pocketing each photograph one by one, said,

“Then, you’re not taking any, I see.”

“What’s that beer for?”

“It’s a gift. I bought it at the corner liquor store for a pre-celebration. Please have one.”

The master clapped his hands to call the maid to uncork it. The master, Meitei, Dokusen, Kangetsu, and Tofu all respectfully raised their glasses to toast Sampei’s romantic fortune. Sampei, looking quite pleased, said,

“I invite everyone here to the reception. Will you all come? You will, won’t you?”

“I don’t want to,” the master replied immediately. “Why not? It’s a once-in-a-lifetime grand event for me. Don’t you want to come? It seems a bit unfeeling.”

“It’s not unfeeling, but I won’t go.”

“Don’t you have a kimono? I can lend you a haori and hakama. You should at least make an appearance, sir. I can introduce you to some famous people.”

“Not a chance.”

“Your stomach will get better.”

“It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t.”

“If you’re going to be that stubborn, then there’s no helping it. How about you, will you come?”

「I suppose I shall go. If possible, I would like to attain the honor of being a mediator. Champagne, three times nine cups, and a spring evening. — What, the mediator is Suzuki Tojuro? I thought as much. This is unfortunate, but it cannot be helped. Even if there are two mediators, it would be too many; I will simply attend as a mere human.」

「What about you?」

「Me? I am a leisurely man, living off the wind and moon, fishing among the white water lilies and red smartweed.」

「What is that? A selection of Chinese poetry?」

「I don’t really understand it.」

「You don’t understand? That’s troubling. Kangetsu, you will come, won’t you? Given our past relations.」

「I will certainly attend; it would be a shame to miss the band playing my composition.」

「Indeed. And what about you, Tofu?」

「Well, I would like to recite a new-style poem in front of the two of them.」

「That sounds delightful. I must say, I have never experienced such joy since my birth.

So, I will have another beer,」 he said, downing the beer he had bought for himself and turning bright red. The short autumn day finally came to an end, and looking into the hibachi, where the remnants of rolled tobacco were scattered, I saw that the fire had long since gone out. Even the carefree group seemed to have lost some of their enthusiasm, as Dokusen stood up first, saying, “It’s getting quite late. Shall we head home?” Following him, others chimed in, “I’m going home too,” and they all made their way to the entrance. The room became lonely, much like after a performance at a theater. The master finished his dinner and entered the study. His wife adjusted the collar of her chilly undergarment and sewed a freshly washed garment. The children lined up their pillows and went to sleep. The maid had gone to fetch hot water. Even those who seemed carefree, when probed to the depths of their hearts, produced a somewhat sad sound. Though he appeared enlightened, Dokusen still had his feet firmly planted on the ground. It may be easygoing, but Meitei’s world is not a painted world. Kangetsu had finally stopped polishing jewels and brought his wife from his homeland. This is only natural. However, if the natural continues for too long, it must surely become tedious. Tofu will likely realize, after ten years, the folly of recklessly dedicating new-style poems. As for Sampei, it is difficult to determine whether he is a man of the water or a man of the mountains. If he can consider himself fortunate to treat others to three cups of sake in his lifetime, that would be splendid. Suzuki Tojuro rolls on and on. If he rolls, he gets muddy. Even if he gets muddy, he has more leeway than those who cannot roll. It has been over two years since I was born a cat and have lived in the human world. I thought there could be no other with such insight as myself, but recently, a stranger named Cartel Muru suddenly raised a ruckus, which surprised me a bit. Upon closer inquiry, I learned that he had actually died a hundred years ago, but out of sheer curiosity, he had purposely become a ghost to surprise me, having traveled from the distant underworld. This cat, when meeting his mother, had set out with a fish in his mouth as a greeting, but halfway there, he could no longer contain himself and ended up eating it. Being such a disobedient one, he was also quite talented, and it is said that he once composed a poem that astonished his master. If such a remarkable figure had already appeared a century ago, then a good-for-nothing like me should have long since taken my leave and returned to the realm of nothingness. The master will soon die of a stomach ailment. Old man Kaneda is already dead from greed. Most of the autumn leaves have fallen.

If dying is the fate of all things, and if living is not particularly useful, then perhaps dying sooner is the wiser choice. According to various teachers, human destiny seems to lead to suicide. If one is careless, even a cat must be born into such a constricting world. It is a terrifying thought. I feel somewhat vexed. Perhaps I should drink Sampei’s beer to lift my spirits. I made my way to the kitchen. The door rattled in the autumn wind and was slightly ajar, allowing the breeze to blow in. The lamp had somehow gone out, and shadows were cast from the moonlight through the window. Three cups were lined up on the tray, two of which were half-filled with brown liquid. What was in the glass felt cold, even if it was hot water. Especially under the chilly moonlight of the night, this liquid, quietly sitting next to the fire extinguisher, was already cold before it even touched my lips, making me not want to drink it at all. But one must try things. Sampei drank it and turned bright red, breathing heavily. Surely a cat could become cheerful if it drank too. After all, who knows when I might die? I should do whatever I can while I’m alive. There’s no use regretting it from the shadows of the grave. I resolved to drink boldly, and with determination, I thrust my tongue into the liquid and began to lap it up, only to be startled. It felt as if the tip of my tongue had been pricked by a needle. I cannot understand why humans drink such rotten things for amusement, but it is certainly something a cat cannot finish. It simply does not suit a cat to drink beer. This is terrible, I thought, as I withdrew my tongue, but then reconsidered. Humans often say that good medicine is bitter, and when they catch a cold, they grimace and drink strange things. Do they drink to heal, or heal to drink? This has been a question for me, but now seems like a good opportunity to solve it with beer. If it makes my stomach bitter, then that’s that; if I become as merry as Sampei, it would be an unprecedented windfall, and I could share it with the neighborhood cats. Well, let’s see what happens; I’ll leave it to fate and resolved to tackle it again, sticking my tongue out once more. It’s hard to drink with my eyes open, so I closed them tightly and began to lap again. When I finally managed to finish a cup of beer after enduring much, a strange phenomenon occurred. At first, my tongue felt prickly, and my mouth felt painfully compressed from the outside, but as I drank, it gradually became easier, and by the time I finished the first cup, it was no longer particularly difficult. Feeling confident, I tackled the second cup without any trouble. I even lapped up the spill on the tray as if to clean it up. For a while afterward, I remained still, observing my own movements.

Gradually, my body warmed. The edges of my eyes felt flushed. My ears burned. I felt the urge to sing. I wanted to dance like a cat. I felt like telling the master, Meitei, and Dokusen to eat shit. I wanted to scratch old man Kaneda. I wanted to nibble at my wife’s nose. Various thoughts swirled in my mind. Finally, I felt a strong urge to stand. Once upright, I wanted to stagger about. This is amusing, I thought, and felt the urge to go outside. Upon going out, I wanted to greet the moon, saying, “Good evening.” It was all quite delightful. While thinking that this must be what they call being in a daze, I wandered about aimlessly, my feet moving haphazardly as if on a stroll, and I felt increasingly sleepy. I could not tell if I was sleeping or walking. I intended to keep my eyes open, but they felt exceedingly heavy. At this point, it was all over. Whether it was the sea or the mountains, I wouldn’t be surprised. Just as I thought to stretch my front paw forward, I suddenly heard a splash, and in a moment of realization — I had been caught. I had no time to think about how I had been caught. I only realized that I had been caught, and whether I did or didn’t, everything afterward became a chaotic mess. **Chapter 1**

When I came to, I was floating on the water. In my distress, I scratched wildly with my claws, but all I could grasp was water, and as soon as I clawed, I sank again. With no other choice, I jumped up with my hind legs and scratched with my front legs, producing a grating sound and feeling a slight response. Finally, just my head floated above the surface, so I looked around to see where I was, and I found myself in a large jar. This jar had been filled with water plants known as water hibiscus until summer, but then a crow came and devoured the hibiscus, using up the water. When the water is used, it decreases. When it decreases, the crow stops coming. I had thought earlier that the water had diminished quite a bit, and I hadn’t seen the crow lately, but I never imagined that I would be using the water in this place instead of the crow. The edge of the water was more than four inches away. Even stretching my legs, I couldn’t reach it. Jumping up wouldn’t help either. If I remained calm, I would only sink. Struggling only resulted in my claws scraping against the jar, and when I did manage to scrape, I would float slightly, but as soon as I relaxed, I would immediately sink again. Sinking was painful, so I would scratch again. Before long, my body began to tire. My mind was anxious, but my legs became less responsive. Eventually, I couldn’t tell whether I was scratching to sink or sinking to scratch. In that moment of pain, I thought this: to suffer such torment was simply a desire to rise above the jar.

I wanted to rise, but I knew I couldn’t. My legs were less than three inches long. Even if my body floated on the surface of the water, and I stretched my front legs as far as I could, there was no way for my claws to grip the edge of the jar, which was more than five inches high. If I couldn’t grip the edge of the jar, no matter how much I scratched or how much I panicked, I could never escape, even if I spent a hundred years wearing myself down. It was futile to try to escape from something I knew I couldn’t. It was this insistence on the impossible that caused my suffering. It was pointless. To seek out suffering and willingly submit to torture was foolish. “Enough already. Do as you please. I’ll stop scratching,” I decided, relinquishing my front legs, hind legs, head, and tail to the forces of nature and resisting no longer. Gradually, I began to feel more at ease. I couldn’t tell whether I was in pain or grateful. I couldn’t discern whether I was in the water or on the tatami mat; it was all unclear. No matter where I was or how I was, it didn’t matter. I was simply at ease. No, I couldn’t even feel the very essence of ease. I severed the sun and moon, ground the heavens and earth into powder, and entered the mysterious tranquility. I would die. I would die and attain this tranquility. Tranquility could only be attained through death. Namu Amida Butsu, Namu Amida Butsu. Grateful, grateful.
